Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A frog sits very still at the edge of the pond.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It waits for a bug to fly close enough.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in a flash.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The whole catch takes less than one second to finish.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A frog sits still at the pond.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It waits for a bug to come close.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its tongue is long and sticky.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The tongue snaps out and grabs the bug.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The whole catch is very fast.

questions.q: What is a frog's tongue like?
questions.a: A frog's tongue is long, pink and very sticky.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. waiting) and paragraph D (i.e. the catch).
Tell how a frog catches a bug.
questions.a: It sits very still at the edge of the pond and waits for a bug to come close. Then its long sticky tongue snaps out and grabs the bug in less than one second.

questions.q:
sticky: able to hold on to things that touch it.
snaps: moves out very fast and then back again.
Describe the connection between sitting still and catching a bug.
questions.a: The frog sits very still and waits for a bug to fly close enough, so the bug comes near without being scared away.

articles.note: Paragraph A and paragraph B are both about waiting. Ask why the writer gave waiting two paragraphs when the catch only gets one.

articles.title: The Crossing Guard
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crossing guard stands at the corner by the school.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When the cars stop, she waves the children across the street.

paras.label: E
paras.text: She stays in the road until the last child is safe.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crossing guard stands by the school.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She wears a bright vest so drivers see her.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She holds up a sign that says stop.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then she waves the children across.

paras.label: E
paras.text: She waits until every child is safe.

questions.q: Why does the crossing guard wear a bright vest?
questions.a: She wears a bright vest so every driver can see her.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the stop sign) and paragraph E (i.e. staying until the end).
Tell what a crossing guard does.
questions.a: She stands at the corner by the school in a bright vest, holds up a sign that tells cars to stop, waves the children across, and stays in the road until the last child is safe.

questions.q:
vest: a bright coat with no sleeves, worn so people can see you.
guard: a person whose job is keeping others safe.
Describe the connection between the sign and the children crossing.
questions.a: She holds up a round sign that tells cars to stop, and when the cars stop she waves the children across the street.

articles.note: The order is the lesson here: sign first, then cars stop, then children cross. Ask what would happen if those swapped.

articles.title: Why a Cat Purrs
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is why a purr does not stop between breaths.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most cats purr when they feel safe and warm.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some cats also purr when they are hurt or scared.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat purrs with the muscles in its throat.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shake happens when it breathes in and out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So a purr does not stop between breaths.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most cats purr when they feel safe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some purr when they are hurt or scared.

questions.q: What part of a cat makes the purr?
questions.a: A cat purrs by shaking the muscles in its throat very fast.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why a purr never stops) and paragraph E (i.e. purring when hurt).
Tell how and why a cat purrs.
questions.a: A cat shakes the muscles in its throat very fast, both breathing in and breathing out, so the purr never stops between breaths. Most cats purr when they feel safe, and some purr when they are hurt or scared.

questions.q:
muscle: a part inside the body that can pull and move.
purr: the soft rumbling sound a cat makes.
Describe the connection between breathing and the sound of a purr.
questions.a: The shake happens when the cat breathes in and when it breathes out, which is why a purr does not stop between breaths.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the surprise and children will want to talk about it. The text says some cats purr when hurt; it does not say why, and that is worth admitting.

articles.title: The Mail Carrier's Bag
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each street goes in order, so the first house comes first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She walks the same route every day and knows every dog.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mail carrier sorts the mail into streets.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each street is in order, so the first house is first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Her bag is heavy at the start.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She walks the same route every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mail at the bottom is the last stop.

questions.q: What does the mail carrier do before she leaves?
questions.a: She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the order) and paragraph E (i.e. the bottom of the bag).
Tell how a mail carrier gets the mail to the right houses.
questions.a: She sorts the mail into streets before she leaves, puts each street in order so the first house comes first, and walks the same route every day. The letters at the bottom of the bag are the last stop.

questions.q:
sort: to put things into groups that belong together.
route: the same path a person takes each day.
Describe the connection between sorting the mail and the bag getting lighter.
questions.a: Each street goes in order so the first house comes first, which is why her bag is heavy at the start and light at the end.

articles.note: Children often miss that the bottom of the bag is the end of the route. It follows from paragraph B, so read those two together.

articles.title: Bees and Flowers
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bee lands on a flower to drink the sweet nectar.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She flies to the next flower and some pollen rubs off.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That pollen helps the flower make seeds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bees get food and flowers get seeds, so both of them win.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bee lands on a flower to drink.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow pollen sticks to her legs.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She flies to the next flower.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some pollen rubs off and helps make seeds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bees get food and flowers get seeds.

questions.q: What sticks to the bee's legs?
questions.a: Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the next flower) and paragraph E (i.e. both of them win).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: Bees and flowers help each other. A bee drinks nectar and pollen sticks to her legs. She rubs some off on the next flower, and that pollen helps the flower make seeds.

questions.q:
nectar: the sweet juice inside a flower.
pollen: the yellow dust a flower makes.
Describe the connection between the bee's legs and the flower's seeds.
questions.a: Pollen sticks to the hairs on her legs, and when she flies to the next flower some pollen rubs off and helps that flower make seeds.

articles.note: The main topic is the trade, not the bee. Ask what the last paragraph adds that the first four do not.

articles.title: The Fire Station
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire station is open all day and all night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants already open.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire station is open all night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The truck is backed in so it can drive out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Boots and coats wait by the truck.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A firefighter can step in fast.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Every second saved helps.

questions.q: Why is the truck backed in?
questions.a: The truck is backed in so it can drive straight out.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the waiting boots) and paragraph E (i.e. seconds saved).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A fire station is set up so firefighters can leave fast. The truck is backed in, the boots and coats wait by the truck with the pants open, and a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds.

questions.q:
station: the building where fire trucks and firefighters stay.
second: a very short piece of time.
Describe the connection between the open pants and getting to the fire.
questions.a: The pants are already open so a firefighter can step in and pull them up in seconds, and every second saved is a second sooner at the fire.

articles.note: Everything here is one idea in five parts: be fast. Ask the child to say the idea in their own words before retelling the details.

articles.title: How Rain Falls
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The vapor rises up into the cold air above.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Up high it cools and sticks to tiny bits of dust.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then they fall back down as rain.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The sun warms a puddle and the water rises.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The vapor goes up into cold air.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Up high it cools into tiny drops.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Drops join until they are too heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then they fall as rain.

questions.q: What makes the drops fall?
questions.a: Many drops join together until they are too heavy to float.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the sun and the puddle) and paragraph D (i.e. the drops joining).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: Water goes up and comes back down. The sun turns a puddle into vapor, the vapor rises into cold air and cools onto bits of dust, and the drops join until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.

questions.q:
vapor: water that has turned into air you cannot see.
float: to stay up without falling.
Describe the connection between the sun and the rain.
questions.a: The sun warms a puddle and the water turns into vapor, and that vapor is what rises, cools and falls back down as rain.

articles.note: This is a circle and the text does not say so. Ask where the rain goes next, and whether paragraph A could come after paragraph E.

articles.title: The Library Card
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library card has your name and a long number on it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number tells the computer which books you took home.

paras.label: C
paras.text: You may keep a book for three weeks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A card is free, and the books you borrow are free too.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A library card has your name and a number.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number tells the computer what you took.

paras.label: C
paras.text: You may keep a book for three weeks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The card is free and the books are free.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When you bring it back, someone else can read it.

questions.q: How long may you keep a book?
questions.a: You may keep a book for three weeks.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the number) and paragraph E (i.e. bringing a book back).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A library card lets you borrow books for free. It has your name and a number that tells the computer which books you took, you may keep a book for three weeks, and when you bring it back someone else can read it.

questions.q:
borrow: to take something for a while and then give it back.
free: costing no money.
Describe the connection between bringing a book back and other readers.
questions.a: When you bring a book back, someone else can read it.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the point of the whole system and it comes last. Ask why the writer saved it for the end.

articles.title: A Seed Grows
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.3 connections · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed holds a tiny plant and a packed lunch for it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water makes the hard coat swell until it cracks open.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A root goes down first, before anything goes up.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then a green shoot pushes up toward the light.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Once the first leaves open, the plant can make its own food.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed holds a tiny plant and its food.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water makes the hard coat crack open.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A root goes down first.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then a green shoot pushes up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When leaves open, the plant makes its own food.

questions.q: What goes out of the seed first?
questions.a: A root goes down first, before anything goes up.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the packed lunch) and paragraph E (i.e. making its own food).
Tell the main topic of this text.
questions.a: A seed grows in order. It holds a tiny plant and food for it, water cracks the coat open, a root goes down first, a shoot pushes up, and once the leaves open the plant makes its own food.

questions.q:
root: the part of a plant that grows down into the soil.
shoot: the new green stem that pushes up.
Describe the connection between the packed lunch and the first leaves.
questions.a: A seed holds a packed lunch for the tiny plant, and once the first leaves open the plant can make its own food instead.

articles.note: Paragraph A and paragraph E are a pair: food that came with the seed, then food the plant makes. The three middle paragraphs sit between them in order.

articles.title: The Sun and the Puddle
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: On Monday the rain left a big puddle on the path.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By Tuesday the sun was out all morning.

paras.label: C
paras.text: By lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun turned the water into a vapor you cannot see.

paras.label: E
paras.text: But a puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Rain left a big puddle on the path.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sun came out all morning.

paras.label: C
paras.text: By lunch the puddle was small.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun turned the water into vapor.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A puddle in the shade was still there.

questions.q: What happened to the puddle in the shade?
questions.a: A puddle in the shade was still there on Wednesday.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the sun) and paragraph E (i.e. the shade).
Tell what this text is about.
questions.a: The sun dried a puddle. Rain left a big puddle, the sun was out all morning, and by lunch it was only a damp ring. A puddle in the shade was still there the next day.

questions.q:
damp: a little bit wet.
shade: a place the sun does not reach.
Describe the connection between the sun and the puddle drying.
questions.a: The sun was out all morning and turned the water into vapor you cannot see, so by lunch the puddle was only a damp ring.

articles.note: The shade puddle is the proof and it comes last. Ask the child what it shows that paragraphs A to D do not.

articles.title: The Bell and the Line
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The bell rings at the end of recess every day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When it rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A teacher counts the children before the line goes in.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The bell is the start of all of it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The bell rings at the end of recess.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The children stop playing and walk to the line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The line forms on the yellow paint.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A teacher counts the children.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The bell starts all of it.

questions.q: Where does the line form?
questions.a: The line forms on the yellow paint by the door.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. walking to the line) and paragraph D (i.e. the counting).
Tell what happens after the bell rings.
questions.a: The bell rings at the end of recess, the children stop playing and walk to the line on the yellow paint, and a teacher counts them before the line goes in.

questions.q:
recess: the time outside for playing.
form: to come together into a shape, like a line.
Describe the connection between the bell and the children lining up.
questions.a: When the bell rings, the children stop playing and walk to the line, so the bell is the start of all of it.

articles.note: Paragraph E names the connection outright. Cover it and see whether the child can say it before reading it.

articles.title: Why the Beach Changes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Early in the morning the beach is wide and flat.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By afternoon the water has come far up the sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That pull makes the water rise and fall twice every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The wide beach comes back again by night.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the morning the beach is wide.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By afternoon the water comes up the sand.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The moon pulls on the ocean.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water rises and falls twice a day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The wide beach comes back by night.

questions.q: How many times a day does the water rise and fall?
questions.a: That pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the moon) and paragraph E (i.e. night).
Tell why the beach changes.
questions.a: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day. So a beach that is wide in the morning is covered by afternoon and wide again by night.

questions.q:
pull: to draw something toward you.
ocean: the very large body of salt water.
Describe the connection between the moon and the water on the sand.
questions.a: The moon pulls on the ocean as the Earth turns, and that pull makes the water rise and fall twice a day.

articles.note: The cause is invisible and far away, which is hard at this age. Keep the child on what they can see in paragraphs A, B and E first.

articles.title: The Farmer and the Market
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A farmer picks beans early, while the air is still cool.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She packs them in boxes and drives to the market.

paras.label: D
paras.text: By eight o'clock her table is full and the doors open.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Beans picked the day before would already be soft.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A farmer picks beans early while it is cool.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She packs them and drives to the market.

paras.label: D
paras.text: By eight her table is full.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Older beans would be soft.

questions.q: Why does the farmer pick beans early?
questions.a: Cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. why cool matters) and paragraph E (i.e. older beans).
Tell why the farmer picks early.
questions.a: She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones. She packs them and drives to the market, and by eight o'clock her table is full.

questions.q:
crisp: firm and fresh, so it snaps.
market: a place where people sell food.
Describe the connection between the cool morning air and the beans on the table.
questions.a: She picks beans early while the air is still cool, because cool beans stay crisp longer than warm ones do.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the comparison that makes the reason land. Read B and E together.

articles.title: The Fly and the Web
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A spider's web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fly cannot tell the two kinds apart.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When a fly hits a sticky thread, the whole web shakes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A web has sticky threads and plain ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The spider walks only on the plain ones.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fly cannot tell them apart.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When a fly hits a sticky thread, the web shakes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The spider feels the shake and goes there.

questions.q: Why does the spider not stick to its own web?
questions.a: The spider walks only on the plain threads, so it never sticks.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the fly not knowing) and paragraph D (i.e. the shake).
Tell how a spider knows a fly is caught.
questions.a: A web has sticky threads and plain ones mixed together, and the spider walks only on the plain ones. A fly cannot tell them apart, so when it hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes and the spider feels it.

questions.q:
thread: one thin line of a web.
plain: not sticky, just ordinary.
Describe the connection between the shaking web and the spider finding the fly.
questions.a: When a fly hits a sticky thread the whole web shakes, and the spider feels the shake and knows just where to go.

articles.note: Two connections sit in this text: why the spider is safe, and how it gets the news. Ask the child for both.

articles.title: What Hibernate Means
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The book says the bear will hibernate all winter long.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its heart beats slower and its body stays cool.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In spring the bear wakes up thin and very hungry.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The book says the bear will hibernate all winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The bear does not eat for months.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its heart beats slower and it stays cool.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In spring it wakes up hungry.

questions.q: What does hibernate mean?
questions.a: Hibernate is a word for a long, deep winter sleep.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. what the word means) and paragraph E (i.e. waking up).
Tell what hibernate means and what a bear does.
questions.a: Hibernate means a long, deep winter sleep. A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, its heart beats slower and its body stays cool, and in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.

questions.q:
hibernate: to sleep deeply all winter.
spring: the season that comes after winter.
Describe the connection between not eating and waking up thin.
questions.a: A bear that hibernates does not eat for many months, so in spring it wakes up thin and very hungry.

articles.note: RI.1.4 is asking about a word, so paragraph B is the answer and the rest is evidence. Ask the child which paragraph gives them the meaning.

articles.title: Words That Tell Where
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map uses small words to tell you where to go.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Above means higher up, and below means lower down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Beside means right next to something else on the map.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Between means in the middle of two other things.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If you miss those small words, the map cannot help you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map uses small words to tell where.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Above means higher. Below means lower.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Beside means next to.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Between means in the middle of two things.

paras.label: E
paras.text: If you miss them, the map will not help.

questions.q: What does between mean?
questions.a: Between means in the middle of two other things.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. above and below) and paragraph E (i.e. missing the words).
Tell what this text teaches.
questions.a: A map uses small words to tell you where to go. Above means higher up and below means lower down, beside means right next to, and between means in the middle of two things. If you miss those words the map cannot help you.

questions.q:
beside: right next to something.
between: in the middle of two things.
Describe the connection between the small words and using a map.
questions.a: A map uses small words to tell you where to go, so if you miss those small words the map cannot help you.

articles.note: These are the words that trip children up on every map all year. Have them put a finger on two things and say what is between them.

articles.title: What Melt Means
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Ice melts into plain water when it gets warm enough.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Butter melts in a hot pan and spreads out flat.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crayon left on a sunny sill can melt too.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Heat is what makes all of those things melt.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Melt means to change from hard to runny.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Ice melts into water when it is warm.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Butter melts in a hot pan.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A crayon in the sun can melt.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Heat makes all of them melt.

questions.q: What does melt mean?
questions.a: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the meaning) and paragraph E (i.e. what they all share).
Tell what melt means and give examples.
questions.a: Melt means to change from hard into something soft and runny. Ice melts into water, butter melts in a hot pan, and a crayon on a sunny sill can melt. Heat is what makes all of those things melt.

questions.q:
melt: to change from hard into soft and runny.
heat: warmth that can change things.
Describe the connection between the three examples in the middle.
questions.a: Ice, butter and a crayon are all different, and heat is what makes all of those things melt.

articles.note: The shape is a definition, three examples and the thing they share. Ask what all three have in common before reading paragraph E.

articles.title: Signs at the Pool
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sign at the pool says NO DIVING in big letters.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another sign says to WALK and not to run.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third sign tells you how deep the water is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sign at the pool says NO DIVING.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Diving means going in head first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another sign says to walk, not run.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third sign tells how deep the water is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Read the signs to stay safe.

questions.q: What does diving mean?
questions.a: Diving means going in head first instead of feet first.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. what diving means) and paragraph D (i.e. the depth sign).
Tell what the signs at the pool say.
questions.a: One sign says NO DIVING, which means going in head first. Another says to walk and not run, and a third tells you how deep the water is. Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

questions.q:
diving: going into water head first.
deep: going far down from the top.
Describe the connection between reading the signs and staying safe.
questions.a: Reading those signs before you swim keeps you safe.

articles.note: The word children get wrong is diving, because they use it for any jump. Paragraph B is there for exactly that.

articles.title: Float and Sink
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer questions to help determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Float means to stay up on top of the water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A cork floats, and a small rock sinks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A big boat floats even though it is very heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So what matters is not just weight but shape too.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Float means to stay on top of the water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sink means to go down to the bottom.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A cork floats and a rock sinks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A big boat floats, and it is heavy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So weight is not the only thing.

questions.q: What does sink mean?
questions.a: Sink means to go all the way down to the bottom.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the cork and the rock) and paragraph D (i.e. the boat).
Tell what float and sink mean.
questions.a: Float means to stay up on top of the water and sink means to go down to the bottom. A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big heavy boat floats too, so what matters is not just weight but shape.

questions.q:
float: to stay up on top of water.
sink: to go down to the bottom.
Describe the connection between the boat and the rest of the text.
questions.a: A cork floats and a small rock sinks, but a big boat floats even though it is very heavy, so what matters is not just weight but shape too.

articles.note: Paragraph D breaks the rule paragraph C sets up, and that is deliberate. Ask the child why a heavy boat does not sink.

articles.title: The List at the Front
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first page of this book is a list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The list shows every part of the book in order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next to each part is the page it starts on.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If you want frogs, the list sends you to page nine.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You do not have to turn every page to find it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first page of this book is a list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It shows every part in order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each part has a page number.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If you want frogs, go to page nine.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You do not turn every page.

questions.q: What is next to each part on the list?
questions.a: Next to each part is the page it starts on.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. finding frogs) and paragraph E (i.e. not turning every page).
Tell what the list at the front is for.
questions.a: The first page is a list that shows every part of the book in order, with the page each part starts on. If you want frogs the list sends you to page nine, so you do not have to turn every page.

questions.q:
list: names written one under another.
page number: the number that tells you which page you are on.
Describe the connection between the list and finding what you want.
questions.a: Next to each part is the page it starts on, so the list sends you straight to page nine instead of turning every page.

articles.note: This is a table of contents and the text never uses the term. Name it after the child has used it, not before.

articles.title: The Word List at the Back
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the back of the book there is a word list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It holds the hard words from every page.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.

paras.label: D
paras.text: After each word is a short line that tells what it means.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can look up a word without asking anyone.

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the back of the book is a word list.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It holds the hard words.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words are in ABC order.

paras.label: D
paras.text: After each word is what it means.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You can look up a word by yourself.

questions.q: What order are the words in?
questions.a: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. ABC order) and paragraph E (i.e. looking it up yourself).
Tell what the word list at the back is for.
questions.a: The back of the book has a list of the hard words from every page, in ABC order, with a short line after each one telling what it means. You can look up a word without asking anyone.

questions.q:
ABC order: the order of the letters of the alphabet.
means: what a word is telling you.
Describe the connection between ABC order and finding a word fast.
questions.a: The words are in ABC order, so they are easy to find and you can look one up without asking anyone.

articles.note: This is a glossary. Point out that it only holds words from this book, which is what makes it different from a dictionary.

articles.title: Headings Tell You Where
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A heading is the dark line above a part of a page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It says in a few words what that part is about.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: You can read just the headings to find what you need.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Headings save you from reading the whole page.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A heading is the dark line above a part.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It tells what that part is about.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A heading that says Eggs means eggs come next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: You can read just the headings.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Headings save you reading the whole page.

questions.q: What does a heading tell you?
questions.a: It says in a few words what that part is about.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the Eggs heading) and paragraph E (i.e. saving reading).
Tell what headings do.
questions.a: A heading is the dark line above a part of a page, and it says in a few words what that part is about. A heading that says Eggs tells you eggs come next, so you can read just the headings to find what you need.

questions.q:
heading: the dark line of words above a part of a page.
about: what something is telling you.
Describe the connection between reading headings and reading the whole page.
questions.a: You can read just the headings to find what you need, which saves you from reading the whole page.

articles.note: Have the child find a heading in any book on the shelf and say what will come under it before they read it.

articles.title: Buttons You Can Tap
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A screen has small pictures you can tap with a finger.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tiny house always takes you back to the start.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A round glass means you can search for something.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An arrow that curls back means undo what you just did.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A screen has small pictures you can tap.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A tiny house takes you back to the start.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A round glass means you can search.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A curled arrow means undo.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pictures mean the same on most screens.

questions.q: What does the tiny house do?
questions.a: A tiny house always takes you back to the start.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the curling arrow) and paragraph E (i.e. every screen).
Tell what the small pictures on a screen do.
questions.a: A screen has small pictures you tap with a finger. A tiny house takes you back to the start, a round glass means search, and an arrow that curls back means undo. They mean the same thing on almost every screen.

questions.q:
tap: to touch a screen once with a finger.
undo: to take back what you just did.
Describe the connection between learning these pictures and using a new screen.
questions.a: The pictures mean the same thing on almost every screen, so learning them once helps on a screen you have never used.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the useful part and children will skip it for the pictures. It is why learning three icons is worth the time.

articles.title: The Numbers at the Bottom
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Know and use various text features, such as headings, a table of contents, a glossary and icons, to locate key facts or information in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Look at the very bottom corner of this page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A small number sits there, and the next page is one more.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also let you stop reading and find your place again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A book with no page numbers is hard to talk about.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Look at the bottom corner of the page.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A small number sits there.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The next page is one more.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Numbers help you find your place again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They also let the list point at a page.

questions.q: Where do you find the page number?
questions.a: Look at the very bottom corner of this page.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. pointing from the list) and paragraph D (i.e. finding your place).
Tell what page numbers are for.
questions.a: A small number sits at the bottom corner of each page, and the next page is one more. Page numbers let the list at the front point at a page, and they let you stop reading and find your place again.

questions.q:
corner: the spot where two edges of a page meet.
place: the spot you stopped at.
Describe the connection between page numbers and the list at the front.
questions.a: Page numbers let a list at the front point at a page.

articles.note: Best done with a real book open. Ask the child to find page nine two ways: by turning, and by using the list.

articles.title: What the Picture Shows
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish between information provided by pictures or other illustrations and information provided by the words in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.9 comparing texts · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The words say the bird has a long bill.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The picture shows you just how long that bill is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words do not say what color the bird is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: But the picture shows that the bird is bright blue.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So both parts of the page tell you different things.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The words say the bird has a long bill.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The picture shows how long it is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The words do not say the color.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The picture shows it is bright blue.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both parts tell different things.

questions.q: What does the picture tell you that the words do not?
questions.a: The picture shows that the bird is bright blue.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. how long the bill is) and paragraph D (i.e. the color).
Tell what the words do and what the picture does.
questions.a: The words say the bird has a long bill and the picture shows just how long. The words do not say the color, but the picture shows the bird is bright blue. Both parts of the page tell you different things.

questions.q:
bill: the hard mouth of a bird.
color: red, blue, green and the rest.
Describe the connection between the words and the picture on this page.
questions.a: Both parts of the page tell you different things, because the words give the long bill and the picture gives the bright blue.

articles.note: Cover the picture, read the words, and ask what the child still does not know. Then uncover it. That is the whole standard in one move.

articles.title: The Words Say More
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish between information provided by pictures or other illustrations and information provided by the words in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.9 comparing texts · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The photo shows a big bear standing in a river.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see its fur, its claws and the water.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The photo cannot tell you that the bear is hungry.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It cannot tell you the fish come here every fall.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The words have to say those things for you.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The photo shows a bear in a river.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see its fur and the water.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The photo cannot say the bear is hungry.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It cannot say when the fish come.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The words say those things.

questions.q: What can you see in the photo?
questions.a: You can see its fur, its claws and the water.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. hungry) and paragraph D (i.e. when the fish come).
Tell what the photo shows and what it cannot.
questions.a: The photo shows a big bear standing in a river, and you can see its fur, its claws and the water. It cannot tell you the bear is hungry or that the fish come every fall, so the words have to say those things.

questions.q:
photo: a picture made with a camera.
claws: the sharp hard nails on an animal's foot.
Describe the connection between what a photo cannot show and the words.
questions.a: The photo cannot tell you that the bear is hungry or when the fish come, so the words have to say those things for you.

articles.note: This is the other half of the standard from What the Picture Shows. Read the two together if you can.

articles.title: A Picture of a Beak
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish between information provided by pictures or other illustrations and information provided by the words in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.9 comparing texts · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The page shows two different birds side by side.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One beak is thin and sharp, like a needle.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other beak is wide and flat, like a spoon.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Together the picture and the words tell you why it is shaped that way.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The page shows two birds side by side.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One beak is thin like a needle.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other beak is wide and flat.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The words say the thin one drinks from flowers.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Together they tell you why.

questions.q: What are the two beaks like?
questions.a: One beak is thin and sharp, like a needle, and the other is wide and flat, like a spoon.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the thin beak) and paragraph D (i.e. what the words add).
Tell what the page shows about beaks.
questions.a: The page shows two birds side by side. One beak is thin and sharp like a needle, and the other is wide and flat like a spoon. The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers, so the picture and the words together tell you why it is shaped that way.

questions.q:
beak: the hard mouth of a bird.
needle: a thin sharp tool for sewing.
Describe the connection between the shape of the beak and what the bird eats.
questions.a: The words say the thin one drinks from deep flowers, and the picture shows that beak is thin and sharp like a needle.

articles.note: Shape and job is the big idea underneath. Ask what the wide flat beak might be for before the child reads anything else.

articles.title: The Map and the Words
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish between information provided by pictures or other illustrations and information provided by the words in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.9 comparing texts · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map of the zoo shows where each animal lives.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see that the lions are near the gate.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The map cannot tell you when the lions are fed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The words under the map say feeding is at two.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You need both to plan your day at the zoo.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A zoo map shows where each animal lives.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see the lions near the gate.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The map cannot say when they are fed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The words say feeding is at two.

paras.label: E
paras.text: You need both to plan your day.

questions.q: What does the map show you?
questions.a: A map of the zoo shows where each animal lives, and you can see that the lions are near the gate.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what the map cannot say) and paragraph D (i.e. the words under it).
Tell what the map does and what the words do.
questions.a: The zoo map shows where each animal lives, so you can see the lions near the gate. The map cannot tell you when the lions are fed, but the words under it say feeding is at two, so you need both to plan your day.

questions.q:
map: a picture that shows where things are.
feeding: the time an animal is given food.
Describe the connection between the map and the words under it.
questions.a: The map shows where the lions are and the words say feeding is at two, so you need both to plan your day at the zoo.

articles.note: Where and when is a clean split for this age. Ask which question the map answers and which one the words answer.

articles.title: What a Photo Cannot Tell You
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Distinguish between information provided by pictures or other illustrations and information provided by the words in a text.
 Spiral: RI.1.5 text features · RI.1.7 illustrations · RI.1.9 comparing texts · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photo shows a volcano with gray smoke above it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see the gray smoke and the dark rock.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A photo cannot tell you how hot that rock is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It cannot tell you the smoke smells like old eggs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only words can tell you both of those things.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photo shows a volcano with smoke.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can see the smoke and the rock.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A photo cannot say how hot it is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It cannot say what the smoke smells like.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only words can tell you that.

questions.q: What can you see in the photo?
questions.a: You can see the gray smoke and the dark rock.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. how hot) and paragraph D (i.e. the smell).
Tell what a photo can show and what it cannot.
questions.a: A photo of a volcano shows the gray smoke and the dark rock. It cannot tell you how hot the rock is or that the smoke smells like old eggs, so only words can tell you those things.

questions.q:
volcano: a mountain that can push out hot rock and smoke.
smells: what your nose tells you about something.
Describe the connection between what you cannot see and what words do.
questions.a: A photo cannot tell you how hot the rock is or what the smoke smells like, so only words can tell you both of those things.

articles.note: Heat and smell are the two things no picture carries. That is a rule a child can take to every book on the shelf.

paras.label: A

paras.text: One points from the soil up the stem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The last points out of the leaf.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The arrows show where the water goes.

questions.q: How many arrows are on the picture?
questions.a: A picture of a plant has three arrows drawn on it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the arrow from the soil) and paragraph E (i.e. what the arrows show).
Tell what the arrows on the plant picture show.
questions.a: A plant picture has three arrows. One points down from the cloud to the leaf, one points from the soil up through the stem, and the last points back out of the leaf. Together they show the way the water travels.

stem: the part of a plant that holds it up.

paras.label: E

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bee picture has small words beside it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A line runs from each word to a part.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One word says wing and points to the wing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: These words are called labels.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Labels teach you the name of each part.

questions.q: What are the small words called?
questions.a: Those small words beside a picture are called labels.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the lines) and paragraph E (i.e. what labels do).
Tell what labels do on a picture.
questions.a: A picture of a bee has small words beside it, and a thin line runs from each word to one part. One word says wing and its line goes to a wing. Those words are called labels, and they let a picture teach you the name of each part.

questions.q:
label: a small word beside a picture that names a part.
wing: the part a bee flies with.
Describe the connection between the line and the label.
questions.a: A thin line runs from each word to one part, so the word wing goes with the wing and not with something else.

articles.note: The line is the part children ignore, and it is the part that makes a label a label. Ask what would happen without the lines.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: Second, germs can make you sick.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Third, soap takes the germs off.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is why the sink is by the door.

questions.q: What is the third reason?
questions.a: Third, soap and water take the germs right off.

questions.a: Germs on your hands can get on your food, germs you cannot see can still make you sick, and soap and water take the germs right off. Those three reasons are why the sink is by the door.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another reason is that light keeps the stem strong.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

questions.a: One reason is that leaves make food out of light.

Tell why a plant needs sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One reason is we learn the way out.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Another is that nobody has to think fast.

paras.text: A third is that the teacher can count us.

paras.text: The second page tells how a bee stings.

articles.standard_text:
Standard: Identify basic similarities in and differences between two texts on the same topic.
 Spiral: RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.6 pictures and words · RI.1.8 reasons · RI.1.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Both of these books are about snow in winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One book shows how a single snowflake is made in a cloud.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other book shows how a town clears its roads.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both books say that snow is water that froze.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One book is mostly pictures and one is mostly words.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Both books are about snow.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One shows how a snowflake is made.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other shows how a town clears roads.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both say snow is water that froze.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One is mostly pictures and one is mostly words.

questions.q: What do both books say?
questions.a: Both books say that snow is water that froze.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. clearing roads) and paragraph E (i.e. pictures and words).
Tell how the two snow books are alike and different.
questions.a: Both are about snow in winter and both say snow is water that froze. One shows how a snowflake is made in a cloud and the other shows how a town clears its roads, and one book is mostly pictures while the other is mostly words.

questions.q:
snowflake: one small piece of falling snow.
clears: takes away so a road is open.
Describe the connection between the two books' topics.
questions.a: Both books say snow is water that froze, but one is about how it forms and the other is about what people do once it lands.

articles.note: One book is about nature and one about people, on the same topic. That split is worth naming out loud.

articles.title: How a Turtle Hides
articles.standard_text:
Standard: With prompting and support, read informational texts appropriately complex for grade 1.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A turtle carries its own hard house on its back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When something scares it, the turtle pulls its head in.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its legs fold in behind strong plates of shell.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When the bird gives up, the turtle just walks away.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A turtle carries its house on its back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: When it is scared, it pulls its head in.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its legs fold in behind the shell.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A bird can peck the shell and get nothing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the turtle walks away.

questions.q: What does the turtle pull in first?
questions.a: When something scares it, the turtle pulls its head in.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the legs) and paragraph D (i.e. the bird pecking).
Tell how a turtle hides.
questions.a: A turtle carries a hard house on its back. When something scares it, it pulls its head in and folds its legs behind strong plates of shell. A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing, and when the bird gives up the turtle walks away.

questions.q:
shell: the hard cover on a turtle's back.
peck: to hit with a beak.
Describe the connection between the shell and the bird giving up.
questions.a: A hungry bird can peck the shell and get nothing, so the bird gives up and the turtle walks away.

articles.note: Nothing happens in paragraph D, and that is the point. Ask what the turtle did to win.

articles.title: The Ice Cream Truck
articles.standard_text:
Standard: With prompting and support, read informational texts appropriately complex for grade 1.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: The ice cream truck plays the same song every day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The song tells you the truck is close before you see it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The driver keeps the freezer running the whole time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If the freezer stops, the ice cream turns to soup.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is why the truck never parks for long.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The ice cream truck plays the same song.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The song tells you the truck is close.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The driver keeps the freezer running.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If it stops, the ice cream melts.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is why the truck does not park long.

questions.q: What does the song tell you?
questions.a: The song tells you the truck is close before you see it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the freezer) and paragraph E (i.e. not parking long).
Tell how an ice cream truck works.
questions.a: The truck plays the same song every day, which tells you it is close before you see it. The driver keeps the freezer running the whole time, because if it stops the ice cream turns to soup, and that is why the truck never parks for long.

questions.q:
freezer: a cold box that keeps things frozen.
parks: stops and stays in one place.
Describe the connection between the freezer and how long the truck stays.
questions.a: If the freezer stops the ice cream turns to soup, which is why the truck never parks for long.

articles.note: The sound comes before the sight, and children know this from life. Start there and the rest follows.

articles.title: Why Leaves Have Veins
articles.standard_text:
Standard: With prompting and support, read informational texts appropriately complex for grade 1.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hold a leaf up to the light and look closely.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Thin lines run from the stem out to the edges.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Those lines are tubes that carry water through the leaf.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also hold the flat part of the leaf open.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hold a leaf up to the light.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Thin lines run from the stem to the edges.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Those lines carry water through the leaf.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also hold the leaf open and flat.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A leaf with broken lines dries out.

questions.q: What do the thin lines carry?
questions.a: Those lines are tubes that carry water through the leaf.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. holding the leaf open) and paragraph E (i.e. a broken leaf).
Tell what the veins in a leaf do.
questions.a: Thin lines run from the stem out to the edges of a leaf. They are tubes that carry water through the leaf, and they also hold the flat part open. A leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.

questions.q:
vein: a thin tube in a leaf that carries water.
limp: soft and drooping.
Describe the connection between the veins and the leaf staying flat.
questions.a: The veins hold the flat part of the leaf open, so a leaf with broken veins goes limp and dries out.

articles.note: Two jobs for one part, which is a useful idea early. Hold a real leaf to a window while you read paragraph A.

articles.title: The Bus Driver's Mirror
articles.standard_text:
Standard: With prompting and support, read informational texts appropriately complex for grade 1.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school bus has a long wide mirror above the driver.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The mirror lets her see every row without turning around.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She checks it once before she lets the bus move.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She checks it again each time the door opens.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mirror is how one adult watches fifty children.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school bus has a long mirror above the driver.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The mirror lets her see every row.

paras.label: C
paras.text: She checks it before the bus moves.

paras.label: D
paras.text: She checks it each time the door opens.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One adult can watch fifty children.

questions.q: What does the mirror let the driver see?
questions.a: The mirror lets her see every row without turning around.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. before the bus moves) and paragraph E (i.e. one adult and fifty children).
Tell what the bus driver's mirror is for.
questions.a: A school bus has a long mirror above the driver that lets her see every row without turning around. She checks it before the bus moves and again each time the door opens, which is how one adult watches fifty children.

questions.q:
mirror: glass that shows what is behind you.
row: a line of seats side by side.
Describe the connection between the mirror and the driver not turning around.
questions.a: The mirror lets her see every row without turning around, so she can watch the children and the road at once.

articles.note: Paragraph E is the point and it is a number. Ask how else one person could watch fifty.

articles.title: How a Zipper Works
articles.standard_text:
Standard: With prompting and support, read informational texts appropriately complex for grade 1.
 Spiral: RI.1.1 key details · RI.1.2 main topic · RI.1.4 word meaning · RI.1.8 reasons
 Lower range: LL 100 – 220

paras.label: A
paras.text: A zipper has two rows of small metal teeth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The slider pulls the two rows together as it goes up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Pulling the slider down unhooks them again in order.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A zipper has two rows of small teeth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The slider pulls the rows together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each tooth hooks beside the one across.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Pulling down unhooks them again.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A stuck zipper has one tooth out of line.

questions.q: What does the slider do?
questions.a: The slider pulls the two rows together as it goes up.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. hooking) and paragraph E (i.e. a zipper that catches).
Tell how a zipper works.
questions.a: A zipper has two rows of small metal teeth. The slider pulls the rows together as it goes up, and each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across. Pulling the slider down unhooks them in order, and a zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.

questions.q:
slider: the part you pull on a zipper.
teeth: the small metal pieces that hook together.
Describe the connection between the teeth and a zipper that catches.
questions.a: Each tooth hooks into the gap beside the one across, so a zipper that catches has one tooth out of line.

articles.note: Children can test paragraph E on their own coat. Look for the one tooth that is bent.

articles.title: The Bird That Builds with Mud
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A barn swallow builds its nest out of mud. It does not carry the mud in its feet. It carries it in its beak, one small ball at a time.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bird lands at the edge of a puddle. It picks up mud and grass together. The grass holds the mud, the way sticks hold a wall together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it flies to a barn or a bridge. It presses the ball onto the wall and waits. The mud dries hard in the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A nest takes about a thousand trips. Two birds work together for a week or more. The nest ends up shaped like a cup.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same pair may come back the next year. They fix the old nest instead of building a new one. That saves them a thousand trips.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A barn swallow builds its nest out of mud. It carries the mud in its beak. It takes one small ball at a time.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bird lands by a puddle. It picks up mud and grass. The grass holds the mud together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it flies to a barn. It presses the ball onto the wall. The mud dries hard.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A nest takes about a thousand trips. Two birds work for a week. The nest looks like a cup.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The same pair may come back next year. They fix the old nest. That saves a thousand trips.

questions.q: How does a barn swallow carry mud?
questions.a: It carries the mud in its beak, one small ball at a time.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the puddle) and paragraph D (i.e. a thousand trips).
Summarize how a barn swallow builds a nest.
questions.a: It picks up mud and grass at a puddle, carries one ball at a time in its beak, and presses each ball onto a wall until the mud dries hard. A nest takes about a thousand trips.

questions.q:
beak: the hard mouth of a bird.
puddle: a small pool of water on the ground.
Describe the connection between the grass and the mud.
questions.a: The grass holds the mud together, the way sticks hold a wall together.

articles.note: A thousand trips is the number to put on the board. Ask the class to guess first, then read paragraph D.

articles.title: The First Traffic Light
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first traffic light in America was turned on in 1914. It stood on a corner in Cleveland, Ohio. It had only two colors, red and green.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There was no yellow light yet. A loud buzzer sounded before the color changed. Drivers heard the buzz and knew to slow down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A police officer sat in a small booth nearby. He pushed a switch by hand to change the light. The light could not change on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cars were new then, and so were the rules. Before the light, a police officer stood in the street and waved his arms all day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Yellow was added a few years later. Today most lights change by themselves, and nobody sits in a booth.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first traffic light in America came on in 1914. It stood in Cleveland, Ohio. It had two colors. Red and green.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There was no yellow light yet. A loud buzzer sounded first. Drivers heard it and slowed down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A police officer sat in a small booth. He pushed a switch by hand. The light could not change on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cars were new then. So were the rules. Before the light, an officer stood in the street and waved.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Yellow came a few years later. Now most lights change by themselves.

questions.q: Where was the first traffic light, and when?
questions.a: It was turned on in 1914 on a corner in Cleveland, Ohio.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the buzzer) and paragraph C (i.e. the officer in the booth).
Summarize what the first traffic light was like.
questions.a: It had only red and green, a buzzer sounded before the color changed, and a police officer in a booth pushed a switch by hand to change it.

questions.q:
buzzer: a thing that makes a loud sound to warn people.
booth: a very small room for one person.
Describe the connection between having no yellow light and the buzzer.
questions.a: There was no yellow light yet, so a loud buzzer sounded before the color changed and drivers knew to slow down.

articles.note: Who, what, where and when are all in paragraph A. Let students find each one and say which question it answers.

articles.title: How a Seed Drinks
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed looks dry and hard. Inside it is a tiny plant, waiting. The plant cannot grow until the seed gets water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water soaks in through a small hole in the seed coat. The hole is smaller than the point of a pencil.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The seed swells as it drinks. Sometimes the seed coat splits open. That is the first sign that a seed is alive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water wakes up the tiny plant. A root pushes down first, before any leaf comes up. The root looks for more water.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A seed can wait a long time for its drink. Some seeds wait one year. A few kinds have waited hundreds of years.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A seed looks dry and hard. Inside is a tiny plant. It waits for water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Water soaks in through a small hole. The hole is in the seed coat. It is very small.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The seed swells as it drinks. The seed coat may split open. That means the seed is alive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The water wakes the tiny plant. A root pushes down first. No leaf comes up yet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A seed can wait a long time. Some seeds wait a year. A few wait much longer.

questions.q: What does a seed need before it can grow?
questions.a: It needs water, because the tiny plant inside cannot grow until the seed gets a drink.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the small hole) and paragraph D (i.e. the root).
Summarize how a seed starts to grow.
questions.a: Water soaks in through a small hole in the seed coat. The seed swells and the coat may split. Then a root pushes down before any leaf comes up.

questions.q:
seed coat: the hard cover around the outside of a seed.
swell: to get bigger.
Describe the connection between the water and the root.
questions.a: The water wakes up the tiny plant, and a root pushes down first to look for more water.

articles.note: Soak beans overnight and bring them in split. Paragraph C stops being a fact and becomes something on the desk.

articles.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Lamp
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before electric lights, a lighthouse burned oil. A keeper lived at the lighthouse and took care of the lamp every single night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The keeper climbed the stairs at sunset. He filled the lamp with oil and lit the wick. Then he waited and watched.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The glass had to stay clean. Smoke from the flame left a gray film. The keeper wiped the glass many times each night.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Around the lamp sat rings of thick glass. The rings bent the light into one strong beam. Ships could see that beam far out at sea.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A keeper slept in the day. If the lamp went out, a ship might not see the rocks. So someone stayed awake all night, every night.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Long ago a lighthouse burned oil. A keeper lived there. He took care of the lamp every night.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The keeper climbed the stairs at sunset. He filled the lamp with oil. He lit the wick.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The glass had to stay clean. Smoke left a gray film. The keeper wiped it many times.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Rings of thick glass sat around the lamp. They bent the light into one beam. Ships saw it far away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A keeper slept in the day. If the lamp went out, a ship might hit rocks. Someone stayed awake all night.

questions.q: Why did the keeper wipe the glass?
questions.a: Smoke from the flame left a gray film on the glass, so he wiped it many times each night.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the rings of glass) and paragraph E (i.e. staying awake).
Summarize what a lighthouse keeper did each night.
questions.a: He climbed the stairs at sunset, filled the lamp with oil and lit the wick. He wiped smoke off the glass many times and stayed awake all night.

questions.q:
wick: the string in a lamp that holds the flame.
beam: a line of light that shines out in one direction.
Describe the connection between the rings of glass and the ships.
questions.a: The rings bent the light into one strong beam, so ships could see that beam far out at sea.

articles.note: Why questions are the hardest of the six. Paragraphs C and E both answer one, and both answers are a whole sentence away from the question.

articles.title: Why a Cat Has Whiskers
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
 Spiral: RI.2.2 main topic · RI.2.3 connections · RI.2.4 word meaning · RI.2.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 330 – 430

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat's whiskers are not just hair. Each one grows from a deep spot in the skin. That spot is full of nerves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Whiskers feel things the cat does not touch. Moving air bends a whisker a little. The cat knows something is near.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Whiskers also measure. A cat's whiskers are about as wide as its body. If the whiskers fit through a gap, the cat fits too.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A cat uses whiskers most in the dark. Eyes need light. Whiskers work with no light at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Whiskers fall out and grow back. That is normal. But a cat with cut whiskers bumps into things.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A cat's whiskers are not just hair. Each one grows deep in the skin. That spot is full of nerves.

paras.label: B
