paras.label: F
paras.text: Fewer letters from the children survive. They tell of being split from brothers and sisters on the same platform. Some spent decades trying to find each other.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both kinds of document are evidence. The files alone describe a rescue. The letters alone describe a loss. The programme was both at once.

questions.q: Why does the article say the Society's records are one-sided?
questions.a: They were written by the people running the programme, who had every reason to count a placement as a success unless something had plainly gone wrong.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the Society's own records) and paragraph F (i.e. the letters written by the children).
Summarize what the orphan trains were and why they are hard to judge.
questions.a: Between 1854 and 1929 about two hundred thousand children were sent west by train to families they had never met. Some were adopted and some were taken as unpaid farm labour. The Society's records count placements as successes and the children's letters describe families separated, so each kind of evidence tells a different story.

questions.q:
almshouse: a public institution where people with no money were housed.
placement: the act of putting a child with a family, which is also the word the Society used when counting its results.
Describe the connection between who wrote a document and what that document shows.
questions.a: The Society's files were written by the people running the programme and describe a rescue, while the letters were written by the children and describe being separated from brothers and sisters.

articles.note: A good answer cites at least two documents with different authors, i.e. the Society's records and the children's letters. Noticing who wrote a source is the move RI.7.1 is building toward.

articles.title: The Bird That Builds a Compost Heap
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most birds sit on their eggs. The malleefowl of southern Australia does not, and the alternative it has worked out takes the better part of a year to run.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In autumn the male scrapes a pit several metres across and fills it with leaves and twigs. Rain soaks the pile, and the material begins to rot, which releases heat exactly the way a garden compost heap does.

paras.label: C
paras.text: When the pile is warm enough the bird covers it with sand, and the female lays her eggs inside. An egg sits in the mound for seven or eight weeks, and nothing about the arrangement is adjustable from outside.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The temperature has to stay close to thirty-three degrees. Too cool and the eggs do not develop; too warm and they die. The rotting leaves do not hold a steady temperature on their own.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the male tests the mound. He pushes his beak into the sand, and the sensitivity of his bill and mouth tells him whether the inside is warm or cool, and then he adds sand or digs it away.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Later in the season the rotting slows and the sun takes over as the main source of heat. The bird's work changes with it: he opens the mound in the morning and closes it before the afternoon.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A chick digs its own way out, which can take fifteen hours, and then runs. Its parents do not feed it, do not recognise it, and may be standing a few metres away while it leaves.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most birds sit on their eggs. The malleefowl of southern Australia does not. Its method takes most of a year.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In autumn the male scrapes a pit several metres wide. He fills it with leaves and twigs. Rain soaks the pile. The material rots, and rotting gives off heat, just like a compost heap.

paras.label: C
paras.text: When the pile is warm, the bird covers it with sand. The female lays her eggs inside. An egg stays there for seven or eight weeks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The temperature must stay near thirty-three degrees. Too cool and the eggs do not grow. Too warm and they die. Rotting leaves do not hold a steady temperature.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the male tests the mound. He pushes his beak into the sand. His bill and mouth tell him if it is warm or cool. Then he adds sand or digs some away.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Later the rotting slows. The sun becomes the main source of heat. The bird changes his work. He opens the mound in the morning and closes it in the afternoon.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A chick digs its own way out. That can take fifteen hours. Then it runs. Its parents do not feed it and do not know it.

questions.q: How does the male malleefowl know whether to add sand or dig it away?
questions.a: He pushes his beak into the sand, and the sensitivity of his bill and mouth tells him whether the inside of the mound is warm or cool.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why the temperature matters) and paragraph E (i.e. how the bird tests and corrects it).
Summarize how a malleefowl incubates its eggs without sitting on them.
questions.a: The male fills a pit with leaves and twigs that rot and give off heat, then covers it with sand for the female to lay in. He tests the mound with his beak and adds or removes sand to hold it near thirty-three degrees, and later he opens and closes it as the sun takes over from the rotting.

questions.q:
incubate: to keep eggs at the temperature they need in order to develop.
mound: here, the pile of rotting material and sand the bird builds and manages, not a natural hill.
Describe the connection between the rotting slowing down and the change in the bird's daily work.
questions.a: Once the rotting slows the sun becomes the main source of heat, so the bird opens the mound in the morning and closes it before the afternoon instead of only adding or removing sand.

articles.note: Three separate pieces of evidence show the mound is managed rather than just built, i.e. the beak test, the adding and removing of sand, and the switch to opening and closing. Push for more than one.

articles.title: The Blizzard That Buried the Wires
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In March 1888 a storm stalled over the north-east of the United States and snowed for three days. Drifts in New York City reached the second floor of some buildings, and about four hundred people died.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city above the streets was a tangle of wire. Telegraph, telephone, fire alarm and electric light companies had each strung their own lines, and in places the poles carried so many that they blocked the light.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Wet snow freezes onto a wire and builds a sleeve of ice around it. The weight of that sleeve, multiplied across a span, is far more than the wire was built to hold, and the poles came down across the streets.

paras.label: D
paras.text: With the wires down, the city could not send a fire alarm, could not call a doctor, and could not reach the trains that were stopped outside it. Food deliveries stopped for days in some neighbourhoods.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Arguments for putting the lines underground had been made for years before the storm. They had lost, mainly because burying a line cost far more than hanging one and because the companies owning the poles saw no reason to pay.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The storm did not introduce a new argument. What it changed was the price of ignoring the old one, and within a few years New York had begun moving its wires into conduits beneath the pavement.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Boston and other cities followed. The ice storm is sometimes described as the cause, which is not quite right: the engineering case was already made, and the storm settled who was going to pay for it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In March 1888 a storm stalled over the north-east United States. It snowed for three days. Drifts in New York reached second-floor windows. About four hundred people died.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Above the streets was a tangle of wire. Telegraph, telephone, fire alarm and electric light companies all strung their own lines. In places the poles blocked the light.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Wet snow freezes onto a wire. It builds a sleeve of ice. The weight across a long span is far more than the wire can hold. The poles came down across the streets.

paras.label: D
paras.text: With the wires down, the city could not send a fire alarm. It could not call a doctor. It could not reach the stopped trains. Food deliveries stopped for days.

paras.label: E
paras.text: People had argued for burying the lines for years. The argument lost. Burying a line cost much more than hanging one, and the companies saw no reason to pay.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The storm did not add a new argument. It changed the price of ignoring the old one. Within a few years New York began moving wires under the pavement.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Boston and other cities did the same. People sometimes call the storm the cause. That is not quite right. The case was already made. The storm settled who would pay.

questions.q: Why did the overhead wires fail during the storm?
questions.a: Wet snow freezes onto a wire and builds a sleeve of ice, and the weight of that sleeve across a span is far more than the wire was built to hold, so the poles came down.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why burying the lines had lost the argument before) and paragraph F (i.e. what the storm actually changed).
Summarize what the 1888 blizzard did to New York's wires and what followed.
questions.a: Three days of snow brought down the overhead telegraph, telephone, fire alarm and light wires, so the city could not send an alarm or call a doctor. Burying the lines had been argued for years and had lost on cost, and after the storm New York began moving its wires into conduits beneath the pavement.

questions.q:
conduit: a pipe or channel laid underground to carry wires.
stalled: here, a storm that stopped moving and stayed over one area instead of passing through.
Describe the connection between the cost of burying a line and the delay in doing it.
questions.a: Burying a line cost far more than hanging one and the companies owning the poles saw no reason to pay, so the argument for underground wires lost for years before the storm.

articles.note: The last paragraph is the one to slow down on. The text explicitly refuses the simple cause, i.e. "the engineering case was already made, and the storm settled who was going to pay for it."

articles.title: The Lead in the Greenland Ice
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Snow that falls on the Greenland ice sheet does not melt. It is buried by the next year's snow, compressed into ice, and stays where it is, in order, for thousands of years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A drilled core brings that order up as a column. Summer and winter snow differ in texture, so the layers can be counted the way tree rings are counted, and a depth can be converted into a date.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The ice also traps whatever was in the air. Dust from a desert, ash from an eruption and the chemistry of the atmosphere itself are all held in place, which makes the core a record and not just a measurement.

paras.label: D
paras.text: In cores covering the last three thousand years, the lead content rises sharply, holds high for several centuries, and then collapses. The rise begins around 600 BCE and the collapse falls in the third century CE.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Lead does not blow off a mountain by itself in those quantities. Smelting silver releases it, and silver smelting on a large scale is exactly what the Greek and then the Roman economies did to make coins.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The collapse is the harder part of the claim and the more interesting one. It lines up with a period of plague and political crisis in the Roman world, when mining output is known from other sources to have fallen.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The ice does not say Rome. It says lead, at a depth that corresponds to a date. Everything after that is an argument built by putting the ice beside coins, mine workings and written records.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Snow that falls on the Greenland ice sheet does not melt. Next year's snow buries it. It is pressed into ice. It stays in order for thousands of years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A drilled core brings that order up as a column. Summer and winter snow look different. So the layers can be counted, like tree rings. A depth becomes a date.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The ice also traps what was in the air. Desert dust, volcanic ash and the chemistry of the air are all held in place. That makes the core a record.

paras.label: D
paras.text: In cores from the last three thousand years, lead rises sharply. It stays high for centuries. Then it collapses. The rise starts near 600 BCE. The fall is in the third century CE.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Lead does not blow off a mountain in those amounts. Smelting silver releases it. Greek and then Roman economies smelted silver on a large scale to make coins.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The collapse is the harder claim. It matches a time of plague and political crisis in the Roman world. Other sources show mining output fell then.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The ice does not say Rome. It says lead at a certain depth. The rest is an argument. It puts the ice beside coins, mines and written records.

questions.q: How can a depth in an ice core be turned into a date?
questions.a: Summer and winter snow differ in texture, so the layers can be counted the way tree rings are counted and a depth converted into a date.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what the lead measurements show) and paragraph G (i.e. what the ice does and does not say on its own).
Summarize what the lead in Greenland ice shows and how far the evidence reaches.
questions.a: Snow buried on the ice sheet keeps a layered record that traps what was in the air, so the layers can be counted and dated. Lead rises around 600 BCE, holds high, and collapses in the third century CE, which matches large-scale silver smelting and then a crisis in the Roman world, but the ice only shows lead at a depth and the rest is argued from coins and written records.

questions.q:
core: a column of ice drilled out whole so its layers stay in the order they formed.
smelting: heating ore to separate out a metal, which in the case of silver also releases lead.
Describe the connection between smelting silver and the lead measured in the ice.
questions.a: Smelting silver releases lead, and Greek and Roman economies smelted silver on a large scale to make coins, which is why lead does not blow off a mountain by itself in those quantities.

articles.note: The last paragraph draws the line between measurement and argument, i.e. "the ice does not say Rome." A student who cites only the lead curve has half the case.

articles.title: The Canal and the Mosquito
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The French began digging a canal across Panama in 1881 and gave up eight years later. The engineering had defeated them, and so had a death rate that reached into the thousands.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow fever and malaria killed workers faster than the company could replace them. Hospitals of the period set the legs of beds in pans of water to keep ants off the patients, which bred mosquitoes beside every sickbed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: By the time the United States took the project over in 1904, Carlos Finlay and Walter Reed had shown that yellow fever is carried by a mosquito. William Gorgas was given the job of acting on that finding.

paras.label: D
paras.text: His campaign was not medical in the ordinary sense. Crews drained standing water, oiled ponds, screened buildings and fumigated houses across the whole zone, and yellow fever disappeared from the isthmus within two years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The engineering changed too. Rather than cutting a channel at sea level, the American plan dammed the Chagres River to make a lake and lifted ships over the high ground in locks.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither decision would have worked alone. A workforce that is dying cannot build a lock system, and a lock system that does not exist cannot be saved by healthy workers.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The canal opened in 1914. It is usually told as a story about concrete and excavation, and the second half of the story is a mosquito that had to be removed from the ground the concrete stood on.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The French began a canal across Panama in 1881. They gave up eight years later. The engineering beat them. So did a death rate in the thousands.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Yellow fever and malaria killed workers faster than the company could replace them. Hospitals set bed legs in pans of water to keep ants off. That bred mosquitoes beside every bed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The United States took over in 1904. By then Carlos Finlay and Walter Reed had shown that a mosquito carries yellow fever. William Gorgas was told to act on it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: His campaign was not medical in the usual way. Crews drained water, oiled ponds, screened buildings and fumigated houses. Yellow fever left the isthmus in two years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The engineering changed too. The American plan did not cut a channel at sea level. It dammed the Chagres River to make a lake and lifted ships in locks.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither choice would have worked alone. Dying workers cannot build locks. Healthy workers cannot save locks that do not exist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The canal opened in 1914. People tell it as a story about concrete. The other half is a mosquito that had to be removed first.

questions.q: Why did hospitals of the period make the mosquito problem worse?
questions.a: They set the legs of beds in pans of water to keep ants off the patients, which bred mosquitoes beside every sickbed.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the campaign against the mosquito) and paragraph E (i.e. the change to a lock and lake design).
Summarize the two changes that let the canal be finished.
questions.a: The French gave up in 1889 after yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers. After 1904 William Gorgas drained and oiled standing water, screened buildings and fumigated houses until yellow fever disappeared, and the American plan dammed the Chagres River to lift ships in locks instead of cutting at sea level. Neither change would have worked without the other.

questions.q:
isthmus: a narrow strip of land joining two larger landmasses, which is what Panama is.
fumigate: to fill a space with smoke or chemical vapour in order to kill insects.
Describe the connection between the health campaign and the engineering plan.
questions.a: A workforce that is dying cannot build a lock system, and a lock system that does not exist cannot be saved by healthy workers, so neither decision would have worked alone.

articles.note: RI.7.2 wants two central ideas held at once. A summary that covers only the mosquitoes or only the locks has found one idea and stopped.

articles.title: The Factory Whistle
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before factories, most work was measured by the task. A weaver finished a length of cloth, a farmer brought in a field, and how long either took was a private matter between the worker and the work.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A mill cannot run that way. Water wheels and then steam engines drove every machine in a building from one shaft, so the whole floor had to start together and stop together or the power was wasted.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The whistle enforced that. Workers were paid for hours rather than output, which meant that for the first time an employer had a direct financial interest in exactly where a worker was at seven in the morning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Clocks became common in ordinary houses in the same decades, and so did arguments about them. Mill owners were accused of running the factory clock slow at the start of a shift and fast at the end.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea grew out of the first. Once time was the unit being bought, time became the thing to bargain over, and the ten-hour day and then the eight-hour day were demands that could not have been phrased earlier.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The slogan of the eight-hour movement divided a day into three: eight hours of work, eight of rest, and eight for what we will. It is an argument about time that only makes sense once time is being counted.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The whistle is therefore not only a signal. It marks the point at which the working day stopped being a description of what got done and became a quantity that two sides could argue about.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before factories, most work was measured by the task. A weaver finished a length of cloth. A farmer brought in a field. How long it took was their own business.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A mill cannot run that way. One shaft drove every machine in the building. The whole floor had to start and stop together, or the power was wasted.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The whistle made that happen. Workers were paid for hours, not output. Now an employer cared exactly where a worker was at seven in the morning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Clocks became common in houses in the same years. So did arguments about them. People accused mill owners of running the factory clock slow, then fast.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea grew from the first. Time was now the thing being bought. So time became the thing to bargain over. The ten-hour day and the eight-hour day were new demands.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The eight-hour movement had a slogan. It split the day in three: eight hours of work, eight of rest, and eight for what we will. That argument needs time to be counted.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the whistle is not only a signal. It marks when the working day stopped describing what got done. It became a quantity two sides could argue about.

questions.q: Why did a mill have to start and stop all its machines together?
questions.a: Water wheels and then steam engines drove every machine in a building from one shaft, so the whole floor had to start together and stop together or the power was wasted.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. being paid for hours rather than output) and paragraph E (i.e. time becoming something to bargain over).
Summarize the two ideas this article develops about time and work.
questions.a: Work used to be measured by the task, but a mill driven from one shaft had to start and stop together, so workers were paid for hours and the whistle enforced it. Once time was the unit being bought it also became the thing to bargain over, which is why the ten-hour and eight-hour day could be demanded.

questions.q:
output: how much a worker produces, as opposed to how long they spend producing it.
shaft: the turning rod that carried power from one engine to every machine on a factory floor.
Describe the connection between being paid by the hour and the demand for an eight-hour day.
questions.a: Once time was the unit being bought, time became the thing to bargain over, so the ten-hour day and then the eight-hour day were demands that could not have been phrased earlier.

articles.note: The two ideas are measurement and bargaining, and the second depends on the first. Ask which paragraph is the hinge, i.e. paragraph E.

articles.title: What Lives in a Gut
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A human intestine holds a large population of bacteria. Counting them is harder than it sounds, and older textbook figures were estimates built on estimates, but the number is in the trillions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Most of these organisms cannot be grown in a dish. For a century that put them beyond study, because the standard method in microbiology was to isolate something and raise it on its own.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sequencing changed the question. Instead of growing an organism, a laboratory can read genetic material straight out of a sample and work out what was there from the sequences it finds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That produced a catalogue, and a catalogue invited a second question, which is harder: does the mixture do anything, or is it simply present the way dust is present in a house?

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some of the evidence is strong. Gut bacteria break down fibres that human enzymes cannot, and they make certain vitamins, and a person whose gut flora is wiped out by antibiotics is more easily infected by other organisms.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Other claims run ahead of their evidence. Studies linking gut bacteria to mood or behaviour are mostly in mice, often with small numbers, and a correlation in a mouse colony is not a mechanism in a person.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both things are true at once, and a careful article says so. The catalogue is real and growing; the question of what the catalogue causes is open and is being answered slowly.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A human intestine holds a large population of bacteria. Counting them is hard. Old textbook figures were estimates built on estimates. The number is in the trillions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Most of these organisms cannot be grown in a dish. For a century that put them out of reach. Microbiology worked by isolating one thing and raising it alone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sequencing changed the question. A laboratory does not have to grow an organism. It can read genetic material straight from a sample and work out what was there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That gave scientists a catalogue. A catalogue raises a harder question. Does the mixture do anything? Or is it just present, like dust in a house?

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some evidence is strong. Gut bacteria break down fibres our enzymes cannot. They make some vitamins. A person whose gut flora is wiped out is infected more easily.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Other claims run ahead of the evidence. Studies linking gut bacteria to mood are mostly in mice. The numbers are often small. A pattern in mice is not a mechanism in a person.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both things are true at once. A careful article says so. The catalogue is real and growing. What it causes is still an open question.

questions.q: Why could gut bacteria not be studied for so long?
questions.a: Most of these organisms cannot be grown in a dish, and the standard method in microbiology was to isolate something and raise it on its own.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the claims the evidence supports) and paragraph F (i.e. the claims that run ahead of it).
Summarize what is known about gut bacteria and what is not.
questions.a: A human intestine holds trillions of bacteria that mostly cannot be grown in a dish, so sequencing was needed to catalogue them. Some effects are well supported, such as breaking down fibres and making vitamins, while claims about mood rest mostly on small studies in mice.

questions.q:
sequencing: reading the order of the chemical letters in genetic material, which identifies an organism without growing it.
correlation: two things happening together, which is not the same as one causing the other.
Describe the connection between having a catalogue and asking a harder question.
questions.a: Once sequencing produced a catalogue of what is there, it invited the second question of whether the mixture does anything or is simply present the way dust is present in a house.

articles.note: The two ideas are what sequencing made possible and what it has not yet settled. Paragraph F is the one students skip, i.e. "a correlation in a mouse colony is not a mechanism in a person."

articles.title: The Typewriter and the Office Door
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first commercially successful typewriter went on sale in 1874. It was slow to catch on, partly because a typed letter struck some recipients as rude, as though the writer had not troubled to use a pen.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What changed was the volume of paper. Railways, insurance firms and mail-order companies generated records faster than clerks could copy them, and a machine that produced legible text at speed solved a problem those firms actually had.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An office before the typewriter was almost entirely male. Clerking was a career with a ladder, and a young man who began copying letters could expect to be given responsibility over time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The typewriter was new, so no one held it. Firms hiring typists could pay less by hiring women, and within thirty years the great majority of typists in the United States were women.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That gave many women their first access to paid work outside a factory or a home, and the training schools and the wages were real. It also built a job with a ceiling on it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Typing was defined from the start as a separate track rather than the first rung of the clerical ladder. The men kept the ladder, and the new entrants were given a room with a door on it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both halves of that are the history. A machine opened an occupation to a group that had been shut out of it, and the same machine fixed the shape of the occupation they were let into.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first typewriter that sold well went on sale in 1874. It caught on slowly. Some people thought a typed letter was rude. The writer had not bothered to use a pen.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What changed was the volume of paper. Railways, insurance firms and mail-order companies made records faster than clerks could copy them. A machine that wrote fast and clearly solved a real problem.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An office before the typewriter was almost all male. Clerking was a career with a ladder. A young man who copied letters could expect more responsibility later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The typewriter was new, so nobody held it. Firms could pay less by hiring women. Within thirty years most typists in the United States were women.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That gave many women their first paid work outside a factory or a home. The schools and the wages were real. It also built a job with a ceiling.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Typing was a separate track from the start. It was not the first rung of the clerical ladder. The men kept the ladder. The new workers got a room with a door.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both halves are the history. A machine opened a job to people shut out of it. The same machine fixed the shape of that job.

questions.q: Why did firms begin to want typewriters?
questions.a: Railways, insurance firms and mail-order companies generated records faster than clerks could copy them, and a machine that produced legible text at speed solved a problem those firms actually had.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the access the job gave) and paragraph F (i.e. the ceiling built into it).
Summarize the two things the typewriter did to office work.
questions.a: Firms adopted the typewriter because they were producing records faster than clerks could copy them. Because the machine was new and nobody held it, firms hired women at lower pay, which gave many women their first paid work outside a factory or a home, and also fixed typing as a separate track from the clerical ladder.

questions.q:
clerical: to do with office work such as copying, filing and correspondence.
ceiling: here, a limit on how far a worker can be promoted, not part of a room.
Describe the connection between the typewriter being a new machine and who was hired to use it.
questions.a: Because the typewriter was new, no one held it, so firms hiring typists could pay less by hiring women and within thirty years most typists in the United States were women.

articles.note: The gain and the limit are one story, not a good half and a bad half. A summary that reports only the opportunity has dropped an idea the text develops.

articles.title: The Ring of Coral
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A coral atoll is a ring of low islands around a lagoon, often far out in deep ocean. The shape is strange enough to need explaining: a ring of shallow-water animals with thousands of metres of water just outside it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Reef-building corals need sunlight, because the algae living in their tissue supply much of their food. That confines them to roughly the top forty metres, which makes a reef in the deep ocean a contradiction.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Charles Darwin proposed an answer in 1842 after seeing atolls on the Beagle voyage. A volcano builds an island, coral grows as a fringe around its shore, and the volcano then subsides slowly beneath the sea.

paras.label: D
paras.text: If the coral grows upward at about the rate the island sinks, the reef stays in the sunlight while the land inside it disappears. What is left is a ring with a lagoon where the mountain used to be.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea is about how such a claim gets settled. Darwin's account predicted something specific: beneath an atoll there should be a great thickness of shallow-water coral sitting on volcanic rock.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Nobody could test that for a century. Drilling at Enewetak Atoll in 1952 went down more than a kilometre through coral limestone and struck basalt, which is what the prediction required and what a rival explanation did not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the atoll is two stories. One is how a ring of islands forms, and the other is how an idea proposed from the deck of a ship waited a hundred years for a drill.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A coral atoll is a ring of low islands around a lagoon. It often sits far out in deep ocean. The shape needs explaining. Shallow-water animals sit beside very deep water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Reef corals need sunlight. Algae live in their tissue and supply much of their food. So corals stay in about the top forty metres. A reef in the deep ocean is a contradiction.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Charles Darwin gave an answer in 1842. He had seen atolls on the Beagle voyage. A volcano builds an island. Coral grows around its shore. Then the volcano sinks slowly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The coral grows up at about the rate the island sinks. So the reef stays in the sunlight. The land inside it disappears. A ring is left, with a lagoon in the middle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea is how such a claim gets settled. Darwin predicted something exact. Under an atoll there should be thick shallow-water coral sitting on volcanic rock.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Nobody could test that for a century. In 1952 a drill at Enewetak Atoll went down more than a kilometre through coral limestone. It struck basalt. That is what the prediction needed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So an atoll is two stories. One is how a ring of islands forms. The other is how an idea waited a hundred years for a drill.

questions.q: Why can reef-building corals only live near the surface?
questions.a: The algae living in their tissue supply much of their food and need sunlight, which confines reef-building corals to roughly the top forty metres.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. how the ring is left behind) and paragraph F (i.e. the drilling at Enewetak).
Summarize Darwin's explanation of atolls and how it was tested.
questions.a: Reef corals need sunlight so they live near the surface, which makes a ring of reef in deep ocean strange. Darwin proposed that a volcano builds an island, coral fringes it, and the volcano subsides while the coral grows upward, leaving a ring around a lagoon. His account predicted thick shallow-water coral on volcanic rock, and drilling at Enewetak in 1952 went through more than a kilometre of coral limestone and struck basalt.

questions.q:
subside: to sink gradually, which is what the volcano does beneath the reef.
lagoon: the shallow body of water enclosed by the ring of a coral atoll.
Describe the connection between the rate the coral grows and the rate the island sinks.
questions.a: If the coral grows upward at about the rate the island sinks, the reef stays in the sunlight while the land inside it disappears, which leaves a ring with a lagoon.

articles.note: The second idea is about testing, not coral. Ask what the drill would have found if Darwin had been wrong, i.e. not a kilometre of shallow-water limestone sitting on basalt.

articles.title: The Chemist Who Fed and Poisoned
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text, for example how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Plants need nitrogen, and the air is nearly four fifths nitrogen, but the atmospheric form is locked in a bond so stable that almost nothing alive can break it. Farming therefore depended on manure, on clover, and on mined deposits that were running down.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1909 Fritz Haber combined nitrogen and hydrogen under great pressure and heat over a catalyst and produced ammonia. Carl Bosch turned the laboratory result into an industrial process, and by 1913 a factory was making fertilizer out of air.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is difficult to overstate what followed. A large share of the nitrogen in the body of a person alive today passed through that reaction, and the population the earth now supports is not reachable by the older methods.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same chemistry has another use. Explosives need fixed nitrogen too, and when war came in 1914 the process that was feeding Germany was also supplying the material its artillery fired.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Haber went further than supplying it. He argued for chemical weapons, developed the method, and stood on the field at Ypres in April 1915 when chlorine was released from cylinders toward the French line.

paras.label: F
paras.text: His wife Clara Immerwahr was a chemist too, the first woman to take a doctorate in chemistry at her university. She opposed the work, and days after Ypres she shot herself in their garden.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the ammonia synthesis. He left Germany in 1933 when the new government's laws reached him, and he died the following year. No summary of him holds still.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Plants need nitrogen. The air is almost four fifths nitrogen. But that form is locked in a very stable bond. Almost nothing alive can break it. So farming relied on manure, clover and mined deposits.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1909 Fritz Haber combined nitrogen and hydrogen. He used great pressure, heat and a catalyst. He made ammonia. Carl Bosch turned it into an industry. By 1913 a factory made fertilizer out of air.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What followed is hard to overstate. Much of the nitrogen in your body passed through that reaction. The older methods could not feed the population the earth now holds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same chemistry has another use. Explosives also need fixed nitrogen. War came in 1914. The process feeding Germany also supplied its artillery.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Haber did more than supply it. He argued for chemical weapons. He developed the method. He stood at Ypres in April 1915 when chlorine was released toward the French line.

paras.label: F
paras.text: His wife Clara Immerwahr was a chemist. She was the first woman to take a chemistry doctorate at her university. She opposed the work. Days after Ypres she shot herself.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Haber won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ammonia. He left Germany in 1933 when the new laws reached him. He died the next year. No summary of him holds still.

questions.q: Why could farmers not simply use the nitrogen already in the air?
questions.a: The atmospheric form is locked in a bond so stable that almost nothing alive can break it, so farming depended on manure, on clover and on mined deposits.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what the fertilizer made possible) and paragraph E (i.e. what Haber did at Ypres).
Summarize what Fritz Haber did and why he is hard to sum up.
questions.a: Haber found a way to combine nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia, and Bosch made it industrial, so fertilizer could be made out of air and far more people could be fed. The same fixed nitrogen makes explosives, and Haber argued for chemical weapons and was at Ypres when chlorine was released, so no summary of him holds still.

questions.q:
catalyst: a substance that lets a reaction happen that would otherwise be too slow, without being used up itself.
fixed nitrogen: nitrogen in a form living things or factories can actually use, rather than the locked form in the air.
Describe the connection between the fertilizer process and the artillery shells.
questions.a: Explosives need fixed nitrogen too, so when war came in 1914 the process that was feeding Germany was also supplying the material its artillery fired.

articles.note: RI.7.3 asks how a person, an event and an idea act on each other. The idea here is fixed nitrogen, and it reaches both a wheat field and a gun. Resist letting students settle on good man or bad man.

articles.title: The Seed Collection Under Siege
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text, for example how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Nikolai Vavilov spent the 1920s and 1930s collecting seed. He travelled across five continents gathering varieties of wheat, rice, maize and potato, and by 1940 his institute in Leningrad held the largest such collection in the world.

paras.label: B
paras.text: His reasoning was that a crop grown everywhere from one or two varieties is fragile. The wild and local relatives of that crop carry resistance to diseases that have not arrived yet, and once those varieties are gone they cannot be recovered.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument made him enemies. Trofim Lysenko rejected the genetics the collection was built on and had the backing of the state, and Vavilov was arrested in 1940 and died in prison in 1943.

paras.label: D
paras.text: German forces encircled Leningrad in September 1941. The siege lasted nearly nine hundred days, and starvation in the city killed hundreds of thousands of people during the first winter alone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The institute held tonnes of rice, maize, wheat and several thousand varieties of potato, in a building in the middle of a starving city. The staff moved the collection into a basement and took turns guarding it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Several of them died of starvation at their posts. Alexander Stchukin was found at his desk with a packet of groundnuts; Dmitri Ivanov died surrounded by sacks of rice he had not opened.

paras.label: G
paras.text: They were not protecting food. They were protecting the ability to grow food later, which is an abstraction, and the collection they kept has supplied breeding programmes ever since.

paras.text: Nikolai Vavilov collected seed in the 1920s and 1930s. He travelled five continents. He gathered kinds of wheat, rice, maize and potato. By 1940 his institute in Leningrad held the largest such collection on earth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: His reasoning was simple. A crop grown everywhere from one or two kinds is fragile. Wild and local relatives carry resistance to diseases that have not come yet. Once they are gone they cannot be got back.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument made him enemies. Trofim Lysenko rejected the genetics behind the collection. The state backed Lysenko. Vavilov was arrested in 1940. He died in prison in 1943.

paras.label: D
paras.text: German forces surrounded Leningrad in September 1941. The siege lasted nearly nine hundred days. Starvation killed hundreds of thousands in the first winter alone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The institute held tonnes of rice, maize and wheat. It held thousands of kinds of potato. The building stood in a starving city. Staff moved the collection to a basement and guarded it in turns.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Several of them starved at their posts. Alexander Stchukin was found at his desk with a packet of groundnuts. Dmitri Ivanov died among sacks of rice he had not opened.

paras.label: G
paras.text: They were not protecting food. They were protecting the ability to grow food later. That is an abstraction. The collection has supplied plant breeders ever since.

questions.q: Why did Vavilov think a collection of crop varieties was necessary?
questions.a: A crop grown everywhere from one or two varieties is fragile, and the wild and local relatives carry resistance to diseases that have not arrived yet, which cannot be recovered once those varieties are gone.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the conflict with Lysenko) and paragraph F (i.e. the staff who died guarding the seed).
Summarize what the Leningrad seed collection was and what happened to it during the siege.
questions.a: Vavilov gathered crop varieties from five continents because a crop grown from one or two varieties is fragile and lost relatives cannot be recovered. He was arrested in 1940 and died in prison, and when Leningrad was besieged from 1941 his staff moved the collection to a basement and guarded it, several of them starving at their posts rather than eat it.

questions.q:
variety: a distinct form of a crop, differing from others of the same species in traits such as disease resistance.
abstraction: an idea that cannot be seen or eaten, such as the ability to grow food in a future year.
Describe the connection between an idea about plant disease and the decision those staff made.
questions.a: They were protecting the ability to grow food later rather than food itself, because the wild and local relatives in the collection carry resistance to diseases that have not arrived yet.

articles.note: The interaction runs from an idea to a choice. Paragraph G names it, i.e. "they were protecting the ability to grow food later, which is an abstraction."

articles.title: The Bridge That Shook Itself Apart
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text, for example how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in July 1940 and fell into the water four months later. Film of the collapse shows the deck twisting through an angle that looks impossible for a road to survive even briefly.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bridge was slender by design. Its engineer, Leon Moisseiff, had argued that a deck could be made lighter and shallower than previous practice allowed, and the theory he used had been applied successfully on other spans.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also moved from the day it opened. Drivers reported the deck rising and falling, local people called it Galloping Gertie, and the motion was treated as a nuisance to be damped rather than a warning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The usual classroom explanation is resonance: wind gusts arriving at the frequency the bridge liked to vibrate at, pushing it like a child on a swing. That explanation is in a great many textbooks and it is wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What happened is aeroelastic flutter. The deck's own twisting changed the way air flowed around it, that altered flow pushed the deck further in the direction it was already going, and the motion fed itself from a steady wind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The difference matters because the two have different cures. Resonance is avoided by changing a frequency. Flutter is avoided by changing the shape of the deck so that twisting does not generate a force that deepens the twist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Bridges built afterwards use open trusses or slotted decks that let air through. The lesson was not that the engineers miscalculated an old problem; it was that they had met a new one and named it wrongly for years.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in July 1940. It fell four months later. Film of the collapse shows the deck twisting. The angle looks impossible for a road to survive.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The bridge was slender by design. Its engineer, Leon Moisseiff, argued a deck could be lighter and shallower than before. The theory he used had worked on other spans.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It moved from the day it opened. Drivers felt the deck rise and fall. Locals called it Galloping Gertie. People treated the motion as a nuisance, not a warning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The usual classroom answer is resonance. Gusts arrive at the frequency the bridge likes, pushing it like a swing. That answer is in many textbooks. It is wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What happened is aeroelastic flutter. The twisting deck changed how air flowed around it. The changed flow pushed the deck further the way it was already going. The motion fed itself.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The difference matters. The two have different cures. You avoid resonance by changing a frequency. You avoid flutter by changing the deck's shape, so twisting does not deepen the twist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Later bridges use open trusses or slotted decks. Air passes through. The lesson was not a miscalculation. The engineers met a new problem and named it wrongly for years.

questions.q: What is aeroelastic flutter, as the article describes it?
questions.a: The deck's own twisting changed the way air flowed around it, and that altered flow pushed the deck further in the direction it was already going, so the motion fed itself from a steady wind.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the resonance explanation) and paragraph F (i.e. why the difference between the two changes the cure).
Summarize what brought the Tacoma Narrows Bridge down and why the common explanation is wrong.
questions.a: A slender deck moved from the day the bridge opened and twisted itself apart four months later. The usual explanation is resonance from gusts arriving at the bridge's own frequency, but the cause was aeroelastic flutter, in which the twisting changed the airflow and the changed airflow deepened the twist. The two have different cures, so later bridges change the deck's shape to let air through.

questions.q:
resonance: pushing something at the frequency it already vibrates at, so the motion grows.
truss: an open framework of beams, used here instead of a solid deck so that air can pass through.
Describe the connection between naming the cause correctly and designing later bridges.
questions.a: Resonance is avoided by changing a frequency while flutter is avoided by changing the shape of the deck, so bridges built afterwards use open trusses or slotted decks that let air through.

articles.note: This one is about an idea being corrected, not a villain. The sentence to hold students to is in paragraph G, i.e. "they had met a new one and named it wrongly for years."

articles.title: The Nurse Who Drew a Diagram
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text, for example how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Florence Nightingale arrived at the British military hospital at Scutari in 1854, during the war in the Crimea. Soldiers were dying there in numbers that nobody in London had expected or could explain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She began counting. The hospital kept records so poorly that even the number of deaths was uncertain, and her first work was not nursing but building a system that produced a trustworthy figure every month.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What the figures showed was that most of the dead had not been killed by their wounds. They were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery, contracted in the hospital, in a building standing over a blocked sewer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Reporting a table of monthly deaths to a government committee is a way of being ignored. Nightingale drew the numbers instead, as wedges radiating from a centre, with the area of each wedge standing for the deaths in a month.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The diagram splits each wedge by cause, and the part representing preventable disease dwarfs the part representing wounds. A reader does not have to follow an argument to see it; the picture makes the comparison before the text does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The sanitary commission dug out the sewers and improved ventilation, and the death rate fell. Attributing that fall entirely to the diagram would be too neat, because several changes happened together.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What is not in doubt is the method. Nightingale was elected the first woman fellow of the Royal Statistical Society in 1858, and the argument she made was carried by a drawing that an official could not put aside.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Florence Nightingale reached the British military hospital at Scutari in 1854. The war in the Crimea was on. Soldiers were dying there in numbers nobody in London expected.

paras.label: B
paras.text: She began counting. The hospital kept poor records. Even the number of deaths was uncertain. Her first work was not nursing. It was building a system that gave a trustworthy figure each month.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The figures showed something clear. Most of the dead were not killed by wounds. They died of typhus, cholera and dysentery. They caught them in the hospital, which stood over a blocked sewer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A table of monthly deaths is easy for a committee to ignore. So Nightingale drew the numbers. She used wedges around a centre. The area of each wedge stood for one month's deaths.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each wedge is split by cause. The part for preventable disease dwarfs the part for wounds. A reader does not need to follow an argument. The picture makes the comparison first.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The sanitary commission dug out the sewers. They improved the air. The death rate fell. Crediting that only to the diagram would be too neat. Several changes happened at once.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The method is not in doubt. Nightingale became the first woman fellow of the Royal Statistical Society in 1858. A drawing carried her argument, and officials could not set it aside.

questions.q: What did Nightingale's figures show about how the soldiers were dying?
questions.a: Most of the dead had not been killed by their wounds but were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery contracted in the hospital, which stood over a blocked sewer.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why she drew the numbers) and paragraph F (i.e. the caution about what caused the death rate to fall).
Summarize what Nightingale counted and why she drew it.
questions.a: At Scutari she first built a system that produced a trustworthy monthly figure, and the figures showed most soldiers were dying of disease caught in the hospital rather than of wounds. Because a table is easy to ignore, she drew the deaths as wedges whose area showed each month, split by cause, so the size of the preventable part could be seen before the argument was read.

questions.q:
preventable: able to be stopped by action taken beforehand, which is what the diagram showed most of the deaths were.
sanitary: to do with cleanliness and drainage, especially the removal of sewage.
Describe the connection between the form of her diagram and the effect it had on officials.
questions.a: The area of each wedge stood for the deaths in a month and each wedge was split by cause, so a reader could see that preventable disease dwarfed wounds without having to follow an argument.

articles.note: Paragraph F is deliberate restraint, i.e. "several changes happened together." A student who says the diagram saved the soldiers has gone past what the text will support.

articles.title: The Eruption That Cancelled a Summer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text, for example how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Mount Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa, erupted in April 1815. It was the largest eruption anywhere in recorded history, and it removed roughly a third of the height of the mountain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The local destruction was immediate. Ash buried villages, and the kingdoms on the slopes ceased to exist. What happened afterwards was slower and reached places that had never heard of the mountain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An eruption of that size pushes sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, above the weather. There it forms tiny droplets of sulphuric acid that scatter sunlight back into space and stay aloft for a year or more.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The following year, 1816, is remembered in New England and in Europe as the year without a summer. Snow fell in June in Massachusetts, frost killed crops through the growing season, and harvests failed across much of Europe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The consequences were social. Food prices rose, people in Switzerland and elsewhere went hungry, and the failed harvests pushed families off farms in Vermont and New Hampshire and westward into Ohio and Indiana.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Nobody at the time connected any of it to a mountain in the Dutch East Indies. The link was argued much later, from ice cores holding the sulphate layer, from tree rings recording a cold year, and from ships' logs and parish records.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the shape of the story: an event, then a mechanism nobody could see, then consequences on another continent, and only afterwards a chain of evidence joining them together.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Mount Tambora erupted in April 1815. It stands on the island of Sumbawa. It was the largest eruption in recorded history. It took off about a third of the mountain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The local damage was immediate. Ash buried villages. The kingdoms on the slopes ended. What came next was slower. It reached places that had never heard of the mountain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An eruption that size pushes sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. That is above the weather. There it makes tiny droplets of acid. They scatter sunlight back to space and stay up for a year.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next year, 1816, is called the year without a summer. Snow fell in June in Massachusetts. Frost killed crops all season. Harvests failed across much of Europe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The effects were social. Food prices rose. People in Switzerland and elsewhere went hungry. Failed harvests pushed families off farms in Vermont and New Hampshire. They moved west to Ohio and Indiana.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Nobody then linked any of it to a mountain in the Dutch East Indies. The link was argued much later. It came from ice cores, tree rings, ships' logs and parish records.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the shape of the story. An event. Then a mechanism nobody could see. Then effects on another continent. Only afterwards, a chain of evidence joining them.

questions.q: How does an eruption cool the planet for a year or more?
questions.a: It pushes sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, above the weather, where it forms tiny droplets of sulphuric acid that scatter sunlight back into space and stay aloft.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the social consequences of the failed harvests) and paragraph F (i.e. how the link was argued later).
Summarize what Tambora did in 1815 and 1816.
questions.a: The eruption buried villages on Sumbawa and pushed sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where droplets of acid scattered sunlight for more than a year. The following summer failed in New England and Europe, prices rose and families left farms in Vermont and New Hampshire for the west, and the link to the mountain was only argued later from ice cores, tree rings and written records.

questions.q:
stratosphere: the layer of atmosphere above the weather, where droplets can stay aloft for a year or more.
mechanism: the physical process that connects a cause to an effect, here the scattering of sunlight.
Describe the connection between a failed harvest and families moving west.
questions.a: Food prices rose and harvests failed, which pushed families off farms in Vermont and New Hampshire and westward into Ohio and Indiana.

articles.note: The last paragraph names the structure of the article itself, i.e. event, mechanism, consequence, evidence. Worth having students label the paragraphs with those four words.

articles.title: What a Scientist Means by Significant
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary speech, significant means important. A significant change in the weather is one you would notice, and a significant amount of money is an amount worth having.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a research paper the word is doing a different job. It describes how likely a result is to have come up by chance alone, and it says nothing at all about whether the result is large or whether it matters.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The usual test asks a narrow question. Suppose the treatment does nothing: how often would an experiment like this one produce a difference at least this big anyway? If the answer is below one in twenty, the result is called statistically significant.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That threshold is a convention. It was not derived; it was chosen, and it could have been one in fifty or one in ten without anything in nature changing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A study of two hundred thousand people can find a statistically significant difference that is far too small to be worth acting on. A study of twelve people can miss a large and real effect and report no significant difference.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is why a headline reading SIGNIFICANT DROP IN RISK is almost unreadable on its own. It may mean the drop is unlikely to be chance, which is a claim about the statistics, and not about the size of the drop.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The word has not been misused by the scientists. It has been borrowed by headline writers from a field where it has a technical meaning, and dropped into a sentence where readers supply the everyday one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary speech, significant means important. A significant change in the weather is one you would notice. A significant amount of money is worth having.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In a research paper the word does another job. It describes how likely a result is to come from chance alone. It says nothing about whether the result is large or whether it matters.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The usual test asks a narrow question. Suppose the treatment does nothing. How often would an experiment like this still show a difference this big? If that is under one in twenty, the result is called statistically significant.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That threshold is a convention. Nobody worked it out from nature. It was chosen. It could have been one in fifty or one in ten.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A study of two hundred thousand people can find a significant difference that is far too small to act on. A study of twelve people can miss a large real effect and report nothing significant.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So a headline saying SIGNIFICANT DROP IN RISK is hard to read. It may only mean the drop is unlikely to be chance. That is a claim about statistics, not about size.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Scientists have not misused the word. Headline writers borrowed it from a field where it is technical. Readers then supply the everyday meaning.

questions.q: What narrow question does a significance test actually ask?
questions.a: It asks that if the treatment does nothing, how often an experiment like this one would produce a difference at least this big anyway.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the threshold being a convention) and paragraph E (i.e. how study size changes what the word reports).
Summarize the difference between the everyday and technical meanings of significant.
questions.a: In ordinary speech significant means important, but in a research paper it describes how likely a result is to have come from chance alone and says nothing about size. The one in twenty threshold is a convention, a very large study can find a significant difference too small to act on, and a very small one can miss a real effect.

questions.q:
convention: an agreed practice rather than a fact about nature, such as the one in twenty threshold.
statistically significant: unlikely to have arisen by chance, which is not the same as large or important.
Describe the connection between the size of a study and what a significant result tells you.
questions.a: A study of two hundred thousand people can find a statistically significant difference that is far too small to be worth acting on, and a study of twelve people can miss a large and real effect and report no significant difference.

articles.note: RI.7.4 asks about the impact of a word choice. The last paragraph refuses the easy blame, i.e. "the word has not been misused by the scientists." Ask who the sentence does hold responsible.

articles.title: Mistakes Were Made
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: English lets a writer build a sentence that names an action without naming whoever performed it. The window was broken. The order was given. Mistakes were made.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This is the passive voice with the actor removed. It is not a fault in itself: a scientist writing the sample was heated to 90 degrees is using it because the identity of whoever did the heating is genuinely beside the point.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In an official report the same construction does other work. Funds were misallocated tells a reader that money went where it should not have gone and withholds the one fact a reader most wants, which is by whom.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Compare two sentences carrying the same facts. The inspector did not visit the site for three years names a person and an omission. Inspections were not carried out names neither, and the second is what tends to appear in print.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The effect is not only about blame. A sentence with no actor is also a sentence with nothing to fix. If inspections were not carried out, the problem is a process; if an inspector did not visit, the problem is a job somebody holds.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Readers can test a document quickly. Take any sentence describing something going wrong and ask whether a person or an organization appears as the subject, and keep count across a page.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Writers are not always hiding. Sometimes the actor is unknown, and sometimes naming one person for a failure shared by many would be its own distortion. The question is whether the pattern holds everywhere in a document or only where the news is bad.

paras.label: A
paras.text: English lets a writer name an action without naming who did it. The window was broken. The order was given. Mistakes were made.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This is the passive voice with the actor dropped. It is not a fault by itself. A scientist writes the sample was heated to 90 degrees because who heated it does not matter.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In an official report the same form does other work. Funds were misallocated tells a reader money went wrong. It holds back the fact the reader most wants. By whom?

paras.label: D
paras.text: Compare two sentences with the same facts. The inspector did not visit the site for three years names a person and an omission. Inspections were not carried out names neither. The second one gets printed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The effect is not only about blame. A sentence with no actor has nothing to fix. If inspections were not carried out, the problem is a process. If an inspector did not visit, the problem is a job.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Readers can test a document fast. Find a sentence about something going wrong. Ask whether a person or an organization is the subject. Keep count down the page.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Writers are not always hiding. Sometimes nobody knows who acted. Sometimes blaming one person for a shared failure is its own distortion. The question is whether the pattern appears everywhere or only where the news is bad.

questions.q: Why is the passive voice not a fault in itself?
questions.a: A scientist writing that the sample was heated to 90 degrees is using it because the identity of whoever did the heating is genuinely beside the point.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. a sentence with no actor having nothing to fix) and paragraph G (i.e. when leaving the actor out is honest).
Summarize what the agentless passive does in an official report.
questions.a: A sentence like funds were misallocated names an action without naming who performed it, so it withholds the fact a reader most wants. It also leaves nothing to fix, because a process is at fault rather than a job somebody holds, and readers can test a document by asking whether a person appears as the subject where the news is bad.

questions.q:
passive voice: a sentence form in which the thing acted on becomes the subject, as in the order was given.
agentless: here, a passive sentence that never says who performed the action.
Describe the connection between naming an actor and being able to fix a problem.
questions.a: If inspections were not carried out the problem is a process, and if an inspector did not visit the site the problem is a job somebody holds, so a sentence with no actor is a sentence with nothing to fix.

articles.note: Give students a real report and have them count. The test in paragraph F is the lesson, i.e. whether the pattern holds everywhere or only where the news is bad.

articles.title: What a Doctor Means by Positive
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A positive test result sounds like bad news and a negative one like good news, and in a clinic the words carry neither meaning. Positive means the test detected what it looks for. Negative means it did not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: No test detects perfectly. Two numbers describe how a test fails: how often it misses the thing when the thing is there, and how often it reports the thing when the thing is absent.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second kind of failure is the one that surprises people. A test can be ninety-nine per cent accurate in the ordinary sense and still produce more wrong positives than right ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Suppose a condition affects one person in ten thousand, and a million people are tested. About a hundred of them have it. If the test wrongly flags one healthy person in a hundred, that is roughly ten thousand false positives.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So of everyone told they tested positive, the great majority do not have the condition. Nothing is wrong with the test. The arithmetic depends on how rare the condition is, which is a fact about the population and not about the test.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is why a result is usually described as a screen rather than a diagnosis, and why a positive screen is followed by a second and different test rather than by treatment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The everyday meanings of the words make all of this harder to explain. A patient hearing positive hears a verdict, when the clinician said only that one instrument responded, and said nothing yet about what is true.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A positive result sounds like bad news. A negative one sounds like good news. In a clinic the words mean neither. Positive means the test found what it looks for. Negative means it did not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: No test is perfect. Two numbers describe how a test fails. How often does it miss the thing when it is there? How often does it report the thing when it is not?

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second failure surprises people. A test can be ninety-nine per cent accurate in the ordinary sense. It can still give more wrong positives than right ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Suppose a condition affects one person in ten thousand. A million people are tested. About a hundred have it. The test wrongly flags one healthy person in a hundred. That is about ten thousand false positives.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So most people told they tested positive do not have the condition. Nothing is wrong with the test. The arithmetic depends on how rare the condition is. That is a fact about the population.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This is why a result is called a screen and not a diagnosis. A positive screen leads to a second, different test. It does not lead straight to treatment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The everyday meanings make this hard to explain. A patient hears positive as a verdict. The clinician said only that one instrument responded. Nothing has been said yet about what is true.

questions.q: Why can an accurate test still produce more wrong positives than right ones?
questions.a: If a condition affects one person in ten thousand and the test wrongly flags one healthy person in a hundred, testing a million people gives about a hundred real cases and roughly ten thousand false positives.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the worked example with a million people) and paragraph F (i.e. why a positive screen is followed by a second test).
Summarize what positive means on a test and why it is often misread.
questions.a: Positive means the test detected what it looks for and negative means it did not, and neither is a verdict. Because a rare condition gives few real cases, even a small rate of wrong positives can outnumber them, so a result is a screen rather than a diagnosis and is followed by a second and different test.

questions.q:
false positive: a result reporting the thing is present when it is absent.
screen: a first test used to decide who needs further testing, rather than to decide what is true.
Describe the connection between how rare a condition is and how a positive result should be read.
questions.a: The arithmetic depends on how rare the condition is, so when a condition affects one person in ten thousand the great majority of those told they tested positive do not have it.

articles.note: The technical meaning and the connotation pull in opposite directions here, which is exactly RI.7.4. Paragraph G states it, i.e. "a patient hearing positive hears a verdict."

articles.title: The Words on a Census Form
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A census looks like an act of counting, and counting looks like the plainest thing a government can do. The form, though, is a list of words, and each word decides what can be counted at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A question offering a fixed list of boxes can only return the categories on the list. A person whose situation is not on it either picks the nearest box or is recorded as other, and both outcomes change the total.

paras.label: C
