paras.text: Categories also change between censuses. The wording used for a household, for an occupation, for a family relationship has been rewritten many times, and each rewrite breaks the comparison with the census before it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is not carelessness. A category that no longer matches how people actually live produces numbers that are precise and useless, so the words have to be revised, and revising them has a cost that is paid in continuity.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The stakes are real, because census counts are not only descriptions. They are used to draw electoral boundaries, to distribute funding and to decide where a hospital or a school is built.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So a change of wording is a political event as well as a technical one. Hearings are held about single questions, and the arguments are about who will appear in the resulting figures and who will not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading an old census well means reading its form first. The number in a column answers the question that was printed, which is often not the question a modern reader assumes it answers.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A census looks like counting. Counting looks like the plainest thing a government does. But the form is a list of words. Each word decides what can be counted.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A question with a fixed list of boxes returns only those categories. A person who does not fit picks the nearest box, or is recorded as other. Both change the total.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Categories also change between censuses. The wording for a household, a job or a family tie has been rewritten many times. Each rewrite breaks the comparison with the last census.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is not carelessness. A category that no longer matches how people live gives numbers that are precise and useless. So the words are revised. The cost is paid in continuity.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The stakes are real. Census counts are not only descriptions. They draw electoral boundaries. They share out funding. They decide where a hospital or school is built.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So changing a word is political as well as technical. Hearings are held about single questions. The arguments are about who will show up in the figures and who will not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: To read an old census well, read its form first. A number answers the question that was printed. That is often not the question a modern reader assumes.

questions.q: Why does a question with a fixed list of boxes limit what a census can find?
questions.a: It can only return the categories on the list, so a person whose situation is not on it either picks the nearest box or is recorded as other, and both outcomes change the total.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why categories are revised despite the cost) and paragraph E (i.e. what census counts are used for).
Summarize why the wording on a census form matters.
questions.a: A census can only count the categories its words offer, so people who do not fit pick the nearest box or are recorded as other. Rewriting a category keeps it matching how people live but breaks comparison with earlier censuses, and because counts draw boundaries and distribute funding, changing a word is political as well as technical.

questions.q:
category: a named group on a form, which determines what the count is able to record.
continuity: the ability to compare one census with the one before, which is lost when wording changes.
Describe the connection between revising a category and losing the comparison with earlier counts.
questions.a: A category that no longer matches how people actually live produces numbers that are precise and useless, so the words have to be revised, and each rewrite breaks the comparison with the census before it.

articles.note: The closing instruction is practical, i.e. read the form before the number. Give students two census forms from different decades and ask what changed between them.

articles.title: What Natural Means on a Label
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two words on a food package can look like a matched pair and work completely differently. Organic is defined in regulation, with rules about what may be used in growing and processing, and an inspection behind the claim.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Natural, in the United States, has no comparable definition for most foods. A manufacturer using it is making a claim that no specific standard sits behind, which is why the same word can appear on products made in very different ways.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Readers supply the missing meaning themselves. Natural carries a strong connotation of unprocessed, of grown rather than made, and that connotation does the work a definition would otherwise do.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Neither word is a measure of nutrition. An organic biscuit and a conventional biscuit are both biscuits, and the certification describes how the ingredients were produced rather than what they do in a body.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some terms are defined in a narrower way than readers expect. A claim about serving size, for instance, is measured against a serving the manufacturer states, which may be smaller than anyone eats at one sitting.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The useful habit is to move from the front of the package to the back. The front is designed and the words on it are chosen; the ingredient list and the nutrition panel are formats a regulator specifies.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of this makes the front of the package a lie. It makes it an advertisement, which is a different kind of writing with a different purpose, and reading it as though it were a report is the error.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two words on a package can look alike and work very differently. Organic is defined in regulation. There are rules about growing and processing. An inspection sits behind the claim.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Natural, in the United States, has no such definition for most foods. A maker using it makes a claim with no standard behind it. So the same word appears on very different products.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Readers fill in the missing meaning. Natural suggests unprocessed. It suggests grown rather than made. That suggestion does the work a definition would do.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Neither word measures nutrition. An organic biscuit and a normal biscuit are both biscuits. The certificate describes how ingredients were produced, not what they do in a body.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Some terms are narrower than readers expect. A claim about serving size is measured against a serving the maker states. That may be smaller than anyone eats at once.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A useful habit is to move from the front of the package to the back. The front is designed and its words are chosen. The ingredient list and nutrition panel follow a format a regulator sets.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of this makes the front a lie. It makes it an advertisement. That is a different kind of writing with a different purpose. Reading it as a report is the error.

questions.q: How do the words organic and natural differ on a package in the United States?
questions.a: Organic is defined in regulation with rules about growing and processing and an inspection behind the claim, while natural has no comparable definition for most foods.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. readers supplying the meaning themselves) and paragraph F (i.e. moving from the front of the package to the back).
Summarize why the front of a food package should be read differently from the back.
questions.a: Organic is defined in regulation while natural has no standard behind it for most foods, so readers supply a connotation of unprocessed that does the work a definition would. Neither word measures nutrition, and the ingredient list and nutrition panel follow a format a regulator specifies while the front is an advertisement whose words are chosen.

questions.q:
connotation: what a word suggests beyond its strict meaning, such as natural suggesting unprocessed.
certification: an inspected guarantee that stated rules were followed, which stands behind organic and not behind natural.
Describe the connection between a word having no definition and readers trusting it anyway.
questions.a: Natural carries a strong connotation of unprocessed, of grown rather than made, and that connotation does the work a definition would otherwise do.

articles.note: Bring in three real packages. The exercise is to sort every phrase on them into defined, undefined and format set by a regulator.

articles.title: The Inverted Pyramid
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most stories told out loud build toward their ending. A news report does the opposite. It puts the outcome in the first sentence and then works backwards into detail, context and quotation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shape has a name. It is called the inverted pyramid, because the widest and heaviest material sits at the top and the paragraphs narrow in importance as they go down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The habit is usually traced to the telegraph. A wire could fail mid-message and transmission was charged by the word, so a correspondent who buried the outcome risked sending the least useful part of the story first.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second pressure came from the page. An editor fitting stories into a fixed column cut from the bottom, and a story written as a pyramid could lose its last three paragraphs and still make sense.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structure shapes what a reader takes away. Someone who reads only the opening gets the outcome and no qualification, and the conditions, the uncertainties and the dissenting voice all live further down.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is why two readers of the same article can disagree about what it said. They did not read the same amount of it, and the parts they missed are the parts carrying the hedges.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Online the shape is loosening, because a page has no bottom to cut from. Some outlets now use a chronological or a question-and-answer form, and the reader has to work out which shape they are in.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most spoken stories build toward an ending. A news report does the opposite. It puts the outcome in the first sentence. Then it works backwards into detail, context and quotes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The shape has a name. It is the inverted pyramid. The heaviest material sits at the top. The paragraphs get less important as they go down.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The habit is usually traced to the telegraph. A wire could fail mid-message. Transmission cost money by the word. A reporter who buried the outcome risked sending the least useful part first.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The page pushed the same way. An editor fitting stories into a column cut from the bottom. A story in pyramid form could lose three paragraphs and still make sense.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structure shapes what a reader keeps. Someone who reads only the opening gets the outcome and no qualification. The conditions, the doubts and the other side sit further down.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So two readers of one article can disagree about what it said. They did not read the same amount. The parts they missed carry the hedges.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Online the shape is loosening. A web page has no bottom to cut from. Some outlets use a timeline or a question-and-answer form. A reader has to work out which shape they are in.

questions.q: Why did an editor's habit of cutting from the bottom reward the inverted pyramid?
questions.a: A story written as a pyramid could lose its last three paragraphs and still make sense, because the paragraphs narrow in importance as they go down.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what a reader of only the opening misses) and paragraph G (i.e. how the shape is loosening online).
Summarize the inverted pyramid and what it does to readers.
questions.a: A news report puts the outcome first and works backwards into detail, because a telegraph could fail mid-message and an editor cut stories from the bottom. The conditions and the dissenting voice live further down, so a reader who stops early takes away the outcome without the qualification.

questions.q:
hedge: a phrase that limits a claim, such as so far or in most cases.
inverted pyramid: the news structure in which the most important material comes first and importance narrows downward.
Describe the connection between where the hedges sit and readers disagreeing about an article.
questions.a: Someone who reads only the opening gets the outcome and no qualification, so two readers can disagree because the parts they missed are the parts carrying the hedges.

articles.note: RI.7.5 asks how sections contribute to the whole. Have students cut a real article after paragraph two and describe what claim they are now left holding.

articles.title: Why a Field Guide Is Not Alphabetical
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dictionary is alphabetical because a reader already knows the word. A field guide cannot be, because a reader holding an unknown leaf has nothing to look it up under.

paras.label: B
paras.text: So a guide is organized by what can be observed. Trees are grouped by leaf arrangement and shape, birds by silhouette and habitat, rocks by hardness and lustre, and the organization is the first half of the identification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Many guides go further and provide a key. A key is a chain of paired choices: leaves opposite or alternate, edge toothed or smooth, and each answer sends the reader to another pair.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Each step removes roughly half the possibilities. A set of six or seven choices can therefore separate one species out of a hundred, which is far quicker than reading a hundred descriptions.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The design has a cost. A key only works if every choice can be answered from the specimen in hand, so a key built on flowers is useless in November and one built on bark is uncertain on a young tree.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Good guides handle that by offering more than one route in, such as a winter key and a summer key, and by admitting where a pair of species cannot be separated on what a reader can see outdoors.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The organization is therefore an argument about how identification happens. The order of the pages is a claim that these features, in this sequence, are the ones a person in a field can actually use.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dictionary is alphabetical because the reader knows the word already. A field guide cannot be. A reader holding an unknown leaf has nothing to look it up under.

paras.label: B
paras.text: So a guide is organized by what can be seen. Trees go by leaf arrangement and shape. Birds go by outline and habitat. Rocks go by hardness and shine. That order is half the work.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Many guides add a key. A key is a chain of paired choices. Are the leaves opposite or alternate? Is the edge toothed or smooth? Each answer sends you to another pair.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Each step cuts the possibilities roughly in half. Six or seven choices can pick one species out of a hundred. That is far faster than reading a hundred descriptions.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The design has a cost. Every choice must be answerable from the specimen you hold. A key built on flowers is useless in November. One built on bark is unsure on a young tree.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Good guides offer more than one route in. There may be a winter key and a summer key. They also admit when two species cannot be told apart outdoors.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the organization is an argument. The order of the pages claims that these features, in this order, are the ones a person in a field can use.

questions.q: Why can a field guide not be arranged alphabetically?
questions.a: A reader holding an unknown leaf has nothing to look it up under, so the guide is organized by what can be observed instead.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. how a key narrows the possibilities) and paragraph E (i.e. the cost of building a key on one feature).
Summarize how a field guide is organized and why.
questions.a: Because a reader does not know the name, a guide groups by observable features such as leaf shape or silhouette, and many add a key of paired choices that each remove about half the possibilities. The cost is that every choice must be answerable from the specimen in hand, so good guides offer a winter route as well as a summer one.

questions.q:
key: a chain of paired either-or choices that leads a reader to an identification.
specimen: the individual plant, animal or rock a person actually has in front of them.
Describe the connection between each choice removing half the possibilities and the number of steps a key needs.
questions.a: Because each step removes roughly half the possibilities, a set of six or seven choices can separate one species out of a hundred.

articles.note: The last paragraph is the RI.7.5 move, i.e. "the order of the pages is a claim." Have students write the first two couplets of a key for the shoes in the room.

articles.title: The Shape of a Court Opinion
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A written court opinion is not organized like an argument someone would make out loud. It has fixed parts in a fixed order, and knowing the order tells a reader what each passage is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It usually opens with the facts, told flatly. Who did what, when, and what the lower courts decided. This section is meant to be uncontroversial, and where the parties disagree about a fact the opinion says so.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then comes the question presented, narrowed as far as the court can narrow it. A case about a search is not decided as a case about privacy in general, and the narrowing is deliberate.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The holding is the answer to that question, and it is the part that binds other courts. It is often a single sentence, and it is often shorter than readers expect.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reasoning follows, and it is the longest part. It walks through earlier decisions, statutes and the consequences of ruling each way, and it has to explain why the earlier cases point where the court says they point.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A dissent is printed after. Its author lost, so the dissent binds nobody, and its purpose is to mark exactly where the disagreement lies rather than to restate the whole dispute.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading the parts in order prevents a common error. A sentence quoted from the reasoning, or worse from the dissent, is often repeated as though it were the holding, which is the one part that actually decided anything.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A court opinion is not built like a spoken argument. It has fixed parts in a fixed order. Knowing that order tells a reader what each passage is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It usually opens with the facts, told flatly. Who did what, and when. What the lower courts decided. This part aims to be uncontroversial. If the parties disagree, the opinion says so.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next comes the question presented. The court narrows it as far as it can. A case about a search is not decided as a case about privacy in general. The narrowing is on purpose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The holding answers that question. It is the part that binds other courts. It is often one sentence. It is often shorter than readers expect.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reasoning follows. It is the longest part. It walks through earlier cases, statutes and consequences. It must show why those cases point where the court says.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A dissent is printed after. Its author lost. A dissent binds nobody. Its job is to mark where the disagreement lies, not to restate the whole dispute.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading the parts in order stops a common error. People quote the reasoning, or the dissent, as if it were the holding. The holding is the part that decided anything.

questions.q: Which part of an opinion binds other courts?
questions.a: The holding, which is the answer to the question presented, and it is often a single sentence and shorter than readers expect.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the narrowing of the question) and paragraph F (i.e. what a dissent is for).
Summarize the parts of a court opinion and what each is for.
questions.a: An opinion gives the facts flatly, then narrows the question presented, then states the holding, which is the part that binds other courts. The reasoning that follows is the longest part and explains why earlier cases point where the court says, and a dissent printed after binds nobody and marks where the disagreement lies.

questions.q:
holding: the court's answer to the question it took the case to decide, and the part that binds other courts.
dissent: an opinion by a judge who disagreed with the decision, which does not bind anyone.
Describe the connection between not knowing the parts and misreading a quotation.
questions.a: A sentence quoted from the reasoning, or from the dissent, is often repeated as though it were the holding, which is the one part that actually decided anything.

articles.note: Hand out one short opinion with the headings removed and have students label the five parts. The dissent is usually the one they mislabel.

articles.title: The Order of a Checklist
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In October 1935 the United States Army Air Corps watched a new Boeing bomber take off at Wright Field, climb, stall and crash. Two of the crew died, including the pilot, who was among the most experienced in the service.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The aircraft was sound. A gust lock, which holds the control surfaces still on the ground, had been left engaged, and the pilot had simply not got to it among everything else the new machine required.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The conclusion at the time was that the design was too much aeroplane for one man to fly. The response was not to simplify the aeroplane. It was to write down the steps.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A checklist is not a set of instructions, and the difference matters. Instructions teach somebody who does not know how; a checklist catches somebody who knows perfectly well and is going to miss one item anyway.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So its structure is unusual. Items are short, they are stated as actions with a confirming response, and there are few of them, because a list long enough to be thorough is long enough to be skipped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order is not arbitrary either. Items are grouped by pause points in the task, such as before starting engines or before takeoff, so the list is read at a moment when stopping costs nothing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The same form has since been taken into operating theatres and construction. What travelled was not the aviation content but the structure, which is the part that does the work.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In October 1935 the Army Air Corps watched a new Boeing bomber take off at Wright Field. It climbed, stalled and crashed. Two crew died, including a very experienced pilot.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The aircraft was sound. A gust lock holds the control surfaces still on the ground. It had been left on. The pilot had not got to it among everything else the new machine needed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: People concluded the design was too much aeroplane for one man to fly. The response was not to simplify the aeroplane. It was to write down the steps.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A checklist is not a set of instructions. The difference matters. Instructions teach someone who does not know how. A checklist catches someone who knows and will still miss an item.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So its structure is unusual. Items are short. Each is an action with a spoken response. There are few of them. A list long enough to be thorough is long enough to be skipped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order is not random either. Items are grouped at pause points, such as before starting engines or before takeoff. The list is read when stopping costs nothing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The same form later moved into operating theatres and building sites. What travelled was not the flying content. It was the structure, which is the part that works.

questions.q: What is the difference between instructions and a checklist?
questions.a: Instructions teach somebody who does not know how, while a checklist catches somebody who knows perfectly well and is going to miss one item anyway.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the items are short and few) and paragraph F (i.e. why they are grouped at pause points).
Summarize why checklists were invented and how their structure follows from that.
questions.a: After a Boeing bomber crashed in 1935 because a gust lock was left engaged, the response was not to simplify the aircraft but to write down the steps. A checklist catches someone who already knows what to do, so its items are short, stated as actions with a confirming response, few enough not to be skipped, and grouped at pause points where stopping costs nothing.

questions.q:
gust lock: a device holding an aircraft's control surfaces still on the ground, which must be released before flight.
pause point: a moment in a task where stopping to check costs nothing, used to position items on a list.
Describe the connection between a list being long and a list being skipped.
questions.a: A list long enough to be thorough is long enough to be skipped, which is why the items are short and there are few of them.

articles.note: Paragraph G is the transfer, i.e. "what travelled was not the aviation content but the structure." Ask students to write a six-item checklist for leaving the classroom and defend the order.

articles.title: Why a Treaty Has a Preamble
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.3 interactions · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A treaty opens with a passage that promises nothing. It names the parties, recalls earlier agreements and states what the signatories are trying to achieve, in sentences that often begin with desiring or recognising.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Readers skip it, reasonably enough, because the obligations are further down. The articles that follow are numbered, and each one states something a party must do, must not do, or may do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The preamble still does work, and the work shows up later. When two governments disagree about what an article means, the stated purpose becomes part of how the article is read.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is not an informal custom. The international rules on interpreting treaties direct an interpreter to read a term in its context, and they define that context to include the preamble.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Which is why the preamble is argued over in negotiation. A word there costs nothing today and may decide a dispute in twenty years, so delegations fight about language that appears to bind nobody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The structure also separates the kinds of commitment. Aspiration goes at the top where it cannot be enforced, and obligation goes into numbered articles where it can, and a reader can tell which is which by location alone.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Treating the preamble as decoration therefore misreads the document. It is the part that says what the rest is for, placed where a lawyer can reach it when the text alone runs out.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A treaty opens with a passage that promises nothing. It names the parties. It recalls earlier agreements. It states what the signatories want. Sentences often begin with desiring or recognising.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Readers skip it. That is fair, because the duties come later. The articles that follow are numbered. Each states what a party must do, must not do, or may do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The preamble still does work. The work appears later. When two governments disagree about an article, the stated purpose becomes part of how it is read.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is not a loose custom. The international rules on reading treaties say a term must be read in its context. They define that context to include the preamble.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the preamble is argued over in talks. A word there costs nothing today. It may settle a dispute in twenty years. Delegations fight over language that seems to bind nobody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The structure also sorts the kinds of promise. Aspiration sits at the top, where it cannot be enforced. Obligation sits in numbered articles, where it can. Location tells you which is which.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So treating the preamble as decoration misreads the document. It says what the rest is for. It sits where a lawyer can reach it when the text runs out.

questions.q: When does a preamble actually get used?
questions.a: When two governments disagree about what an article means, the stated purpose becomes part of how the article is read.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why delegations argue over the preamble) and paragraph F (i.e. how location separates aspiration from obligation).
Summarize what a preamble is for and why it is not decoration.
questions.a: A preamble names the parties and states what they are trying to achieve without creating obligations, which sit in the numbered articles. Because the rules on interpreting treaties define context to include the preamble, its wording is argued over in negotiation, and the structure lets a reader tell aspiration from obligation by location alone.

questions.q:
preamble: the opening passage of a treaty, stating purpose rather than obligation.
aspiration: something the parties hope for, as opposed to something they are bound to do.
Describe the connection between where a sentence sits in a treaty and whether it can be enforced.
questions.a: Aspiration goes at the top where it cannot be enforced and obligation goes into numbered articles where it can, so a reader can tell which is which by location alone.

articles.note: The structural claim is that position carries legal weight. Compare the preamble and article one of any treaty and ask which sentences could be broken.

articles.title: Who Paid for the Study
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the end of a research paper there is usually a short paragraph nobody reads. It says who funded the work and whether any author has a financial interest in the result.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paragraph exists because funding is known to shift findings. Across many fields, studies paid for by an industry reach conclusions favourable to that industry more often than independently funded studies of the same question.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is rarely fraud. A funder influences which questions get asked, which comparison a new product is tested against, how long a trial runs and whether a study that came out badly is published at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A reader who treats the disclosure as a verdict gets it wrong in the other direction. Industry funds a great deal of genuine research, and a study is not refuted by who paid for it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What the disclosure does is tell a reader where to look harder. It is a reason to check the comparison group, the length of the trial and whether the measure reported is the one the study originally set out to measure.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Good authors go further and say so themselves. A paper may state that a funder had no role in the design or in the decision to publish, which is a claim the authors are putting their names behind.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the paragraph is not an accusation and not a clearance. It is information about the position the work was written from, offered so that a reader can weigh it rather than guess at it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the end of a research paper there is a short paragraph nobody reads. It says who funded the work. It says whether any author gains financially from the result.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paragraph exists because funding shifts findings. In many fields, studies paid for by an industry favour that industry more often than independent studies of the same question.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is rarely fraud. A funder shapes which questions are asked. It shapes what a product is compared against, how long a trial runs, and whether a bad result is published.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A reader who treats the disclosure as a verdict goes wrong the other way. Industry funds much real research. A study is not refuted by who paid for it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What the disclosure does is show where to look harder. Check the comparison group. Check the length of the trial. Check whether the measure reported is the one they set out to measure.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Good authors say more. A paper may state that the funder had no role in the design or in the choice to publish. The authors put their names behind that claim.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the paragraph is not an accusation. It is not a clearance either. It is information about where the work was written from. A reader can weigh it instead of guessing.

questions.q: How does a funder usually influence a result, according to the article?
questions.a: Rarely by fraud, but by influencing which questions get asked, which comparison a product is tested against, how long a trial runs and whether a study that came out badly is published at all.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why a disclosure is not a verdict) and paragraph E (i.e. what a reader should check instead).
Summarize what a funding disclosure tells a reader.
questions.a: It says who paid for the work and whether an author gains from the result, and it exists because industry-funded studies more often favour that industry. It is not a refutation, because industry funds genuine research, so what it offers is a reason to check the comparison group, the length of the trial and whether the reported measure is the original one.

questions.q:
disclosure: a statement revealing an interest that a reader would want to know about.
comparison group: what a new treatment is tested against, which a funder may influence.
Describe the connection between knowing who funded a study and knowing where to look harder.
questions.a: Because a funder influences the comparison, the length of the trial and whether a bad result is published, the disclosure tells a reader to check those things rather than to accept or reject the study.

articles.note: RI.7.6 asks how an author marks their own position against others. Paragraph F is that move in miniature, i.e. the authors stating the funder had no role.

articles.title: The Plaque That Was Replaced
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A monument usually carries a small plaque, and the plaque is a piece of writing with an author, a date and a purpose, even though it rarely names any of the three.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A plaque written in 1910 and a plaque written in 2010 about the same event will differ in more than tone. They differ in what they treat as needing explanation and in who the sentences assume is reading.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An older text often uses the passive voice and words such as settled or pacified. A newer one more often names the parties, gives numbers, and states who died, which is a choice about what counts as the event.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Where a plaque has been replaced, some sites keep the old one mounted beside the new. The pairing lets a visitor compare, and it also makes the first plaque into an exhibit rather than a statement.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Replacement is argued about, and the arguments are not only about history. One side says a text that misdescribes an event should be corrected like any other error. The other says removing it hides that the misdescription was once official.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A careful new plaque does something that answers both. It states the event, and then it states what the earlier plaque said and when, which distinguishes the position it is taking from the position it replaced.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the move worth noticing. Any writer can assert. Marking where your account differs from an earlier one, and saying so on the same panel, is a harder and more useful thing to do.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A monument usually carries a small plaque. The plaque is a piece of writing. It has an author, a date and a purpose. It rarely names any of the three.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A plaque from 1910 and one from 2010 about the same event differ in more than tone. They differ in what needs explaining. They differ in who the sentences assume is reading.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An older text often uses the passive voice. It uses words like settled or pacified. A newer one names the parties, gives numbers and says who died. That is a choice about what counts as the event.

paras.label: D
paras.text: At some sites the old plaque stays mounted beside the new one. A visitor can compare them. The pairing also turns the first plaque into an exhibit rather than a statement.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Replacement is argued about. The arguments are not only about history. One side says a wrong text should be corrected. The other says removing it hides that the wrong text was once official.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A careful new plaque answers both. It states the event. Then it says what the earlier plaque said, and when. That marks the difference between the two positions.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the move worth noticing. Anyone can assert. Saying where your account differs from an earlier one, on the same panel, is harder and more useful.

questions.q: How do older and newer plaques about the same event tend to differ?
questions.a: An older text often uses the passive voice and words such as settled or pacified, while a newer one more often names the parties, gives numbers and states who died.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the argument about replacing a plaque) and paragraph F (i.e. what a careful new plaque does).
Summarize the argument about replacing a plaque and how a new one can answer it.
questions.a: A plaque is writing with an author and a purpose, and an older one often uses the passive voice while a newer one names parties and gives numbers. One side says a text that misdescribes an event should be corrected and the other says removing it hides that it was once official, and a careful new plaque states the event and then states what the earlier plaque said and when.

questions.q:
plaque: a mounted panel of text at a site, which carries an author and a date even when it names neither.
exhibit: something displayed to be examined, rather than a statement a visitor is asked to accept.
Describe the connection between keeping the old plaque and what a visitor can do.
questions.a: The pairing lets a visitor compare the two texts, and it makes the first plaque into an exhibit rather than a statement.

articles.note: This is RI.7.6 about a text of forty words. Bring two plaque texts for the same event and have students mark every verb.

articles.title: The Choices in a Nature Film
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A nature documentary presents itself as a window. The camera appears simply to have been there, and the animals appear to be doing what they would have done anyway.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Much of that is true, and the patience behind it is real. A sequence of a few minutes can rest on months in a hide, and the behaviour on screen is behaviour that happened.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sound is a different matter. Microphones cannot usually record a small animal at a distance over wind, so footsteps, wingbeats and rustling are commonly created afterwards in a studio and matched to the picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The score does more than fill silence. Music tells a viewer whether a hunt is a tragedy or a triumph, and the same footage of the same hunt can be cut to make either, without a single frame changing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Narration carries a position too. Calling an animal a mother rather than a female, or saying it is determined rather than that it continued, invites a viewer to read intention into behaviour nobody can ask about.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of this is deception by itself. A film has to choose a sound, a score and a sentence, and refusing to choose is not available; silence and a flat voice are choices as well.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What a viewer can do is notice the choosing. Watching a sequence once with the sound off is usually enough, because the story the pictures tell alone is frequently a looser and less certain one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A nature documentary looks like a window. The camera seems simply to have been there. The animals seem to be doing what they would have done anyway.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Much of that is true. The patience behind it is real. A few minutes of film can rest on months in a hide. The behaviour on screen did happen.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sound is different. A microphone usually cannot record a small animal at a distance over wind. So footsteps, wingbeats and rustling are often made later in a studio.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The music does more than fill silence. It tells a viewer whether a hunt is a tragedy or a triumph. The same footage can be cut either way. Not one frame has to change.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Narration carries a position too. Call an animal a mother, not a female. Say it is determined, not that it continued. That invites viewers to read intention into behaviour.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of this is deception by itself. A film must choose a sound, a score and a sentence. Refusing to choose is not possible. Silence and a flat voice are choices too.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A viewer can notice the choosing. Watch a sequence once with the sound off. The story the pictures tell alone is usually looser and less certain.

questions.q: Why is the sound in a nature film usually made in a studio?
questions.a: Microphones cannot usually record a small animal at a distance over wind, so footsteps, wingbeats and rustling are created afterwards and matched to the picture.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what the music decides) and paragraph F (i.e. why choosing is unavoidable).
Summarize the choices a nature film makes and why noticing them matters.
questions.a: The behaviour filmed is real and takes months to capture, but the sound is usually created in a studio, the music decides whether a hunt reads as tragedy or triumph, and the narration can invite viewers to read intention into behaviour. None of this is deception because refusing to choose is not available, so a viewer can watch a sequence with the sound off and see a looser story.

questions.q:
score: the music written or chosen for a film, which shapes how a scene is read.
hide: a concealed structure a camera operator waits in, sometimes for months.
Describe the connection between the narration's word choice and what a viewer concludes.
questions.a: Calling an animal a mother rather than a female, or saying it is determined rather than that it continued, invites a viewer to read intention into behaviour nobody can ask about.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the fair-minded turn, i.e. "refusing to choose is not available." Students who conclude that documentaries lie have missed it.

articles.title: The Editorial and the News Story
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A newspaper prints two kinds of writing about the same events and signals the difference in ways a hurried reader can miss. One kind reports. The other argues, and is supposed to say so.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A news story is built to be checkable. Claims are attributed, the people criticised are offered a reply, and the reporter's own view is meant not to appear in the sentences at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An editorial drops all three constraints on purpose. It takes a position, it is unsigned because it speaks for the paper rather than a person, and it is placed on a page set aside for that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The signals are physical as well. A different column width, a standing label, a box, sometimes a different typeface, all of which say to a reader that the rules just changed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Online, almost all of that disappears. A link shared in a message arrives without the page, without the column width and often without the label, and both kinds of writing look identical on a phone.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the work falls to the reader, and there are quick tests. Are claims attributed to someone who could be asked? Does anyone disagreeing get quoted? Is the writer named, and does the piece recommend something?

paras.label: G
paras.text: An editorial is not a lesser thing than a report. A paper arguing openly for a position, over its own name, is doing something honest. The difficulty is only that the frame around it has been stripped off.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A newspaper prints two kinds of writing about the same events. It signals the difference in ways a hurried reader misses. One kind reports. The other argues, and should say so.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A news story is built to be checked. Claims are attributed. People who are criticised get a chance to reply. The reporter's own view should not appear.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An editorial drops all three on purpose. It takes a position. It is unsigned, because it speaks for the paper, not a person. It sits on a page kept for that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The signals are physical too. A different column width. A standing label. A box. Sometimes a different typeface. All of it tells a reader the rules just changed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Online almost all of that is gone. A shared link arrives without the page, the column width, and often the label. Both kinds look the same on a phone.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the work falls to the reader. There are quick tests. Are claims attributed to someone who could be asked? Is anyone who disagrees quoted? Is the writer named? Does the piece recommend something?

paras.label: G
paras.text: An editorial is not a lesser thing. A paper arguing openly, over its own name, is being honest. The trouble is that the frame around it has been stripped off.

questions.q: What three constraints does an editorial drop on purpose?
questions.a: It takes a position rather than keeping the writer's view out, it is unsigned because it speaks for the paper, and it does not have to offer a reply to the people it criticises.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the physical signals on a printed page) and paragraph E (i.e. what happens to those signals online).
Summarize the difference between a news story and an editorial and why it is harder to see online.
questions.a: A news story attributes claims, offers a reply to those criticised and keeps the reporter's view out, while an editorial takes a position, is unsigned and sits on its own page. Print marks the difference with column width, labels and typeface, and a link shared on a phone arrives without any of that, so a reader has to test for attribution, quoted disagreement and a recommendation.

questions.q:
attribute: to say who a claim comes from, so a reader could go and ask them.
editorial: an unsigned piece arguing a position on behalf of the publication rather than a person.
Describe the connection between losing the page and losing the signal.
questions.a: A link shared in a message arrives without the page, the column width and often the label, so both kinds of writing look identical and the reader has to test the piece instead.

articles.note: The four tests in paragraph F are the takeaway. Run them on one shared link in class and see which of the four it fails.

articles.title: The Paragraph Where an Author Admits the Limits
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Near the end of a research paper there is usually a section headed limitations. It is written by the authors, about their own work, and it lists the reasons their conclusion might be wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That is an unusual thing for any writer to do. Most writing argues for its claim and leaves the weaknesses for an opponent to find, and a section volunteering them looks at first like a tactical error.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is not. A paper that names its weaknesses is telling a reader where its claim stops, and a claim with a stated edge is more useful than one that appears to apply everywhere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The section also marks the author's position against other work. Saying that a sample was drawn from one city distinguishes this paper from one claiming a national result, without having to criticise the other paper directly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader can judge the section itself. A good one names limits that actually threaten the conclusion. A weak one lists things that sound humble and change nothing, such as calling for further research.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The absence of such a section is informative too. Press releases and advertisements never include one, and that is the clearest difference between a document reporting a result and a document selling it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the paragraph most readers skip is the one that shows most about how a text was written. It is where an author draws a line around their own claim rather than waiting for somebody else to draw it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Near the end of a research paper there is often a section headed limitations. The authors write it about their own work. It lists reasons their conclusion might be wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That is an odd thing for a writer to do. Most writing argues for its claim. It leaves the weak points for an opponent to find. Volunteering them looks like a mistake.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is not. A paper that names its weak points tells a reader where its claim stops. A claim with a stated edge is more useful than one that seems to apply everywhere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The section also marks the author's position against other work. Saying a sample came from one city sets this paper apart from one claiming a national result. No direct criticism is needed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader can judge the section itself. A good one names limits that really threaten the conclusion. A weak one lists humble-sounding things that change nothing, like calling for more research.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The absence of such a section says something too. Press releases and advertisements never have one. That is the clearest difference between reporting a result and selling it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the paragraph most readers skip shows the most about how a text was written. The author draws a line around their own claim instead of waiting for someone else to draw it.

questions.q: Why is naming a weakness not a tactical error?
questions.a: A paper that names its weaknesses is telling a reader where its claim stops, and a claim with a stated edge is more useful than one that appears to apply everywhere.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how to judge the section itself) and paragraph F (i.e. what it means when there is no such section).
Summarize what a limitations section does.
questions.a: It is written by the authors about their own work and lists why the conclusion might be wrong, which tells a reader where the claim stops and distinguishes the paper from work making a broader claim. A good one names limits that threaten the conclusion, and press releases and advertisements never include one at all.

questions.q:
limitations: the section in which authors state the reasons their own conclusion might not hold.
sample: the particular group actually studied, which may not represent everyone the claim could be applied to.
Describe the connection between having no limitations section and what a document is for.
questions.a: Press releases and advertisements never include one, which is the clearest difference between a document reporting a result and a document selling it.

articles.note: Pair this with a press release about the same finding. The comparison in paragraph F does the teaching by itself.

articles.title: The Speech on the Page and in the Air
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject, for example how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.9 comparing accounts · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A speech exists twice. There is a text, which can be read in silence at any speed, and there is a delivery, which happened once, at a particular pace, in a particular room, in front of people who answered back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The text is the version that gets quoted and taught. It can be searched, marked up and compared, and every reader of it receives exactly the same words in exactly the same order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The recording carries what the page cannot hold. Pace, volume, the length of a pause, a voice that tightens or steadies, and the sound of an audience responding, which changes what the next sentence has to do.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Sometimes the two versions are not even the same words. Speakers cut, repeat and add, and the most remembered passage of a speech is occasionally one that was not in the prepared text at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Martin Luther King's address in Washington in 1963 is the familiar example. The closing section that nearly everyone can name was not in the typed draft, and the recording is the only evidence of how it arrived.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This matters for how a claim gets studied. A historian comparing a draft, a delivered recording and a newspaper transcript of the same speech has three documents, and they will not agree.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Neither version is the real one. The text is what was planned and the recording is what happened, and a reader who has only met one of them has met half of the event.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A speech exists twice. There is a text. It can be read in silence at any speed. There is a delivery. It happened once, at one pace, in one room, before people who answered back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The text is the version that gets quoted and taught. It can be searched, marked and compared. Every reader gets the same words in the same order.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The recording holds what a page cannot. Pace. Volume. The length of a pause. A voice that tightens or steadies. An audience responding, which changes what the next sentence must do.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Martin Luther King's 1963 address in Washington is the familiar case. The closing section almost everyone can name was not in the typed draft. The recording is the only evidence of how it arrived.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This matters for study. A historian may hold a draft, a recording and a newspaper transcript of one speech. That is three documents. They will not agree.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Neither version is the real one. The text is what was planned. The recording is what happened. A reader who knows only one has met half the event.

questions.q: What does a recording carry that a text cannot?
questions.a: Pace, volume, the length of a pause, a voice that tightens or steadies, and the sound of an audience responding, which changes what the next sentence has to do.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the closing section that was not in the draft) and paragraph F (i.e. the three documents a historian ends up with).
Summarize why a speech has to be studied in more than one form.
questions.a: A text can be read at any speed and gives every reader the same words, while a recording carries pace, pauses and the audience's response. The two are sometimes not even the same words, because speakers cut and add, so a draft, a recording and a transcript are three documents that will not agree.

questions.q:
delivery: the performance of a speech, including pace, volume and pause, as distinct from its words.
transcript: a written record of what was said, which may differ from both the draft and the recording.
Describe the connection between an audience responding and what the speaker does next.
questions.a: The sound of an audience responding changes what the next sentence has to do, which is part of why a delivery differs from a prepared text.

articles.note: RI.7.7 is best taught by doing it. Read a passage aloud flat, then play the recording, and ask what changed when nothing in the words did.

articles.title: Three Ways to Look at a Heart
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject, for example how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.9 comparing accounts · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A doctor listening through a stethoscope is reading a heart by sound. Valves closing make the two familiar beats, and a sound that does not belong, such as a murmur, suggests blood moving where it should not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound is immediate and cheap, and it is also crude. It tells a listener that something is irregular long before it tells them what, and two different problems can produce a similar noise.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An electrocardiogram records something else entirely. It is not sound but electrical activity, drawn as a line, and it shows the timing and the sequence of the signal that makes the muscle contract.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That makes it excellent for rhythm and nearly blind to structure. A trace can show that the signal is arriving in the wrong order while saying nothing about whether a valve is thickened.

paras.label: E
paras.text: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to build a moving picture. It shows the chambers filling and emptying and the valves opening, which is the structural question the first two instruments cannot answer.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Each instrument is a different medium reporting on the same organ, and each is strongest exactly where the others are weak. A clinician choosing between them is choosing what kind of question to ask.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The same holds outside medicine. A table, a photograph and a recording of one event are not three copies of it, and deciding which to trust means first deciding what you are trying to find out.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A doctor with a stethoscope reads a heart by sound. Closing valves make the two familiar beats. A sound that does not belong, like a murmur, suggests blood moving where it should not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound is immediate and cheap. It is also crude. It says something is wrong long before it says what. Two different problems can make a similar noise.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An electrocardiogram records something else. It is not sound. It records electrical activity and draws it as a line. It shows the timing of the signal that makes the muscle contract.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So it is excellent for rhythm and almost blind to structure. A trace can show a signal arriving in the wrong order. It says nothing about a thickened valve.

paras.label: E
paras.text: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to build a moving picture. It shows the chambers filling and emptying. It shows the valves opening. That is the question the other two cannot answer.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Each instrument is a different medium reporting on one organ. Each is strongest where the others are weak. A clinician choosing between them is choosing what to ask.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The same is true outside medicine. A table, a photograph and a recording of one event are not three copies. Choosing what to trust means deciding what you want to find out.

questions.q: Why is an electrocardiogram nearly blind to structure?
questions.a: It records electrical activity drawn as a line, so it shows the timing and sequence of the signal while saying nothing about whether a valve is thickened.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the limits of listening) and paragraph E (i.e. what ultrasound adds).
Summarize the three ways of examining a heart and what each one is for.
questions.a: A stethoscope reads the heart by sound, which is immediate and cheap but crude. An electrocardiogram records electrical activity as a line, which is excellent for rhythm and blind to structure. An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to show the chambers and valves moving, so each medium is strongest where the others are weak.

questions.q:
murmur: a sound in the heartbeat that does not belong, suggesting blood is moving where it should not.
ultrasound: sound too high to hear, used to build a moving picture of structures inside the body.
Describe the connection between choosing an instrument and choosing a question.
questions.a: Each instrument is strongest exactly where the others are weak, so a clinician choosing between them is choosing what kind of question to ask.

articles.note: The last paragraph generalises the standard, i.e. a table, a photograph and a recording are not three copies. Ask what question each of those three is best at.

articles.title: The Night the Radio Play Aired
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject, for example how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.9 comparing accounts · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: On the evening of October 30, 1938, a radio drama adapted H. G. Wells's novel about a Martian invasion. The company broadcast it as a series of news bulletins interrupting a music programme.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form was the point. A listener tuning in late heard what sounded like an announcer breaking into a dance band with reports from New Jersey, and the dramatic structure borrowed the authority of a medium people trusted.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The next morning's newspapers described a nation in panic. Headlines reported crowds in the streets, people fleeing cities and switchboards overwhelmed, and that account entered textbooks and stayed there.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Later research questioned nearly all of it. The programme had a small audience that night, surveys taken immediately afterwards found few listeners who believed an invasion was underway, and the widespread flight is poorly evidenced.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There are also reasons why newspapers would tell it that way. Radio was taking advertising revenue from print, and a story about a reckless new medium frightening the public served the older one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So there are three things to compare: a novel, a broadcast that changed the novel's form without changing its plot, and a press account of the broadcast that may say more about newspapers than about listeners.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The lesson is not that nobody was alarmed, because some people clearly were. It is that the size of a reaction is a claim like any other, and it needs evidence that is not simply another headline.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On the evening of October 30, 1938, a radio drama used H. G. Wells's novel about a Martian invasion. The company broadcast it as news bulletins interrupting a music programme.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form was the point. A listener tuning in late heard an announcer breaking into a dance band with reports from New Jersey. The drama borrowed the authority of a trusted medium.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next morning the newspapers described a nation in panic. Headlines told of crowds in the streets, people fleeing and switchboards jammed. That account went into textbooks and stayed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Later research questioned nearly all of it. The audience that night was small. Surveys taken soon after found few listeners who believed it. The mass flight is poorly evidenced.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There are reasons newspapers would tell it that way. Radio was taking advertising from print. A story about a reckless new medium frightening people served the older one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So there are three things to compare. A novel. A broadcast that changed its form but not its plot. A press account that may say more about newspapers than about listeners.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The lesson is not that nobody was alarmed. Some clearly were. It is that the size of a reaction is a claim. It needs evidence that is not just another headline.

questions.q: How did the broadcast change the novel without changing its plot?
questions.a: It was presented as a series of news bulletins interrupting a music programme, so the drama borrowed the authority of a medium people trusted.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what later research found) and paragraph E (i.e. why newspapers had a reason to tell it that way).
Summarize the three versions this article asks a reader to compare.
questions.a: There is the novel, the broadcast that retold it as news bulletins interrupting a music programme, and the newspaper account of a nation in panic. Later research found a small audience and few listeners who believed it, and newspapers were losing advertising to radio, so the press account may describe newspapers more than listeners.

questions.q:
bulletin: a short news announcement interrupting other programming, which is the form the drama borrowed.
survey: a set of questions put to a sample of people, used here to test what listeners actually believed.
Describe the connection between radio taking advertising from print and the way the story was reported.
questions.a: Radio was taking advertising revenue from print, so a story about a reckless new medium frightening the public served the older one.

articles.note: Three media and a contested claim about one of them. The final sentence is the standard in a line, i.e. "the size of a reaction is a claim like any other."

articles.title: A Bird Call in Three Forms
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject, for example how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.9 comparing accounts · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Older field guides describe a bird's song in words. A phrase such as a clear whistled three-note call, falling at the end, is a sentence doing a job that sentences are not well suited to.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some guides use mnemonics instead, inventing English words that sound like the song. These are memorable and they are also a trap, because once a listener has learned one, the bird begins to sound like the phrase.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A recording solves the obvious problem and creates a new one. It is exact, but it is gone as soon as it is played, and a listener cannot hold the beginning of a song beside the end of it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A spectrogram is the third form. Time runs across the page, pitch runs up it, and the energy of the sound is drawn as marks, so a song that lasts two seconds becomes a shape that can be examined for as long as you like.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The shape shows things the ear struggles with. Two songs that sound alike can have clearly different slopes, and a note too fast to count by ear appears as four separate marks on the page.

paras.label: F
paras.text: No form is complete. The description is portable, the recording is faithful, the spectrogram is analysable, and birders in practice use all three in the same morning.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is why modern guides print spectrograms beside the text and link to recordings. The guide is not offering the same information three times; it is offering three things that each survive a different kind of use.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Older field guides describe a bird's song in words. A clear whistled three-note call, falling at the end. That is a sentence doing a job sentences are bad at.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some guides use mnemonics. They invent English words that sound like the song. These are memorable. They are also a trap. Once you learn one, the bird starts to sound like the phrase.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A recording solves the obvious problem and makes a new one. It is exact. But it is gone once played. A listener cannot hold the start of a song beside its end.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A spectrogram is the third form. Time runs across the page. Pitch runs up it. The sound is drawn as marks. A two-second song becomes a shape you can study for as long as you like.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The shape shows what the ear struggles with. Two songs that sound alike can have clearly different slopes. A note too fast to count appears as four separate marks.

paras.label: F
paras.text: No form is complete. The description travels. The recording is faithful. The spectrogram can be analysed. Birders use all three in one morning.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So modern guides print spectrograms beside the text and link to recordings. They are not giving the same thing three times. They are giving three things that survive different uses.

questions.q: What does a spectrogram let a person do that listening does not?
questions.a: Time runs across the page and pitch up it, so a song that lasts two seconds becomes a shape that can be examined for as long as you like.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. why a mnemonic is a trap) and paragraph E (i.e. what the shape shows that the ear misses).
Summarize the three ways a bird's song can be presented and what each is good for.
questions.a: A written description is portable but words are poor at carrying sound, a mnemonic is memorable but makes the bird sound like the phrase, a recording is exact but gone once played, and a spectrogram draws time against pitch so the song can be examined. Guides print all of them because each survives a different kind of use.

questions.q:
spectrogram: a drawing of sound with time across the page and pitch up it.
mnemonic: an invented phrase that sounds like a song, used as a memory aid.
Describe the connection between a recording being exact and a recording being hard to study.
questions.a: It is exact, but it is gone as soon as it is played, so a listener cannot hold the beginning of a song beside the end of it.

articles.note: Play one call, then show its spectrogram, then read the written description. Ask which one they would want in a pocket and which one at a desk.

articles.title: When a Trial Is Televised
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject, for example how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.9 comparing accounts · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A court produces a written record of everything said in it. A transcript is complete, in order, and dull, and for most of history it was the only way the public could learn what happened in a room they were not in.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cameras change the available evidence. A viewer sees hesitation, posture and whether a witness looked at the person they were accusing, none of which the transcript records and some of which jurors are told to weigh.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is the argument in favour. Proceedings are supposed to be public, a transcript is public only to people who will read two hundred pages, and a broadcast is public in a way an ordinary person can actually use.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument against is that a camera is not a window. Coverage is edited, the minute selected for a news bulletin is chosen because something happened in it, and hours of procedure are what a trial mostly is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is also an effect on the room. Lawyers, witnesses and judges who know they are being recorded behave differently, and a system that depends on candid testimony has reason to worry about that.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Different courts have settled this differently. Some allow cameras, some allow audio only, some allow sketch artists and nothing else, and each rule is a judgement about which record does least damage.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A student comparing a clip with the transcript of the same hour is doing the whole exercise. The question is not which is accurate, because both are, but what each medium selects and what it leaves out.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A court writes down everything said in it. A transcript is complete, in order, and dull. For most of history it was the only way the public learned what happened.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Cameras change the evidence available. A viewer sees hesitation and posture. A viewer sees whether a witness looked at the accused. The transcript records none of that.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is the argument in favour. Proceedings are meant to be public. A transcript is public only to people who will read two hundred pages. A broadcast is public in a usable way.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument against is that a camera is not a window. Coverage is edited. The minute chosen for a bulletin is chosen because something happened. A trial is mostly hours of procedure.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is also an effect on the room. Lawyers, witnesses and judges behave differently when recorded. A system that needs candid testimony has reason to worry.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Courts have settled this differently. Some allow cameras. Some allow audio only. Some allow sketch artists and nothing more. Each rule judges which record does least harm.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A student comparing a clip with the transcript of the same hour is doing the whole exercise. The question is not which is accurate. Both are. It is what each one selects and leaves out.

questions.q: What can a viewer see that a transcript does not record?
questions.a: Hesitation, posture and whether a witness looked at the person they were accusing, some of which jurors are told to weigh.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the argument for cameras) and paragraph D (i.e. the argument that a camera is not a window).
Summarize the argument about televising trials.
questions.a: A transcript is complete but only public to people who will read it, while a broadcast shows hesitation and posture and is public in a usable way. Against that, coverage is edited and selects the minute where something happened, and people in the room behave differently when recorded, so courts have settled on different rules.

questions.q:
transcript: the complete written record of what was said in a proceeding.
candid: honest and unguarded, which is what testimony is supposed to be and what recording may affect.
Describe the connection between editing and what a viewer concludes about a trial.
questions.a: The minute selected for a news bulletin is chosen because something happened in it, while hours of procedure are what a trial mostly is.

articles.note: The closing sentence resets the question from accurate to selective, which is the RI.7.7 habit worth building.

articles.title: The Argument for a Later School Start
articles.standard_text:
