Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The case for starting secondary school later runs like this. Adolescent sleep timing shifts later for biological reasons, a start before eight o'clock cuts sleep rather than moving it, and short sleep damages learning, mood and safety.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first claim is the strongest. The shift in timing at puberty has been measured in laboratories and across many countries, and it is not explained away by phones or by homework.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second follows reasonably. If the body clock has moved and the alarm has not, the hours are taken off the front of the night, and surveys of teenagers consistently show exactly that pattern.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third claim is where the evidence gets mixed. Studies of districts that moved their start times report gains in attendance and in reported sleep, and the findings on grades are smaller and less consistent.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One result is often quoted on its own: a fall in teenage car crashes after a district moved its start. That study is real, but a single district over a few years is a thin base for a general claim.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a cost side the argument sometimes skips. Bus schedules, after-school work, sport and the care of younger siblings all move with the bell, and those effects fall unevenly across families.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The argument is therefore strong at its foundation and weaker at its edges. A reader who accepts the biology is not thereby obliged to accept every number attached to it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The case for a later school start runs like this. Teenage sleep timing shifts later for biological reasons. A start before eight cuts sleep rather than moving it. Short sleep harms learning, mood and safety.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first claim is the strongest. The shift at puberty has been measured in labs and in many countries. Phones and homework do not explain it away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second follows well. If the body clock moves and the alarm does not, hours come off the front of the night. Surveys of teenagers show that pattern.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third claim is where the evidence gets mixed. Districts that moved their start report better attendance and more sleep. The findings on grades are smaller and less consistent.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One result is often quoted alone. Teenage car crashes fell after one district moved its start. The study is real. One district over a few years is a thin base for a general claim.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a cost side the argument skips. Buses, after-school jobs, sport and caring for younger siblings all move with the bell. Those effects fall unevenly across families.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the argument is strong at its base and weaker at the edges. A reader who accepts the biology need not accept every number attached to it.

questions.q: Which part of this argument does the article call strongest, and why?
questions.a: The shift in adolescent sleep timing, because it has been measured in laboratories and across many countries and is not explained away by phones or by homework.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the car crash result quoted on its own) and paragraph F (i.e. the costs the argument skips).
Summarize the argument for a later start and where its evidence weakens.
questions.a: Adolescent sleep timing shifts later for biological reasons, an early alarm takes hours off the front of the night, and short sleep harms learning and safety. The biology is well measured, the findings on grades are smaller and less consistent, a widely quoted crash result rests on one district, and costs such as buses and childcare fall unevenly.

questions.q:
body clock: the internal timing system that sets when a person becomes sleepy, which shifts later at puberty.
unevenly: here, falling harder on some families than others, which is how the costs are described.
Describe the connection between the body clock moving and the alarm staying put.
questions.a: If the body clock has moved and the alarm has not, the hours are taken off the front of the night, which is the pattern surveys of teenagers show.

articles.note: RI.7.8 is about sufficiency, not agreement. A student can support the policy and still mark paragraph E as a claim resting on too little.

articles.title: The Case Against the New Stadium
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city is asked to help pay for a stadium, and the proposal arrives with an economic impact study. The study projects jobs, visitor spending and tax revenue, and the numbers are large.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Such studies are usually commissioned by the party that wants the stadium, which does not make them wrong but does tell a reader which assumptions to check first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The main objection economists raise is substitution. Money a local family spends at a game is mostly money it would otherwise have spent on something else in the same city, so the regional total moves far less than the gross figure suggests.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second objection concerns the jobs. Stadium employment is heavily part-time and seasonal, and a headline counting positions rather than full-time equivalents can describe the same work several times over.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third concerns what the money could have done instead. A subsidy spent on a stadium is not available for a bus route or a school roof, and a fair comparison is against that alternative, not against nothing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The case in favour is not empty. A stadium can anchor a district that was emptying, and a city may reasonably decide that having a team is worth paying for as a civic good rather than an investment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the distinction the argument turns on. Saying a stadium will pay for itself is a claim about economics that the evidence mostly does not support. Saying it is worth having anyway is a different claim, and an honest one.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city is asked to help pay for a stadium. The proposal comes with an economic impact study. It projects jobs, visitor spending and tax revenue. The numbers are large.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Such studies are usually paid for by the side that wants the stadium. That does not make them wrong. It does tell a reader which assumptions to check first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The main objection is substitution. Money a local family spends at a game is mostly money it would have spent elsewhere in the same city. So the regional total moves far less than the figure suggests.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second objection is about jobs. Stadium work is largely part-time and seasonal. A headline counting positions, not full-time equivalents, can describe the same work several times.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third asks what the money could have done. A subsidy spent here is not available for a bus route or a school roof. The fair comparison is against that, not against nothing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The case in favour is not empty. A stadium can anchor a district that was emptying. A city may decide a team is worth paying for as a civic good, not an investment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is the distinction. Saying a stadium will pay for itself is an economic claim the evidence mostly does not support. Saying it is worth having anyway is a different claim, and an honest one.

questions.q: What is the substitution objection?
questions.a: Money a local family spends at a game is mostly money it would otherwise have spent on something else in the same city, so the regional total moves far less than the gross figure suggests.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what the money could have done instead) and paragraph G (i.e. the two different claims a supporter might make).
Summarize the objections to a stadium subsidy and the distinction the article ends on.
questions.a: Impact studies are usually commissioned by the side that wants the stadium, and economists object that local spending is substituted rather than added, that jobs are part-time and can be counted more than once, and that the subsidy is not available for a bus route or a school roof. The honest version of the case is that a team is worth having as a civic good, not that the stadium will pay for itself.

questions.q:
substitution: spending that moves from one local business to another rather than being new to the area.
full-time equivalent: a way of counting jobs by total hours, so part-time work is not counted as if it were full-time.
Describe the connection between who commissioned a study and how a reader should use it.
questions.a: Such studies are usually commissioned by the party that wants the stadium, which does not make them wrong but tells a reader which assumptions to check first.

articles.note: The last paragraph separates two claims that get said in one breath. Ask students which of the two a given sentence in a real proposal is making.

articles.title: The Argument for Culling the Deer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park proposes to reduce its deer population by shooting. The argument offered is ecological: the herd has no large predators, numbers have risen, and the browsing is preventing the forest from regenerating.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The regeneration claim can be tested directly. Fencing a plot excludes deer, and if seedlings grow inside the fence and not outside it, the deer are the explanation rather than soil, light or rainfall.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Exclosure studies of that kind are strong evidence, and they are also local. A result from one plot in one forest supports a claim about that forest and not automatically about a park two counties away.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument's second step is weaker in an interesting way. Showing that deer are causing the damage does not by itself show that this cull, at this size, at this time of year, will fix it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Opponents propose alternatives, including fertility control, fencing valuable areas and reintroducing predators. Each has an evidence base, and each works at a different scale and over a different timescale.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The arguments that are hardest to assess are the ones not made in ecological terms at all. Objections about shooting in a public park, or about what a park is for, are real positions, and an impact study cannot settle them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A careful reader sorts the claims before judging them: what is measured, what is predicted, and what is a value. Mixing the three is what makes these disputes feel unresolvable when they are not.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park proposes to cut its deer numbers by shooting. The argument is ecological. The herd has no large predators. Numbers have risen. Browsing stops the forest regrowing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The regrowth claim can be tested. Fence a plot to keep deer out. If seedlings grow inside and not outside, the deer are the cause, not soil, light or rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Such exclosure studies are strong evidence. They are also local. A result from one plot supports a claim about that forest. It does not automatically cover a park two counties away.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second step is weaker in an interesting way. Showing deer cause the damage does not show that this cull, at this size, at this time of year, will fix it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Opponents suggest alternatives. Fertility control. Fencing valuable areas. Bringing back predators. Each has evidence. Each works at a different scale and over a different time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The hardest arguments to assess are not ecological at all. Objections about shooting in a public park, or about what a park is for, are real positions. An impact study cannot settle them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A careful reader sorts the claims first. What is measured. What is predicted. What is a value. Mixing the three makes these disputes feel unresolvable when they are not.

questions.q: How does fencing a plot test whether deer are causing the damage?
questions.a: Fencing excludes deer, so if seedlings grow inside the fence and not outside it, the deer are the explanation rather than soil, light or rainfall.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why showing the cause does not justify this cull) and paragraph G (i.e. sorting measured, predicted and value claims).
Summarize the argument for a cull and how a reader should assess it.
questions.a: The claim is that deer have no predators, numbers have risen and browsing prevents regeneration, which fencing can test directly. Exclosure evidence is strong but local, showing deer cause the damage does not show this particular cull will fix it, alternatives exist, and objections about what a park is for are values an impact study cannot settle.

questions.q:
exclosure: a fenced plot built to keep animals out so their effect can be measured.
regenerate: here, for a forest to grow new trees that replace the old ones.
Describe the connection between a study being local and the strength of a general claim.
questions.a: A result from one plot in one forest supports a claim about that forest and not automatically about a park two counties away.

articles.note: Paragraph G gives students a sorting task they can use anywhere. Run it on the article itself and label each paragraph measured, predicted or value.

articles.title: The Claim That Scores Fell
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A headline reports that reading scores have fallen. Before the explanations begin, a reader has several questions, and the answers decide whether there is anything to explain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is who was tested. If more students sat the test this year, including students who would not have sat it before, the average can fall while no individual student has got worse.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is whether the test changed. A revised test is not the old test, and comparing a score from one with a score from the other requires a statistical bridge that may or may not have been built.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is what the line is measured against. A score can fall relative to last year, relative to a decade ago, or relative to a standard that somebody set, and those are three different claims.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is the size of the change. Test scores move slightly every year for reasons nobody can name, and a change inside that ordinary range is not a trend no matter how it is reported.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of these questions is a reason to dismiss the report. Sometimes scores really do fall, and an article that answers all four and still reports a drop has made its case.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The habit worth building is the order of operations. Establish that the change is real before arguing about its cause, because a confident explanation of a change that did not happen is worse than no explanation.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A headline says reading scores have fallen. Before the explanations start, a reader has questions. The answers decide whether there is anything to explain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is who was tested. Suppose more students sat the test this year, including some who would not have before. The average can fall while no student got worse.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is whether the test changed. A revised test is not the old test. Comparing a score from each needs a statistical bridge. That bridge may not have been built.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is what the line is measured against. A score can fall against last year, against a decade ago, or against a standard somebody set. Those are three different claims.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is the size of the change. Scores move a little every year for reasons nobody can name. A change inside that ordinary range is not a trend, however it is reported.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of this is a reason to dismiss the report. Sometimes scores really do fall. An article that answers all four questions and still reports a drop has made its case.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The habit to build is the order of operations. Show the change is real before arguing about its cause. A confident explanation of a change that did not happen is worse than none.

questions.q: How can an average fall without any individual student doing worse?
questions.a: If more students sat the test this year, including students who would not have sat it before, the average can fall while no individual student has got worse.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the ordinary year-to-year movement) and paragraph G (i.e. the order of operations).
Summarize the four questions to ask about a report that scores fell.
questions.a: Ask who was tested, because adding students can lower an average without anyone doing worse; whether the test changed, because comparing two tests needs a statistical bridge; what the score is measured against, since last year, a decade ago and a standard are three claims; and how large the change is, because scores move slightly every year. Establish the change is real before arguing about its cause.

questions.q:
average: a single figure summarising a group, which can move because the group changed rather than because its members did.
trend: a change large and sustained enough to be more than ordinary year-to-year movement.
Describe the connection between the test changing and the comparison between two years.
questions.a: A revised test is not the old test, so comparing a score from one with a score from the other requires a statistical bridge that may or may not have been built.

articles.note: Give students a real score headline and the four questions. Most articles answer one of the four, and which one is usually revealing.

articles.title: The Claim About Plastic Straws
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.5 structure · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Campaigns to ban plastic straws spread quickly, helped by a video of a turtle with a straw lodged in its nostril. The argument was that straws are unnecessary, replaceable and harmful, and all three are defensible.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The weak link is scale. By weight, straws are a very small share of the plastic entering the ocean, and the large contributors are discarded fishing gear and waste escaping from a relatively small number of rivers.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That does not make a ban pointless. Harm is not only a question of mass, a light object can kill an animal that swallows it, and an item nobody needs is an easy thing to stop producing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It does make one particular sentence false. A campaign claiming that banning straws will substantially reduce ocean plastic is making a quantitative claim, and the quantities do not support it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Supporters often shift ground when pressed, and the second argument is more interesting than the first. Straws are a starting point, the claim goes, and a person who changes one habit becomes easier to persuade about larger ones.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a claim about psychology rather than about plastic, and it has its own evidence, which is mixed. Some studies find a small action increases later commitment, others find it substitutes for one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the honest version of the campaign is narrower and harder to put on a poster. It says straws are a cheap thing to stop doing and that the main sources lie elsewhere and are harder to reach.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Campaigns to ban plastic straws spread fast. A video of a turtle with a straw in its nostril helped. The argument was that straws are needless, replaceable and harmful. All three are defensible.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The weak link is scale. By weight, straws are a very small share of the plastic entering the ocean. The big sources are lost fishing gear and waste from a small number of rivers.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That does not make a ban pointless. Harm is not only about mass. A light object can kill an animal that swallows it. An item nobody needs is easy to stop making.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It does make one sentence false. Claiming a straw ban will greatly reduce ocean plastic is a claim about quantity. The quantities do not support it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Supporters often shift ground when pressed. The second argument is more interesting. Straws are a starting point. Change one habit and a person is easier to persuade about bigger ones.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a claim about psychology, not plastic. It has its own evidence, and the evidence is mixed. Some studies find a small action builds later commitment. Others find it replaces one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the honest version is narrower and harder to put on a poster. Straws are a cheap thing to stop. The main sources lie elsewhere and are harder to reach.

questions.q: Which sentence in the campaign does the article say is false, and why?
questions.a: The claim that banning straws will substantially reduce ocean plastic, because that is a quantitative claim and by weight straws are a very small share of the plastic entering the ocean.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why a ban is not pointless) and paragraph F (i.e. the mixed evidence about small actions).
Summarize what is sound and what is unsupported in the straw argument.
questions.a: Straws are unnecessary, replaceable and able to harm an animal that swallows one, so a ban is not pointless. By weight they are a small share of ocean plastic compared with fishing gear and a few rivers, so claiming a ban will substantially reduce ocean plastic is unsupported, and the fallback that small actions lead to larger ones rests on mixed evidence.

questions.q:
quantitative: expressed as an amount, so that it can be checked against measurements.
shift ground: to move to a different argument when the first one is challenged.
Describe the connection between harm and mass in this argument.
questions.a: Harm is not only a question of mass, because a light object can kill an animal that swallows it, even though by weight straws are a very small share of the plastic entering the ocean.

articles.note: This is the clearest RI.7.8 case in the set: a conclusion worth supporting attached to a number that does not hold it up. Keep the two apart.

articles.title: Two Accounts of the Dust Bowl
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1930s the southern plains of the United States lost a great deal of their topsoil to the wind. Dust storms darkened the sky as far east as the Atlantic coast, and families abandoned farms across several states.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A government film made in 1936 presented the disaster as the result of ploughing. Native grass had held the soil through dry years for a very long time, the argument ran, and the plough removed what the drought then exposed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The evidence for that account is agricultural. Wheat acreage on the plains expanded enormously during and after the First World War, and the land that blew was overwhelmingly land that had been broken.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many people who lived there told it differently. Their accounts emphasise the drought itself, which was severe and prolonged, and the fact that farmers had been encouraged by government, by railroads and by prices to plough exactly where they ploughed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The evidence for that account is also real. Rainfall records show a genuine extreme, and the promotional literature urging settlement on the plains was produced by the same institutions that later explained what went wrong.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two accounts do not disagree about many facts. They disagree about which facts are the centre of the story, and therefore about whether this was a natural event made worse by farming or a farming event made visible by weather.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A reader comparing them should notice what each leaves at the edges. The film is thin on who encouraged the ploughing; the local accounts are thin on what ploughing did. Neither gap is an accident.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1930s the southern plains of the United States lost much of their topsoil to wind. Dust storms darkened skies as far east as the Atlantic. Families left farms across several states.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A government film from 1936 blamed ploughing. Native grass had held the soil through dry years for a very long time. The plough removed what the drought then exposed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The evidence for that is agricultural. Wheat acreage on the plains grew hugely during and after the First World War. The land that blew was mostly land that had been broken.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many people who lived there told it differently. They stressed the drought, which was severe and long. They stressed that government, railroads and prices had urged farmers to plough there.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That evidence is real too. Rainfall records show a true extreme. The advertisements urging settlement came from the same bodies that later explained what went wrong.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two accounts agree on most facts. They disagree about which facts are the centre. Was this a natural event worsened by farming, or a farming event made visible by weather?

paras.label: G
paras.text: A reader should notice what each leaves at the edges. The film says little about who urged the ploughing. The local accounts say little about what ploughing did. Neither gap is an accident.

questions.q: What evidence supports the account that blames ploughing?
questions.a: Wheat acreage on the plains expanded enormously during and after the First World War, and the land that blew was overwhelmingly land that had been broken.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the account given by people who lived there) and paragraph G (i.e. what each account leaves at the edges).
Summarize the two accounts of the Dust Bowl and how they differ.
questions.a: A 1936 government film blamed ploughing, supported by the huge expansion of wheat acreage and the fact that the land that blew had been broken. Local accounts stressed a severe drought and the government, railroads and prices that had urged farmers to plough there. They agree on most facts and disagree about which are the centre of the story.

questions.q:
topsoil: the upper layer of soil that crops grow in, which is what the wind removed.
acreage: the amount of land under a crop, used here as evidence of how much grassland was broken.
Describe the connection between who produced the promotional literature and who later explained the disaster.
questions.a: The literature urging settlement on the plains was produced by the same institutions that later explained what went wrong, which is part of why local accounts emphasise encouragement.

articles.note: RI.7.9 is about emphasis, not contradiction. Paragraph F states it directly, i.e. they disagree about which facts are the centre.

articles.title: Two Papers on One Fossil
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 2003 a team excavating a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores found a small skeleton. The individual had stood about a metre tall and had a brain roughly a third the size of a modern human's.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first paper described a new species. Its evidence was the proportions of the limbs, the shape of the wrist bones and the pelvis, and the fact that the remains were dated to a period when modern humans were already in the region.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A second group published a different reading of the same bones. In their account the skeleton was a modern human affected by a condition that reduces growth and brain size, and the unusual features were pathology rather than ancestry.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both papers cited measurements, and in several cases the same measurements. The disagreement was about which features are diagnostic: a wrist bone that develops early is harder to explain as illness than overall body size is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Evidence accumulated that favoured the first reading. More individuals were found at the site, which is difficult to explain if the first was a single affected person, and stone tools in the deposit covered a long span of time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second group did not simply concede, and that is normal. A claim is usually abandoned gradually as new evidence makes it more expensive to maintain, rather than at a moment when someone announces they were wrong.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading both papers side by side teaches more than reading the winner. The same bones supported two accounts, and what settled it was not argument but material that neither team had when they wrote.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 2003 a team digging a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores found a small skeleton. The person had stood about a metre tall. The brain was roughly a third of a modern human's.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first paper described a new species. Its evidence was the limb proportions, the wrist bones and the pelvis. The remains dated to a time when modern humans were already in the region.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A second group read the same bones differently. To them the skeleton was a modern human with a condition that reduces growth and brain size. The odd features were illness, not ancestry.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both papers cited measurements. Sometimes the same ones. The argument was about which features count. A wrist bone that forms early is harder to explain as illness than body size is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Evidence built up favouring the first reading. More individuals were found at the site. That is hard to explain if the first was one affected person. Stone tools covered a long span of time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second group did not simply give in. That is normal. A claim is usually dropped slowly, as new evidence makes it costly to hold. It rarely ends with someone announcing they were wrong.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading both papers together teaches more than reading the winner. The same bones supported two accounts. What settled it was material neither team had when they wrote.

questions.q: What did the two papers disagree about, given that both cited measurements?
questions.a: They disagreed about which features are diagnostic, since a wrist bone that develops early is harder to explain as illness than overall body size is.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the evidence that accumulated afterwards) and paragraph F (i.e. how a claim is usually abandoned).
Summarize the dispute over the Flores skeleton.
questions.a: One team described a new species from the limb proportions, wrist bones and pelvis, and another read the same bones as a modern human affected by a condition reducing growth and brain size. More individuals and a long span of stone tools made the first reading stronger, and the dispute was settled by material neither team had when they wrote.

questions.q:
diagnostic: a feature that distinguishes one group from another, as opposed to one that could have several causes.
pathology: disease or abnormal development, offered here as an alternative explanation for unusual bones.
Describe the connection between finding more individuals and the strength of the two readings.
questions.a: More individuals were found at the site, which is difficult to explain if the first was a single affected person, so the evidence favoured the new species reading.

articles.note: Paragraph F is worth dwelling on. Students expect science to end in a concession, and it more often ends in a cost that rises until nobody pays it.

articles.title: The Two Texts of a Treaty
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in New Zealand in 1840. It exists in two versions, one in English and one in Māori, and the difference between them has shaped the country's law ever since.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The English text has Māori chiefs ceding sovereignty to the Crown. That is a strong word in English law, and it describes the transfer of the ultimate authority to govern.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Māori text uses kāwanatanga, a word built from the transliteration of governor. It conveys something closer to governorship than to sovereignty, and it is not the word a Māori speaker would have reached for to mean full authority.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same Māori text then guarantees the chiefs tino rangatiratanga over their lands and treasures. That phrase does carry the sense of full authority, which produces a document promising in one clause what the other appears to take.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Almost all of the roughly five hundred signatures were made on the Māori text. That matters, because the people signing were agreeing to the document in front of them and in their own language.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Historians differ on how deliberate the gap was. Some read it as the haste and imprecision of a translation made overnight; others point out that the translator knew both languages well and that the softer word served the Crown's purpose.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Modern practice does not pick one text and discard the other. It asks what the parties understood themselves to be agreeing to, which is a question the existence of two texts makes unavoidable.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in New Zealand in 1840. It exists in two versions. One is English. One is Māori. The difference has shaped the country's law ever since.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The English text has Māori chiefs ceding sovereignty to the Crown. In English law that is a strong word. It means handing over the final authority to govern.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Māori text uses kāwanatanga. The word is built from the word governor. It is closer to governorship than to sovereignty. It is not the word a Māori speaker would use for full authority.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same Māori text then guarantees the chiefs tino rangatiratanga over their lands and treasures. That phrase does mean full authority. So one clause promises what the other seems to take.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Nearly all of the roughly five hundred signatures were on the Māori text. That matters. The people signing agreed to the document in front of them, in their own language.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Historians differ on how deliberate the gap was. Some call it haste in an overnight translation. Others note the translator knew both languages well, and the softer word suited the Crown.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Modern practice does not pick one text and drop the other. It asks what the parties understood they were agreeing to. Two texts make that question unavoidable.

questions.q: Why does the Māori text appear to promise in one clause what another takes?
questions.a: It uses kāwanatanga, which is closer to governorship than sovereignty, and then guarantees the chiefs tino rangatiratanga over their lands and treasures, which does carry the sense of full authority.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. which text was actually signed) and paragraph F (i.e. how historians differ about the gap).
Summarize why the Treaty of Waitangi has two texts and why it matters.
questions.a: The English text has chiefs ceding sovereignty, while the Māori text uses kāwanatanga, closer to governorship, and then guarantees tino rangatiratanga, which means full authority. Almost all the signatures were on the Māori text, historians differ over whether the gap was haste or purpose, and modern practice asks what the parties understood rather than choosing one text.

questions.q:
cede: to give up or hand over, used in the English text for the transfer of sovereignty.
transliteration: writing a word from one language in the letters and sounds of another, as kāwanatanga is built from governor.
Describe the connection between which text was signed and how the treaty is read today.
questions.a: Almost all of the roughly five hundred signatures were made on the Māori text, and the people signing were agreeing to the document in front of them in their own language, so modern practice asks what the parties understood themselves to be agreeing to.

articles.note: Two authors, one event, two documents, and the difference is a single word in each. This is the sharpest RI.7.9 example in the set.

articles.title: Why the Big Animals Vanished
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the end of the last ice age, most of the very large land mammals disappeared. Mammoths, giant ground sloths and others vanished from several continents within a span that is short by geological standards.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One explanation puts the cause on people. Extinctions on each landmass tend to follow the arrival of modern humans, the pattern repeats on islands reached much later, and the species lost are overwhelmingly large and slow-breeding.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other explanation puts the cause on climate. The end of the ice age reorganised vegetation across whole continents, and an animal adapted to one kind of grassland does not simply move when the grassland changes composition.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Each account emphasises evidence the other treats as secondary. The first points at timing and at island cases; the second points at pollen records and at species that disappeared where hunting evidence is scarce.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Africa is the case both must address. It lost proportionally fewer large mammals than other continents, and each explanation has an answer, which is that its animals evolved alongside humans or that its climate shifted less.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The disagreement has narrowed over time, and most researchers now argue for a combination in which small populations under climate stress were finished by hunting they could otherwise have absorbed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A combined answer is not a compromise for the sake of peace. It is what the evidence supports, and it is harder to state than either original claim, which is one reason the simpler versions persist in print.

paras.label: A
paras.text: At the end of the last ice age, most very large land mammals disappeared. Mammoths and giant ground sloths vanished from several continents. By geological standards it happened fast.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One explanation blames people. Extinctions on each landmass follow the arrival of modern humans. The pattern repeats on islands reached much later. The lost species are mostly large and slow to breed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The other blames climate. The end of the ice age reorganised plants across whole continents. An animal adapted to one grassland does not simply move when the grassland changes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Each account stresses evidence the other treats as minor. The first points to timing and islands. The second points to pollen records and to species lost where hunting evidence is thin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Africa is the case both must answer. It lost fewer large mammals in proportion. One side says its animals evolved alongside humans. The other says its climate shifted less.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The gap has narrowed. Most researchers now argue for a combination. Small populations under climate stress were finished by hunting they could otherwise have survived.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A combined answer is not a compromise for peace. It is what the evidence supports. It is harder to state than either simple claim, which is why the simple ones stay in print.

questions.q: What evidence supports the explanation that blames people?
questions.a: Extinctions on each landmass tend to follow the arrival of modern humans, the pattern repeats on islands reached much later, and the species lost are overwhelmingly large and slow-breeding.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how each explanation handles Africa) and paragraph G (i.e. why a combined answer is not a compromise).
Summarize the two explanations for the loss of the large mammals.
questions.a: One account blames people, citing extinctions following human arrival, the same pattern on islands, and the loss of large slow-breeding species. The other blames climate, citing the reorganisation of vegetation and pollen records. Both must explain why Africa lost proportionally fewer, and most researchers now argue that climate stress left small populations that hunting finished.

questions.q:
slow-breeding: producing few young over a long life, which makes a population slow to recover from losses.
pollen record: preserved pollen in sediments, used to show what plants grew in a place at a given time.
Describe the connection between climate stress and hunting in the combined explanation.
questions.a: Small populations already under climate stress were finished by hunting they could otherwise have absorbed.

articles.note: Students often want a winner. The useful question is what each side would accept as a decisive observation, which is harder and more honest.

articles.title: Two Histories of One Strike
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
 Spiral: RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.6 point of view · RI.7.8 claims and evidence · RI.7.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1892 the steelworks at Homestead, Pennsylvania locked out its union workers over a wage dispute. The company brought in three hundred armed Pinkerton agents by barge, and the fighting that followed killed men on both sides.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A history written from company records describes a firm protecting property. In that account the workers seized the plant, the agents were guards hired to restore lawful access, and the violence began when the barges were fired on.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A history written from union records and local newspapers describes a town defending itself. In that account the company had planned the lockout for months, the agents arrived armed at four in the morning, and the townspeople were resisting an invasion.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both accounts can cite documents. Company correspondence shows advance planning; union minutes show the plant was occupied; the Pinkerton agents were armed and so were the workers, and both facts appear in testimony.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The difference shows up in sequence and in naming. One account begins with the occupation of the plant and the other with the decision to break the union, and where one writes guards the other writes agents.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those choices are not decoration. A reader who accepts the starting point has largely accepted the conclusion, because the first event in a story is the one everything after it is a response to.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The practical skill is to notice the first sentence. Ask what happened before it, and whether the author had to choose not to start there.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1892 the steelworks at Homestead, Pennsylvania locked out its union workers over wages. The company brought in three hundred armed Pinkerton agents by barge. The fighting killed men on both sides.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A history from company records describes a firm protecting property. The workers seized the plant. The agents were guards hired to restore lawful access. The violence began when the barges were fired on.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A history from union records and local papers describes a town defending itself. The company had planned the lockout for months. The agents arrived armed at four in the morning. The townspeople resisted an invasion.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both can cite documents. Company letters show advance planning. Union minutes show the plant was occupied. The agents were armed and so were the workers. Both facts appear in testimony.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The difference shows in sequence and in naming. One account starts with the occupation. The other starts with the decision to break the union. One writes guards. The other writes agents.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those choices are not decoration. Accept the starting point and you have mostly accepted the conclusion. The first event is the one everything after it answers.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The practical skill is to notice the first sentence. Ask what happened before it. Ask whether the author chose not to start there.

questions.q: How do the two accounts differ in where they begin?
questions.a: One account begins with the occupation of the plant and the other with the decision to break the union.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the documents both accounts can cite) and paragraph F (i.e. why the starting point carries the conclusion).
Summarize how two histories of Homestead differ.
questions.a: A company account describes a firm protecting property from workers who seized the plant, and a union account describes a town resisting armed agents who arrived at four in the morning after months of planning. Both cite real documents, and they differ in sequence and in naming, which matters because the first event in a story is the one everything after it is a response to.

questions.q:
lockout: an employer shutting workers out of a workplace during a dispute, as distinct from workers walking out.
sequence: the order in which events are told, which can carry an argument without stating one.
Describe the connection between choosing a starting point and reaching a conclusion.
questions.a: A reader who accepts the starting point has largely accepted the conclusion, because the first event in a story is the one everything after it is a response to.

articles.note: Give students the two opening sentences only, with no other text, and ask what each one has already decided.

articles.title: The Second That Was Added to a Year
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6-8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: There are two ways to say what time it is. One counts the rotation of the earth. The other counts oscillations of a caesium atom, which is far steadier than the planet.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The planet is not a reliable clock. Tides exert a drag that slows the rotation over long periods, and shorter wobbles come from the atmosphere, the oceans and movements of material deep inside the earth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Atomic time does not wobble, so the two slowly separate. Left alone for long enough, clock noon would drift away from the sun being overhead, by a small amount at first and then by a visible one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The fix adopted in 1972 was the leap second. When the gap approaches a limit, an extra second is inserted into the last minute of a day, and that minute officially contains sixty-one seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It works, and it causes trouble. Computer systems that assume every minute has sixty seconds have failed at the insertion, and a leap second cannot be scheduled far ahead because the earth's wobbles are not predictable.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2022 the international body responsible voted to stop inserting them by 2035, letting the gap grow and dealing with it in a larger correction much later.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decision is a trade. Timekeeping that follows the sky is being loosened in favour of timekeeping that computers can rely on, and a thing that has been true for all of history, that noon means the sun is overhead, becomes approximately true instead.

paras.label: A
paras.text: There are two ways to say what time it is. One counts the rotation of the earth. The other counts oscillations of a caesium atom. The atom is far steadier than the planet.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The planet is not a reliable clock. Tides drag on it and slow the rotation over long periods. Shorter wobbles come from the air, the oceans and movements deep inside the earth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Atomic time does not wobble. So the two slowly separate. Left long enough, clock noon would drift from the sun being overhead. First a little, then visibly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The fix adopted in 1972 was the leap second. When the gap nears a limit, a second is added to the last minute of a day. That minute officially holds sixty-one seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It works, and it causes trouble. Computers that assume sixty seconds in a minute have failed at the insertion. A leap second cannot be planned far ahead, because the wobbles are not predictable.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2022 the international body voted to stop adding them by 2035. The gap will grow. A larger correction will deal with it much later.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decision is a trade. Time that follows the sky is loosened in favour of time computers can rely on. Noon meaning the sun overhead becomes approximately true.

questions.q: Why do atomic time and earth time separate?
questions.a: Tides exert a drag that slows the rotation, and shorter wobbles come from the atmosphere, the oceans and movements of material deep inside the earth, while atomic time does not wobble.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the trouble leap seconds cause) and paragraph G (i.e. what the 2035 decision trades away).
Summarize the leap second and why it is being abandoned.
questions.a: Earth's rotation is slowed by tides and wobbled by the atmosphere and oceans, so it drifts from atomic time. Since 1972 a leap second has been inserted to keep clock noon near the sun overhead, but computers assuming sixty-second minutes have failed and the insertions cannot be scheduled far ahead, so the practice is to stop by 2035.

questions.q:
oscillation: one complete back-and-forth cycle, counted in an atom to define a second.
leap second: an extra second inserted into the last minute of a day to keep clock time near the earth's rotation.
Describe the connection between the earth's wobbles and the scheduling of leap seconds.
questions.a: A leap second cannot be scheduled far ahead because the earth's wobbles are not predictable.

articles.note: A good place to ask what a standard is for. The last paragraph says what is being given up, which most coverage of this decision leaves out.

articles.title: The Ship That Was Built Too Tall
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6-8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: The warship Vasa sailed from Stockholm on its first voyage in August 1628. It travelled roughly 1,300 metres, heeled over in a gust, took water through its open gunports and sank in the harbour.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The ship was extraordinarily ornamented and carried two full decks of guns. It was also narrow for its height, and it had far too little ballast in the hold to balance the weight above the waterline.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The problem was known before it sailed. An officer had thirty men run from side to side across the deck while the ship lay at the quay, and the rolling became dangerous enough that he stopped the test.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The test was not reported upward in any way that stopped the launch. The king had ordered the ship, the king was at war, and the people who knew were not the people who decided.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Shipbuilding then had no written calculation of stability. A master shipwright worked from proportions carried in his head and from ships that had worked before, and this ship had been altered during construction.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The inquiry afterwards found nobody at fault. The shipwright had died, the surviving builders said they had followed instruction, and the instruction had come from a king nobody was going to name.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Vasa was raised almost intact in 1961, because the Baltic is too brackish for the shipworm that would have eaten it anywhere else. The failure is in a museum, which is a rare thing for a failure to be.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The warship Vasa sailed from Stockholm on its first voyage in August 1628. It went about 1,300 metres. A gust heeled it over. Water came through the open gunports. It sank in the harbour.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The ship was heavily ornamented. It carried two full decks of guns. It was narrow for its height. It had far too little ballast to balance the weight above the waterline.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The problem was known before it sailed. An officer had thirty men run from side to side on deck at the quay. The rolling grew dangerous. He stopped the test.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The test was not reported upward in a way that stopped the launch. The king had ordered the ship. The king was at war. The people who knew were not the people who decided.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Shipbuilding then had no written calculation of stability. A master shipwright used proportions he carried in his head and ships that had worked before. This ship had been altered during building.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The inquiry found nobody at fault. The shipwright had died. The surviving builders said they followed instruction. The instruction came from a king nobody would name.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Vasa was raised almost whole in 1961. The Baltic is too brackish for the shipworm that would have eaten it elsewhere. The failure sits in a museum, which failures rarely do.

questions.q: What did the test at the quay show?
questions.a: Thirty men running from side to side across the deck made the rolling dangerous enough that the officer stopped the test.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why the test did not stop the launch) and paragraph F (i.e. what the inquiry concluded).
Summarize why Vasa sank and why nobody was held responsible.
questions.a: The ship was narrow for its height with two gun decks and too little ballast, so a gust heeled it over and water came through the open gunports. A test at the quay had shown the danger but did not stop a launch the king wanted, there was no written calculation of stability at the time, and the inquiry found nobody at fault.

questions.q:
ballast: heavy material carried low in a ship to balance the weight above the waterline.
brackish: slightly salty, less salty than the open sea, which is why the shipworm could not live there.
Describe the connection between who knew about the problem and who could act on it.
questions.a: The people who knew were not the people who decided, and the test was not reported upward in any way that stopped the launch.

articles.note: Paragraph D is the sentence to hold onto, i.e. the people who knew were not the people who decided. It describes a great many failures since.

articles.title: The Forest That Is One Tree
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6-8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: In central Utah there is a stand of quaking aspen covering about forty-three hectares. It looks like a forest of perhaps forty thousand separate trees, and it is one organism.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Aspen reproduce mainly by sending up new stems from a spreading root system. Each stem is genetically identical to the others, and the whole connected mass is called a clone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Testing that is not a matter of looking. Genetic sampling across the stand returns the same profile, the stems are male throughout, and they leaf out and turn colour together in a way neighbouring stands do not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The organism has been given a name, Pando, and an age, and the age is the contested part. Estimates have ranged from several thousand to tens of thousands of years, and the methods behind them disagree.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The difficulty is that no individual stem is old. A stem lives perhaps a hundred and fifty years, so the age being claimed belongs to the root system, and a root system does not keep rings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The clone is also in trouble. Surveys find plenty of mature stems and very few young ones, which is what a population looks like when something is eating the new growth faster than it appears.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Fenced areas within the stand have begun to regenerate, which points at browsing by deer and elk. It is an unusual conservation problem: the patient is not dying, it is failing to replace itself.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In central Utah a stand of quaking aspen covers about forty-three hectares. It looks like a forest of perhaps forty thousand trees. It is one organism.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Aspen mostly reproduce by sending up new stems from a spreading root system. Each stem is genetically identical. The whole connected mass is called a clone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Testing that takes more than looking. Genetic samples across the stand match. The stems are all male. They leaf out and turn colour together, which nearby stands do not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The organism has a name, Pando, and an age. The age is contested. Estimates run from several thousand to tens of thousands of years. The methods behind them disagree.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The difficulty is that no single stem is old. A stem lives maybe a hundred and fifty years. The age belongs to the root system. A root system does not keep rings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The clone is in trouble. Surveys find many mature stems and very few young ones. That is what happens when something eats new growth faster than it appears.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Fenced areas inside the stand have started to regrow. That points at browsing by deer and elk. It is an unusual case. The patient is not dying. It is failing to replace itself.

questions.q: What evidence shows the stand is a single organism?
questions.a: Genetic sampling across the stand returns the same profile, the stems are male throughout, and they leaf out and turn colour together in a way neighbouring stands do not.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the age is hard to establish) and paragraph G (i.e. what the fenced areas point at).
Summarize what Pando is and what is happening to it.
questions.a: A forty-three hectare stand of aspen in Utah is one organism, shown by matching genetic samples, all-male stems and synchronised leafing. Its age is contested because no stem is older than about a hundred and fifty years and a root system keeps no rings, and surveys find many mature stems and few young ones, with fenced areas regenerating, which points at browsing.

questions.q:
clone: a group of genetically identical stems connected by one root system.
browsing: animals eating leaves and young shoots, which is what the fenced plots suggest is happening.
Describe the connection between the age claimed and what no stem can show.
questions.a: A stem lives perhaps a hundred and fifty years, so the age being claimed belongs to the root system, and a root system does not keep rings.

articles.note: Pairs well with the deer article. The exclosure evidence is the same instrument doing the same job in a different argument.

articles.title: The Parts That Had to Fit
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6-8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: A craftsman building a musket fitted every part to the gun in front of him. A lock from one weapon would not fit another, and a broken part was repaired by a person with files rather than replaced from a box.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Making parts interchangeable sounds like a small change and is not. It requires that two parts made months apart in different places fall within a tolerance, which means the tolerance has to be written down and measurable.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So the real invention was not a machine. It was a system of gauges, a go gauge that a correct part passes and a no-go gauge it must not pass, together with the discipline of using them on every part.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Eli Whitney is often credited, on the strength of a demonstration in Washington in 1801 in which he assembled locks from mixed parts. Later examination of his surviving muskets suggests the parts were not in fact interchangeable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What actually produced the system was slower and less quotable. Armouries in Massachusetts and Virginia worked at it for decades, and interchangeability arrived in the 1840s at considerable expense.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The consequence reached far past weapons. Interchangeable parts made repair possible without a craftsman, made assembly a sequence of simple steps, and made the production line thinkable.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The story is usually told as a flash of genius because that shape is easier to remember. The accurate version is about measurement, record-keeping and forty years of institutional patience.

Interchangeability required written, measurable tolerances and a system of go and no-go gauges used on every part. tolerance: the range of sizes a part may have and still fit, which must be written down to be checked.

articles.note: A good test of whether students can hold two things at once, i.e. that the famous demonstration happened and that it did not show what it is said to show.

articles.title: What the Permafrost Holds
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6-8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.7.1 citing evidence · RI.7.2 central ideas · RI.7.4 word meaning · RI.7.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 820 – 920

paras.label: A
paras.text: Permafrost is ground that has stayed below freezing for at least two consecutive years, and in parts of Siberia, Alaska and Canada it runs hundreds of metres deep and has been frozen for a very long time.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Frozen ground does not rot. Plants and animals that died there were buried and held rather than broken down, so the permafrost contains an enormous quantity of carbon that never completed its decay.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Estimates put that store at well over a thousand billion tonnes, which is roughly twice the carbon currently in the atmosphere. The figure is uncertain, because measuring it means drilling across a region the size of a continent.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Thawing releases it, and the form matters. Decay with oxygen produces carbon dioxide; decay in waterlogged ground without oxygen produces methane, which traps far more heat per molecule over the following decades.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The worry is that this is a feedback. Warming thaws ground, thawed ground releases gas, and the released gas contributes to further warming, which is a loop that does not require anyone to do anything more to continue.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The size and speed of that loop are genuinely unsettled. Thaw is patchy, some ground collapses abruptly while some warms slowly, and plants growing on thawed land take up carbon of their own.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the honest statement has a wide range in it. The store is real and large, the mechanism is understood, and how much arrives this century is a number nobody can yet give with confidence.

questions.q: Why does permafrost hold so much carbon?
questions.a: Frozen ground does not rot, so plants and animals that died there were buried and held rather than broken down, leaving carbon that never completed its decay.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why the form of the gas matters) and paragraph F (i.e. why the size of the loop is unsettled).
Summarize what permafrost holds and what is uncertain about it.
questions.a: Permafrost has stayed frozen for a very long time, so material that died there never finished decaying and the store is estimated at well over a thousand billion tonnes of carbon. Thaw releases carbon dioxide where there is oxygen and methane where there is not, which creates a feedback, but thaw is patchy and plants take up carbon, so how much arrives this century is not known with confidence.

questions.q:
permafrost: ground that has remained below freezing for at least two consecutive years.
feedback: a loop in which an effect adds to the cause that produced it.
Describe the connection between waterlogged ground and the gas that is released.
questions.a: Decay with oxygen produces carbon dioxide, while decay in waterlogged ground without oxygen produces methane, which traps far more heat per molecule over the following decades.

articles.note: The last paragraph models what a confident statement about an uncertain quantity sounds like. Have students write one of their own in the same shape.

articles.title: The Fossil That Was Predicted
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Fossils of fish are common in rocks of a certain age, and fossils of four-legged land animals are common in younger rocks. For a long time the interval between them held very little, and that gap was the problem.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A team led by Neil Shubin decided not to search where fossils had already been found. They reasoned instead about where to look, which meant deciding first what kind of rock the animal would have to be in.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reasoning had three parts. The rock had to date from roughly 375 million years ago, it had to have formed in shallow fresh water rather than deep ocean, and it had to be exposed at the surface rather than buried under a city or a forest.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Very few places satisfy all three. Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic, does, and the team spent four summers there before finding anything, which is most of the story and the part usually left out.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What they found in 2004 was an animal with the scales and fins of a fish, a flat head with eyes on top, a neck, and inside its fin the bones of a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Several pieces of evidence support the claim that this animal sits between fish and land vertebrates. The anatomy is one. The age of the rock is another. The presence of a neck, which fish do not have, is a third.

paras.label: G
paras.text: But the strongest is the prediction. The anatomy could have been argued over afterwards; what could not be argued over is that the team said what they expected to find, said where, and then went to that place and found it.

paras.label: A

questions.q: What three conditions did the rock have to meet?
questions.a: It had to date from roughly 375 million years ago, to have formed in shallow fresh water rather than deep ocean, and to be exposed at the surface rather than buried.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the three pieces of supporting evidence) and paragraph G (i.e. why the prediction outweighs them).
Summarize how the team found the fossil and why the find is strong evidence.
questions.a: Rather than searching where fossils were already known, they reasoned that the animal must lie in rock about 375 million years old, formed in shallow fresh water and exposed at the surface, which pointed to Ellesmere Island. After four summers they found an animal with fish scales and fins but a neck and the bones of a shoulder, elbow and wrist, and the prediction made beforehand is stronger evidence than the anatomy alone.

questions.q:
vertebrate: an animal with a backbone, which includes both fish and four-legged land animals.
exposed: here, rock lying at the surface where it can be examined, rather than buried under soil or buildings.
Describe the connection between choosing where to dig and the strength of the result.
questions.a: The team said what they expected to find and said where, so going to that place and finding it is evidence that could not be argued over afterwards the way anatomy could.

articles.note: RI.8.1 asks for the evidence that supports a claim most strongly, which means ranking. Paragraph F offers three and paragraph G names a fourth that beats them. Make students defend the order.

articles.title: Who Reached the Pole First
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1909 two American explorers claimed to have reached the North Pole. Frederick Cook said he had arrived in April 1908, and Robert Peary said he had arrived in April 1909, and each disputed the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There is nothing at the Pole to photograph. It is sea ice, indistinguishable from the ice for many kilometres around it, and it drifts, so a party cannot leave a marker and expect anyone to find it again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That leaves navigation records as the evidence. A traveller establishes position from the height of the sun, measured with a sextant, combined with an accurate time and careful arithmetic recorded as they go.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cook's case collapsed quickly. His supporting records were thin, and two Inuit companions described a route that did not go far north, and a separate claim he had made about climbing Denali was shown to be false.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Peary's case is argued about still. His party covered distances on the return journey that are difficult to match, and his diary for the days at the Pole is strikingly bare, and he took no navigator with him who could confirm the readings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Weighing this means ranking kinds of evidence. A diary entry is weaker than a sextant observation, a sextant observation is weaker if nobody independent witnessed it, and a travel speed can be compared against other expeditions.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Most historians now treat the first confirmed surface arrival as a later one. The honest statement is not that Peary lied but that the record he left cannot carry the claim, which is a different and more careful thing to say.

paras.text: In 1909 two American explorers claimed to have reached the North Pole. Frederick Cook said April 1908. Robert Peary said April 1909. Each disputed the other.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

questions.q: Why can a claim to have reached the North Pole not be settled by a photograph or a marker?
questions.a: It is sea ice, indistinguishable from the ice for many kilometres around, and it drifts, so a party cannot leave a marker and expect anyone to find it again.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how the kinds of evidence rank against each other) and paragraph G (i.e. the careful way to state the conclusion).
Summarize the dispute over who reached the North Pole and how it is judged.
questions.a: Cook claimed 1908 and Peary 1909, and there is nothing at the Pole to photograph, so navigation records are the evidence. Cook's case collapsed because his records were thin and companions described a different route, while Peary's is still argued over because of implausible return distances, a bare diary and no independent navigator, so the careful conclusion is that his record cannot carry the claim.

questions.q:
sextant: an instrument measuring the angle of the sun above the horizon, used to work out position.
independent: here, a witness with no stake in the claim, whose confirmation would strengthen the record.
Describe the connection between the absence of an independent navigator and the strength of Peary's claim.
questions.a: A sextant observation is weaker if nobody independent witnessed it, and he took no navigator with him who could confirm the readings.

articles.note: The last sentence models the distinction worth teaching, i.e. a record that cannot carry a claim is not the same as a lie. Students reach for the accusation first.

articles.title: The Bones Inside a Flipper
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A whale's flipper is a stiff paddle used for steering. From outside it resembles the fin of a fish, which is unsurprising, because both are solving the same problem in the same medium.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Inside it does not resemble a fin at all. An x-ray shows one long bone, then two bones side by side, then a cluster of small ones, then rows of finger bones, which is the arrangement in a human arm.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A fish fin contains nothing of the kind. It is supported by many thin rays of bone or cartilage, lying parallel to one another and jointed to nothing, and the similarity between a flipper and a fin ends at the skin.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same arrangement appears in a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a mole's digging hand, and in each the proportions differ enormously while the sequence and the connections stay the same.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Two kinds of evidence are available for the claim that these animals share an ancestor. One is that the limbs look similar from outside. The other is that the bones occur in the same order and the same joints.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second is far stronger, and the fish fin is why. Outward similarity can be produced by a shared problem, since anything swimming fast will end up streamlined, and a shared problem explains nothing about ancestry.

paras.label: G
paras.text: An arrangement that serves no present purpose is harder to explain away. There is no reason a steering paddle needs finger bones, and the best explanation for their being there is that they were inherited from an animal that used them.

paras.text: A whale's flipper is a stiff paddle used for steering. From outside it looks like a fish's fin. That is no surprise. Both solve the same problem in the same medium.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same arrangement is in a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a mole's digging hand. The proportions differ hugely. The order and the joints stay the same.
