paras.label: F
paras.text: That belief did not survive the laboratory. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound from living organisms, from starting materials that were not. The boundary turned out not to exist.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The word stayed where the boundary had been. A technical term can outlive its justification. It keeps a shape that matches nothing. That is when an everyday meaning moves in beside it.

questions.q: What makes a compound organic in chemistry?
questions.a: It contains carbon in the relevant arrangements, whatever its origin, which is why petrol and most plastics are organic.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the older meaning of the word) and paragraph F (i.e. Wöhler's synthesis of urea).
Summarize the two meanings of organic and how they came apart.
questions.a: In a supermarket organic describes rules about how food was produced, backed by certification, while in chemistry it means a compound containing carbon, so petrol and most plastics qualify. The word originally meant from a living organism because chemists believed such compounds needed a vital force, and Wöhler's synthesis of urea in 1828 removed that boundary while the word stayed.

questions.q:
synthesis: making a compound from simpler starting materials, as Wöhler made urea.
vital force: the supposed property of living things once believed necessary to produce certain compounds.
Describe the connection between a boundary disappearing and a word changing meaning.
questions.a: A technical term can outlive its own justification and keep a shape that no longer matches anything, which is when an everyday meaning moves in beside it.

articles.note: Compare with grade 7's What Natural Means on a Label. Same shelf, different word, and this one has a technical meaning that is genuinely at odds with the shelf.

articles.title: How a Paragraph Builds a Definition
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Take a paragraph defining the word species in a biology textbook and read it one sentence at a time. The paragraph is short, and almost every sentence in it is doing a different job from the one before.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence usually offers the definition plainly: a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. On its own that sentence sounds complete, which is the effect it is written to have.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second sentence almost always narrows it. It adds a condition such as under natural conditions, which excludes animals that will breed only in captivity, and the definition is now smaller than it was a sentence ago.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third sentence tends to introduce the trouble. Bacteria do not interbreed at all, many plants hybridise freely across what everyone calls species, and fossils cannot be tested for anything of the kind.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth does repair work. It either admits that the definition covers some organisms and not others, or it introduces a second definition used where the first fails, and either move changes the status of sentence one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the opening sentence is not the definition the paragraph delivers. It is a first approximation the rest of the paragraph edits, and a reader who stops after it has the version the author already decided was insufficient.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This shape is everywhere in technical writing. Claim, narrow, complicate, repair, and the sentence most often quoted elsewhere is the first one, which is the only sentence in the paragraph the author did not mean to stand alone.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Take a paragraph defining the word species in a biology textbook. Read it one sentence at a time. The paragraph is short. Almost every sentence does a different job from the one before.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence usually gives the definition plainly. A species is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. On its own it sounds complete. It is written to sound that way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second sentence almost always narrows it. It adds a condition like under natural conditions. That excludes animals that breed only in captivity. The definition is now smaller.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third sentence brings the trouble. Bacteria do not interbreed at all. Many plants hybridise across what everyone calls species. Fossils cannot be tested for any of this.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth repairs. It admits the definition covers some organisms and not others. Or it adds a second definition for where the first fails. Either move changes the first sentence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the opening sentence is not the definition the paragraph delivers. It is a first try that the rest edits. A reader who stops there has the version the author already called insufficient.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This shape is everywhere in technical writing. Claim, narrow, complicate, repair. The sentence quoted elsewhere is usually the first, the only one not meant to stand alone.

questions.q: What job does the second sentence of such a paragraph usually do?
questions.a: It narrows the definition by adding a condition such as under natural conditions, which excludes animals that will breed only in captivity.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the repair sentence) and paragraph F (i.e. why the opening sentence is not the definition).
Summarize the four jobs the sentences of a definition paragraph do.
questions.a: The first states the definition plainly so it sounds complete, the second narrows it with a condition, the third introduces cases it fails on such as bacteria and fossils, and the fourth repairs by admitting a limit or adding a second definition. The opening sentence is a first approximation the rest of the paragraph edits.

questions.q:
hybridise: to breed across what are normally treated as separate species and produce offspring.
approximation: a first version that is close enough to begin with and is expected to be corrected.
Describe the connection between quoting the first sentence and misrepresenting the paragraph.
questions.a: The first sentence is the one the rest of the paragraph edits, so a reader who stops after it has the version the author already decided was insufficient.

articles.note: RI.8.5 is about one paragraph. Give students a definition paragraph with the sentences numbered and ask them to label each with claim, narrow, complicate or repair.

articles.title: The Sentence That Concedes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of a well-made argument there is usually a sentence that appears to work against it. It grants something to the other side, and it is placed deliberately rather than let in by accident.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is easy to spot once you look. It begins with although, admittedly, it is true that, or of course, and whatever follows is a point the writer is not disputing and does not intend to come back and dispute later.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A reader might expect such a sentence to weaken the paragraph. It generally strengthens it, because an argument that never grants anything signals either that the writer has not met the objections or has decided not to mention them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sentence after a concession is where the work happens. It usually begins with but, yet or however, and it does not deny what was just granted; it argues that the granted point does not reach the conclusion.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That pairing is what makes a concession safe to make. The writer accepts a fact and then disputes its weight, and a reader who understands that structure will not mistake the concession for a change of mind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A concession can also be used badly. A writer may grant a small point while leaving the serious objection unmentioned, which produces the appearance of fairness at a very low price.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the test is what gets conceded, not whether anything does. Find the strongest objection you can think of and ask whether the paragraph names it, because a concession that avoids the hard one is a performance.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of a good argument there is usually a sentence that seems to work against it. It grants something to the other side. It is placed on purpose, not let in by accident.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is easy to spot once you look. It starts with although, admittedly, it is true that, or of course. What follows is a point the writer is not disputing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: You might expect such a sentence to weaken the paragraph. It usually strengthens it. An argument that grants nothing suggests the writer has not met the objections, or chose not to mention them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sentence after a concession does the work. It usually starts with but, yet or however. It does not deny what was granted. It argues that the granted point does not reach the conclusion.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That pairing makes a concession safe to make. The writer accepts a fact and then disputes its weight. A reader who sees the structure will not mistake it for a change of mind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A concession can be used badly. A writer may grant a small point and leave the serious objection unmentioned. That looks like fairness at a very low price.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the test is what gets conceded, not whether anything does. Think of the strongest objection. Ask whether the paragraph names it. A concession that avoids the hard one is a performance.

questions.q: What does the sentence after a concession usually do?
questions.a: It begins with but, yet or however, and rather than denying what was granted it argues that the granted point does not reach the conclusion.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why a concession strengthens an argument) and paragraph F (i.e. how a concession can be used badly).
Summarize how a concession works inside a paragraph.
questions.a: A concession sentence grants a point to the other side, signalled by although or of course, and the sentence after it disputes the weight of what was granted rather than denying it. Granting nothing suggests the writer has not met the objections, but granting only a small point while leaving the serious one unmentioned produces the appearance of fairness cheaply.

questions.q:
concession: a sentence granting a point to the opposing side within one's own argument.
weight: how much a granted fact actually supports a conclusion, which is what the following sentence disputes.
Describe the connection between which objection is conceded and whether the fairness is real.
questions.a: A writer may grant a small point while leaving the serious objection unmentioned, so the test is to find the strongest objection and ask whether the paragraph names it.

articles.note: This is the structural half of RI.8.6, taught a standard early. Students who can find the concession can usually find the author's position straight afterwards.

articles.title: The Paragraph That Reports Nothing Happened
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A result that shows no effect is harder to write up than one that shows an effect, and it is harder to publish, and for a long time most of them were never written up at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paragraph reporting such a result has an unusual job. It has to establish that the study could have found an effect if one had been there, because otherwise the finding is indistinguishable from having run a poor experiment.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So it opens by stating what was measured and how precisely. A confidence interval appears early, and a narrow interval around zero says something quite different from a wide one that includes large effects in both directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next sentences describe the study's power, which is the chance it had of detecting an effect of a given size. A study with low power that finds nothing has found nothing about the world.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only then does the paragraph state the result, and careful writing states it as a bound rather than as an absence. The phrasing is not we found no effect but any effect is smaller than this.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That distinction matters more than it looks. An absence is unprovable, a bound is a measurement, and the second can be combined with other studies while the first cannot be combined with anything.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Such paragraphs are now easier to find because trials are registered before they run, so a study that reports nothing can be matched against the plan it was registered with, and one that is never reported leaves a visible gap.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A result that shows no effect is harder to write up than one that shows an effect. It is harder to publish. For a long time most were never written up at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paragraph reporting such a result has an unusual job. It must show the study could have found an effect if one existed. Otherwise the finding looks like a poor experiment.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So it opens by saying what was measured and how precisely. A confidence interval appears early. A narrow interval around zero says something very different from a wide one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next sentences describe the study's power. That is the chance it had of detecting an effect of a given size. A low-powered study that finds nothing has found nothing about the world.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only then does the paragraph state the result. Careful writing states a bound, not an absence. Not we found no effect, but any effect is smaller than this.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That distinction matters more than it looks. An absence cannot be proved. A bound is a measurement. A bound can be combined with other studies. An absence cannot be combined with anything.

paras.label: G
paras.text: These paragraphs are easier to find now. Trials are registered before they run. A study that reports nothing can be checked against its plan. One never reported leaves a visible gap.

questions.q: Why must such a paragraph describe the study's power?
questions.a: Power is the chance the study had of detecting an effect of a given size, and a study with low power that finds nothing has found nothing about the world.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. stating a bound rather than an absence) and paragraph G (i.e. what registration changed).
Summarize how a paragraph reports a result that found no effect.
questions.a: It must first establish that the study could have detected an effect, so it states what was measured and how precisely, gives a confidence interval and describes the study's power. It then states the result as a bound rather than an absence, because a bound is a measurement that can be combined with other studies while an absence cannot.

questions.q:
power: the chance a study had of detecting an effect of a given size if one existed.
bound: a statement that any effect is smaller than a stated size, which is a measurement rather than an absence.
Describe the connection between registering a trial beforehand and noticing a missing result.
questions.a: A study that reports nothing can be matched against the plan it was registered with, and one that is never reported leaves a visible gap.

articles.note: The order of the sentences is the argument. Reporting the result before establishing the power would make the paragraph worthless, and students should be able to say why.

articles.title: The Definitions Section of a Law
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Many laws open with a section that does nothing but define words. It is skipped by almost every reader, including many who are otherwise reading carefully, and it frequently determines the outcome of every dispute the law produces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The convention is a single paragraph built from repeated clauses: in this Act, vehicle means, employee means, premises means. The repetition is deliberate, because a definition that varies in form invites argument about whether the variation meant something.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each clause is doing one of two opposite jobs. Some widen an ordinary word so it covers more than usual, and some narrow it so a familiar word excludes cases a reader would assume were included.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The widening clauses are the ones to watch. A definition saying vehicle includes any device for carrying a person by land is reaching for things nobody would call a vehicle in conversation, and that reach is the law's actual scope.

paras.label: E
paras.text: There is usually a sentence near the end doing something different again. It says that where a word is not defined here it carries its ordinary meaning, which quietly puts a dictionary into the statute.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order within the paragraph matters too. A term used inside another definition has to be defined before or alongside it, so the sequence often reveals which concept the drafters treated as basic.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading this section first changes the rest. A sentence later in the law that looked clear often turns out to be using at least one word in a sense that was fixed in a paragraph the reader skipped.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Many laws open with a section that only defines words. Almost every reader skips it. It frequently decides the outcome of every dispute the law produces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form is one paragraph of repeated clauses. In this Act, vehicle means. Employee means. Premises means. The repetition is deliberate. A definition that varies invites argument about the variation.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each clause does one of two opposite jobs. Some widen an ordinary word to cover more than usual. Some narrow it, so a familiar word excludes cases a reader would assume were in.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The widening clauses are the ones to watch. A definition saying vehicle includes any device for carrying a person by land reaches for things nobody would call a vehicle. That reach is the law's scope.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Near the end there is usually a different kind of sentence. It says that an undefined word carries its ordinary meaning. That quietly puts a dictionary inside the statute.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Order inside the paragraph matters too. A term used in another definition must be defined first or alongside. So the sequence shows which concept the drafters treated as basic.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Reading this section first changes the rest. A sentence that looked clear often uses a word in a sense fixed in a paragraph the reader skipped.

questions.q: What two opposite jobs can a definition clause do?
questions.a: Some widen an ordinary word so it covers more than usual, and some narrow it so a familiar word excludes cases a reader would assume were included.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the sentence about undefined words) and paragraph F (i.e. what the order of definitions reveals).
Summarize what a definitions section does and why it should be read first.
questions.a: It defines words in repeated clauses, each either widening an ordinary word beyond normal use or narrowing it to exclude cases a reader would assume, with a closing sentence giving undefined words their ordinary meaning. The order shows which concepts the drafters treated as basic, and a later sentence that looks clear may use a word in a sense fixed here.

questions.q:
statute: a written law passed by a legislature.
scope: how far a law reaches, which the widening definitions establish rather than the later sentences.
Describe the connection between skipping the definitions and misreading a later sentence.
questions.a: A sentence later in the law that looked clear often turns out to be using at least one word in a sense that was fixed in the paragraph the reader skipped.

articles.note: Bring one real definitions section. Ask which clauses widen and which narrow, then ask what the law would cover without them.

articles.title: One Paragraph of a Forecast Discussion
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.3 connections · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Behind the icons on a weather app there is a document most people never see. Forecasters write a discussion in prose, for other forecasters, explaining how they reached the forecast and where they are unsure.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A paragraph from one of these has a recognisable structure. It opens with the current situation, states what the computer models are showing, notes where the models disagree, and then gives the forecaster's judgement between them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The disagreement sentence is the most informative one in the paragraph. Two models placing a low pressure system a hundred kilometres apart produce very different weather for a particular town, and the public forecast cannot show that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Next comes the reasoning. A forecaster may prefer one model because it has handled this pattern well this season, or because its starting conditions used observations the other one lacked, and the preference is stated with its reason.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Confidence is given explicitly and in words. A paragraph will say high confidence in the timing and low confidence in the amount, which separates two things that a single percentage on a screen merges into one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last sentences usually say what would change the forecast. If the overnight model run shifts the track west, the whole picture changes, and naming that in advance is a commitment rather than a hedge.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The app shows a cloud with a number under it. The same forecast in prose shows the uncertainty, the disagreement, the reason for a choice, and the observation that would overturn it, which is four things the icon cannot carry.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Behind the icons on a weather app is a document most people never see. Forecasters write a discussion in prose, for other forecasters. It explains how they reached the forecast and where they are unsure.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A paragraph from one has a clear structure. It opens with the current situation. It says what the computer models show. It notes where the models disagree. Then it gives the forecaster's judgement.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The disagreement sentence is the most informative. Two models placing a low pressure system a hundred kilometres apart give very different weather for one town. The public forecast cannot show that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Next comes the reasoning. A forecaster may prefer one model because it handled this pattern well this season. Or because its starting data used observations the other lacked. The reason is stated.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Confidence is given in words. A paragraph will say high confidence in the timing and low confidence in the amount. One percentage on a screen merges those two things into one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last sentences say what would change the forecast. If the overnight run shifts the track west, the picture changes. Naming that in advance is a commitment, not a hedge.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The app shows a cloud with a number. The same forecast in prose shows uncertainty, disagreement, the reason for a choice, and what would overturn it. The icon cannot carry four things.

questions.q: Why is the disagreement sentence the most informative?
questions.a: Two models placing a low pressure system a hundred kilometres apart produce very different weather for a particular town, and the public forecast cannot show that.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. confidence being stated in words) and paragraph F (i.e. naming what would change the forecast).
Summarize the structure of a forecast discussion paragraph.
questions.a: It opens with the current situation, states what the models show, notes where they disagree, and gives the forecaster's judgement with a reason for preferring one. Confidence is stated in words so timing and amount are separated, and the closing sentences name the observation that would change the forecast.

questions.q:
model: a computer simulation of the atmosphere, several of which may disagree about the same day.
confidence: here, how sure a forecaster is about a particular element, stated separately for timing and amount.
Describe the connection between naming what would change the forecast and making a commitment.
questions.a: Saying in advance that an overnight shift in the track would change the whole picture is a commitment rather than a hedge, because it states beforehand what would overturn the forecast.

articles.note: Pull a real discussion from a weather service and read one paragraph aloud. Students can usually label all five moves on a second reading.

articles.title: The Paper That Answers Its Critics
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A scientific journal does not only print papers. It prints comments on papers, and replies to those comments, and the whole exchange is published under the names of the people having it, in the same volume as the work being argued about.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sequence is fixed. Someone publishes a result, another researcher writes a comment arguing it is wrong, the original authors reply, and all three appear in the record where anyone can read them together.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What a comment does is narrower than disagreement. It identifies a specific step: an analysis that should have excluded certain data, a control that was missing, an alternative explanation the paper did not rule out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reply is the interesting document, because a reply has only a few honest moves available. The authors can show the step was handled and say where, they can accept the point and state what survives it, or they can present new analysis.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a reply cannot do is ignore the objection and restate the original claim more firmly. Readers can see both texts at once, and a reply that does not engage is visible as such immediately.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The exchange also fixes a date. After a published comment, the objection is on the record, so later work that repeats the original claim without addressing it is making a choice rather than an oversight.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a field's disagreements are worth reading rather than avoiding. A paper on its own shows what its authors concluded; a paper with its comment and reply shows what the authors could defend when someone pushed.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A scientific journal does not only print papers. It prints comments on papers, and replies to those comments. The exchange is published under the names of the people having it.

paras.label: B

paras.label: G

questions.q: What does a comment on a paper usually identify?
questions.a: A specific step, such as an analysis that should have excluded certain data, a control that was missing, or an alternative explanation the paper did not rule out.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the honest moves available in a reply) and paragraph F (i.e. how the exchange fixes a date).
Summarize how comment and reply work and what they reveal.
questions.a: A result is published, a researcher comments naming a specific step that is wrong, and the authors reply, with all three in the record. A reply can show the step was handled, accept the point and say what survives, or present new analysis, but cannot ignore the objection, and after a published comment later work repeating the claim is making a choice.

questions.q:
control: a comparison built into an experiment so that an effect can be attributed to the thing being tested.
on the record: published where anyone can find it, so it cannot later be treated as unknown.
Describe the connection between both texts being published and a weak reply being obvious.
questions.a: Readers can see both texts at once, so a reply that does not engage with the objection is visible as such immediately.

articles.note: RI.8.6 asks how an author responds to conflicting evidence. This article describes the venue built for exactly that, which makes the standard concrete.

articles.title: The Report With a Minority View
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: When a committee is asked to investigate something, it is usually expected to agree. A single report carries more weight than several competing ones, and the people who appointed the committee generally want one answer they can act on.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sometimes a member will not sign. The usual mechanism is a separate statement printed inside the same report, placed after the main findings and labelled as a minority or dissenting view.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The placement is the point. Printing the disagreement inside the document means a reader of the report cannot avoid knowing that it exists, which would not be true if the member had resigned and written elsewhere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A good minority statement is narrow. It does not restate the whole investigation; it names the findings it accepts, identifies the one or two it does not, and says what evidence it thinks was weighed wrongly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The majority then has a decision to make. Some reports respond to the dissent directly in the main text, which strengthens both documents, and some leave it standing unanswered, which tells a reader something as well.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Minority statements have a particular history of being right. A dissent that was ignored at the time is sometimes the part of a report still being quoted decades later, usually after the thing it warned about happened.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is not an argument that dissents are usually correct, because most are not. It is an argument for printing them, since a report that shows its disagreement lets a later reader check who had seen what.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sometimes a member will not sign. The usual mechanism is a separate statement inside the same report. It comes after the main findings. It is labelled a minority or dissenting view.

paras.label: C

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: Minority statements have a history of being right. A dissent ignored at the time is sometimes the part still quoted decades later. Usually after the thing it warned about happened.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is not an argument that dissents are usually correct. Most are not. It is an argument for printing them. A report that shows its disagreement lets a later reader check who saw what.

questions.q: Why does it matter that a dissent is printed inside the report?
questions.a: A reader of the report cannot avoid knowing that it exists, which would not be true if the member had resigned and written elsewhere.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the majority's choice about responding) and paragraph G (i.e. the argument for printing dissents).
Summarize what a minority statement is and why it is printed.
questions.a: When a committee member will not sign, a separate statement is printed inside the same report naming the findings accepted, the one or two rejected and the evidence weighed wrongly. The majority may answer it or leave it standing, and although most dissents are not correct, printing them lets a later reader check who had seen what.

questions.q:
dissent: a statement by a member of a group disagreeing with the group's conclusion.
minority view: the position of the committee members who did not join the main findings.
Describe the connection between leaving a dissent unanswered and what a reader learns.
questions.a: Some reports respond to the dissent directly in the main text, which strengthens both documents, and some leave it standing unanswered, which tells a reader something as well.

articles.note: The last paragraph refuses the romantic version. Students who conclude that the dissenter is usually right have taken the opposite of what the text says.

articles.title: The Review That Weighs Studies
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: On most questions in medicine there is not one study but dozens, and they do not all agree. A systematic review is the document written to deal with that, and its method is as important as its conclusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins before any results are looked at. The authors write down what question they are asking, which studies will count, and how the studies will be assessed, and they publish that plan in advance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order protects against a specific failure. An author who reads the studies first and then writes the inclusion rules can produce any answer they want, simply by setting a boundary that excludes the inconvenient ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The search is then meant to be exhaustive rather than convenient. Reviewers search several databases, look for unpublished work, and write down how many studies they found and how many they excluded at each stage, with reasons.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each included study is assessed for risk of bias. A trial where participants knew which group they were in is not weighted the same as one where nobody did, and the assessment is reported study by study rather than averaged away.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then are results combined, and sometimes they should not be. If the studies measured different things in different populations, a single pooled number hides the disagreement instead of resolving it, and a careful review says so.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion of such a review carries weight because of everything that came before it. A review that announces its answer without showing the plan, the search and the assessment is an opinion with a bibliography.

paras.label: A
paras.text: On most questions in medicine there is not one study but dozens. They do not all agree. A systematic review deals with that. Its method matters as much as its conclusion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins before any results are seen. The authors write down the question, which studies will count, and how studies will be assessed. They publish that plan in advance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order protects against a specific failure. An author who reads the studies first and then writes the rules can produce any answer. They set a boundary that excludes the inconvenient ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The search is meant to be exhaustive, not convenient. Reviewers search several databases and look for unpublished work. They record how many studies they found and excluded, with reasons.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each included study is assessed for risk of bias. A trial where participants knew their group is not weighted like one where nobody did. The assessment is reported study by study.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only then are results combined, and sometimes they should not be. If studies measured different things in different populations, one pooled number hides the disagreement. A careful review says so.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion carries weight because of what came before it. A review that announces an answer without showing the plan, the search and the assessment is an opinion with a bibliography.

questions.q: Why is the plan published before the results are examined?
questions.a: An author who reads the studies first and then writes the inclusion rules can produce any answer they want by setting a boundary that excludes the inconvenient studies.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. assessing risk of bias study by study) and paragraph F (i.e. when results should not be combined).
Summarize what a systematic review does.
questions.a: It writes down the question, the inclusion rules and the assessment method before looking at results, searches exhaustively and records what was excluded and why, assesses each study for risk of bias separately, and only then combines results, saying so when studies measured different things in different populations and should not be pooled.

questions.q:
systematic review: a review that states its method in advance and applies it to every study it finds.
risk of bias: the ways a study's design could have pushed its result in a particular direction.
Describe the connection between the method and the weight of the conclusion.
questions.a: The conclusion carries weight because of the plan, the search and the assessment that came before it, and a review without those is an opinion with a bibliography.

articles.note: This is how a field answers conflicting evidence at scale. Pair it with The Paper That Answers Its Critics, which is the same job for one disagreement.

articles.title: The Textbook That Shows Two Views
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A history textbook has to decide what to do when historians disagree, and on a great many topics they do. The easy option is to pick one account and tell it plainly, and most textbooks written for younger readers do exactly that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There are reasons for it. A reader who does not yet know the basic events cannot evaluate a dispute about them, and a book that opens every topic with a controversy can leave a student unable to say what happened.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The cost appears later. A student taught one account with no sign that there was ever an argument will read a second account as an error, and will have no practice at the thing historians actually do.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Some textbooks handle it by setting two short passages side by side with their sources named, and asking what each emphasises. The arrangement is honest about there being a choice to make.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Done badly it becomes a habit of its own. Presenting every question as two balanced views implies the evidence is always evenly divided, and on many questions it is not, which is its own kind of distortion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The better versions distinguish the cases. Some disagreements are about what the evidence shows, some are about which evidence matters, and some are between a position with substantial support and one with very little.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What a reader can do is check whether a book ever says historians disagree. A textbook that never does is making a claim about its field, and the claim is almost certainly false.

paras.text: A history textbook must decide what to do when historians disagree. The easy option is to pick one account and tell it plainly. Most textbooks for younger readers do that.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: Better versions separate the cases. Some disagreements are about what the evidence shows. Some are about which evidence matters. Some are between a well-supported position and a weak one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A reader can check whether a book ever says historians disagree. A textbook that never does is making a claim about its field. That claim is almost certainly false.

questions.q: What is the argument for telling one account plainly?
questions.a: A reader who does not yet know the basic events cannot evaluate a dispute about them, and a book that opens every topic with a controversy can leave a student unable to say what happened.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the distortion of presenting every question as balanced) and paragraph F (i.e. the kinds of disagreement a better book distinguishes).
Summarize the problem a textbook faces when historians disagree.
questions.a: Telling one account plainly helps a reader who does not yet know the events, but a student taught that way reads a second account as an error. Setting two sourced passages side by side is honest, although presenting every question as balanced implies evidence is always evenly divided, so better books distinguish disagreements about what evidence shows from disagreements about which evidence matters.

questions.q:
account: one historian's telling of events, shaped by which evidence they emphasise.
distortion: a misleading impression created by how material is presented rather than by a false statement.
Describe the connection between a book never mentioning disagreement and a claim about the field.
questions.a: A textbook that never says historians disagree is making a claim about its field, and that claim is almost certainly false.

articles.note: Have students look at their own textbook for the word disagree or its equivalents. The count is usually low enough to be the lesson by itself.

articles.title: The Scientist Who Published a Correction
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Published research is sometimes wrong, and the system has two formal ways of saying so. A correction fixes an error while leaving the conclusion standing, and a retraction withdraws the paper entirely.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The distinction is about reach. A mislabelled axis or a wrong sample size in a table is corrected; an error that undermines the result, or evidence that the data were not what they were said to be, produces a retraction.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Both are published rather than quietly applied. The original paper stays in the record with a notice attached, because papers that have already been cited cannot be removed from the work that cited them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Authors do not always initiate these. Some corrections follow an outside reader finding the problem, and some retractions are issued by a journal over the authors' objection, and the notice usually says which happened.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That makes the wording of a notice worth reading. A notice saying the authors identified an error and reported it describes a different event from one saying the journal was unable to obtain the original data.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The incentives run against admitting anything. A correction is a public statement that a published result was wrong, and the people best placed to find an error are the authors, who have the least to gain from finding it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Which is why the researchers who correct their own work are worth noticing. The number of corrections a field publishes is not a measure of how often it is wrong; it is a measure of how often it says so.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Published research is sometimes wrong. The system has two formal ways of saying so. A correction fixes an error and leaves the conclusion standing. A retraction withdraws the paper.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The distinction is about reach. A mislabelled axis or a wrong sample size is corrected. An error that undermines the result, or data that were not what they were said to be, brings a retraction.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the wording of a notice is worth reading. The authors identified an error and reported it describes one event. The journal was unable to obtain the original data describes another.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So researchers who correct their own work are worth noticing. The number of corrections is not a measure of how often a field is wrong. It measures how often it says so.

questions.q: What is the difference between a correction and a retraction?
questions.a: A correction fixes an error while leaving the conclusion standing, and a retraction withdraws the paper entirely when an error undermines the result or the data were not what they were said to be.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the wording of a notice matters) and paragraph G (i.e. what a count of corrections measures).
Summarize how published research is corrected.
questions.a: A correction fixes an error and leaves the conclusion standing while a retraction withdraws the paper, and both are published with a notice attached because cited papers cannot be removed from the work citing them. Notices differ depending on whether authors reported the problem or a journal acted over their objection, and the incentives run against the people best placed to find an error.

questions.q:
retraction: the formal withdrawal of a published paper, leaving it in the record with a notice attached.
incentive: a reason to act in a particular way, which here runs against admitting an error.
Describe the connection between who is best placed to find an error and who gains least from finding it.
questions.a: The people best placed to find an error are the authors, who have the least to gain from finding it, because a correction is a public statement that a published result was wrong.

articles.note: The closing sentence reverses the obvious reading of a statistic. Ask what a field with zero corrections would most likely be doing.

articles.title: Why Every Flat Map Is Wrong
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A globe shows the earth accurately and is almost useless. It cannot be folded, carried in a pocket, printed in a book or displayed on a screen, and a flat map can do all of those things and cannot be accurate.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This is not a failure of effort. A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, and that is a proved result in geometry rather than a practical limitation that better techniques might remove.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So every projection chooses what to preserve. Mercator keeps angles correct, which is why a compass bearing is a straight line on it, and the price is area: Greenland appears comparable to Africa and is about a fourteenth of its size.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Equal-area projections make the opposite trade. They show the relative sizes of landmasses correctly and distort shape instead, so continents appear stretched, and they are unusable for the navigation Mercator was built for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The choice therefore depends on the job. A sailor and a person comparing the land area of countries need different maps, and arguing about which projection is correct without naming a purpose is arguing about nothing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A globe, a flat map and an interactive map that reprojects as you move each fail differently. The globe cannot show the whole surface at once, the flat map distorts, and the interactive one shows no overview at all.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What a reader can do is look for the projection's name, usually printed small at an edge. A map that does not say which projection it uses has withheld the one fact needed to know what it is distorting.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A globe shows the earth accurately and is almost useless. It cannot be folded, carried in a pocket, printed in a book or shown on a screen. A flat map can do all of that and cannot be accurate.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This is not a failure of effort. A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching. That is a proved result in geometry, not a limit that better techniques could remove.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So every projection chooses what to keep. Mercator keeps angles right, so a compass bearing is a straight line. The price is area. Greenland looks like Africa and is about a fourteenth of its size.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Equal-area projections trade the other way. They show relative sizes correctly and distort shape. Continents look stretched. They are unusable for the navigation Mercator was built for.

paras.text: So the choice depends on the job. A sailor and a person comparing land areas need different maps. Arguing about which projection is correct without naming a purpose is arguing about nothing.

questions.q: What does the Mercator projection preserve, and at what cost?
questions.a: It keeps angles correct, so a compass bearing is a straight line, and the price is area, with Greenland appearing comparable to Africa although it is about a fourteenth of its size.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the purpose decides the projection) and paragraph G (i.e. what a map that names no projection has withheld).
Summarize why no flat map can be accurate and what follows.
questions.a: A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, which is a proved geometric result, so every projection chooses what to preserve. Mercator keeps angles and distorts area while equal-area projections do the reverse, so the right choice depends on the job, and a globe, a flat map and an interactive map each fail in a different way.

questions.q:
projection: a systematic way of representing a curved surface on a flat one, each with its own distortions.
conformal: preserving angles, which is what Mercator does and why it suits navigation.
Describe the connection between naming a purpose and choosing a projection.
questions.a: A sailor and a person comparing the land area of countries need different maps, so arguing about which projection is correct without naming a purpose is arguing about nothing.

articles.note: RI.8.7 asks for advantages and disadvantages of mediums. Paragraph F makes it three mediums rather than two, which is where the comparison gets interesting.

articles.title: The Archive on Paper and on a Server
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter written on good paper and kept dry can be read in five hundred years by anyone who knows the language, with no equipment at all and no intervening effort. That is an unusual property, and it is worth stating plainly before discussing anything digital.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Digital storage is better at almost everything else. A server holds a collection in a fraction of the space, serves it to anyone anywhere, and lets a reader search a million pages for a phrase in under a second.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is worse at lasting. Storage media degrade within decades, and more importantly formats stop being readable, so a file saved in a word processor from thirty years ago may now require software nobody distributes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The response is active rather than passive. Digital preservation means copying collections to new media and migrating them to current formats on a schedule, which is a continuing cost rather than a one-off purchase.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That changes what an archive is. A paper archive survives neglect for a long time and is destroyed by fire or flood; a digital archive survives fire easily and is destroyed by twenty years of nobody paying the bill.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The failures are also differently visible. A damaged page announces itself, while a corrupted file may open and display what looks like the document with a section silently missing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Serious archives therefore use both. The original is kept because it is the thing itself and degrades slowly, and the scan is kept because it can be read, searched and copied, and neither substitutes for the other.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter on good paper, kept dry, can be read in five hundred years with no equipment. That is an unusual property. It is worth saying plainly before discussing anything digital.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Digital storage is better at almost everything else. A server holds a collection in little space. It serves anyone anywhere. It searches a million pages for a phrase in under a second.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is worse at lasting. Media degrade within decades. More importantly, formats stop being readable. A file from a word processor thirty years ago may need software nobody distributes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The response is active, not passive. Digital preservation means copying to new media and migrating to current formats on a schedule. That is a continuing cost, not a one-off purchase.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That changes what an archive is. A paper archive survives neglect and is destroyed by fire or flood. A digital archive survives fire easily and is destroyed by nobody paying the bill.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The failures are differently visible too. A damaged page announces itself. A corrupted file may open and display what looks like the document, with a section silently missing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So serious archives use both. The original is the thing itself and degrades slowly. The scan can be read, searched and copied. Neither replaces the other.

questions.q: Why is format obsolescence more serious than media degrading?
questions.a: A file saved in a word processor thirty years ago may now require software nobody distributes, so the file survives and still cannot be read.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how the two kinds of archive fail differently) and paragraph F (i.e. why a corrupted file is worse than a damaged page).
Summarize the advantages and disadvantages of paper and digital archives.
questions.a: Paper can be read in centuries with no equipment and survives neglect, while digital storage saves space, reaches anyone and allows instant search but degrades and loses format support. Digital preservation is a continuing cost rather than a purchase, a damaged page announces itself while a corrupted file may hide a missing section, so archives keep both.

questions.q:
migration: copying files into a current format so they remain readable as software changes.
obsolescence: a format or medium falling out of use, so that material stored in it can no longer be opened.
Describe the connection between a digital archive's strength against fire and its weakness over time.
questions.a: A digital archive survives fire easily because it can be copied anywhere, and is destroyed by twenty years of nobody paying the bill to keep copying and migrating it.

articles.note: The failure modes are the heart of this. Ask which of the two archives a student would choose for a document that must survive a century with no budget.

articles.title: The Diagram and the Equation
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A physics problem about a block on a slope can be given two ways. One is a diagram with arrows on it. The other is a set of equations, and both describe exactly the same situation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram is better at the first step. It shows how many forces there are, roughly which way each points, and which ones must balance, and a mistake like forgetting friction is visible as a missing arrow.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is worse at the second step. A diagram cannot be solved. Arrows do not combine, an angle drawn by hand is not a measured angle, and a picture does not say what happens when the slope gets steeper.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The equations do what the diagram cannot. They can be rearranged, combined and taken to a limit, and the same expression that answers this problem answers every problem of the same shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They are worse at catching a missing term. An equation with a force left out still looks like an equation, it still solves, and it returns an answer that is wrong without looking wrong.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Which is why physicists teach the diagram first and then do not throw it away. The picture is where the model gets checked, and the symbols are where it gets solved, and a student using only one of them fails in a predictable direction.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is a general point about mediums rather than a point about physics. Each one makes a particular kind of error easy to see, and switching between them is how the errors each one hides get caught.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram is better at the first step. It shows how many forces there are and which way each points. It shows which must balance. Forgetting friction is visible as a missing arrow.

paras.label: E

paras.label: F

paras.label: G

questions.q: What kind of mistake does a diagram make visible?
questions.a: A missing force, such as forgetting friction, shows up as a missing arrow.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why an equation hides a missing term) and paragraph G (i.e. the general point about mediums).
Summarize what a diagram and an equation each do well.
questions.a: A diagram shows how many forces there are and which way they point, so a missing one is visible, but it cannot be solved or taken to a limit. Equations can be rearranged and generalised but an equation with a term left out still solves and returns a wrong answer that does not look wrong, so each medium catches errors the other hides.

questions.q:
limit: in mathematics, what an expression approaches as a quantity is pushed toward an extreme such as a steeper slope.
term: one of the separate quantities added together in an equation, which can be omitted without the equation looking broken.
Describe the connection between using only one medium and failing predictably.
questions.a: The picture is where the model gets checked and the symbols are where it gets solved, so a student using only one of them fails in a predictable direction.

articles.note: The last paragraph generalises past physics, which is the RI.8.7 move. Ask for another pair of mediums that divide checking from solving the same way.

articles.title: The Museum Case and the Scan
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An object in a museum case is the thing itself. It has a size a visitor can stand next to, a surface that catches light, and a presence that comes partly from knowing it is not a copy.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is also almost unreachable. It can be seen from one side, at one distance, in one building, by whoever can travel there, and it cannot be handled, turned over or looked at from underneath.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A high-resolution scan reverses nearly all of that. It can be rotated, enlarged, measured, lit from any angle, examined by a researcher on another continent, and handed to a class in a school with no museum nearby.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The scan also supports work the object cannot. Measurements can be taken from it without touching anything, tool marks can be exaggerated with artificial lighting, and a fragment can be compared with a fragment held elsewhere.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it loses is scale and material. A screen gives no sense of mass, a surface rendered smoothly loses the roughness a hand would feel, and nothing in a file tells a viewer that an object is heavy.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also the question of what a scan is of. A scan is a measurement made at a moment with a particular instrument, so it records the object as it is now, including damage, restoration and the decisions of whoever did the scanning.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Treating the two as alternatives is the error. A scan does not replace an object any more than a photograph of a person replaces them, and an object in a case does not give a researcher the measurements they need.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An object in a museum case is the thing itself. It has a size a visitor can stand next to. It has a surface that catches light. Part of its presence is knowing it is not a copy.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also what a scan is of. It is a measurement made at a moment with one instrument. It records the object as it is now, including damage, restoration and the scanner's choices.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Treating the two as alternatives is the error. A scan no more replaces an object than a photograph replaces a person. And an object in a case does not give a researcher measurements.

questions.q: What work does a scan support that the object cannot?
questions.a: Measurements can be taken without touching anything, tool marks can be exaggerated with artificial lighting, and a fragment can be compared with a fragment held elsewhere.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what a scan loses) and paragraph F (i.e. what a scan is actually a record of).
Summarize the advantages and disadvantages of an object and a scan.
questions.a: An object in a case is the thing itself with real scale and presence but can only be seen from one side in one building and cannot be handled. A scan can be rotated, measured and sent anywhere and supports work the object cannot, but it loses scale and material and records the object as it was at one moment with one instrument.

questions.q:
render: to produce an image of an object from measured data, which can smooth a surface the original does not have.
restoration: repair work done to an object, which a scan records as part of the object's present state.
Describe the connection between a scan being a measurement and what it records.
questions.a: A scan is a measurement made at a moment with a particular instrument, so it records the object as it is now, including damage, restoration and the decisions of whoever did the scanning.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the one students skip, i.e. a scan is dated. Ask what a scan made before a restoration would be worth.

articles.title: The Photograph That Is Not a Photograph
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums, for example print or digital text, video or multimedia, to present a particular topic or idea.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.9 conflicting texts · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A famous image of a nebula looks like a photograph of something a traveller could fly past and see. It is not, and almost everything that makes it striking is a decision rather than an observation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The telescope did not record colour. It recorded brightness through a series of narrow filters, each admitting light of one particular wavelength, and each exposure came back as a grey image.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Those filters are usually chosen for chemistry rather than appearance. One admits the light emitted by hydrogen, another by oxygen, another by sulphur, so each grey frame is a map of where one element is.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The colour image is built by assigning each frame to red, green or blue and combining them. The assignment is a choice, and a different assignment of the same data produces an image with completely different colours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is not deception, and the people doing it say so in the caption. The point is to make a scientific distinction visible, so two regions in different colours differ in composition, which a true-colour image would not show.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The trouble is what happens to the image afterwards. It is reproduced without its caption, and a reader who meets it on a screen has no way of knowing that the colours encode elements rather than appearance.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The medium is doing the work here. A labelled diagram of the same data would be read as an interpretation, and the same information in the form of a photograph is read as a view, because that is what photographs usually are.

questions.q: What did the telescope actually record?
questions.a: Brightness through a series of narrow filters, each admitting light of one particular wavelength, with each exposure coming back as a grey image.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the colour assignment is not deception) and paragraph G (i.e. why the medium changes how it is read).
Summarize how such an image is made and why it misleads once shared.
questions.a: A telescope records brightness through narrow filters chosen for chemistry, so each grey frame maps one element, and a colour image is built by assigning frames to red, green and blue. The purpose is to make composition visible and the caption says so, but the image is reproduced without its caption and a photograph is read as a view rather than an interpretation.

questions.q:
filter: a device admitting only light of a particular wavelength, so each exposure records one part of the spectrum.
encode: to represent one thing by another, as colour here represents which element is present.
Describe the connection between the form of the image and how a reader treats it.
questions.a: A labelled diagram of the same data would be read as an interpretation, and the same information in the form of a photograph is read as a view, because that is what photographs usually are.

articles.note: The claim is about the medium rather than about honesty. Ask what would change if the same data were published as a labelled map instead.

articles.title: Does the Full Moon Change Behaviour?
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: The belief that a full moon changes human behaviour is widespread and old. Nurses, police officers and teachers report busier nights, and the reports are sincere, numerous and offered as evidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Testing it is straightforward, because the moon's phase is known in advance for every date in history. Researchers can take years of records and compare the nights without deciding anything after the fact.

paras.label: C
paras.text: This has been done many times with births, emergency admissions, crimes and calls to police lines. Reviews gathering those studies together have repeatedly found no consistent effect.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reports are still worth explaining rather than dismissing. A busy night followed by someone saying it must be a full moon creates a memory that joins the two; a busy night with no moon mentioned creates no such memory.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is a mechanism, and it predicts what should be found: the belief should be strongest among people who work nights, which it is, and the effect should vanish when records are counted, which it does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A particular kind of argument is often offered in reply. The moon moves the tides, people are mostly water, so the moon must move something in a person, and the reasoning is confident and has nothing to do with the question.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Tides are produced by the difference in pull across an ocean-sized object. A person is not large enough for that difference to amount to anything, and in any case an effect this would predict would show up in the records, which it does not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Testing it is straightforward. The moon's phase is known in advance for every date in history. Researchers can take years of records and compare nights without deciding anything afterwards.

paras.label: C
paras.text: This has been done many times. With births, emergency admissions, crimes and calls to police lines. Reviews gathering those studies have repeatedly found no consistent effect.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reports still deserve explaining rather than dismissing. A busy night plus someone saying it must be a full moon creates a memory joining the two. A busy night with no moon mentioned creates none.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is a mechanism, and it predicts things. The belief should be strongest among people who work nights, and it is. The effect should vanish when records are counted, and it does.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A particular reply is often offered. The moon moves the tides. People are mostly water. So the moon must move something in a person. The reasoning is confident and irrelevant.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Tides come from the difference in pull across an ocean-sized object. A person is not large enough for that difference to amount to anything. And such an effect would show in the records.

questions.q: Why is this belief easy to test?
questions.a: The moon's phase is known in advance for every date in history, so researchers can take years of records and compare the nights without deciding anything after the fact.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the mechanism that explains the reports) and paragraph F (i.e. the irrelevant argument offered in reply).
Summarize the evidence about the full moon and the argument offered against it.
questions.a: Phases are known for every date, so records of births, admissions and crimes can be compared, and reviews have repeatedly found no consistent effect. The sincere reports are explained by a busy night and a remark about the moon creating a joint memory, and the reply that the moon moves tides and people are mostly water is irrelevant because tides depend on the difference in pull across an ocean-sized object.

questions.q:
review: a study that gathers many earlier studies and assesses them together.
irrelevant: not bearing on the question at hand, however true or confident the statement may be.
Describe the connection between the tide argument and the records.
questions.a: An effect of the kind that argument predicts would show up in the records of births, admissions and crimes, and it does not.

articles.note: RI.8.8 adds recognising irrelevant evidence. Paragraph F is a true statement about tides doing no work at all, which is the shape students must learn to spot.

articles.title: The Petition With a Thousand Signatures
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A petition arrives at a council meeting with a thousand signatures asking that a road be closed to through traffic. The number is read out at the start, before anything else in the document is described, and it is treated as the strongest part of the case.

paras.label: B
paras.text: For some questions it genuinely is. If the question is whether residents want the road closed, a thousand signatures is direct evidence about what residents want, which is the thing being asked.

paras.label: C
paras.text: For other questions it is no evidence at all. If the claim is that closing the road will reduce accidents, the number of people who believe that has no bearing on whether it is true.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Mixing the two is where petitions go wrong. A document that says a thousand residents agree the closure will improve safety is offering a count of opinions in the place where a traffic study belongs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reverse error is just as common. A council that dismisses a petition because signatures are not data has dismissed real evidence about preference, which is one of the things a council is supposed to weigh.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Some additional questions sharpen it. How many signatories live on the road, how were they asked, and what did the sheet they signed actually say, because a petition is also a survey with no controls.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The habit worth building is to split the document. Mark every sentence that reports what people want and every sentence that claims what will happen, and then ask whether the signatures support the second kind.
