questions.q: When is a signature count genuine evidence?
questions.a: When the question is what residents want, because a thousand signatures is direct evidence about preference, which is the thing being asked.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the reverse error of dismissing a petition) and paragraph G (i.e. the habit of splitting the document).
Summarize when signatures count as evidence and when they do not.
questions.a: A signature count is direct evidence about what people want and no evidence about what a measure will do, so a petition claiming a closure will improve safety offers opinions where a traffic study belongs. Dismissing a petition entirely is the opposite error, since preference is something a council must weigh, and the habit is to mark which sentences claim preference and which claim consequence.

questions.q:
petition: a signed document asking an authority to act, which records preference rather than consequence.
controls: features of a survey that stop the way a question is asked from shaping the answer, which a petition lacks.
Describe the connection between the kind of claim being made and whether signatures support it.
questions.a: Signatures are direct evidence about preference, so they support a sentence about what people want and do not support a sentence about whether closing the road will reduce accidents.

articles.note: Both errors are worth naming, because students who learn the first one often commit the second within a week.

articles.title: The Testimonial in a Health Claim
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An advertisement for a supplement carries a photograph and a quotation. Someone describes the pain they had for years, the product they took, and how much better they feel now, and the account is specific, detailed and convincing in a way a statistic is not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first thing to notice is that it may well be true. Treating a testimonial as a lie misses the point, because the problems with it survive the account being completely honest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most conditions vary. People seek a remedy when symptoms are at their worst, and symptoms at their worst tend to improve afterwards whatever is done, which produces a real recovery with no cause attached.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is also a selection problem. The advertisement contains the people who improved, and the people who took the product and felt nothing were not photographed and did not send a quotation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both of these are why trials use a comparison group. Half receive the product and half do not, neither group knows which, and the question becomes whether the first group improved more than the second.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A testimonial cannot do that arithmetic even in principle. It is one person, with no comparison group and no record of what would have happened otherwise, selected for inclusion precisely because of the outcome, and adding nine more testimonials produces ten of the same thing rather than evidence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Watch for the sentence that follows. Advertisements often pair a testimonial with a phrase such as studies suggest, which borrows the authority of research for a claim the testimonial above it cannot support.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An advertisement for a supplement carries a photograph and a quotation. Someone describes their pain, the product they took, and how much better they feel. The account is specific and convincing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first thing to notice is that it may well be true. Calling a testimonial a lie misses the point. The problems with it survive the account being completely honest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most conditions vary. People look for a remedy when symptoms are worst. Symptoms at their worst tend to improve afterwards whatever is done. That gives a real recovery with no cause attached.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is also a selection problem. The advertisement contains people who improved. People who took the product and felt nothing were not photographed and sent no quotation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why trials use a comparison group. Half get the product and half do not. Neither group knows which. The question becomes whether the first group improved more than the second.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A testimonial cannot do that arithmetic even in principle. One person. No comparison. Selected because of the outcome. Nine more testimonials give ten of the same thing, not evidence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Watch the sentence that follows. Advertisements often pair a testimonial with a phrase like studies suggest. That borrows the authority of research for a claim the testimonial cannot support.

questions.q: Why can a true testimonial still be poor evidence?
questions.a: People seek a remedy when symptoms are at their worst and symptoms tend to improve afterwards whatever is done, so a real recovery occurs with no cause attached.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the selection problem) and paragraph E (i.e. what a comparison group does instead).
Summarize why testimonials cannot support a health claim.
questions.a: A testimonial may be entirely honest, but people seek remedies when symptoms are worst and symptoms then improve anyway, and advertisements contain only the people who improved. A trial compares a group receiving the product with one that is not, which a testimonial cannot do even in principle, and adding more testimonials produces more of the same thing rather than evidence.

questions.q:
testimonial: a personal account of a product's effect, offered as evidence that it works.
comparison group: the people in a trial who do not receive the treatment, against whom the treated group is measured.
Describe the connection between how testimonials are collected and what they can show.
questions.a: The advertisement contains the people who improved, because those who took the product and felt nothing were not photographed and did not send a quotation.

articles.note: Paragraph G is the irrelevant-evidence clause of RI.8.8, i.e. a vague appeal to studies attached to an account that is not one.

articles.title: The Argument That Changes the Subject
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A council is debating whether to put a bus lane on a main road. One speaker argues that the lane will slow deliveries, and a second rises to say that the first speaker does not even live in the district.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That may be true and it is not a reply. The claim on the table is about deliveries, and whether it is correct does not depend in any way on where the person making it sleeps.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Dealing with the speaker rather than the claim is the oldest move in the catalogue. It works because an audience that has lost confidence in a person stops examining what the person said, which is the effect it is produced for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A related move answers a different question than the one asked. Asked whether the lane will slow deliveries, a supporter who replies that the road has needed investment for years has said something true and answered nothing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third version raises the stakes until the question disappears. If the debate becomes whether a speaker is against public transport in general, the specific question about delivery times has quietly left the room.

paras.label: F
paras.text: These are hard to catch in the moment because they feel like continuations. Each new sentence follows the one before it, and the drift away from the question happens one reasonable-sounding step at a time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The defence is to write the question down. Keep the sentence that was actually asked in front of you and check each contribution against it, because a contribution that does not touch it is not part of the argument.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A council is debating a bus lane on a main road. One speaker argues the lane will slow deliveries. A second rises to say the first speaker does not even live in the district.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That may be true and it is not a reply. The claim is about deliveries. Whether it is correct does not depend on where the person making it sleeps.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third version raises the stakes until the question disappears. If the debate becomes whether someone opposes public transport in general, the question about delivery times has left the room.

paras.label: F
paras.text: These are hard to catch in the moment. They feel like continuations. Each sentence follows the one before. The drift happens one reasonable-sounding step at a time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The defence is to write the question down. Keep the sentence that was asked in front of you. Check each contribution against it. One that does not touch it is not part of the argument.

questions.q: Why is pointing out where a speaker lives not a reply?
questions.a: The claim on the table is about deliveries, and whether it is correct does not depend in any way on where the person making it sleeps.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why these moves are hard to catch) and paragraph G (i.e. the defence of writing the question down).
Summarize the three ways an argument can leave its own question.
questions.a: A speaker can be attacked instead of the claim, which works because an audience that loses confidence stops examining what was said; a different question can be answered truthfully and irrelevantly; and the stakes can be raised until the original question disappears. These feel like continuations, so the defence is to keep the question written down and check each contribution against it.

questions.q:
relevant: bearing on the question actually asked, which a true statement may fail to be.
drift: the gradual movement of a discussion away from its question, one reasonable-sounding step at a time.
Describe the connection between each sentence following the last and the question being lost.
questions.a: The moves feel like continuations because each new sentence follows the one before it, so the drift away from the question happens one reasonable-sounding step at a time.

articles.note: Run a short debate in class with the question written on the board, and have one student mark every contribution that does not touch it.

articles.title: The Chart With a Cut Axis
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.5 paragraph structure · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bar chart shows two columns, and the second is visibly twice the height of the first. The impression is immediate, and it is produced by the drawing rather than by the numbers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The key is at the bottom left. The vertical axis does not start at zero; it starts at a value chosen to sit just below the smaller bar, so the part shown is only the top slice of each column.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The effect is dramatic. Two values of 48 and 52 drawn from zero look almost identical, and drawn from 47 one looks twice the other, with the same two numbers printed above them in both versions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cutting an axis is not automatically dishonest. On a line chart tracking a quantity that never goes near zero, such as body temperature, starting at zero wastes the whole chart on empty space and hides the variation that matters.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rule that actually works is about what the shape encodes. A bar says compare these lengths, so a bar chart must start at zero, and a line says watch this move, so a line may legitimately start anywhere.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are other versions of the same trick. A second axis with a different scale, a time range beginning at a convenient year, and unequal spacing along the bottom all change a shape without touching a number.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the first thing to read on any chart is the axes, before the shape. The shape is the part that persuades, and it is produced by decisions that are printed in small type at the edges.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A bar chart shows two columns. The second is visibly twice the height of the first. The impression is immediate. It is produced by the drawing, not by the numbers.

paras.label: B

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read the axes first, before the shape. The shape is the part that persuades. It is produced by decisions printed in small type at the edges.

questions.q: How can 48 and 52 be made to look twice as different?
questions.a: By starting the vertical axis at 47 instead of zero, so only the top slice of each column is shown, while the same two numbers are printed above them.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. when cutting an axis is reasonable) and paragraph E (i.e. the rule about what the shape encodes).
Summarize when a cut axis misleads and when it does not.
questions.a: Starting a vertical axis above zero shows only the top slice of each column, so 48 and 52 can be drawn to look twice as different. A bar encodes length so it must start at zero, while a line encodes movement and may start anywhere, which is why a temperature chart starting at zero would waste the space and hide the variation.

questions.q:
axis: the scaled line along the side or bottom of a chart, whose starting value controls the shape.
encode: to represent a quantity by a visual feature such as length or position, which determines what a chart may do.
Describe the connection between what a bar encodes and the rule about zero.
questions.a: A bar says compare these lengths, so a bar chart must start at zero, while a line says watch this move and may legitimately start anywhere.

articles.note: The point is a rule students can apply, not a blanket suspicion. Give them one chart that cuts its axis correctly and one that does not.

articles.title: Two Inquiries Into One Disaster
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: The space shuttle Challenger broke apart in January 1986, shortly after launch, killing all seven aboard. A presidential commission was appointed, and it produced a report within months.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The commission established the immediate cause without serious dispute. A rubber seal in a joint of a solid rocket booster failed to close the joint at the unusually low temperature on the morning of the launch.

paras.label: C
paras.text: On that point there is no conflict between the texts. The physical finding was agreed by everyone, demonstrated in a public hearing with a piece of the material and a glass of iced water, and it has never been contested.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The conflict is about the second question, which is how the decision to launch was made. The main report describes a flawed decision-making process, and it is written in the measured language of an official document.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Richard Feynman, a member of the commission, did not think the main report said what the evidence showed. His own analysis was published as an appendix, separately, after he made clear he would not otherwise sign.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That appendix reports that management put the chance of a catastrophic failure at about one in a hundred thousand while engineers working on the same hardware put it nearer one in a hundred, and it calls the gap a failure of the organisation rather than of a process.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the two texts agree entirely about the seal and disagree about what the seal demonstrates. One is a disagreement about fact and there is none here; the other is about interpretation, and that is where the whole dispute sits.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The space shuttle Challenger broke apart in January 1986, shortly after launch. All seven aboard died. A presidential commission was appointed. It produced a report within months.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The commission established the immediate cause without serious dispute. A rubber seal in a joint of a solid rocket booster failed to close at the unusually low temperature that morning.

paras.label: C
paras.text: On that point the texts do not conflict. Everyone agreed the physical finding. It was shown in a public hearing with a piece of the material and a glass of iced water. It has never been contested.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The conflict is about the second question. How was the decision to launch made? The main report describes a flawed process. It is written in the measured language of an official document.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Richard Feynman, a commission member, did not think the report said what the evidence showed. His own analysis appeared as a separate appendix, after he made clear he would not otherwise sign.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The appendix reports that management put the chance of catastrophic failure near one in a hundred thousand. Engineers on the same hardware put it nearer one in a hundred. He called the gap an organisational failure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the two texts agree entirely about the seal and disagree about what it shows. One kind of disagreement is about fact, and there is none here. The other is interpretation, and that is the whole dispute.

questions.q: What did the commission establish without dispute?
questions.a: That a rubber seal in a joint of a solid rocket booster failed to close the joint at the unusually low temperature on the morning of the launch.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the appendix was published separately) and paragraph G (i.e. where the two texts actually disagree).
Summarize what the two documents agree and disagree about.
questions.a: Both agree that a rubber seal failed to close at a low temperature, a finding demonstrated publicly and never contested. They disagree about how the launch decision was made, with the main report describing a flawed process and Feynman's separately published appendix reporting that management estimated catastrophic failure at one in a hundred thousand while engineers said one in a hundred, which he called an organisational failure.

questions.q:
appendix: a document attached to a report but standing apart from its main text.
catastrophic failure: a failure that destroys the vehicle, which is what the two estimates disagreed about the likelihood of.
Describe the connection between the two estimates of failure and Feynman's conclusion.
questions.a: Management put the chance at about one in a hundred thousand and engineers at nearer one in a hundred, and he treated that gap as a failure of the organisation rather than of a process.

articles.note: RI.8.9 asks students to locate a disagreement as fact or interpretation. This case is unusually clean, because the factual half is settled and the texts still conflict.

articles.title: Two Counts of the Same Crowd
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: After a large public gathering, two numbers appear. The organisers give one figure, the authorities give another, and the two often differ by a factor of three or more for the same afternoon in the same square.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Neither side has to be lying for this to happen. Counting a crowd is a measurement problem, and a figure depends on decisions that are rarely stated: which area was counted, at what time, and what density was assumed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The standard method multiplies area by density. A photograph taken from above is divided into zones, a density is estimated for each, and the total depends heavily on whether a zone is judged to hold one person per square metre or four.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Time is the second variable. A march passes a point over several hours, so a count at the densest moment and a count of everyone who attended at any point are different quantities, and both can be called the size of the crowd.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Area is the third. Including the side streets and the park at the edge can double a figure, and a photograph taken from one end makes a judgement about the boundary that the caption rarely records.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the first question is not who is right but what each number measures. Two figures three times apart may both be accurate answers to questions that differ in area, in timing and in assumed density.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is a disagreement about fact rather than interpretation, which is what makes it solvable. Publishing the photograph, the zone boundaries and the densities used turns an argument about numbers into an argument about method, which can be settled.

paras.label: A

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

questions.q: What three decisions does a crowd figure depend on?
questions.a: Which area was counted, at what time, and what density was assumed for each zone.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why timing changes the quantity) and paragraph G (i.e. why this disagreement is solvable).
Summarize why two counts of one crowd can differ so much.
questions.a: A crowd figure is produced by multiplying area by assumed density, so it depends on which area was included, at what moment, and whether a zone is judged to hold one person per square metre or four. A march counted at its densest moment and everyone who attended are different quantities, so two figures far apart may both be accurate answers to different questions.

questions.q:
density: the number of people per unit of area, estimated for each zone and multiplying the total.
zone: a section a photograph is divided into so that a separate density can be estimated for each.
Describe the connection between publishing the method and settling the argument.
questions.a: Publishing the photograph, the zone boundaries and the densities used turns an argument about numbers into an argument about method, which can be settled.

articles.note: Pair with grade 8's What Counts as a City. Both are disagreements about fact that dissolve once each side states what it measured.

articles.title: Two Studies That Disagree About Coffee
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: One study reports that coffee drinkers live longer. Another reports no benefit. Both are published, both are large, and both were conducted by competent researchers who are not disputing each other's honesty.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Neither assigned anyone to drink coffee. Both followed groups of people who had already made that choice, recorded what happened over years, and compared the groups, which is the only practical design for a question like this.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That design has a known weakness. People who drink coffee differ from people who do not in many other ways, and some of those ways affect health directly, so a difference in outcome may belong to something else entirely.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Researchers adjust for the differences they can measure. One study may adjust for smoking, income and exercise, and another for those plus diet and existing illness, and the two will then report different numbers from similar data.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The definitions differ too. One study's heavy drinker is four cups a day and another's is two, the populations are from different countries with different drinking habits, and the follow-up periods are different lengths.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So where do they actually disagree? Rarely about a fact. The underlying observations are usually compatible, and the conflict is in interpretation: which adjustments were appropriate and how much a remaining difference should be trusted.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a single nutrition study is almost never worth changing anything for. The useful document is the review that reads a field's studies together and reports where their methods differ, which is where the conflict actually lives.

paras.label: A
paras.text: One study reports that coffee drinkers live longer. Another reports no benefit. Both are published and large. Both come from competent researchers who do not dispute each other's honesty.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Neither assigned anyone to drink coffee. Both followed groups who had already chosen, recorded what happened over years, and compared them. That is the only practical design for this question.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That design has a known weakness. Coffee drinkers differ from non-drinkers in many other ways. Some of those ways affect health directly. A difference in outcome may belong to something else.

paras.label: F

paras.label: G

questions.q: What is the known weakness of following people who already made a choice?
questions.a: People who drink coffee differ from people who do not in many other ways, and some of those ways affect health directly, so a difference in outcome may belong to something else.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the differing definitions) and paragraph F (i.e. where the disagreement actually lies).
Summarize why two coffee studies can disagree.
questions.a: Neither assigns anyone to drink coffee, so both follow people who already chose and differ in other ways that affect health. Researchers adjust for what they can measure and adjust for different things, define a heavy drinker differently and study different populations over different periods, so the observations are usually compatible and the conflict is about which adjustments were appropriate.

questions.q:
adjust: to account statistically for a known difference between groups so it does not explain the result.
follow-up: the period over which a study tracks the people in it after recording their habits.
Describe the connection between the adjustments chosen and the numbers reported.
questions.a: One study may adjust for smoking, income and exercise and another for those plus diet and existing illness, and the two will then report different numbers from similar data.

articles.note: Students expect conflicting studies to mean someone is wrong. The answer here is that the conflict is in interpretation, which the previous article prepared them to name.

articles.title: Two Maps of the Same War
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two newspapers print a map of the same conflict on the same day. The front lines are drawn in different places, the shaded areas differ, and some towns appear on one map and not the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of that is genuine disagreement about fact. Who holds a particular town on a particular morning may be unknown, disputed on the ground, or changing hourly, and two sources with different contacts will say different things.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Much of it is not about facts at all. A map has to decide what counts as holding territory, and a force present on a road in daylight and absent at night is treated as holding it by one convention and not by another.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Shading makes this worse. A solid colour over a district implies uniform control, and a situation where a government holds the towns and someone else moves freely between them cannot be drawn that way honestly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Names carry a position too. A town with two names in two languages has to be labelled somehow, and whichever is chosen is read by someone as a claim, including when the mapmaker meant only to be understood.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What is omitted is hardest to see. A map showing only the front line and not the refugee movements, or only territory and not who controls the electricity, has chosen a subject as much as a style.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Comparing two maps therefore means asking three questions in order. Where do they disagree about who holds what, where do they use different definitions of holding, and what has each chosen not to put on the page at all?

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two newspapers print a map of the same conflict on the same day. The front lines sit in different places. The shaded areas differ. Some towns appear on one map and not the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of that is real disagreement about fact. Who holds a town on a given morning may be unknown, disputed, or changing hourly. Two sources with different contacts will say different things.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Much of it is not about facts. A map must decide what counts as holding territory. A force on a road by day and gone by night is holding it under one convention and not another.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Shading makes this worse. A solid colour over a district implies uniform control. A government holding the towns while someone else moves between them cannot be drawn that way honestly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Names carry a position too. A town with two names in two languages must be labelled somehow. Whichever is chosen is read as a claim, even when the mapmaker meant only to be understood.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What is left out is hardest to see. A map showing the front line and not refugee movements, or territory and not who controls the electricity, has chosen a subject as much as a style.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So comparing two maps means asking three questions in order. Where do they disagree about who holds what? Where do they define holding differently? What has each left off the page?

questions.q: Why can two maps differ without either being wrong about who is where?
questions.a: A map has to decide what counts as holding territory, and a force present on a road in daylight and absent at night is treated as holding it by one convention and not by another.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what solid shading implies) and paragraph G (i.e. the three questions to ask in order).
Summarize why two maps of one conflict differ.
questions.a: Some differences are genuine disagreements about who holds a town on a given morning, but a map must also define what holding means, and solid shading implies uniform control that may not exist. Names carry claims and omissions are hardest to see, so comparing two maps means asking where they disagree on fact, where they define holding differently, and what each left out.

questions.q:
convention: an agreed rule for representing something, such as what counts as holding territory.
omission: what a map leaves out, which shapes the reader's understanding without appearing on the page.
Describe the connection between solid shading and a situation it cannot represent.
questions.a: A solid colour over a district implies uniform control, so a situation where a government holds the towns and someone else moves freely between them cannot be drawn that way honestly.

articles.note: The three questions in paragraph G are the standard restated as a procedure. They work on any two documents, not only maps.

articles.title: Two Dates for the Same Site
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
 Spiral: RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.6 point of view · RI.8.8 claims and evidence · RI.8.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: An archaeological site is excavated and two dates are published for the same layer. One comes from radiocarbon measurement of charcoal, and the other from the position of the layer within the sequence of deposits above and below it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The methods answer slightly different questions. Radiocarbon dates the death of the organism the sample came from, and stratigraphy dates the layer relative to the layers around it, so the two are not measuring the same event.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That gap explains a classic conflict. A piece of charcoal from long-dead wood can be older than the fire it was burned in, so a radiocarbon date may be genuinely correct and still predate the human activity it is being used to date.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Material can also move. Burrowing animals, roots and later digging carry small objects downward through a sequence, so a sample can be recovered from a layer it was not deposited in and date that layer wrongly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Calibration adds a further step. Radiocarbon years are not calendar years, and converting between them uses a curve built from tree rings, which has flat stretches where a single measurement corresponds to a range of several centuries.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the first question when two dates conflict is what each one dated. A disagreement between the death of a tree and the position of a layer is not a disagreement about when people were there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Where that does not resolve it, the conflict is real and is usually settled by more samples. Several dates from several materials in several layers constrain a sequence in a way one measurement from one piece of charcoal never can.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A site is excavated and two dates are published for the same layer. One comes from radiocarbon measurement of charcoal. The other comes from the layer's position in the sequence of deposits.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The methods answer slightly different questions. Radiocarbon dates the death of the organism the sample came from. Stratigraphy dates a layer relative to those around it. They measure different events.

paras.label: G

questions.q: What does a radiocarbon measurement actually date?
questions.a: The death of the organism the sample came from, which is not necessarily the same event as the human activity being dated.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. how material moves between layers) and paragraph E (i.e. what calibration adds).
Summarize why two dates for one layer can conflict.
questions.a: Radiocarbon dates the death of an organism while stratigraphy dates a layer relative to those around it, so charcoal from long-dead wood can be older than the fire it burned in. Material can also move downward through a sequence, and calibration curves have flat stretches covering centuries, so the first question is what each date dated and the remainder is settled by more samples.

questions.q:
stratigraphy: dating a layer by its position relative to the layers deposited above and below it.
calibration: converting a radiocarbon measurement into calendar years using a curve built from tree rings.
Describe the connection between old wood and a date that is both correct and misleading.
questions.a: A piece of charcoal from long-dead wood can be older than the fire it was burned in, so a radiocarbon date may be genuinely correct and still predate the human activity it is being used to date.

articles.note: The first move is always what did each one measure. Students who reach for which is right have skipped the step that resolves most of these.

articles.title: The Experiment That Weighed the Earth
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1798 Henry Cavendish published a measurement of the density of the earth. He did it in a shed in his garden, with two lead spheres, two smaller ones, a wooden rod and a wire.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Gravity between everyday objects is extraordinarily weak. Two lead balls on a table attract each other with a force far too small to feel, and the problem was not understanding the effect but detecting it at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His apparatus turned a tiny force into a visible rotation. A rod with a small lead ball at each end hung horizontally from a thin wire, and twisting the wire even slightly required almost no force.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two large spheres were then brought up beside the small ones. Their attraction swung the rod, the wire twisted, and the angle of the twist gave the size of the force, since the stiffness of the wire had been measured beforehand.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The hard part was everything else. A person in the room warms one side of the air, a draught moves the rod more than gravity does, so Cavendish observed through a telescope from outside and worked the apparatus with pulleys.

paras.label: F
paras.text: From the force he obtained the density of the earth, about five and a half times that of water, which is more than any surface rock and was the first real evidence of a dense metallic interior.

paras.label: G
paras.text: His result stood for a century within about one per cent. The experiment is still run in teaching laboratories today, and students using modern equipment in a climate-controlled building rarely do much better.

questions.q: How did the apparatus make a tiny force measurable?
questions.a: A rod with a small lead ball at each end hung from a thin wire, so bringing large spheres alongside swung the rod and twisted the wire, and the angle gave the force because the wire's stiffness had been measured beforehand.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the precautions against draughts and body heat) and paragraph F (i.e. what the density implied about the interior).
Summarize Cavendish's experiment and its result.
questions.a: Gravity between everyday objects is too weak to feel, so Cavendish hung a rod with lead balls from a thin wire and brought large spheres alongside, reading the force from the angle of twist. He observed through a telescope from outside to avoid draughts and body heat, and obtained a density about five and a half times that of water, which was the first evidence of a dense metallic interior.

questions.q:
density: mass per unit of volume, which is what Cavendish measured for the earth as a whole.
torsion: the twisting of a wire or rod, used here to turn a very small force into a readable angle.
Describe the connection between the measured density and what lies inside the earth.
questions.a: The density came out at about five and a half times that of water, which is more than any surface rock, and that was the first real evidence of a dense metallic interior.

articles.note: The interesting work is in paragraph E. Ask what the experiment would have measured if he had stayed in the room, which is the answer to why it is hard.

articles.title: The City That Reversed Its River
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Chicago grew beside a lake it drank from and a river it used as a drain. The river ran into the lake, which meant the city's sewage arrived back at the intake pipes that supplied its drinking water.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The consequences were measured in outbreaks. Typhoid and cholera moved through the city repeatedly through the nineteenth century, and extending the water intake further out into the lake bought time rather than a solution.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The solution adopted was to make the river run the other way. A canal was cut from the river toward the Des Plaines, deep enough that water would flow away from the lake and toward the Mississippi watershed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It worked, in the sense that the engineering did what it was designed to do. The river reversed in 1900, the intake pipes stopped receiving the city's own waste, and deaths from waterborne disease in Chicago fell sharply.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It also moved the problem downstream. The state of Missouri sued, arguing that Chicago was sending its sewage toward St Louis, and the case went to the Supreme Court, which did not stop the canal.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There were effects nobody litigated. The canal connected two watersheds that had been separate, and species have since moved between them in both directions, which is a consequence still being managed today.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The story is usually told as engineering triumph or as environmental warning. It is more useful as neither, since what it actually shows is a real problem genuinely solved by an action whose consequences were larger than the problem.

paras.text: Chicago grew beside a lake it drank from and a river it used as a drain. The river ran into the lake. So the city's sewage arrived back at the pipes that supplied its drinking water.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: E

paras.label: F

questions.q: Why did extending the water intake not solve the problem?
questions.a: The river still ran into the lake, so extending the intake further out bought time rather than a solution.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the lawsuit from Missouri) and paragraph F (i.e. the joining of two watersheds).
Summarize what Chicago did to its river and what followed.
questions.a: The river carried the city's sewage into the lake it drank from, causing repeated typhoid and cholera outbreaks, so a canal was cut deep enough to reverse the flow toward the Mississippi watershed. The river reversed in 1900 and waterborne deaths fell, Missouri sued over sewage sent downstream, and the canal joined two watersheds so species have moved between them ever since.

questions.q:
watershed: the area of land whose water drains into one river system, two of which the canal connected.
intake: the pipe through which a city draws its drinking water, here from the same lake the river emptied into.
Describe the connection between solving the city's problem and creating one elsewhere.
questions.a: Reversing the river stopped the intake pipes receiving the city's own waste and sent it toward St Louis instead, which is why Missouri sued.

articles.note: The last paragraph refuses both available morals. Ask students which of the two they were forming while reading, and what the text offers instead.

articles.title: The Bacteria That Eat Rock
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every familiar food chain starts with sunlight. Plants capture it, animals eat the plants, other animals eat those, and tracing any meal backwards far enough arrives at a leaf and then at the sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some organisms do not begin there. Certain bacteria obtain energy by driving chemical reactions on minerals, taking electrons from iron or sulphur compounds in rock, and they require no light at any stage.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They live where that chemistry is available, which turns out to be a very large volume. They have been recovered from boreholes kilometres deep, from the rock beneath the ocean floor, and from water that has been isolated underground for a long time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Life down there runs slowly. Estimates of generation times in some deep communities run to centuries rather than hours, which is difficult to study because an experiment outlasts the researcher by a wide margin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The total is genuinely uncertain and genuinely large. Published estimates put a substantial fraction of all bacterial cells on earth below the surface, and the range between the low and high estimates is itself wider than most ecosystems.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The finding matters beyond the organisms. It means energy and carbon move through rock in ways geology alone does not describe, and that some mineral deposits have had biological help in forming.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It also changes a question. If life does not require a star's light but only a source of chemical energy and liquid water, then the places worth examining for it are not limited to the surfaces of planets.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every familiar food chain starts with sunlight. Plants capture it. Animals eat the plants. Trace any meal back far enough and you reach a leaf, and then the sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some organisms do not begin there. Certain bacteria get energy by driving chemical reactions on minerals. They take electrons from iron or sulphur compounds in rock. They need no light at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They live where that chemistry exists, which is a very large volume. They have been recovered from boreholes kilometres deep, from rock beneath the ocean floor, and from long-isolated underground water.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Life down there runs slowly. Some deep communities are estimated to reproduce over centuries, not hours. That is hard to study. An experiment outlasts the researcher by a wide margin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The total is genuinely uncertain and genuinely large. Published estimates put a large share of all bacterial cells below the surface. The range between low and high estimates is very wide.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The finding matters beyond the organisms. Energy and carbon move through rock in ways geology alone does not describe. Some mineral deposits have had biological help in forming.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It also changes a question. If life needs no starlight, only chemical energy and liquid water, then the places worth examining are not limited to the surfaces of planets.

questions.q: How do these bacteria obtain energy?
questions.a: By driving chemical reactions on minerals, taking electrons from iron or sulphur compounds in rock, with no light required at any stage.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why deep life is hard to study) and paragraph G (i.e. how the finding changes where to look for life).
Summarize what rock-eating bacteria are and why they matter.
questions.a: Certain bacteria take electrons from iron or sulphur compounds in rock and need no light, and they have been found kilometres deep and beneath the ocean floor, reproducing over centuries in some communities. A large and uncertain share of all bacterial cells may be below the surface, which means energy and carbon move through rock in ways geology does not describe and that life needs only chemical energy and liquid water.

questions.q:
borehole: a narrow hole drilled deep into rock, from which deep samples are recovered.
generation time: how long an organism takes to reproduce, which in some deep communities is estimated in centuries.
Describe the connection between not needing light and where life might be found.
questions.a: If life does not require a star's light but only a source of chemical energy and liquid water, the places worth examining for it are not limited to the surfaces of planets.

articles.note: Paragraph E is honest about a wide uncertainty without abandoning the claim, which is the habit grade 8 has been building since RI.8.1.

articles.title: The Day the Clocks Were Standardised
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of history every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over that town, so clocks in two places a hundred kilometres apart genuinely disagreed, and nothing was wrong with either.

paras.label: B
paras.text: This caused no difficulty while travel was slow. A journey taking two days absorbed a few minutes of difference without anyone noticing, and local time was both accurate and sufficient.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Railways removed that tolerance. A timetable has to state a departure time, and a train crossing many towns in an afternoon cannot leave at a different noon in each, so railway companies began publishing their own time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The result was worse than either system alone. A station could be running on railway time while the town outside ran on local time, so the clock on the platform and the clock on the church disagreed by minutes that mattered.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In November 1883 the railway companies of North America adopted a shared scheme of time zones. Within each zone every clock read the same, and the boundaries were drawn where the companies found them convenient.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Governments followed rather than led. An international conference the following year fixed a prime meridian for the purpose of reckoning longitude and time, and national legislation in many countries came later still.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a unit everyone treats as natural was settled by companies with a scheduling problem. The hour on a phone descends from a decision about trains, and it was adopted because coordination was worth more than accuracy to the sun.

paras.text: For most of history every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over that town. Clocks a hundred kilometres apart genuinely disagreed. Nothing was wrong with either.

paras.label: B

questions.q: Why did local time stop working?
questions.a: A timetable has to state a departure time, and a train crossing many towns in an afternoon cannot leave at a different noon in each.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the period when two systems ran at once) and paragraph F (i.e. governments following rather than leading).
Summarize how standard time came about.
questions.a: Every town once kept its own noon, which worked while travel was slow, but railway timetables could not state a departure time across many towns, so companies published their own time and stations disagreed with the towns outside them. In November 1883 North American railway companies adopted shared time zones, and governments and international agreement followed afterwards.

questions.q:
prime meridian: the line of longitude agreed as the zero point from which longitude and time are reckoned.
tolerance: here, the amount of difference a system can absorb before it causes a problem.
Describe the connection between a scheduling problem and the time on a phone.
questions.a: A unit everyone treats as natural was settled by companies with a scheduling problem, so the hour on a phone descends from a decision about trains.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 7's leap second article. Both are about a standard being chosen rather than discovered, a century apart and in opposite directions.

articles.title: The Detector a Kilometre Underground
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.8.1 citing evidence · RI.8.2 central idea · RI.8.4 word meaning · RI.8.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 870 – 970

paras.label: A
paras.text: A neutrino is a particle with almost no mass and no electric charge, and it passes through matter as though the matter were not there. Enormous numbers from the sun are going through this page and through you now.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Detecting something that barely interacts requires a great deal of material and a great deal of patience. A detector is built as a very large tank of liquid, watched by thousands of light sensors, waiting for the rare occasion when one neutrino hits a nucleus.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The difficulty is not the signal. It is everything else. Cosmic rays strike the atmosphere constantly and the particles they produce would swamp a detector at the surface, with real events lost in an enormous background.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So the detectors are put underground, in mines and under mountains. A kilometre of rock stops almost everything else while leaving neutrinos entirely unaffected, which is the one situation where being hard to stop is useful.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first such experiment produced a famous problem. It measured neutrinos from the sun and found about a third of the number the understood physics of the sun predicted, and the shortfall persisted for three decades.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Two explanations competed. Either the model of the sun was wrong, or the neutrinos were changing on the way, into kinds the detector could not see, and settling it required a detector sensitive to all three kinds.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That experiment reported in 2001 and found the total was right. The neutrinos had been changing type in flight, which meant they have a small mass, which the existing theory of particles had said they did not.

paras.text: A neutrino has almost no mass and no electric charge. It passes through matter as if the matter were not there. Enormous numbers from the sun are going through this page and through you now.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Detecting something that barely interacts needs a lot of material and a lot of patience. A detector is a very large tank of liquid, watched by thousands of light sensors, waiting for a rare hit.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D
paras.text: So detectors go underground, in mines and under mountains. A kilometre of rock stops almost everything else and leaves neutrinos unaffected. Being hard to stop is useful here.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first such experiment produced a famous problem. It measured neutrinos from the sun. It found about a third of the predicted number. The shortfall lasted three decades.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Two explanations competed. Either the model of the sun was wrong. Or the neutrinos were changing on the way, into kinds the detector could not see. Settling it needed a detector sensitive to all three.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That experiment reported in 2001. The total was right. The neutrinos had been changing type in flight. So they have a small mass, which the existing theory of particles had said they did not.

questions.q: Why are neutrino detectors built underground?
questions.a: Cosmic rays striking the atmosphere produce particles that would swamp a detector at the surface, and a kilometre of rock stops almost everything else while leaving neutrinos unaffected.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the shortfall in solar neutrinos) and paragraph G (i.e. what the 2001 result showed).
Summarize the solar neutrino problem and how it was settled.
questions.a: Neutrinos barely interact, so detectors are enormous tanks placed a kilometre underground where rock removes the cosmic ray background. An early experiment found about a third of the neutrinos the physics of the sun predicted, and either the model was wrong or the neutrinos were changing type in flight, which a detector sensitive to all three kinds confirmed in 2001, showing they have a small mass.

questions.q:
cosmic ray: a high-energy particle arriving from space, whose products would otherwise swamp a detector.
shortfall: the gap between what was measured and what was predicted, here about two thirds of the expected neutrinos.
Describe the connection between neutrinos changing type and their having mass.
questions.a: The 2001 result showed the total was right and the neutrinos had been changing type in flight, which means they have a small mass, contrary to what the existing theory of particles had said.

articles.note: A thirty-year disagreement where both sides were testable and one was right. Worth putting beside the RI.8.9 articles, where most disagreements are not like this.

articles.title: The Case for an Asteroid
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between the rocks of the Cretaceous and those of the Paleogene there is a thin layer of clay, a centimetre or two thick, which can be found at sites on several continents. Below it there are certain fossils and above it there are not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1980 a team including Walter and Luis Alvarez reported that this layer contains iridium at concentrations far above anything in the rocks around it. Iridium is rare in the earth's crust and common in asteroids, which is where the argument begins.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A single anomaly is a curiosity. What turned it into a claim was that the same enrichment appeared at site after site, in marine rocks and in terrestrial ones, at the same stratigraphic position, which rules out a local explanation.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second line is physical rather than chemical. The layer contains quartz grains with microscopic fracture patterns that form only under shock pressures, of a kind produced by impacts and not by volcanoes, however large.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third line is the spherules: tiny beads of once-molten rock, thickest in sites around the Gulf of Mexico and thinning with distance, which is the pattern debris thrown from a single point would leave.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The prediction that followed was specific. A body large enough to do this would leave a crater on the order of a hundred and fifty kilometres across, of exactly that age, and for eleven years nobody could produce one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The Chicxulub structure, buried under sediment at the edge of the Yucatán, was identified in 1991 from gravity and magnetic surveys and from drill cores. Its size and its age matched, and the crater had been found by people looking for oil.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A rival explanation existed throughout and has not vanished. The Deccan Traps, enormous volcanic eruptions in India, were active across the same interval, and the live question is no longer whether an impact happened but how the two causes divide the responsibility.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between the rocks of the Cretaceous and the Paleogene lies a thin clay layer, one or two centimetres thick. It is found at sites on several continents. Below it there are certain fossils. Above it there are not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1980 a team including Walter and Luis Alvarez reported that this layer holds iridium far above the levels around it. Iridium is rare in the earth's crust and common in asteroids. That is where the argument starts.

paras.label: C
paras.text: One anomaly is a curiosity. What made it a claim was that the same enrichment turned up site after site. In marine rocks and land rocks. At the same level. A local explanation cannot cover that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second line is physical, not chemical. The layer holds quartz grains with microscopic fracture patterns. Those form only under shock pressures. Impacts make them. Volcanoes, however large, do not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third line is the spherules. They are tiny beads of once-molten rock. They are thickest around the Gulf of Mexico and thin with distance. Debris thrown from one point would leave that pattern.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The prediction that followed was specific. A body that size would leave a crater about a hundred and fifty kilometres across, of exactly that age. For eleven years nobody could produce one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The Chicxulub structure lies buried under sediment at the edge of the Yucatán. It was identified in 1991 from gravity and magnetic surveys and drill cores. Its size and age matched. Oil prospectors had found it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A rival explanation existed all along and has not gone. The Deccan Traps, huge eruptions in India, were active over the same interval. The live question is not whether an impact happened. It is how the two causes share the blame.

questions.q: Why does finding iridium at many sites matter more than finding it at one?
questions.a: The same enrichment appeared at site after site, in marine rocks and in terrestrial ones, at the same stratigraphic position, which rules out a local explanation.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the prediction of a crater) and paragraph H (i.e. the rival volcanic explanation).
Summarize the evidence for an impact and what remains disputed.
questions.a: A thin clay layer between Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks holds iridium far above surrounding levels at sites on several continents, along with shocked quartz that only impacts produce and spherules thickest around the Gulf of Mexico. The predicted crater was found at Chicxulub in 1991 with matching size and age, while the Deccan Traps erupted over the same interval, so the dispute is now about how the two causes divide responsibility.

questions.q:
iridium: a metal rare in the earth's crust and common in asteroids, whose concentration in the clay layer began the argument.
spherule: a tiny bead of once-molten rock, thrown out by an impact and settling thickest nearest its source.
Describe the connection between the thickness of the spherule layer and the location of the impact.
questions.a: The spherules are thickest at sites around the Gulf of Mexico and thin with distance, which is the pattern debris thrown from a single point would leave.

articles.note: RI.9-10.1 wants strong AND thorough evidence. Four independent lines plus a confirmed prediction is what thorough looks like, and paragraph H shows that thorough does not mean settled.

articles.title: Reading the Domesday Book
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1086, twenty years after the conquest of England, William I ordered a survey of the land he had taken. Commissioners went into the shires, put questions to juries of local men, and the answers were compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It records, manor by manor, who held the land before the conquest and who held it now, how much ploughland there was, how many mills and how many people of various legal categories, and what the whole was worth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: For a historian this is an extraordinary document and a treacherous one. It is the earliest systematic survey of its kind in Europe, and almost everything a modern reader wants to know from it is something it was not built to record.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It does not count people. It counts heads of households of particular legal statuses, which means a population figure derived from it rests on an assumed household size, and different assumptions produce totals that differ by millions.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It was also made for a purpose. The survey existed to establish who owed what, so the categories are the categories of obligation, and a person who owed nothing to anyone the king could tax has a weak claim on appearing at all.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are also known gaps. London and Winchester are absent, several northern areas are covered thinly or not at all, and the survey was taken in a decade when parts of the north had been devastated by the king's own armies.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a claim built on it has to be careful about its own shape. The book supports strong statements about landholding and about relative value, and much weaker ones about how many people lived anywhere.

paras.label: H
paras.text: This is not a defect peculiar to medieval sources. Every record was made by someone for a reason, and the first question to ask of any of them is what it was built to capture, because that determines what it can be asked.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1086, twenty years after the conquest of England, William I ordered a survey of the land he had taken. Commissioners went into the shires. They questioned juries of local men. The answers became Domesday Book.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It records, manor by manor, who held the land before the conquest and who held it now. How much ploughland. How many mills. How many people of various legal categories. What the whole was worth.

paras.label: C
paras.text: For a historian this is extraordinary and treacherous. It is the earliest systematic survey of its kind in Europe. Almost everything a modern reader wants from it is something it was not built to record.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It does not count people. It counts heads of households of particular legal statuses. A population figure from it rests on an assumed household size. Different assumptions give totals millions apart.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It was also made for a purpose. The survey existed to establish who owed what. The categories are categories of obligation. Someone who owed nothing the king could tax has a weak claim on appearing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are known gaps. London and Winchester are absent. Several northern areas are thin or missing. The survey came a decade after the king's own armies had devastated parts of the north.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a claim built on it must be careful about its shape. The book supports strong statements about landholding and relative value. It supports much weaker ones about how many people lived anywhere.

paras.label: H
paras.text: This is not a medieval problem. Every record was made by someone for a reason. The first question to ask of any of them is what it was built to capture. That decides what it can be asked.

questions.q: Why can Domesday Book not give a population figure directly?
questions.a: It counts heads of households of particular legal statuses rather than people, so any population figure rests on an assumed household size, and different assumptions produce totals differing by millions.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the purpose the survey was made for) and paragraph G (i.e. which claims it can and cannot support).
Summarize what Domesday Book records and what it cannot be used for.
questions.a: It records manor by manor who held land before and after the conquest, the ploughland, mills, people by legal category and the value of the whole. Because it was made to establish who owed what, it counts households of particular statuses rather than people and omits London, Winchester and much of the north, so it supports strong claims about landholding and weak ones about population.

questions.q:
manor: the unit of landholding the survey was organised around.
obligation: what a landholder owed, which is what the survey's categories were built to record.
Describe the connection between the survey's purpose and who appears in it.
questions.a: The survey existed to establish who owed what, so a person who owed nothing to anyone the king could tax has a weak claim on appearing at all.

articles.note: The closing paragraph generalises from one source to all of them. Ask students what a school attendance register was built to capture, and what it therefore cannot be asked.

articles.title: How Old the Earth Is
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: The question of the earth's age was argued for centuries from the wrong kind of evidence. Estimates were built from the thickness of sediments, from the saltiness of the oceans, and from how long a molten body would take to cool.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each of those rests on an assumed rate. If sediment has always accumulated at today's rate, a thickness gives a time, and the answer is only as good as an assumption nobody could test.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Radioactivity changed the problem. Certain elements decay into others at rates that do not depend on temperature, pressure or chemistry, so a mineral containing a parent element and its daughter product carries a clock that started when it formed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The difficulty was choosing what to measure. Rocks at the surface have been melted, weathered and recycled, so the oldest rock anyone can find gives a minimum age for the crust and not an age for the planet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Clair Patterson's solution in the early 1950s was to date meteorites instead, on the argument that the solar system's material formed at one time, so an undisturbed meteorite dates the formation of everything including the earth.

paras.label: F
paras.text: He measured lead isotopes in material from the Canyon Diablo meteorite and obtained an age of about 4.55 billion years. The figure has been refined since and has not been overturned, which is unusual for a first measurement of anything.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Getting it required solving a different problem first. Lead is everywhere in a modern laboratory, from petrol, paint and solder, and Patterson had to build rooms clean enough that his samples were not reading the twentieth century.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That work had a second result he did not set out to produce. Having measured industrial lead in order to exclude it, he had the data to show how much of it there was, and he spent much of his later career arguing for its removal from fuel.

questions.q: Why does the oldest rock on earth not give the age of the planet?
questions.a: Rocks at the surface have been melted, weathered and recycled, so the oldest rock anyone can find gives a minimum age for the crust rather than an age for the planet.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the contamination problem) and paragraph H (i.e. the second result of solving it).
Summarize how the age of the earth was established.
questions.a: Earlier estimates rested on assumed rates of sedimentation, salting or cooling, while radioactive decay provides a clock independent of conditions. Surface rocks have been recycled, so Patterson dated meteorites instead, obtaining about 4.55 billion years, and to do it he had to build laboratories clean enough that industrial lead did not contaminate the samples.

questions.q:
isotope: a form of an element differing in mass, whose proportions change in a known way as decay proceeds.
contamination: unwanted material entering a sample, which here would have made the measurement read modern lead.
Describe the connection between the clean laboratory and Patterson's later career.
questions.a: Having measured industrial lead in order to exclude it from his samples, he had the data to show how much of it there was, and he spent much of his later career arguing for its removal from fuel.

articles.note: The strong evidence here is a rate that does not depend on conditions, which is exactly what the earlier estimates lacked. Ask students to name the assumption each older method could not test.

articles.title: The Photographs at the Mill
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1908 and 1924 Lewis Hine photographed children at work in the United States for the National Child Labor Committee. He photographed them in textile mills, in canneries, in mines and on streets, and the pictures were made to be used.

paras.label: B
paras.text: They were made in difficult conditions. Employers did not want a photographer inside, so Hine often entered claiming to be an insurance inspector or a machinery salesman, and he worked quickly and left.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What makes the photographs evidence rather than illustration is what he wrote on them. Hine recorded names, ages as given, how long each child had worked, the name of the mill and the date, in notes attached to the images.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He also solved a measurement problem. Children did not always know their ages and employers had reason to overstate them, so Hine learned the height of the buttons on his own coat and photographed children standing beside him.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That detail is what moves a picture from affecting to usable. A legislator presented with a photograph can be told that the child is a particular height, in a particular mill, on a particular date, and the claim can be checked.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The photographs were not neutral and were never offered as neutral. Hine was employed by an organisation campaigning for legislation, he chose what to photograph, and the committee chose which images to print.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That does not weaken them as evidence of what they show. A photograph taken to make an argument still records that a child of that height was standing at that machine, and the caption is checkable against mill records.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The useful distinction is between the evidence and the case. Hine's pictures are strong evidence that children of certain ages worked in certain places, and the argument that this should be illegal is a separate claim the photographs support rather than prove.
