questions.q: How did Hine establish a child's height?
questions.a: He learned the height of the buttons on his own coat and photographed children standing beside him, so a height could be read from the image.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. that the photographs were not neutral) and paragraph H (i.e. the distinction between evidence and case).
Summarize what makes Hine's photographs usable as evidence.
questions.a: He recorded names, ages as given, time worked, the mill and the date with each image, and used the buttons on his own coat as a scale so a child's height could be read from the photograph. He worked for a campaigning organisation and chose what to photograph, but the pictures still record a child of a given height at a given machine and the captions can be checked against mill records.

questions.q:
caption: the written record attached to a photograph, which is what turns it into checkable evidence.
neutral: without a position, which these photographs were never claimed to be.
Describe the connection between the photographs being evidence and the argument being separate.
questions.a: The pictures are strong evidence that children of certain ages worked in certain places, and the claim that this should be illegal is a separate argument they support rather than prove.

articles.note: Paragraph H is the move students find hardest, i.e. that evidence made for a cause can still be good evidence. Make them state what exactly the photographs prove.

articles.title: The Case That Smoking Causes Cancer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: By the late 1940s lung cancer was rising sharply in several countries, and the increase was too large and too fast to be explained by better diagnosis alone. Several possible causes were proposed, including tar from road surfacing and exhaust from cars.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill compared patients who had lung cancer with similar patients who did not, and asked both groups about their histories. Smoking separated the groups more sharply than anything else they measured.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A comparison of that kind has a known weakness. People who smoke may differ from people who do not in ways that themselves cause illness, and asking someone with a diagnosis to recall their past invites a kind of error the healthy group does not face.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So they ran a second study in the other direction. They enrolled British doctors in 1951, recorded their smoking before anyone was ill, and followed them for decades, which removed the problem of recall entirely.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result held and sharpened. The more a person smoked, the higher their risk, and the risk of someone who stopped fell over the years that followed, which is the pattern a cause produces and a mere association generally does not.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The objection that could not be answered by any one study was that both smoking and cancer might be caused by something else. There was no way to settle it experimentally, because assigning people to smoke for twenty years is not an experiment anyone may run.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Bradford Hill's response in 1965 was to set out what, in the absence of an experiment, should be looked for: a strong association, found repeatedly in different populations, with the cause preceding the effect, a dose relationship, and a plausible mechanism.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Those are not a formula and he said so explicitly. They are a description of what a thorough case looks like when the decisive experiment cannot be done, which is the situation in most of the questions that matter.

paras.label: A
paras.text: By the late 1940s lung cancer was rising sharply in several countries. The increase was too large and too fast for better diagnosis alone. Proposed causes included tar from road surfacing and car exhaust.

paras.label: D

paras.label: G

paras.label: H
paras.text: These are not a formula, and he said so plainly. They describe what a thorough case looks like when the decisive experiment cannot be run. That is the situation in most questions that matter.

questions.q: Why did Doll and Hill run a second study following doctors forward?
questions.a: Recording smoking before anyone was ill removed the problem of asking someone with a diagnosis to recall their past, which invites an error the healthy group does not face.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the objection no single study could answer) and paragraph G (i.e. what Bradford Hill set out instead).
Summarize how the case that smoking causes cancer was built.
questions.a: Lung cancer rose too fast for better diagnosis, and comparing patients with and without it showed smoking separated the groups most sharply. Because recall is unreliable, a second study followed doctors from 1951 recording smoking before illness, and risk rose with amount and fell after stopping. Since no experiment could be run, Bradford Hill set out what a thorough case requires: strength, repetition, the cause preceding the effect, a dose relationship and a plausible mechanism.

questions.q:
dose relationship: a pattern in which more exposure produces more effect, which supports a causal reading.
recall: a participant's memory of their own past, which is less reliable in someone who already has a diagnosis.
Describe the connection between the impossibility of an experiment and Bradford Hill's criteria.
questions.a: Assigning people to smoke for twenty years is not an experiment anyone may run, so he described what a thorough case should look like in the absence of one.

articles.note: The last paragraph matters as much as the list, i.e. he said explicitly that these are not a formula. Students reach for checklists, and this is a checklist that refuses to be one.

articles.title: What a Thermometer Had to Settle
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: An early thermometer could show that today was warmer than yesterday and could not say by how much, because there was no agreement about what the numbers on the side of the tube meant.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The instrument itself was not the difficulty. A sealed tube of liquid that expands with heat works perfectly well, and several were in use by the seventeenth century, each marked according to its maker's own scheme.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The problem was reproducibility. To compare a reading in one city with a reading in another, both instruments have to be marked against the same reference, and a reference has to be something that happens identically everywhere.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two candidates emerged. Ice melting and water boiling both occur at a temperature that does not change while the change of state is going on, so either can be found again by anyone with ice or a kettle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Boiling turned out to be the awkward one. Water boils at a temperature that depends on air pressure, so a thermometer calibrated in a mountain town and one calibrated at a port will disagree at the top of the scale.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The refinement was to specify the pressure as well. Once the steam point is defined as the boiling temperature at a stated atmospheric pressure, the reference becomes reproducible, and that condition is part of the definition rather than a footnote.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Scales were then built between the fixed points and the choice of how many divisions is arbitrary. Nothing in nature requires a hundred steps between melting and boiling, and the number was chosen because people have ten fingers.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea develops in two directions at once. A measurement needs an instrument, and it needs a shared definition of what the instrument's marks mean, and the second of those took far longer and mattered more.

questions.q: Why does a fixed point have to be a change of state?
questions.a: Ice melting and water boiling occur at a temperature that does not change while the change of state is going on, so either can be found again by anyone with ice or a kettle.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why boiling was awkward) and paragraph G (i.e. why the number of divisions is arbitrary).
Summarize what had to be settled before temperatures could be compared.
questions.a: A thermometer works without agreement about its markings, so readings in two cities could not be compared until both were calibrated against references that occur identically everywhere. Melting and boiling served, but boiling depends on air pressure, so the pressure became part of the definition, and the number of divisions between the fixed points was chosen arbitrarily.

questions.q:
fixed point: a reproducible temperature, such as melting ice, used to calibrate an instrument.
reproducible: able to be produced again identically by anyone, which is what a reference condition must be.
Describe the connection between air pressure and two thermometers disagreeing.
questions.a: Water boils at a temperature that depends on air pressure, so a thermometer calibrated in a mountain town and one calibrated at a port will disagree at the top of the scale.

articles.note: RI.9-10.2 asks how a central idea is refined by specific details. The pressure condition in paragraph F is the refinement, and without it the idea in paragraph C does not work.

articles.title: The Invention of the Weekend
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A two-day break at the end of the week feels like a natural division of time. It is about a century old in most places where it exists, and it was assembled out of several unrelated pressures rather than designed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The older pattern was one day. A sabbath, observed on different days by different communities, had been a day without work for a very long time, and the day before it was an ordinary working day.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Industrial workers took an unofficial second day anyway. The practice of not returning on Monday after a Sunday was common enough in nineteenth-century Britain to have a name, Saint Monday, and employers disliked it intensely.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first official concession ran the other way. Factories began closing early on Saturday, which gave workers an afternoon and gave employers a workforce that arrived on Monday, and a half-day was a compromise rather than a principle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A different pressure operated in the United States. Factories employing both Jewish and Christian workers faced two different sabbaths, and closing on both Saturday and Sunday was simpler than running a plant at half strength twice a week.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then came an argument from the employers' own side. Henry Ford adopted a five-day week in 1926 and argued publicly that workers with time and wages would buy goods, including cars, which made leisure a business proposition.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of these pressures was about rest. Religious observance, absenteeism, the practicalities of two sabbaths and the creation of consumers each produced the same result for a different reason.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why the shape persisted once assembled. A pattern supported by several independent interests is harder to reverse than one argued for on a single ground, and nobody has had to defend the weekend since.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. Ford's argument about consumers) and paragraph H (i.e. why the pattern persisted).
Summarize how the two-day weekend came about.
questions.a: A single sabbath was the older pattern, workers took an unofficial Monday anyway, and factories conceded a Saturday half-day to secure a Monday workforce. American factories with both Jewish and Christian workers found closing both days simpler, and Ford argued in 1926 that workers with time and wages would buy goods, so several unrelated interests produced the same result.

questions.q:
sabbath: a day set aside without work, observed on different days by different communities.
concession: something granted in a negotiation, here a Saturday half-day offered in exchange for Monday attendance.
Describe the connection between several interests supporting a pattern and its persistence.
questions.a: A pattern supported by several independent interests is harder to reverse than one argued for on a single ground, which is why nobody has had to defend the weekend since.

articles.note: The central idea only appears in paragraph G, after four separate causes have been laid out. Ask students where they first expected it and why the article withholds it.

articles.title: The Antibiotic Nobody Will Develop
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics. This is not a surprise or a failure; it is what a population under selection does, and every antibiotic in use has a finite working life for that reason.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The response has to be a supply of new ones. For several decades that supply existed, as a sequence of discoveries from soil organisms produced classes of drug that worked by different mechanisms.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That supply has thinned to almost nothing. Very few genuinely new classes have reached patients since the 1980s, and the reasons are only partly scientific.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The economics work against it in an unusual way. A new antibiotic that works against resistant infections is immediately placed in reserve, used as little as possible to protect it, which means a successful drug is one that barely sells.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Compare that with a medicine for a long-term condition. A drug taken daily for thirty years by a large population returns its development cost, and a drug taken for ten days by a small number of patients, deliberately rarely, does not.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the incentive points at the wrong target. The better an antibiotic is, the more carefully it will be rationed, and the more carefully it is rationed the less its maker earns, which is a structure that discourages exactly the drug most needed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Proposed fixes separate payment from sales. A government can pay a fixed sum for access to a drug regardless of how much is used, which makes the developer's return depend on the product existing rather than on its being prescribed.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea is therefore not about bacteria. Resistance is a biological process and the shortage of new drugs is an economic one, and a policy aimed at only one of them is aimed at half the problem.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics. That is not a surprise or a failure. It is what a population under selection does. Every antibiotic in use has a finite working life for that reason.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The response must be a supply of new ones. For decades that supply existed. A sequence of discoveries from soil organisms produced classes of drug that worked by different mechanisms.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That supply has thinned to almost nothing. Very few genuinely new classes have reached patients since the 1980s. The reasons are only partly scientific.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The economics work against it in an unusual way. A new antibiotic effective against resistant infections goes straight into reserve. It is used as little as possible. So a successful drug barely sells.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Compare a medicine for a long-term condition. A drug taken daily for thirty years by many people returns its development cost. A drug taken for ten days by few patients, deliberately rarely, does not.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the incentive points at the wrong target. The better an antibiotic is, the more carefully it is rationed. The more carefully it is rationed, the less its maker earns.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Proposed fixes separate payment from sales. A government can pay a fixed sum for access regardless of use. The developer's return then depends on the product existing, not on its being prescribed.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the central idea is not about bacteria. Resistance is a biological process. The shortage of new drugs is an economic one. A policy aimed at one of them is aimed at half the problem.

questions.q: Why does a successful new antibiotic barely sell?
questions.a: A new antibiotic that works against resistant infections is immediately placed in reserve and used as little as possible to protect it.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the incentive points the wrong way) and paragraph G (i.e. how a fixed payment changes it).
Summarize why new antibiotics are not being developed.
questions.a: Resistance is what a population under selection does, so new drugs are needed, but very few new classes have reached patients since the 1980s. A new antibiotic is held in reserve and used rarely, so the better it is the less it earns, and proposed fixes pay a fixed sum for access so the return depends on the drug existing rather than on prescriptions.

questions.q:
selection: the process by which organisms better suited to a pressure leave more descendants, which produces resistance.
incentive: a financial reason to act, which here rewards the opposite of what is needed.
Describe the connection between rationing a drug and the money its maker earns.
questions.a: The better an antibiotic is, the more carefully it will be rationed, and the more carefully it is rationed the less its maker earns.

articles.note: The central idea arrives last and reframes everything before it. Ask students to state what they thought the article was about after paragraph C.

articles.title: The Credit Score
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Lending money to a stranger requires a judgement about whether they will repay it. For most of the history of banking that judgement was made by a person who knew the applicant, or thought they did.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That system had obvious failures. A decision resting on an individual's impression could rest on anything, and the characteristics a lender noticed depended on who the lender was and who had walked through the door.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Statistical scoring was offered as a correction. Instead of asking a manager what they thought, a lender could ask what had happened to many thousands of previous borrowers with similar records, and attach a number to the answer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The method has real advantages, and they are not only about efficiency. A formula applies the same rule to everyone, it can be examined, and a decision it produces can be audited in a way an impression cannot.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The refinement is that a model trained on past lending learns what past lending did. If a group was historically refused credit, the data contains few records of them repaying, and a model can reproduce an old pattern while using none of the old reasons.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A second refinement concerns what the number is about. A score predicts the behaviour of people with similar records, which is a statement about a group, and it is then used to make a decision about one person who may not resemble their group.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The score also became something else. Once it existed it was used for insurance, for renting a flat and sometimes for employment, so a measure built to predict repayment began deciding questions it was never validated against.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea is not that scoring is worse than a manager's judgement. It is that replacing a judgement with a number moves the decision rather than removing it, and the question becomes what went into the number and what it was tested on.

questions.a: A formula applies the same rule to everyone, it can be examined, and a decision it produces can be audited in a way an impression cannot.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how a model can reproduce an old pattern) and paragraph G (i.e. the score being used beyond lending).
Summarize how credit scoring changed lending decisions.
questions.a: Lending once rested on a manager's impression, which could rest on anything, so statistical scoring applied one examinable rule to everyone. A model trained on past lending can reproduce an old pattern without the old reasons, a score describes a group and is applied to an individual, and the number spread to insurance, renting and employment without being validated for them.

questions.q:
audit: to examine a decision afterwards against the rule it was supposed to follow.
validated: tested to show a measure actually predicts what it is being used to predict.
Describe the connection between historical refusals and what a model learns.
questions.a: If a group was historically refused credit the data contains few records of them repaying, so a model can reproduce an old pattern while using none of the old reasons.

articles.note: Paragraph H refuses the comfortable conclusion in both directions. Make students state what the article does NOT say about managers.

articles.title: The Metre That Was a Mistake
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences defined a new unit of length as one ten-millionth of the distance from the north pole to the equator, measured along the meridian passing through Paris.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The choice was deliberate and political. A unit taken from the earth belonged to nobody in particular, unlike a king's foot, and the definition could in principle be recovered by anyone anywhere who was willing to do the survey.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Doing the survey was another matter. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent six years measuring the arc between Dunkirk and Barcelona by triangulation, through a revolution and a war, and the work nearly destroyed both of them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Méchain discovered an inconsistency in his own measurements at Barcelona and could not resolve it. He did not report it, he continued working on the problem privately for years, and he died on a journey to extend the survey.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The metre was fixed anyway, as a platinum bar, in 1799. The bar was slightly short of the definition it was built from, by an amount that follows partly from the survey and partly from the shape of the earth being imperfectly known.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the standard and its definition had come apart almost immediately. For most of the nineteenth century the metre was in practice the length of a particular object in a particular vault, whatever the original definition said.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Later definitions moved away from objects entirely. The metre was tied to a wavelength of light in 1960, and since 1983 it has been defined by fixing the speed of light, so the unit is now derived from a constant rather than from an artefact.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea develops from ambition to artefact and back to constant. Each step was an attempt to make the unit independent of any particular object, and the first attempt failed in a way that took most of two centuries to repair.

questions.q: Why was a unit taken from the earth considered preferable?
questions.a: A unit taken from the earth belonged to nobody in particular, unlike a king's foot, and could in principle be recovered by anyone anywhere willing to do the survey.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. Méchain's unresolved inconsistency) and paragraph G (i.e. the move to defining the metre by a constant).
Summarize how the definition of the metre changed.
questions.a: It was defined in 1791 as one ten-millionth of the distance from pole to equator so that it belonged to nobody, but the survey was difficult and the platinum bar fixed in 1799 was slightly short of its own definition. triangulation: measuring a long distance by building a chain of triangles whose angles can be observed.

Describe the connection between the aim of the 1791 definition and the 1983 one.
questions.a: Each step was an attempt to make the unit independent of any particular object, which the earth-based definition sought and the bar undermined, and which fixing the speed of light finally achieved.

articles.note: RI.9-10.2 wants the shape of the development, not only the end point. The idea returns to where it started, two centuries and one failure later.

articles.title: How an Accident Investigation Proceeds
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: When an airliner is lost, an investigation begins within hours, and its sequence is prescribed. The order is not administrative tidiness; it exists because doing the steps in a different order produces worse answers.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first phase gathers facts and draws no conclusions. Wreckage is located and documented in place, recorders are recovered, maintenance records are collected, air traffic recordings are secured and witnesses are interviewed while memories are fresh.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Those activities are divided among groups with narrow remits. One group handles structures, another systems, another operations, another weather, and each produces a factual report without offering an explanation.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The separation is deliberate. A group that has formed a theory will interpret what it finds in light of the theory, and keeping the factual phase free of explanation is the main defence against finding what you expect.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Only afterwards does analysis begin, and it proceeds by testing proposed sequences against the facts already established. A proposed cause has to account for every recorded fact, and a single fact it cannot accommodate is fatal to it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The investigation then produces a probable cause and contributing factors, in those words. The phrasing is careful because the conclusion is an inference from physical evidence rather than something anybody observed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further rule that shapes the whole process. The inquiry does not assign blame or liability, and its findings are kept separate from legal proceedings, because a process that could produce punishment would not produce candid witnesses.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The order therefore encodes a theory of error. Facts before explanation, explanation tested against all facts, conclusion stated as probability, and no punishment attached, each step protecting the next one from a way the process could go wrong.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the wording of the conclusion) and paragraph G (i.e. why blame is kept out).
Summarize the order an accident investigation follows and why.
questions.a: Facts are gathered first by groups with narrow remits who offer no explanation, because a group with a theory interprets what it finds in light of it. Analysis then tests proposed sequences against every established fact, the conclusion is stated as a probable cause because it is an inference, and blame is kept out so that witnesses will speak candidly.

questions.q:
remit: the specific area a group is responsible for, which keeps each factual report narrow.

Describe the connection between keeping blame out and the quality of the evidence.

articles.note: RI.9-10.3 is about the order in which points are made. Paragraph H names what the order is defending against at each step, which is the analysis the standard asks for.

articles.title: How a Prosecution Is Built
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A criminal charge is not a story about what someone did. It is a claim that particular facts exist, and those facts are specified in advance by the definition of the offence rather than chosen by whoever is presenting them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Every offence breaks down into elements. A charge of theft, for instance, requires that property belonged to someone else, that it was taken, and that it was taken with a particular intention, and each element is a separate thing to be proved.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order of a case follows from that structure. A prosecutor must establish every element, so the presentation is organised around them, and evidence that is interesting but touches no element has no place in the case at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This is why some apparently damning material is excluded. Evidence that a defendant has behaved badly before may tell a jury a great deal about the person and establish none of the elements of the offence charged.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The standard of proof then applies to the whole. A juror must be sure of each element, so a case that establishes four elements convincingly and the fifth weakly has not established the offence, however strong the overall impression.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The defence does not have to offer an alternative account. It can simply contest one element, and a case built on five pillars can be defeated by removing one of them, which is why the defence often concentrates its effort narrowly.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That asymmetry is deliberate. The state has greater resources than a defendant, so the burden is placed entirely on the prosecution and the standard is set high, as a structural counterweight rather than a statement about guilt.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading a trial this way changes what looks important. The dramatic evidence is often not the decisive evidence, and the decisive question is usually which element is weakest and whether anything in the case repairs it.

questions.a: The separate facts the definition of the offence requires, such as that property belonged to someone else, that it was taken, and that it was taken with a particular intention.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the defence can concentrate narrowly) and paragraph G (i.e. why the burden is placed on the prosecution).
Summarize how the structure of an offence shapes a trial.
questions.a: An offence is defined as a set of elements, each of which must be proved, so the case is organised around them and evidence touching no element has no place. A juror must be sure of each one, so a weak fifth element defeats a strong case, the defence need only contest one, and the burden rests on the prosecution as a counterweight to the state's resources.

element: one of the separate facts a definition of an offence requires to be proved.
burden of proof: the obligation to establish a claim, placed here entirely on the prosecution.
Describe the connection between the structure of elements and what the defence must do.
questions.a: A case built on five pillars can be defeated by removing one of them, so the defence can contest a single element rather than offering an alternative account.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 7's The Shape of a Court Opinion. That one was about reading a decision, and this is about how the material reaching it was ordered.

articles.title: Differential Diagnosis
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A patient arrives with chest pain. That single fact is consistent with a heart attack, a blood clot in the lung, a tear in a major artery, inflammation, a cracked rib, indigestion and anxiety, among others.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A clinician does not test for all of them. Testing is expensive, slow and not harmless, and a strategy that investigated everything would deliver its answers after the patient needed them.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So the list is built and then ordered, and it is ordered by two things at once: how likely each possibility is, and how much damage it does if it is missed for an hour.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those two criteria do not agree. Indigestion is far more likely than a tear in the aorta, and the tear kills faster, so the order of investigation is not the order of probability and cannot be.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first tests are therefore chosen to exclude rather than to confirm. A question is asked that would be answered differently if the dangerous possibility were present, which narrows the list fastest where narrowing matters most.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Each result reshapes the list rather than ending it. A normal reading reduces one possibility and slightly raises the relative standing of the rest, and the working diagnosis is whatever currently sits at the top, held provisionally.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The provisional status is the part that is easy to lose. Once a diagnosis has been written down it begins attracting supporting observations, and later findings that do not fit tend to be explained rather than counted against it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Hence the standard instruction to revisit the list when a patient does not improve as expected. The failure to respond is itself a result, and it is evidence about the diagnosis rather than only about the treatment.

articles.title: How a Case Is Appealed
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: An appeal is widely imagined as a second trial. It is not, and almost everything surprising about appellate courts follows from that one fact.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An appeal is generally a review of the first proceeding, not a repetition of it. There is no jury, no witnesses, and in most cases no new evidence; the court works from the record made below and from written arguments.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What can be raised is therefore limited. An appellant usually must identify a specific error of law, such as evidence wrongly admitted or a legal test wrongly stated, rather than argue that the outcome was unjust.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reason is a view about who is best placed to judge what. A trial court saw the witnesses and heard them answer, and an appellate court reading a transcript is in a worse position to weigh whether someone was believable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So different questions carry different standards of review. Findings of fact are disturbed only where no reasonable court could have made them, while questions of law are considered afresh, because reading a statute does not require having been in the room.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A further consequence is that an argument not made below usually cannot be made above. A point that was available at trial and was not raised is generally treated as given up, which places weight on decisions made early by people under pressure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The remedy also differs from what people expect. An appellate court that finds an error frequently does not substitute its own result; it sends the matter back to be done again correctly, which can mean another hearing rather than an ending.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The order of the system therefore separates two jobs. One court decides what happened, another decides whether the law was applied correctly to it, and the reason the second cannot simply redo the first is that it was not there.

paras.label: A
paras.text: An appeal is widely imagined as a second trial. It is not. Almost everything surprising about appellate courts follows from that one fact.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An appeal is generally a review of the first proceeding, not a repetition. There is no jury and no witnesses. In most cases there is no new evidence. The court works from the record and written arguments.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So what can be raised is limited. An appellant usually must identify a specific error of law. Evidence wrongly admitted. A legal test wrongly stated. Not simply that the outcome was unjust.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The reason is a view about who judges what best. A trial court saw the witnesses answer. An appellate court reading a transcript is worse placed to weigh whether someone was believable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So different questions carry different standards of review. Findings of fact are disturbed only if no reasonable court could have made them. Questions of law are considered afresh. Reading a statute needs no presence in the room.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Another consequence is that an argument not made below usually cannot be made above. A point available at trial and not raised is treated as given up. That puts weight on early decisions made under pressure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The remedy differs from what people expect too. An appellate court finding an error often does not substitute its own result. It sends the matter back to be done again correctly. That can mean another hearing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the system separates two jobs. One court decides what happened. Another decides whether the law was applied correctly. The second cannot redo the first because it was not there.

questions.q: Why are findings of fact rarely disturbed on appeal?
questions.a: A trial court saw the witnesses and heard them answer, and an appellate court reading a transcript is in a worse position to weigh whether someone was believable.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. arguments not raised below) and paragraph G (i.e. what an appellate remedy usually is).
Summarize what an appeal is and how it differs from a trial.
questions.a: An appeal reviews the first proceeding rather than repeating it, with no jury, witnesses or usually new evidence, so an appellant must identify a specific error of law. Findings of fact are disturbed only if no reasonable court could have made them while questions of law are considered afresh, points not raised below are treated as given up, and the usual remedy is to send the matter back rather than substitute a result.

questions.q:
standard of review: the test an appellate court applies, which differs for questions of fact and of law.
record: the documented account of the first proceeding, which is what an appellate court works from.
Describe the connection between who was present and which questions each court decides.
questions.a: A trial court saw the witnesses so it decides what happened, and an appellate court considers questions of law afresh because reading a statute does not require having been in the room.

articles.note: The connections drawn between the points are the lesson here. Every feature in the article follows from the single claim in paragraph B.

articles.title: Two Ways to Assemble a Genome
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A genome cannot be read end to end. The available chemistry produces short fragments, so a sequence is assembled by reading many overlapping pieces and working out how they must fit together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That works while the sequence is varied. Overlaps are found by matching, and matching is reliable where a stretch of sequence appears once, which is true of a great deal of a genome and not of all of it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Repeated regions break it. If a sequence of several thousand characters occurs in twenty places, fragments from those places look identical, and an assembly program has no way to know which copy a fragment came from.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two projects took opposite approaches to that problem in the 1990s. The public consortium built a map first, breaking the genome into large known pieces and locating each one before any of it was sequenced in detail.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That order is slow and it makes the repeats tractable. A fragment is known to come from a particular mapped piece, so the ambiguity is contained inside a region small enough to resolve.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The rival approach, taken by a company, reversed the order. It sequenced fragments from the whole genome at once and relied on computation and on very large numbers of reads to resolve the overlaps afterwards.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is faster and it depends on the repeats being resolvable by sheer volume, which was the point in dispute. Both projects published in 2001, and the later consensus is that the fast method worked partly because the mapped data existed to check against.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is an argument about the order of operations rather than about technique. Map then sequence, or sequence then compute, and the choice determines what is hard, what is fast and what you can be confident of at the end.

paras.label: B

questions.q: Why do repeated regions make assembly difficult?
questions.a: If a sequence of several thousand characters occurs in twenty places, fragments from those places look identical and an assembly program has no way to know which copy a fragment came from.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how mapping first contains the ambiguity) and paragraph G (i.e. what the later consensus was).
Summarize the two approaches to assembling a genome.
questions.a: Sequencing produces short fragments assembled by overlap, which fails in repeated regions where fragments look identical. The public consortium mapped large pieces first so ambiguity stayed inside a small region, while a company sequenced the whole genome at once and resolved overlaps by computation, and the later view is that the faster method benefited from the mapped data existing to check against.

questions.q:
assembly: reconstructing a long sequence from many short overlapping reads.
consortium: a group of institutions working together, here on the public sequencing project.
Describe the connection between the order chosen and what becomes difficult.
questions.a: Map then sequence, or sequence then compute, and the choice determines what is hard, what is fast and what you can be confident of at the end.

articles.note: The analysis the article unfolds is a comparison of two orders for the same job. Ask which order a student would choose if the genome had no repeats at all.

articles.title: Hedging in a Scientific Abstract
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: An abstract is the part of a paper most people read and the only part many people read. It is a few hundred words, it is free to access when the paper often is not, and it is what a journalist works from.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its vocabulary is unusually careful, and the care is not decoration. Words such as suggests, may, is consistent with, and appears to each mark a different distance between what was observed and what is being claimed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Consider three versions of one finding. The drug reduced mortality, the drug was associated with reduced mortality, and the data are consistent with a reduction in mortality describe the same numbers and make three different claims.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first asserts a cause. The second asserts only that two things occurred together. The third says the observation would not be surprising if the effect existed, which is compatible with the effect not existing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading these as interchangeable is the single most common error. A reader who treats all three as the drug works has translated a careful sentence into a claim its authors deliberately did not make.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The hedges also accumulate. A sentence carrying two of them is not twice as cautious; it is often marking two separate uncertainties, one about the measurement and one about what the measurement means.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a known failure in the other direction. Studies comparing abstracts with results sections have found abstracts that state conclusions more confidently than the data behind them support, which has its own literature and its own name.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the practical habit is to read the hedges as load-bearing. They are the sentence's statement about its own strength, and a reader who strips them out has removed the part that said how much to believe.

questions.a: The first asserts a cause, the second asserts only that two things occurred together, and the third says the observation would not be surprising if the effect existed, which is compatible with it not existing.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how hedges accumulate) and paragraph G (i.e. the failure in the other direction).
Summarize what hedges do in a scientific abstract.

Treating them as interchangeable turns a careful sentence into a claim the authors avoided, and abstracts are also known sometimes to state conclusions more confidently than their own data support.

questions.q:
hedge: a word marking how far a claim goes beyond what was observed.
associated with: occurring together, which is a weaker claim than causing.
Describe the connection between removing a hedge and changing a claim.

articles.note: RI.9-10.4 asks for the cumulative impact of word choices. Rewrite one real abstract with every hedge removed and read both aloud.

articles.title: The Language of a Court Opinion
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A newspaper report and a court opinion about the same case are written in different languages. Both are English, both are about the same events, and almost every choice in one would be wrong in the other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A newspaper says the court decided. An opinion says we hold, and the distinction is not formality: hold marks the one part of the document that binds other courts, and a sentence that said decided would not mark it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: An opinion also marks what it is not deciding. Phrases such as we need not reach that question or assuming without deciding are doing precise work, telling later readers that a point was left open on purpose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its uncertainty is phrased institutionally. Rather than we do not know, an opinion says the record does not disclose, which locates the gap in the material before the court rather than in the court's understanding.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Terms of art carry definitions a dictionary will not give. Malice, consideration and reasonable each mean something specific and non-obvious, and a reader who supplies the everyday meaning will misread the sentence confidently.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A newspaper has the opposite obligations. It must be comprehensible on one reading to someone with no background, so it replaces terms of art with approximations and states conclusions without the qualifications that produced them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Neither is a defective version of the other. The opinion is written to be applied by courts in cases nobody has yet brought, and the report is written to be understood this morning by people who will not read it twice.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is what matters. A single substitution looks harmless, and a report that makes forty of them has produced a text with a different meaning, built entirely out of reasonable individual choices.

questions.q: Why does an opinion say we hold rather than the court decided?
questions.a: Hold marks the one part of the document that binds other courts, and a sentence that said decided would not mark it.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. how an opinion phrases uncertainty) and paragraph F (i.e. a newspaper's opposite obligations).
Summarize how the language of an opinion differs from that of a report.
questions.a: An opinion uses we hold to mark what binds other courts, marks what it is not deciding, phrases uncertainty as the record does not disclose, and uses terms of art with non-obvious definitions. A newspaper must be clear on one reading so it substitutes approximations and drops qualifications, and the effect is cumulative rather than the result of any single choice.

questions.q:
term of art: a word with a precise technical meaning inside a field, different from its everyday sense.
cumulative: building up across many small choices rather than arising from one.
Describe the connection between a newspaper's audience and its vocabulary.
questions.a: It must be comprehensible on one reading to someone with no background, so it replaces terms of art with approximations and states conclusions without the qualifications that produced them.

articles.note: This is the example the standard itself names. Put a real opinion beside a real report of the same case and count the substitutions.

articles.title: Why a Patent Reads Like That
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A patent is written in a style that is nearly unreadable, and almost all of it is deliberate. The document has to do a job that ordinary description cannot do, and the style is what the job requires.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The operative part is the claims, a numbered list at the end. Everything before them describes the invention; only the claims define what is protected, and a feature described at length and left out of the claims is given away.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each claim is a single sentence, however long. It has to be, because a claim defines a boundary, and dividing a boundary into separate sentences would create an ambiguity about how the pieces combine.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Particular words carry fixed meanings established by decades of litigation. A device comprising three parts has at least those three and may have others; a device consisting of three parts has those and nothing more.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The indefinite article is similarly load-bearing. A fastener generally means one or more fasteners, so a competitor using two has not escaped the claim, and this is a settled reading rather than a quirk of grammar.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Later references must attach to earlier ones. Said fastener points back to a fastener introduced before it, and a term that appears first with said refers to nothing, which is an objection an examiner will raise.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The specification before the claims does its own work. It must describe the invention well enough that a skilled person could build it, because a patent is a bargain: protection in exchange for a disclosure the public eventually gets.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the effect of the whole is a document optimised against a reader who is looking for a way out. Every habit that makes it hard to read exists because some earlier patent was read cleverly and lost.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. what the specification must do) and paragraph H (i.e. who the style is written against).
Summarize why a patent is written as it is.
questions.a: Only the numbered claims define what is protected, so a feature described but not claimed is given away, and each claim is one sentence because a boundary split across sentences would be ambiguous. Words such as comprising and the indefinite article carry fixed meanings set by litigation, and the specification must enable a skilled person to build the invention, because a patent exchanges protection for disclosure.

claim: the numbered sentence defining the boundary of what a patent protects.
specification: the descriptive part of a patent, which must enable a skilled person to build the invention.
Describe the connection between past litigation and the style of a modern patent.

articles.note: Students assume obscure writing means careless writing. Here every obscurity has a reason, which makes it a good test of the standard's cumulative-impact clause.

articles.title: What Diplomats Say Instead
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Official statements between governments are written in a register that sounds bland to an outsider and is read as precise by its intended audience. Almost nothing in it means what the same words mean elsewhere.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A frank exchange of views means the parties disagreed. A full and frank exchange means they disagreed sharply. A useful meeting means very little happened, and a historic meeting is the only one of these that means what it says.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The gradations matter because they are a scale. Expressing concern, expressing serious concern, and expressing grave concern are three recognised steps, and moving between them is itself the message being sent.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The vocabulary exists because of what statements do. A government that uses strong language publicly has committed itself, and a crisis is easier to end if nobody has said anything they cannot step back from.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Actions are also graded and also readable. Summoning an ambassador is a public rebuke, recalling your own ambassador for consultations is stronger, and expelling diplomats is stronger again, and all of these are understood as a sequence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The register has a cost. A public reading a statement in ordinary English will underestimate what is happening, because the words that signal a serious deterioration sound mild to anyone not counting the steps.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It also constrains honesty. A government that wants to say something is unacceptable in plain terms must either break the register, which is itself a signal, or accept that its statement will be read as routine.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a language where tone carries the content. A reader has to know the scale before any individual statement means anything, which is the opposite of how ordinary writing is supposed to work.

register: a way of using language appropriate to a particular setting, which here carries meaning of its own.

Describe the connection between the register and what the public understands.
questions.a: A public reading a statement in ordinary English will underestimate what is happening, because the words that signal a serious deterioration sound mild to anyone not counting the steps.

articles.note: The scale is the point rather than any one phrase. Give students three real statements about one event and ask them to order them.

articles.title: The Vocabulary of Risk
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A headline reports that a habit doubles the risk of a disease. The sentence is probably accurate, it is almost certainly incomplete, and the missing piece is the one that would let a reader decide anything.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Doubling is a relative statement. It describes the change in risk and says nothing about the risk it changed, so the same phrase covers a move from one in ten to two in ten and a move from one in a million to two.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The absolute version carries the information a person needs. Risk rose from four in ten thousand to eight in ten thousand is less striking, harder to put in a headline, and the only form in which the size of the effect appears.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both numbers are honest and they are used for different reasons. A relative risk is the right quantity for comparing studies, because it stays stable across populations with different baseline rates, and that is why researchers report it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third form is more useful again for a decision. The number needed to treat says how many people must take a medicine for one of them to benefit, which converts a probability into a count of actual people.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a difference between risk and rate. A risk is a probability over a stated period, so a figure given without its period is incomplete in a way that is easy to miss, since the sentence still reads as though it is finished.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Attributable fraction is another term doing quiet work. It describes how much of the disease in a population would not occur without the exposure, which is a question about the population and not about any individual.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative lesson is that these are not synonyms with different tones. Each quantity answers a different question, and a sentence that supplies only one of them has decided which question the reader is allowed to ask.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative lesson is that these are not synonyms with different tones. Each answers a different question. A sentence supplying only one has decided which question the reader may ask.

questions.q: Why is doubling the risk incomplete on its own?
questions.a: It describes the change in risk and says nothing about the risk it changed, so it covers both a move from one in ten to two in ten and a move from one in a million to two.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the number needed to treat) and paragraph G (i.e. attributable fraction).
Summarize the different ways risk can be stated.
questions.a: A relative risk describes a change without its baseline and stays stable across populations, which is why researchers use it, while an absolute risk gives the size of the effect. The number needed to treat converts a probability into a count of people, a risk requires a stated period, and attributable fraction describes a population rather than an individual.

questions.q:
baseline: the risk before the exposure, which a relative statement leaves out.
number needed to treat: how many people must receive a treatment for one of them to benefit.
Describe the connection between which quantity is reported and what a reader can ask.
questions.a: Each quantity answers a different question, so a sentence that supplies only one of them has decided which question the reader is allowed to ask.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's What a Doctor Means by Positive. Both are about a number whose everyday reading is confidently wrong.

articles.title: Where a Review Article Turns
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A review article surveys what is known about a question. It is the document a newcomer is told to read first, and most of its length is summary of work done by other people.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Summary alone would not justify it. Anyone can list papers, and a review earns its place by doing something the list cannot, which happens in a particular section and can usually be located precisely.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first part establishes the field. It defines the terms, sets out the main findings in a defensible order, and gives the reader enough to follow an argument they could not have followed before.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The turn comes when the review stops reporting and starts adjudicating. A sentence appears saying that two bodies of work are usually treated as compatible and are not, or that a widely cited result has not been replicated.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Everything before that sentence is preparation for it. The definitions were chosen so that the disagreement could be stated, and the order of the summary was chosen so that the two bodies of work would end up adjacent.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What follows the turn is a reorganisation rather than an addition. The field is re-sorted around the distinction the review has drawn, and findings that looked like a sequence are redescribed as answers to two different questions.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A weak review never turns. It reports everything with equal weight, treats every disagreement as a matter for further research, and leaves a reader knowing what has been published and not what to think.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the way to read one is to find the turn first. Locate the paragraph where the author's own position appears, then read backwards to see what the summary was built to make possible.

questions.q: What does a review do that a list of papers cannot?
questions.a: It stops reporting and starts adjudicating, saying for instance that two bodies of work usually treated as compatible are not, or that a widely cited result has not been replicated.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. how the earlier sections prepare for the turn) and paragraph G (i.e. what a weak review does instead).
Summarize the structure of a review article.
questions.a: The first part defines terms and sets out findings in a defensible order, preparing for a turn where the author stops reporting and judges, for instance that two bodies of work are incompatible. What follows re-sorts the field around that distinction, and a weak review never turns, leaving a reader knowing what has been published rather than what to think.

questions.q:
adjudicate: to decide between competing claims rather than only reporting them.
replicated: repeated by other researchers with the same result, which a widely cited finding may never have been.
Describe the connection between the order of the summary and the turn.
questions.a: The order of the summary was chosen so that the two bodies of work would end up adjacent, which is what allows the disagreement to be stated.

articles.note: RI.9-10.5 asks how a larger portion of a text develops a claim. Here the first half exists to make one sentence in the second half possible.

articles.title: The Middle of a Biography
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Biographies are rarely weakest at the beginning or the end. The childhood is documented by family records and the late career by newspapers, and the thin stretch is usually in the middle, before the subject became worth recording.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That stretch is where the book's claim is made. A biography is an argument that a person became who they became for reasons, and the reasons generally operate in exactly the years for which the evidence is poorest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A careful biographer marks the thinness rather than smoothing it. Phrases such as the record is silent, or he may have, or there is no evidence that, are doing structural work by showing where the narrative is carrying weight it cannot support.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The alternative is to fill the gap with context. A chapter about what the city was like, what the trade involved and what people of that class generally did is true, interesting and not about the subject at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That technique is not dishonest and it is easy to misread. A reader moving through a well-written chapter about a milieu can finish it believing they have learned something about a person, when the person has not appeared.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader can test it directly. Take a chapter from the middle and underline every sentence whose subject is the person, and what remains is the evidence the argument rests on.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The structure also explains a familiar complaint. Biographies often feel as though they lose their subject halfway through and recover them later, and that is not a failure of writing but the shape of the surviving material.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the middle is where to judge a biography. The beginning shows the writer can handle documents and the end shows they can handle a public life, and the middle shows what they do when there is nothing to work with.

questions.q: Why is the middle of a biography usually the thinnest part?
questions.a: The childhood is documented by family records and the late career by newspapers, and the middle covers the years before the subject became worth recording.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. filling a gap with context) and paragraph F (i.e. the underlining test).
Summarize why the middle of a biography matters most.
questions.a: The middle covers the years before a subject was worth recording, and it is also where the book's explanation of how they became who they became has to operate. A careful biographer marks the thinness with phrases such as the record is silent, while the alternative is a chapter of context that is true and not about the subject, which a reader can test by underlining sentences whose subject is the person.

questions.q:
milieu: the surroundings and social setting a person lived in, which a chapter may describe in place of the person.
structural: doing work in how a text is built, rather than only conveying information.
Describe the connection between the surviving material and a common complaint about biographies.
questions.a: Biographies often feel as though they lose their subject halfway through and recover them later, which is not a failure of writing but the shape of the surviving material.

articles.note: The underlining test in paragraph F is quick and genuinely revealing. Run it on one chapter and count.

articles.title: The Supplementary File
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most scientific papers now carry a second document. The supplementary materials hold the data, the extra figures, the detail of the methods and the analyses that did not fit, and it is often several times longer than the paper.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The arrangement solves a real constraint. Journals limit length, a reader wants an argument they can follow, and a methods section containing every parameter would be unreadable without serving any reader well.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also moves material across a line. The main text is read by reviewers and editors closely; the supplement is read closely by far fewer people, and what is in it is formally part of the paper and practically less examined.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That creates a predictable shape. Results that complicate the main claim can end up in the supplement without anything being concealed, because every one of them is published and findable and nobody is lying about anything.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader who wants to assess a paper properly therefore has to go there. The supplement is where the sample sizes for each condition sit, where the analyses that were tried appear, and where a figure showing an inconvenient subgroup lives.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It is also where the strongest work often is. A full dataset, a complete protocol and the code used to analyse it are what make a study checkable, and a supplement containing all three is a claim about the authors' confidence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The division therefore refines the paper's argument rather than merely extending it. The main text says what the authors conclude, and the supplement says what they did, and the gap between those two is the thing worth measuring.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Which is why the first question about a paper is increasingly whether the supplement exists and what is in it. A short paper with a long supplement and a short paper with none are making very different offers to a reader.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why complicating results end up there) and paragraph F (i.e. why a full supplement is a claim about confidence).
Summarize what a supplementary file contains and why it matters.
questions.a: It holds data, extra figures, methods detail and analyses that did not fit the length limit, and it is formally part of the paper while being read far less closely. Results complicating the main claim can end up there with nothing concealed, and it is also where a full dataset, protocol and code make a study checkable, so the gap between what authors conclude and what they did is measurable there.

questions.q:
protocol: the complete written plan of how a study was carried out.
subgroup: a smaller set within a study's participants, whose separate result may differ from the overall one.
Describe the connection between how closely a document is read and what ends up in it.
questions.a: The main text is read closely by reviewers and editors while the supplement is read closely by far fewer people, so results that complicate the main claim can end up there without anything being concealed.

articles.note: Paragraph D is careful not to allege bad faith, and the care is the point. The structure produces the effect whether or not anyone intends it.

articles.title: How a Manifesto Is Built
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A manifesto is a document designed to produce action, and its structure is nearly always the same regardless of what it is arguing for. Recognising the structure is most of what it takes to read one critically.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens with a diagnosis. Something is described as wrong, and the description is written to be agreed with by people who will disagree about everything after it, so the opening is usually the least controversial part.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second movement supplies a cause. The wrong thing is attributed to a system, a group or a failure of will, and this is where a reader who accepted the opening is first asked to accept something more.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then come the principles, stated as though they followed from the diagnosis. They generally do not follow in any strict sense; several different sets of principles would be consistent with the same account of what is wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The demands come last, and they are the only part that commits anybody. A manifesto with a vivid diagnosis and vague demands has arranged for agreement without obligation, which is the commonest form the document takes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The transition to the imperative is the hinge. Somewhere the verbs change from describing to instructing, and a reader can usually point at the sentence, because almost everything persuasive happens before it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That ordering is not an accident of style. Agreement is cheapest at the start and most expensive at the end, so the document spends its credibility in the order it was accumulated.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading one backwards is therefore the useful exercise. Start at the demands, ask what the diagnosis would have to say to make them follow, and then check whether the diagnosis actually says it.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why vague demands are common) and paragraph H (i.e. reading the document backwards).
Summarize the structure of a manifesto.
questions.a: It opens with a diagnosis written to be widely agreed with, supplies a cause that asks for more, states principles as though they followed when several sets would fit, and ends with demands, the only part that commits anyone. The verbs turn from describing to instructing at a locatable hinge, and the order spends agreement from cheapest to most expensive.

imperative: the grammatical form that instructs rather than describes, which marks the turn in the document.
diagnosis: the opening account of what is wrong, offered before any cause or demand.
Describe the connection between the order of the sections and the cost of agreeing.
questions.a: Agreement is cheapest at the start and most expensive at the end, so the document spends its credibility in the order it was accumulated.

articles.note: The backwards reading in paragraph H works on any persuasive document. It is the single most transferable exercise in this grade.

articles.title: The Figure That Carries the Paper
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Experienced readers of scientific papers do not read them in order. They read the abstract, then look at the figures, and only then decide whether to read any prose at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That is not laziness. In most experimental papers one figure carries the central claim, and a reader who understands that figure understands what the paper is asserting, with the text serving to say how it was produced.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The figure is usually identifiable. It is the one the abstract refers to most directly, it is often the most complex, and it typically shows the comparison that the whole study was designed to make.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Everything else in the paper is positioned relative to it. Earlier figures establish that the method works and that controls behaved as expected, and later ones extend the claim to another system or rule out an alternative.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the figures have an argumentative order of their own. A reader can follow the logic from the sequence alone, and a paper whose figures do not make sense in order usually has a problem the prose is covering.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The caption is part of the argument rather than a label. It states what was measured, how many times, what the error bars represent and what the statistical test was, and a caption that omits those has moved a claim into a place it cannot be checked.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is also where a paper is most often weak in a visible way. A key figure showing three replicates, or error bars whose definition is unstated, or an axis that begins where the difference looks largest, is readable as such without reading a word.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The structure therefore refines the claim at the level of the whole document. The prose says what the authors think happened, and the figures say what they can show, and reading them in that order keeps the two apart.
