questions.q: How can the central figure usually be identified?
questions.a: It is the one the abstract refers to most directly, it is often the most complex, and it typically shows the comparison the whole study was designed to make.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what a caption must state) and paragraph G (i.e. the weaknesses visible in a figure).
Summarize how the figures in a paper carry its argument.
questions.a: One figure usually carries the central claim, with earlier figures establishing that the method and controls worked and later ones extending it or excluding alternatives, so the sequence has a logic of its own. The caption must state what was measured, how many times, what error bars represent and which test was used, and weaknesses such as three replicates or an unstated error bar are visible without reading the prose.

questions.q:
replicate: one repetition of an experiment, whose number limits how much a figure can show.
control: a comparison condition included to show that an effect is attributable to the thing being tested.
Describe the connection between reading the figures first and judging the paper.
questions.a: The prose says what the authors think happened and the figures say what they can show, so reading them in that order keeps the two apart.

articles.note: Hand out a real paper with the prose removed. Students can usually reconstruct the argument from figures and captions alone, which is the claim this article makes.

articles.title: How a Grant Application Persuades
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research grant application is a persuasive document that is almost never read as one. It is written by scientists, reviewed by scientists, and it uses rhetoric as deliberately as any advertisement.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first task is to establish that a problem matters. The opening pages argue significance, usually by connecting a narrow technical question to something a reader already cares about, and the connection is the part doing the work.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second task is harder and less honest-sounding. An applicant must show that the work is likely to succeed, which in practice means showing it has partly been done already, because a reviewer will not fund a question that might not be answerable.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That produces a known tension. Preliminary data demonstrate feasibility, and an applicant with enough preliminary data to be convincing has performed a good deal of the research they are asking to be funded for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The verbs carry a great deal. We will determine asserts that the experiment will produce an answer; we will investigate concedes that it might not; and a reader who notices which verb appears where has located the applicant's real confidence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Risk is handled by a particular move. A section on potential problems and alternative approaches names the things most likely to fail, which both demonstrates competence and removes the objection from the reviewer's hands.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The rhetoric is not deception and the system knows it. Everyone involved has written these documents, everyone recognises the moves, and the convention is understood as a shared format rather than a set of claims taken at face value.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What that costs is a kind of distortion. Work that cannot be made to look nearly finished is harder to fund, so the format quietly selects for research whose answer is already partly known.

preliminary data: results obtained before funding, used to demonstrate that the proposed work will succeed.
Describe the connection between the need for preliminary data and what gets funded.
questions.a: Work that cannot be made to look nearly finished is harder to fund, so the format quietly selects for research whose answer is already partly known.

articles.note: RI.9-10.6 asks how rhetoric advances a purpose. Paragraph G refuses the cynical reading and paragraph H refuses the comfortable one, which is the pair worth holding.

articles.title: The Shape of a Public Apology
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A public apology from an organisation is a composed document, drafted by several people and approved by more, and it has recognisable parts. Knowing them makes it possible to say precisely what a given statement does and does not do, which is harder than deciding whether it sounded sincere.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A complete apology names the act. It states what was done, in language a person affected would recognise, rather than describing it as an incident, a situation or a matter that has come to attention.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then accepts responsibility in the first person. We did this is a different sentence from mistakes were made, and the difference is the entire question of whether anyone has apologised.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third element is the hardest and the most often missing. An acknowledgement of harm says what the act cost the people it affected, which requires describing their experience rather than the organisation's regret.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A remedy follows, with specifics. What will be done, by when, and how anyone will know it happened, because a promise with no date attached is not checkable and will not be checked.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The best-known failure is the conditional. I am sorry if anyone was offended apologises for a reaction rather than an act, places the reader's sensitivity in question, and commits the speaker to nothing at all.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A second failure is the explanation that arrives too early. A sentence about pressures, resources or circumstances that appears before the acknowledgement of harm reads as a defence, whatever it was intended as.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The rhetoric is doing two jobs at once, which is why these documents are so often strange. They must satisfy people who were harmed and must not create legal liability, and the parts most often missing are precisely the parts a lawyer would remove.

questions.a: Saying what the act cost the people it affected, which means describing their experience rather than the organisation's regret.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the conditional apology) and paragraph H (i.e. the two jobs the document is doing).
Summarize the parts of a complete apology and the common failures.
questions.a: It names the act in recognisable language, accepts responsibility in the first person, acknowledges what the act cost those affected, and sets out a specific remedy with a date. The conditional form apologises for a reaction rather than an act, an early explanation reads as a defence, and the missing parts are those a lawyer would remove to avoid liability.

questions.q:
conditional: phrased as depending on something, as in sorry if anyone was offended, which commits the speaker to nothing.
remedy: the specific action promised to put something right, which is checkable only if it carries a date.
Describe the connection between legal liability and what an apology leaves out.
questions.a: The document must satisfy people who were harmed and must not create legal liability, and the parts most often missing are precisely the parts a lawyer would remove.

articles.note: Bring three real corporate apologies and have students score each against the four parts. The scores are usually low and the pattern of what is missing is consistent.

articles.title: The Advertisement That Shows the Crash
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Road safety campaigns often use frightening images. A slowed shot of an impact, a hospital corridor, a family being told something: the technique is old, widely used and not as effective as it looks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The reasoning behind it is intuitive. A person who understands the consequences will change their behaviour, so making the consequences vivid should produce a change proportional to how vivid they are made.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Research on fear appeals does not support that cleanly. Fear reliably gets attention, and attention is not behaviour, and a message that frightens without offering a response can produce avoidance instead of change.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The finding most often reported is that fear works when paired with efficacy. A viewer must believe both that the danger is real and that there is a specific thing they can do that will work, and the second half is what most frightening advertisements omit.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Without it the available response is to stop watching. A person who feels threatened and powerless can reduce the feeling by dismissing the message, by deciding it does not apply to them, or by looking away.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a targeting problem. The people a campaign most wants to reach are often those most practised at dismissing it, and a message that works on cautious viewers who were never the risk is measuring the wrong audience.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of this makes the technique worthless, and campaigns that pair the image with a concrete instruction have evidence behind them. The instruction is doing much of the work the image is usually credited with.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The rhetorical question is therefore which part persuades. An advertisement is built to be remembered, and a campaign is meant to change what people do, and those two goals come apart more often than the people commissioning them expect.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the targeting problem) and paragraph H (i.e. remembering versus changing behaviour).
Summarize why frightening safety advertisements often fail.

Fear works when paired with a specific action the viewer believes will work, which most such advertisements omit, and the viewers most practised at dismissing a message are often the intended audience.

questions.q:
efficacy: a viewer's belief that a specific action is available and will work.
fear appeal: a persuasive message that works by making a consequence vivid and frightening.
Describe the connection between being memorable and changing behaviour.
questions.a: An advertisement is built to be remembered and a campaign is meant to change what people do, and those two goals come apart more often than the people commissioning them expect.

articles.note: A rhetoric article where the rhetoric is partly ineffective, which is unusual and useful. Ask what evidence would settle whether a particular campaign worked.

articles.title: What a Concession Speech Is For
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A candidate who has lost an election gives a speech. It is an unusual piece of public speaking, because its speaker has no power, no proposal and nothing to gain, and it is nevertheless one of the most consequential speeches in a democracy.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The speech has one job above the others. By accepting the result, the loser tells their own supporters that the process worked, and no institution can do this in their place because it is the losing side that has to be persuaded.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its rhetoric is therefore addressed inward. The audience is not the country generally but the people who voted for the speaker, who are disappointed, who may suspect the result, and who will take their reading of events from them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There are standard elements. The speaker names the winner, congratulates them explicitly, states that they have called them, and usually offers cooperation, and each of those is a signal that the contest has ended rather than paused.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The thanks to supporters do more than they appear to. By praising the campaign as worthwhile, the speaker reframes a loss as a legitimate outcome of a fair process rather than evidence that something was taken.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A concession has no legal effect at all. It does not certify a result, it does not bind anyone, and a candidate who refuses to give one has not changed any official outcome, which makes its function purely rhetorical and not therefore minor.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The absence of the speech is what shows its work. When a concession does not come, supporters are left without the one signal that would tell them the contest is over, and the uncertainty is the thing the convention existed to prevent.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the genre is a case of rhetoric doing institutional work. A speech with no authority behind it performs a function the written rules do not cover, which is why it is treated as a convention rather than a courtesy.

questions.q: Why is a concession speech addressed to the speaker's own supporters?
questions.a: It is the losing side that has to be persuaded the process worked, and no institution can do that in the candidate's place.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. that a concession has no legal effect) and paragraph G (i.e. what its absence reveals).
Summarize what a concession speech does.
questions.a: A candidate with no power tells their own supporters the process worked, since it is the losing side that must be persuaded. The standard elements signal that the contest has ended rather than paused, thanking supporters reframes a loss as a legitimate outcome, and although the speech has no legal effect its absence leaves supporters without the signal the convention existed to supply.

questions.q:
concession: a public acceptance of defeat, which carries no legal force.
convention: a practice followed because it is expected rather than because a rule requires it.
Describe the connection between the speech having no legal effect and its mattering.
questions.a: It certifies nothing and binds nobody, so its function is purely rhetorical, and that function is performing work the written rules do not cover.

articles.note: Rhetoric with institutional consequences and no legal force is a hard idea. The absence argument in paragraph G is what makes it demonstrable.

articles.title: The Briefing After the Failure
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Something has gone wrong in public: a system is down, a product has injured someone, a launch has failed. Within hours an organisation holds a briefing, and almost everything said in it is constrained before anyone speaks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first constraint is that nobody knows yet. A cause takes weeks to establish, and a spokesperson who offers one on the first afternoon will usually be wrong and will have to retract it publicly.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is legal. A statement accepting responsibility becomes evidence, so counsel will remove it, and an organisation speaking honestly on day one may be worsening a position that affects employees and shareholders.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is that silence is read as guilt. An organisation that says nothing will have the gap filled by others, so it must speak while having nothing it is able to say, which is the whole difficulty of the genre.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The resulting rhetoric is recognisable. Statements of concern, a commitment to investigate, a description of what is being done now, and no account of why, because why is the thing that cannot yet be said.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A good briefing is distinguishable from a bad one. It states clearly what is not yet known and when more will be said, it corrects anything already published that is wrong, and it tells people what they should do today.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A bad one fills the same space with reassurance. It describes the organisation's commitment to safety and its long record, which answers a question nobody asked and signals that the speaker's concern is the organisation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the test is where the sentences point. Toward the people affected and what they need now, or toward the institution and how it would like to be seen, and the words available are nearly the same in both cases.

questions.q: Why must an organisation speak before it knows anything?
questions.a: Silence is read as guilt and an organisation that says nothing will have the gap filled by others, so it must speak while having nothing it is able to say.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what a good briefing does) and paragraph H (i.e. the test of where sentences point).
Summarize the constraints on a briefing after a failure.
questions.a: A cause takes weeks to establish so an early explanation will usually be wrong, a statement of responsibility becomes legal evidence, and silence is read as guilt, so an organisation must speak without being able to explain. A good briefing states what is not known, when more will come, corrects errors already published and says what people should do, while a bad one offers reassurance about the organisation.

questions.q:
counsel: the lawyers advising an organisation, whose concern is what a statement may later be used for.
holding statement: a statement issued to fill the space before anything can be explained.
Describe the connection between the legal constraint and what a briefing leaves out.
questions.a: A statement accepting responsibility becomes evidence, so counsel will remove it, which is part of why no account of cause appears.

articles.note: Pairs with The Shape of a Public Apology. One is written when nothing is known and the other when everything is, and the legal pressure shapes both.

articles.title: An Expedition in Three Records
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A scientific expedition generates three quite different documents, written at different times for different readers, and a historian using only one of them will reach a conclusion the other two would not support.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the log. It is written daily, in the field, by people who are tired, and it records positions, weather, what was collected and what went wrong, without knowing which of those will matter.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its value is that it was written before the outcome was known. A log cannot be shaped by how the expedition turned out, and a day that later proved decisive is recorded with no more emphasis than any other.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second is the published narrative, written afterwards for a general audience. It has a shape, with a beginning, a crisis and a resolution, and the events are selected and ordered to produce that shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That narrative is not less true and it is differently organised. Days that produced nothing are compressed into a sentence, and an incident that reads as a turning point may have been one of several similar incidents in the log.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third record is the data: specimens, measurements, photographs, samples. It emphasises what the expedition was for, and it is almost silent about the experience of obtaining any of it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Each medium therefore emphasises a different thing. The log emphasises sequence, the narrative emphasises meaning, and the data emphasise result, and no two of them disagree about any fact.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The useful exercise is to take one day and read it in all three. The day will have a position and a weather note in the log, two paragraphs of significance in the narrative, and three specimen labels in the collection.

Summarize what each of the three records emphasises.

Describe the connection between when a document was written and what it can be shaped by.

articles.note: RI.9-10.7 asks which details each medium emphasises. The closing exercise makes that measurable rather than impressionistic.

articles.title: A Life in Three Tellings
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A person's life can be told as an autobiography, as a biography written by someone else, and as an obituary. The three are built from overlapping facts and they are not three versions of one thing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An autobiography has access nothing else has. Only the subject knows what they intended, what they feared and what they decided not to do, and none of that appears in any external record.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also has the worst possible vantage point. A person is explaining their own life to themselves as well as to a reader, the account was composed after everything had already turned out, and memory reorganises around outcomes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A biography trades access for distance. The writer cannot know what the subject intended and can read letters the subject forgot writing, interview people who disliked them, and compare claims against dates.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its characteristic failure is the opposite one. A biographer has chosen a subject, spent years with them, and must produce a coherent account, which creates pressure toward a thesis that the evidence may only partly support.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An obituary is the most constrained and the most revealing of its moment. It is short, it is written quickly, and it must decide in a few hundred words which two or three things a life is going to be remembered for.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That compression is informative in itself. Obituaries of the same person in different publications select different achievements, and comparing them shows what each audience was assumed to care about.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the emphases are predictable from the form. Intention from the autobiography, verification from the biography, and public meaning from the obituary, and a reader who wants all three has to read all three.

questions.q: What can an autobiography supply that no other account can?
questions.a: What the subject intended, feared and decided not to do, none of which appears in any external record.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the biographer's characteristic failure) and paragraph G (i.e. what comparing obituaries reveals).
Summarize what each of the three forms emphasises.
questions.a: An autobiography alone knows intention but is composed after the outcome, when memory reorganises around it. A biography trades access for distance and can check claims, but the writer must produce a coherent account, which pushes toward a thesis. An obituary compresses a life into a few hundred words, and comparing versions shows what each audience was assumed to value.

questions.q:
vantage point: the position from which an account is written, which determines what can be seen from it.
thesis: the single organising claim a biographer is under pressure to produce.
Describe the connection between when an autobiography is written and what it can show.
questions.a: The account was composed after everything had already turned out and memory reorganises around outcomes, which is why its access to intention comes with the worst possible vantage point.

articles.note: Pairs with The Middle of a Biography under RI.9-10.5. That one was about structure inside a form, and this is about choosing between forms.

articles.title: One Storm, Three Instruments
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A hurricane is described by three kinds of record that agree about very little in detail while describing the same storm. Each is produced by a different instrument, answers a different question, and is trusted by forecasters for a different part of the picture.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A satellite image shows the whole system at once. It gives the shape, the size, the position of the eye and the temperature of the cloud tops, which is a reasonable proxy for how violently air is rising.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What it cannot give is the ground. A satellite sees the tops of clouds, so the wind a person is standing in has to be inferred from what the cloud tops look like, and that inference is where the uncertainty lives.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A forecast model supplies the opposite. It produces wind speeds, pressures and rainfall at every point on a grid, for hours into the future, with a precision the observations never had.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That precision is calculated rather than measured. A model's output is a consequence of its equations and its starting conditions, and running two models on the same morning produces two futures that are both internally consistent.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third record is the surface observation: a buoy reporting pressure, a gauge recording rainfall, a reconnaissance aircraft flying through and measuring directly, and an account from someone who was there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: These are true and they are scattered. An observation describes one point, the points are wherever instruments happen to be, and the worst-affected places are frequently where the instruments stopped reporting.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So each medium emphasises what it can reach. The satellite emphasises structure, the model emphasises what comes next, the observations emphasise what actually occurred, and a forecaster's work is largely the business of holding all three at once.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A hurricane is described by three kinds of record. They agree about very little in detail. They are describing the same storm.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A satellite image shows the whole system at once. It gives shape, size, the position of the eye, and cloud-top temperature, which is a reasonable proxy for how violently air is rising.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What it cannot give is the ground. A satellite sees cloud tops. The wind a person is standing in must be inferred from what those tops look like. The uncertainty lives in that inference.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A forecast model gives the opposite. It produces wind speeds, pressures and rainfall at every point on a grid, hours into the future, with a precision the observations never had.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That precision is calculated, not measured. A model's output follows from its equations and starting conditions. Two models run on one morning give two futures, each internally consistent.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third record is the surface observation. A buoy reporting pressure. A gauge recording rainfall. An aircraft flying through and measuring directly. An account from someone who was there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: These are true and they are scattered. An observation describes one point. The points are wherever instruments happen to be. The worst-affected places are often where instruments stopped reporting.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So each medium emphasises what it can reach. The satellite emphasises structure. The model emphasises what comes next. The observations emphasise what occurred. A forecaster holds all three at once.

questions.q: Why can a satellite not report the wind at ground level?
questions.a: A satellite sees the tops of clouds, so the wind a person is standing in has to be inferred from what the cloud tops look like.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why model precision is calculated rather than measured) and paragraph G (i.e. where observations are missing).
Summarize what each record of a storm emphasises.
questions.a: A satellite shows the whole system's structure but only the cloud tops, so surface wind must be inferred. A model gives values at every grid point hours ahead, but that precision follows from its equations and starting conditions rather than measurement. Surface observations are true but scattered, and the worst-affected places are often where instruments stopped reporting.

questions.q:
proxy: a measurable quantity standing in for one that cannot be observed directly, such as cloud-top temperature for rising air.
reconnaissance: a flight made through a storm specifically to take direct measurements.
Describe the connection between where instruments are and what the observations miss.
questions.a: An observation describes one point, the points are wherever instruments happen to be, and the worst-affected places are frequently where the instruments stopped reporting.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's One Paragraph of a Forecast Discussion. That one showed a forecaster writing about disagreement, and this is what the disagreement is between.

articles.title: The Trial in Three Media
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A criminal trial produces a transcript, and in many jurisdictions also a set of courtroom drawings, and increasingly a podcast or documentary made afterwards. All three describe the same proceeding.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The transcript is complete and nearly unreadable. It records every word in order, including the procedural exchanges, the objections and the long passages where nothing happens, which is most of what a trial is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its completeness is what makes it the reference. Any claim about what was said can be checked against it, and the parts that are boring are not omitted, which is precisely why it can settle a dispute.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A courtroom sketch records something the transcript cannot. It shows where people sat, how they held themselves and who was looking at whom, and in courts that exclude cameras it is the only visual record there is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It is also an interpretation made at speed. An artist chooses a moment, chooses who to put in the frame and chooses what expression to give them, and a face drawn as composed or as anguished is a judgement.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A documentary or podcast adds narrative and removes nearly everything. A trial of six weeks becomes eight hours, which means more than ninety-five per cent of it is gone, and what remains was chosen for being interesting.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That selection is the thing to watch. A series is built around a question, usually whether the verdict was right, and material that bears on that question survives while material that does not is cut whatever its importance was in the room.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the emphases run in opposite directions. The transcript emphasises completeness, the sketch emphasises presence, the documentary emphasises coherence, and only one of them was made without knowing how it ended.

questions.q: Why is the transcript's dullness part of its value?
questions.a: It records every word in order including the parts where nothing happens, so any claim about what was said can be checked against it and it can settle a dispute.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the judgements inside a sketch) and paragraph G (i.e. what a documentary's question selects for).
Summarize what each account of a trial emphasises.
questions.a: The transcript is complete and unreadable, which is what lets it settle disputes about what was said. A sketch shows where people sat and how they held themselves but is an interpretation made at speed. A documentary compresses weeks into hours around a question, usually whether the verdict was right, so material not bearing on it is cut whatever it mattered in the room.

questions.q:
procedural: to do with the conduct of the proceeding rather than the facts in dispute.
coherence: hanging together as a single account, which a documentary produces by selection.
Describe the connection between knowing the ending and how an account is built.
questions.a: Only the transcript was made without knowing how it ended, while a documentary is built around a question about the verdict and selects material accordingly.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's When a Trial Is Televised. That article asked whether cameras should be allowed, and this one asks what each record emphasises once they are.

articles.title: The Study, the Release and the Leaflet
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: One piece of medical research reaches the public through a chain of documents, each written by different people for different readers. There is the paper, then a press release written by the institution that employs the researchers, then news coverage, then sometimes a leaflet handed to patients in a waiting room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The paper is written for specialists and states its claim with its limits attached. It says what population was studied, over what period, with what comparison, and what the authors can and cannot conclude.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The press release is written to be used. Its author wants journalists to cover the work, which rewards a clear claim, and a sentence that is accurate and heavily qualified does not travel.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Research on this chain has found something specific. Where news coverage overstates a finding, the overstatement is frequently already present in the press release rather than introduced by the journalist.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The usual mechanisms are small and identifiable. An association is described in causal language, a result in mice is reported without the species being prominent, and advice to readers is added that the study did not test.

paras.label: F
paras.text: News coverage then compresses further, and the leaflet compresses again. By the last document a qualified finding about a specific population has frequently become a general instruction addressed to the reader.

paras.label: G
paras.text: No one in the chain necessarily did anything wrong. Each document is appropriate for its own audience, and the distortion is produced by the sequence rather than by any single step in it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Which is why the useful comparison is end to end. Put the paper's own statement of its finding beside the leaflet's, and the difference between them is the thing to explain, without assuming that anyone intended it.

paras.text: One piece of medical research reaches the public through a chain of documents. The paper. A press release written by the institution. News coverage. Sometimes a leaflet given to patients.

questions.q: Where does research find that overstatement usually enters the chain?
questions.a: Where news coverage overstates a finding, the overstatement is frequently already present in the press release rather than introduced by the journalist.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the identifiable mechanisms) and paragraph G (i.e. the distortion coming from the sequence).
Summarize how a finding changes as it passes along the chain.
questions.a: The paper states a claim with its limits, the press release rewards a clear claim because a qualified sentence does not travel, and research finds overstatement often enters there rather than in the news. Associations become causal, mouse results lose their species, and advice is added, so by the leaflet a qualified finding about one population has become a general instruction.

questions.q:
press release: a document written by an institution to encourage coverage of its work.
qualified: stated with limits attached, which makes a claim accurate and harder to pass along.
Describe the connection between each document suiting its audience and the final distortion.
questions.a: Each document is appropriate for its own audience, so the distortion is produced by the sequence rather than by any single step in it.

articles.note: The end-to-end comparison in paragraph H is doable in one lesson with a real paper and a real leaflet, and the result is usually larger than students expect.

articles.title: The Study That Could Not Have Shown That
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A report claims that a school programme improves attainment. The evidence offered is that students who took part scored better at the end of the year than students who did not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Before asking whether the difference is real, ask a prior question: could this design have produced the answer being claimed, whatever the result had been? Often the answer is no, and then the size of the difference does not matter.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Here the problem is who took part. If students opted in, or were nominated by teachers, then the two groups differed before the programme started, and a difference at the end was guaranteed by the difference at the beginning.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is not a complaint about the size of the study. Enrolling ten times as many students would produce the same bias ten times more precisely, and a larger sample makes a confident wrong answer rather than a right one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The general form of the error is a design that cannot distinguish between the explanation being offered and at least one other. A result consistent with two explanations supports neither of them over the other.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a useful test that can be applied before any data exist. Ask what the study would have shown if the programme did nothing at all, and if the answer is the same result, the design cannot answer the question.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Applied honestly it is uncomfortable, because it disqualifies a great deal of research that is otherwise careful. Measurement can be precise, analysis can be correct, and the design can still be unable to support the sentence in the summary.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So this is not scepticism about conclusions. It is a question asked earlier than that, about whether the conclusion was reachable, and a study that fails it has not produced weak evidence but evidence about something else.

questions.q: Why does enrolling more students not fix this problem?
questions.a: Enrolling ten times as many students would produce the same bias ten times more precisely, so a larger sample makes a confident wrong answer rather than a right one.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the test that can be applied before any data exist) and paragraph H (i.e. why this is not ordinary scepticism).
Summarize the error and the test for it.
questions.a: If students opted in or were nominated, the groups differed before the programme began, so a difference at the end was guaranteed, and a larger sample only makes the bias more precise. The general form is a design that cannot separate the offered explanation from another, and the test is to ask what the study would have shown if the programme did nothing.

questions.q:
design: how a study is set up, which determines what questions its results can answer.
bias: a systematic difference built into a comparison, which more data does not remove.
Describe the connection between two explanations fitting a result and what the result supports.
questions.a: A result consistent with two explanations supports neither of them over the other, so a design that cannot distinguish them cannot answer the question.

articles.note: RI.9-10.8 asks whether reasoning is valid, not only whether evidence is sufficient. This article is about validity, and the test in paragraph F is the one to make routine.

articles.title: The Argument From Tradition
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A proposal to change something is met with the observation that it has been done this way for a very long time. The observation is usually true, and on its own it establishes nothing about whether the practice is good.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The reason is that age and merit are different properties. A practice persists for many reasons, including that nobody examined it, that changing it was costly, and that the people who found it intolerable had no say.

paras.label: C
paras.text: There is a serious argument nearby, and conflating the two is where most of the confusion lives. The serious version says that a long-standing arrangement may be solving a problem that is no longer visible, so removing it may have consequences nobody has predicted.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That argument is about caution rather than about merit. It says find out what this is for before you remove it, which is a demand for investigation, and it is satisfied by investigating.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fallacious version refuses the investigation. If the answer to what is this for is that it has always been so, the argument has provided no reason, and it will provide exactly the same non-reason next year.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two can be told apart by a single question: what would change your mind? A cautious defender names the thing they are afraid of losing, and a traditional defender cannot name it, because the position does not depend on one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The mirror error is equally common. Treating age as evidence against a practice is the same mistake reversed, and a rule's being old is no more a defect than it is a credential.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the burden sits where it always sits. Whoever wants the practice kept should say what it does, and whoever wants it removed should say what will happen instead, and how long it has existed is not part of either answer.

questions.q: Why does a practice persisting not show that it is good?
questions.a: A practice persists for many reasons, including that nobody examined it, that changing it was costly, and that the people who found it intolerable had no say.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the serious argument nearby) and paragraph F (i.e. the question that separates the two).
Summarize the difference between the cautious and the fallacious argument from tradition.
questions.a: Age and merit are different properties, and a practice may persist because nobody examined it. The serious version warns that an old arrangement may solve a problem no longer visible, which is a demand for investigation and is satisfied by investigating, while the fallacious version refuses it, and the two are separated by asking what would change your mind.

questions.q:
fallacious: reasoning that fails for a structural reason rather than because its facts are wrong.
burden: the obligation to give reasons, which here falls on both sides of the question.
Describe the connection between refusing investigation and giving no reason.
questions.a: If the answer to what is this for is that it has always been so, the argument has provided no reason, and it will provide exactly the same non-reason next year.

articles.note: Students who learn this fallacy often commit the mirror error in paragraph G within a week. Teach both halves at once.

articles.title: The Claim That Proves Itself
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A programme is reported as effective. Asked how effectiveness was determined, the report explains that a programme counts as effective when it meets the criteria, and the criteria turn out to describe what the programme does.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Nothing false has been said. Every sentence may be accurate, the arithmetic may be correct, and the conclusion follows from the premises, which is exactly what makes this difficult to see.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The problem is that the conclusion was contained in the premises from the start. An argument of this shape cannot fail, and an argument that cannot fail has not told you anything about the world.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The form appears constantly in definitions. A natural food is healthier, because healthy eating means eating natural food, is a complete argument that establishes nothing, and it survives because both sentences sound reasonable alone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It also appears in measurement. If a test is validated by comparing it against the judgements of experts, and those experts were trained using the test, the agreement between them is not evidence that either is right.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Detecting it requires a specific move: state the conclusion, then state the premises, then ask whether believing the premises requires already believing the conclusion. If it does, the argument is circular however long it is.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Length is the usual disguise. A circle with two steps is obvious, and a circle with nine steps spread across a forty-page report is nearly invisible, because no reader holds all nine in mind at once.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The test is therefore mechanical rather than intuitive. Write the steps in a list and look for the return, because the feeling that an argument is convincing is produced by exactly the same structure whether or not it is circular.

It appears in definitions and in measurement, as when a test is validated against experts trained on that test, and detection requires listing the steps and asking whether believing the premises requires already believing the conclusion.

questions.q:
premise: a statement an argument starts from and asks a reader to accept.
circular: an argument that arrives back at something it assumed, so it cannot fail.
Describe the connection between the length of a report and the visibility of a circle.
questions.a: A circle with two steps is obvious and one with nine steps spread across forty pages is nearly invisible, because no reader holds all nine in mind at once.

articles.note: The mechanical test in paragraph H matters because intuition is useless here. A circular argument feels exactly as convincing as a sound one.

articles.title: The Only Two Options
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: A council debating a shortfall is told it must either close the library or raise the local tax. The sentence is delivered as an account of the situation and is in fact the most contested claim in the room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Presenting two options as exhaustive is the oldest way to win an argument without having it. A listener who dislikes one is manoeuvred into defending the other, and the question of whether there are others is never reached.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The move is not always illegitimate. Some choices really are binary, and a speaker who has examined the alternatives and found them unavailable is reporting rather than framing, and that is a difference a listener can test.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The test is whether the speaker can say what was excluded and why. A council that has considered reducing opening hours, sharing premises, changing the service or delaying something else has a defensible pair, even if the pair is unwelcome.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fallacious version cannot do this, and usually does not have to. The two options appear in the opening sentence, the discussion moves immediately to which is worse, and by the time anyone asks, the frame has been accepted by everybody arguing inside it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A related move narrows a continuous question into a switch. Spending is not a choice between a service existing and not existing; it is a quantity, and converting a dial into a switch removes every answer except the two ends.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The defence is to ask for the list before the argument. What else was considered, and what ruled it out, which is a question about process rather than about preference and is therefore hard to refuse.

paras.label: H
paras.text: This matters because the frame usually survives the debate. Whichever side wins, the decision made is one of the two that were offered, and the options nobody mentioned remain unexamined until the same shortfall arrives again.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A council debating a shortfall is told it must close the library or raise the local tax. The sentence sounds like an account of the situation. It is the most contested claim in the room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Presenting two options as exhaustive is the oldest way to win an argument without having it. A listener who dislikes one is pushed into defending the other. Whether there are others is never reached.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The move is not always illegitimate. Some choices really are binary. A speaker who examined the alternatives and found them unavailable is reporting rather than framing. A listener can test that difference.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The test is whether the speaker can say what was excluded and why. A council that considered reduced hours, shared premises, a changed service or a delay elsewhere has a defensible pair, even an unwelcome one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fallacious version cannot do this and usually does not have to. The two options appear in the opening sentence. Discussion moves to which is worse. By the time anyone asks, everyone has accepted the frame.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A related move turns a continuous question into a switch. Spending is not a choice between a service existing and not existing. It is a quantity. Turning a dial into a switch removes every answer but the ends.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The defence is to ask for the list before the argument. What else was considered, and what ruled it out. That is a question about process, not preference, and so it is hard to refuse.

paras.label: H
paras.text: This matters because the frame outlasts the debate. Whoever wins, the decision is one of the two offered. The options nobody mentioned stay unexamined until the same shortfall returns.

questions.q: How can a listener test whether a pair of options is genuine?
questions.a: By asking whether the speaker can say what was excluded and why, since a council that considered reduced hours, shared premises or a delay has a defensible pair.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. turning a dial into a switch) and paragraph H (i.e. why the frame outlasts the debate).
Summarize the false dilemma and how to answer it.
questions.a: Presenting two options as exhaustive wins an argument without having it, because a listener who dislikes one defends the other. Some choices are genuinely binary, and the test is whether a speaker can name what was excluded and why, while a related move converts a continuous quantity into a switch, so the defence is to ask for the list before the argument begins.

questions.q:
exhaustive: covering every possibility, which a pair of options is claimed to be and often is not.
frame: the way a question is set up, which determines what answers are available inside it.
Describe the connection between accepting a frame and the options that are never examined.
questions.a: Whichever side wins, the decision made is one of the two that were offered, so the options nobody mentioned remain unexamined until the same shortfall arrives again.

articles.note: The dial-and-switch distinction in paragraph F generalises past budgets. Ask students for three questions that are routinely presented as switches and are not.

articles.title: Moving the Goalposts
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Someone makes a claim and names what would show it to be wrong. A test is run, the named result does not appear, and the claim is restated with a new condition attached that was not mentioned before.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Each individual restatement can be reasonable. Science revises claims constantly, an experiment can genuinely fail for a technical reason, and insisting that a hypothesis die at the first disconfirming result would be bad practice.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The difference is whether the revision was principled or convenient. A principled revision is derived from a reason independent of the failure, and it makes a new prediction that could itself fail, which the original claim no longer can.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A convenient revision does neither. It adds exactly the condition needed to explain away the result just obtained, it is introduced only afterwards, and it makes no prediction that any future test could disappoint.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A claim that has been rescued this way several times reaches a particular state. It is now compatible with every possible observation, which its holder may describe as its strength and which has made it impossible to learn anything from.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The pattern is easiest to see in the history of a dispute rather than at any one moment. Any single revision looks defensible; five of them in sequence, each triggered by a result rather than by an argument, is the whole phenomenon.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The fair way to raise it is to ask before the test, not afterwards. Agreeing in advance on what result would count as a failure converts the question from a dispute about motives into a record anyone can check.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That request is also a test of the claim's holder. Somebody who will state in advance what would change their mind is doing something different from somebody who will not, whatever either of them believes.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That request also tests the claim's holder. Someone who will state in advance what would change their mind is doing something different from someone who will not, whatever either believes.

questions.q: What distinguishes a principled revision from a convenient one?
questions.a: A principled revision is derived from a reason independent of the failure and makes a new prediction that could itself fail, while a convenient one adds exactly the condition needed to explain the result away and predicts nothing.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the state a repeatedly rescued claim reaches) and paragraph G (i.e. asking before the test).
Summarize how goalpost-moving works and how to address it.
questions.a: A claim is restated with a new condition each time a test fails, and any single revision may be reasonable since science revises constantly. The difference is whether the revision comes from an independent reason and makes a new falsifiable prediction, and a claim rescued repeatedly becomes compatible with every observation, so the fair response is to agree in advance what would count as a failure.

questions.q:
disconfirming: a result that counts against a claim rather than for it.
compatible with every observation: unable to be contradicted by anything, which makes a claim uninformative.
Describe the connection between seeing the history of a dispute and recognising the pattern.
questions.a: Any single revision looks defensible, so the pattern appears only across a sequence of them, each triggered by a result rather than by an argument.

articles.note: Paragraph G turns an accusation into a procedure, which is the most useful thing in this set. The accusation is unanswerable and the procedure is not.

articles.title: The Declaration and the Declaration of Sentiments
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In July 1848 a convention at Seneca Falls, New York, adopted a document called the Declaration of Sentiments. It was written to be read against another document, and the resemblance is deliberate down to the sentence rhythms.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its central sentence alters the most familiar line in American political writing by two words. We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men and women are created equal, and the addition is the entire argument.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The structure follows its model exactly. The 1776 Declaration states a principle, lists the grievances establishing that the principle has been violated, and concludes with a claim of right, and the 1848 document does all three in the same order.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The grievances are addressed to a different party. Where the original lists the acts of a king, the Declaration of Sentiments lists the acts of men, in the same accumulating form: he has, he has, he has.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The rhetorical effect depends on the reader knowing the original. An audience that recognises the form is being asked to notice that the argument they already accept, in the version they already accept, extends further than they have taken it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a specific kind of argument, and it is harder to refuse than a new one. A reader who rejects the 1848 document must explain which part of the 1776 reasoning stops short, and where, and on what principle.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The convention did not agree about everything. The resolution demanding the vote was the most contested item, and it passed after Frederick Douglass spoke for it, which is recorded in the proceedings.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Of around three hundred attendees, about a hundred signed. That number is part of the document's history: a text that borrows the authority of a founding document still had to persuade the people in the room.

questions.q: How does the Declaration of Sentiments alter its model's central sentence?
questions.a: It states that all men and women are created equal, and the addition of two words is the entire argument.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the borrowed form is hard to refuse) and paragraph H (i.e. how many attendees signed).
Summarize how the two documents relate.
questions.a: The 1848 Declaration of Sentiments copies the 1776 Declaration's structure of principle, grievances and claim of right, and alters its central sentence to say that all men and women are created equal. The grievances are addressed to men rather than a king in the same accumulating form, so a reader who rejects it must explain where the earlier reasoning stops, and about a hundred of three hundred attendees signed.

questions.q:
grievance: a listed wrong, used in both documents as evidence that a stated principle has been violated.
self-evident: requiring no proof, which is what both documents claim of their central principle.
Describe the connection between borrowing a form and the difficulty of refusing the argument.
questions.a: A reader who rejects the 1848 document must explain which part of the 1776 reasoning stops short, and where, and on what principle.

articles.note: RI.9-10.9 asks how seminal documents address related themes. This pair is the clearest case available, because one was written to be read against the other.

articles.title: Washington's Farewell Address
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In September 1796 Washington announced that he would not seek a third term. The announcement was not a speech; it was a letter published in a Philadelphia newspaper, addressed to the people, and reprinted across the country.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form matters to how it reads. A letter can be longer than a speech, it can be reread, and a reader meets its arguments in the order the writer chose rather than in the order an audience's attention allows.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is also a collaborative document. Washington worked from an earlier draft prepared with Madison and had Hamilton revise it extensively, so the text represents a considered position rather than one man's phrasing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its warnings are specific and they are about structures rather than people. The address argues that a party spirit organised around region will make Americans see each other as rival interests rather than as parties to one arrangement.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second warning concerns foreign attachment. Washington argues against permanent alliances, on the reasoning that an attachment to another nation gives domestic factions an outside interest to serve and a foreign quarrel a route inward.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The address is careful about its own authority. It presents its advice as that of a departing friend rather than as instruction, and it says the writer may be wrong, which is a rhetorical choice as much as a modest one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Its later use has often ignored that. The address has been cited for positions it does not take, and the phrase entangling alliances, frequently attributed to it, is Jefferson's from a different document.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading it beside the Declaration shows two distinct tasks. One text argues for separating from a government, and the other argues about how to hold one together afterwards, and the second is the harder of the two to write.

questions.q: Why does Washington argue against permanent alliances?
questions.a: An attachment to another nation gives domestic factions an outside interest to serve and a foreign quarrel a route inward.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how the address handles its own authority) and paragraph G (i.e. how it has been misused since).
Summarize what the Farewell Address argues and how it was made.
questions.a: Published as a letter rather than delivered, and revised by Hamilton from a draft prepared with Madison, it warns that party spirit organised around region will make Americans see each other as rival interests, and that permanent foreign attachments give factions an outside interest to serve. It offers its advice as a departing friend's and has since been cited for positions it does not take.

questions.q:
faction: a group within a state pursuing its own interest against the whole.
attachment: here, a standing connection to a foreign power, which the address argues against.
Describe the connection between the Declaration's task and this address's task.
questions.a: One text argues for separating from a government and the other argues about how to hold one together afterwards, which the article calls the harder of the two.

articles.note: The misattribution in paragraph G is worth checking in class. Students will find the phrase entangling alliances quoted as Washington's in several places.

articles.title: Two Hundred and Seventy Words
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: The address Lincoln gave at Gettysburg in November 1863 is about two hundred and seventy words long and took perhaps two or three minutes. It was not the main speech of the occasion.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Edward Everett had spoken first, for about two hours, in the manner expected of a dedication: a detailed account of the battle, the campaign and the classical precedents. His address was the one the programme was built around.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Lincoln's begins by dating the nation, and the choice is an argument. Four score and seven years before 1863 is 1776, which places the country's founding at the Declaration rather than at the Constitution of 1787.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That matters because the two documents say different things. The Declaration asserts that all men are created equal; the Constitution as then written accommodated slavery, and choosing the earlier text as the founding is choosing which principle the war defends.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structure is three sentences of work. The past founded a nation on a proposition, the present is testing whether such a nation can endure, and the future is a task handed to the living, and the whole speech moves through those three.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It also refuses to do what dedications do. The speech says the ground cannot be dedicated by anyone present because the dead have already done it, which removes the ostensible purpose of the occasion in a single sentence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The phrase government of the people, by the people, for the people was not original to Lincoln and he is not known to have claimed it was. Its force here comes from its position at the end of a structure that has earned it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Five manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive and they differ. There is no single authoritative text, which means that the most quoted speech in American history exists in several versions, none of them certainly what was said.

questions.a: It places the founding at the Declaration rather than the Constitution, and since the Declaration asserts that all men are created equal while the Constitution as then written accommodated slavery, it chooses which principle the war defends.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the refusal to dedicate) and paragraph H (i.e. the five differing manuscripts).
Summarize the Gettysburg Address and what it does.
questions.a: Lincoln spoke for two or three minutes after Everett's two hours, dating the nation from 1776 and so placing its founding at the Declaration rather than the Constitution. The speech moves from a past founded on a proposition, through a present testing whether such a nation can endure, to a task for the living, and it refuses the occasion's stated purpose by saying the dead have already dedicated the ground.

questions.q:
proposition: a claim put forward to be held or tested, which is how the speech describes the nation's founding.
dedicate: to set apart formally for a purpose, which the speech says cannot be done by those present.
Describe the connection between the choice of founding document and the purpose of the war.
questions.a: The Declaration asserts that all men are created equal while the Constitution as then written accommodated slavery, so choosing the earlier text as the founding chooses which principle the war is defending.

articles.note: Pairs directly with the Declaration of Sentiments article. Both are arguments made by choosing which earlier text to stand on.

articles.title: The Four Freedoms
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: On January 6, 1941, Roosevelt delivered his annual message to Congress. The United States was not at war, the country was divided about whether it should be, and the speech is written in and around that fact.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Most of it is an argument for supplying nations already fighting. It describes the danger of a world in which hostile powers control other continents, and it asks Congress for the authority and the money to send material.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The passage everyone remembers comes at the end and does something different. It names four freedoms that should exist everywhere in the world: of speech, of worship, from want, and from fear.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two of those are familiar from the First Amendment, and two are not. Freedom from want and freedom from fear do not appear in the Bill of Rights, and they are not restrictions on government in the same way the first two are.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That distinction is the argument. A freedom from want requires something to be provided rather than merely not prevented, which asks the state to do rather than to refrain, and it extends a familiar list by changing its kind.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The phrase everywhere in the world does similar work. It converts a statement about American arrangements into a claim about what people are owed anywhere, and that is what makes the passage usable as a foundation for later documents.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It was used that way. The four freedoms are frequently cited in the drafting history of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which includes provisions of both kinds, the restraining and the providing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading it beside Gettysburg shows a difference in method. Lincoln argued by narrowing to a proposition already stated in 1776, and Roosevelt argued by extending a list beyond what any American document had said.
