questions.a: They do not appear in the Bill of Rights and they are not restrictions on government, because a freedom from want requires something to be provided rather than merely not prevented.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the work done by everywhere in the world) and paragraph H (i.e. the contrast with Gettysburg).
Summarize what the Four Freedoms passage does.
questions.a: Most of the 1941 message argues for supplying nations already at war, and the closing passage names four freedoms for everywhere in the world. Two come from the First Amendment and two ask the state to provide rather than refrain, and the phrase everywhere in the world turns a statement about American arrangements into a claim about what people are owed anywhere.

questions.q:
Bill of Rights: the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution, which restrain government action.
provision: a clause in a document setting out something to be done or guaranteed.
Describe the connection between Lincoln's method and Roosevelt's.
questions.a: Lincoln argued by narrowing to a proposition already stated in 1776, and Roosevelt argued by extending a list beyond what any American document had said.

articles.note: The distinction between a freedom from interference and a freedom requiring provision is the hard idea here, and the whole standard's comparison work depends on students holding it.

articles.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1963 Martin Luther King Jr was arrested in Birmingham, Alabama, for taking part in demonstrations. While held, he wrote a long letter, beginning on the margins of a newspaper and continuing on whatever paper could be brought in.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is addressed to a specific audience. Eight white clergymen had published a statement calling the demonstrations unwise and untimely and urging that the matter be pursued in the courts rather than in the streets.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The letter answers them point by point, which shapes everything about it. It is not a speech to supporters; it is a reply to people who considered themselves sympathetic, and that is a harder document to write than either an attack or an appeal.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its central argument concerns the word untimely. King's reply is that there has never been a direct action campaign that was timely in the judgement of those not suffering, and that waiting has been the advice offered in every decade.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second argument addresses the charge of breaking laws. The letter distinguishes just from unjust laws, defines an unjust law as one a majority imposes on a minority but does not bind itself by, and cites Augustine and Aquinas for the distinction.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The passage most often extracted is about the white moderate. King writes that the moderate who prefers order to justice and sets the timetable for someone else's freedom is a greater obstacle than open opposition.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That passage is frequently quoted without its address. It is a sentence written to named recipients who had published a specific statement, and reading it as a general reflection removes the thing it was answering.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Beside the other documents in this group it does something none of them do. The Declaration and the Gettysburg Address state principles, and this letter argues with people who say they accept those principles and dispute the timing.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1963 Martin Luther King Jr was arrested in Birmingham, Alabama, for taking part in demonstrations. While held, he wrote a long letter. It began on newspaper margins and continued on whatever paper reached him.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is addressed to a specific audience. Eight white clergymen had published a statement calling the demonstrations unwise and untimely. They urged that the matter go to the courts rather than the streets.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The letter answers them point by point, and that shapes everything. It is not a speech to supporters. It is a reply to people who thought themselves sympathetic. That is harder to write than an attack or an appeal.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its central argument concerns the word untimely. King replies that no direct action campaign has ever been timely in the judgement of those not suffering, and that waiting has been the advice in every decade.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A second argument answers the charge of breaking laws. The letter separates just from unjust laws. An unjust law is one a majority imposes on a minority and does not bind itself by. Augustine and Aquinas are cited.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The passage most often extracted is about the white moderate. King writes that a moderate who prefers order to justice, and sets the timetable for someone else's freedom, is a greater obstacle than open opposition.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That passage is often quoted without its address. It was written to named recipients who had published a specific statement. Reading it as a general reflection removes what it was answering.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Beside the other documents here it does something none of them do. The Declaration and the Gettysburg Address state principles. This letter argues with people who say they accept those principles and dispute the timing.

questions.q: How does the letter define an unjust law?
questions.a: As one a majority imposes on a minority but does not bind itself by, a distinction for which the letter cites Augustine and Aquinas.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the passage about the white moderate) and paragraph G (i.e. what is lost when it is quoted alone).
Summarize what the letter argues and whom it answers.
questions.a: Written in jail in April 1963, it replies to eight clergymen who had called the demonstrations unwise and untimely. It argues that no direct action campaign has ever been timely in the judgement of those not suffering, distinguishes just from unjust laws by whether a majority binds itself, and argues that a moderate who prefers order to justice is a greater obstacle than open opposition.

questions.q:
direct action: public action such as a demonstration, as distinct from pursuing a claim through courts.
moderate: here, someone who accepts the aim and objects to the method or the timing.
Describe the connection between who the letter answers and what kind of document it is.
questions.a: It replies to people who considered themselves sympathetic and dispute the timing, which is harder to write than either an attack or an appeal, and unlike the Declaration or the Gettysburg Address it argues rather than states principles.

articles.note: Read the clergymen's statement first. The letter is almost unreadable as the reply it is without the four paragraphs it is answering.

articles.title: The Map of the Ocean Floor
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of history the sea floor was assumed to be a featureless plain. Nothing contradicted the assumption, because nobody could see it and the few available soundings were taken by lowering a weighted line.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Echo sounding changed what was available. A ship could record the depth continuously along its track, and by the late 1940s there were thousands of such tracks, each a profile of the bottom along one line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Marie Tharp worked at Lamont, in New York, converting those profiles into maps. She was not permitted on the research vessels for most of the 1950s, so she worked from data collected by colleagues who were.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The method was laborious and the result was new. By plotting profiles against each other she could draw the sea floor as a landscape, with mountains, escarpments and valleys rendered as a physiographic map a non-specialist could read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What appeared in the middle of the Atlantic was not a plain. There was a continuous mountain range, and running along the crest of it was a deep valley, a rift, which she identified from the profiles crossing it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Her colleague Bruce Heezen initially dismissed the rift, reportedly because it supported continental drift, which was then a disreputable idea. The valley implied the sea floor was being pulled apart, which meant continents moved.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The confirmation came from a different dataset. Earthquake epicentres in the Atlantic, plotted independently, fell along a line, and when the two maps were compared the line of earthquakes lay inside the rift she had drawn.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The map did something an argument could not. A physiographic map is readable by anyone, and a feature that had been a disputed interpretation of numbers became a thing a person could point at on a wall.

questions.q: What did Tharp find running along the Mid-Atlantic mountain range?
questions.a: A deep valley, a rift, which she identified from the profiles crossing it.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the independent earthquake data) and paragraph H (i.e. what a map could do that an argument could not).
Summarize how the shape of the ocean floor became known.
questions.a: Echo sounding produced thousands of depth profiles, and Marie Tharp, excluded from research vessels, plotted them against each other to draw the sea floor as a readable landscape. A continuous mountain range with a rift along its crest appeared in the Atlantic, implying the sea floor was pulling apart, and independently plotted earthquake epicentres fell inside the rift she had drawn.

questions.q:
physiographic map: a map drawn to show a landscape as it would look, rather than as contour lines.
epicentre: the point on the surface above where an earthquake originated.
Describe the connection between the rift and the idea that continents move.
questions.a: The valley implied the sea floor was being pulled apart, which meant continents moved, and that was then a disreputable idea.

articles.note: Two independent datasets agreeing is the evidential move from RI.9-10.1, appearing here in a different century and a different science.

articles.title: The Town That Moved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hibbing, Minnesota, sits on the Mesabi Range, and the iron ore that the town existed to mine turned out to extend directly underneath it. The ore was worth more than the location, and so the town was moved.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The decision was not metaphorical. Beginning around 1919 and continuing for several years, buildings were raised on jacks, placed on rollers or wheeled frames, and hauled about three kilometres south to a new site.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Not everything went. Larger structures were demolished rather than moved, some buildings were cut into sections and reassembled, and a number of residents refused for long enough that the process had to be negotiated building by building.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The mining company paid, which is the part that explains the rest. A company willing to meet the cost of moving a town had calculated the value of what lay beneath it, and the arithmetic was not close.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The new Hibbing was planned rather than grown. It was laid out deliberately, and the company's money produced public buildings of a scale the town's size would not otherwise have supported, including a high school with an auditorium modelled on a theatre.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That building is the part of the story usually told, and it is the least representative. An opulent school is a visible benefit, and the invisible cost is a settlement that exists where a company found it convenient.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What was left behind is also visible. The original site is largely a pit, and the ground where the first town stood has been removed, so the place a town used to be is not merely empty but gone.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is a clear case of a general pattern. Where a resource is immobile and a settlement is not, the settlement moves, and the apparent permanence of a town is a judgement about relative value rather than a fact about towns.

questions.q: Why was the town moved rather than the mining stopped?
questions.a: The ore was worth more than the location, and a company willing to meet the cost of moving a town had calculated the value of what lay beneath it.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the school is the least representative part) and paragraph H (i.e. the general pattern).
Summarize what happened at Hibbing and what it shows.
questions.a: Iron ore ran under the town, so from about 1919 buildings were raised on jacks and hauled three kilometres south, with larger ones demolished and some residents negotiating individually. The company paid because the ore was worth more, and the planned new town has public buildings beyond its size while the original site is now a pit.

questions.q:
immobile: unable to be moved, which is true of an ore body and not of a settlement.
opulent: lavish and expensive, as the new high school was for a town of that size.
Describe the connection between the company paying and the scale of the new public buildings.
questions.a: The company's money produced public buildings of a scale the town's size would not otherwise have supported, including a high school with an auditorium modelled on a theatre.

articles.note: Paragraph F is the turn, i.e. the celebrated detail is the unrepresentative one. Ask which part of the story a town's own museum would lead with.

articles.title: The Antenna That Could Not Be Cleaned
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1964 two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, began working with a large horn-shaped antenna originally built for satellite communication.

paras.label: B
paras.text: They wanted to use it for astronomy, which required characterising every source of noise in the instrument. Any signal they later detected would have to be distinguished from whatever the antenna produced on its own.

paras.label: C
paras.text: There was more noise than there should have been. A faint hiss remained after every known source was accounted for, it did not change with the time of day, it did not change with the season, and it came from every direction equally.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They worked through the possibilities methodically. The receiver was checked, the joints were checked, nearby New York City was considered and excluded because the signal did not vary with direction.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A pair of pigeons was nesting in the horn. The birds were removed, the accumulated droppings were cleaned out, and the two men later described the material in a phrase that has outlasted most of the rest of the account.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The noise remained. Having eliminated the instrument, the sky's known sources and the pigeons, they had a measurement of something uniform in every direction at a temperature of a few degrees above absolute zero.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Forty kilometres away at Princeton, a group led by Robert Dicke was preparing to look for exactly that. A hot early universe would have left radiation filling all space, cooled by expansion to a few degrees, and they were building an instrument to find it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two groups published together in 1965, one paper reporting a measurement and one explaining what it was. Penzias and Wilson had found the strongest evidence available for the origin of the universe while trying to clean their equipment.

questions.a: Any signal they later detected would have to be distinguished from whatever the antenna produced on its own.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the possibilities they worked through) and paragraph G (i.e. what the Princeton group was preparing to look for).
Summarize how the cosmic background radiation was found.
questions.a: Penzias and Wilson were characterising the noise in a horn antenna and found a faint hiss that did not vary with time, season or direction. They checked the receiver and joints, excluded New York, removed nesting pigeons and cleaned the horn, and the noise remained, while a Princeton group was separately preparing to look for radiation left by a hot early universe, so the two published together in 1965.

questions.q:
characterise: to measure and describe something fully, here every source of noise an instrument produces.
absolute zero: the lowest possible temperature, a few degrees below the temperature they measured.
Describe the connection between the signal coming from every direction and the explanation.
questions.a: A hot early universe would have left radiation filling all space, cooled by expansion to a few degrees, which is why the measurement was uniform in every direction.

articles.note: The methodical elimination in paragraphs D and E is the part worth slowing down on. The pigeons are memorable and the procedure is the lesson.

articles.title: The Index That Ranked Nations
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: Until 1990 the standard way to compare countries was income per person. It was available, it was comparable, and it had the property of being a number, which made ranking possible and argument easy.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It also measured one thing. A country could raise income per person while life expectancy fell, and the figure would record only improvement, because the figure was not built to notice anything else.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Human Development Index was proposed as a deliberate rival. Designed under Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen among its architects, it combined life expectancy, education and income into a single figure.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Combining them required deciding how much each should count. The index weights the three roughly equally, which is a choice that cannot be derived from anything and had to be defended as reasonable rather than correct.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its designers argued that the simplicity was the point. A rival to income per person had to be as easy to quote, because an index that required a paragraph of explanation would lose to one that required none.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The predictable criticisms arrived immediately. The weights are arbitrary, the components are correlated, and a single number for a country says nothing about distribution within it, which can hide very large inequalities.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some of that was later addressed. An inequality-adjusted version was introduced, which lowers a country's score according to how unevenly its achievements are spread, and the gap between the two figures became its own measure.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode shows what an index is. It is an argument about what matters, compressed into a number so that it can travel, and every criticism of its construction is a criticism of the argument it was built to make.

Its simplicity was deliberate so it could be quoted as easily as income, and criticisms about arbitrary weights and hidden inequality led to an inequality-adjusted version whose gap from the original became its own measure.

questions.q:
index: a single figure combining several measures, built to make comparison possible.
distribution: how something is spread across a population, which a single national figure cannot show.
Describe the connection between an index's construction and the argument it makes.
questions.a: An index is an argument about what matters compressed into a number, so every criticism of how it was built is a criticism of that argument.

articles.note: Paragraph H is the generalisation worth keeping. Ask students what argument a school league table is making, and what it had to decide to weight.

articles.title: The Clock That Runs Slower Downstairs
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 920 – 1020

paras.label: A
paras.text: General relativity predicts that a clock closer to a massive object runs slower than one further away. The prediction is not about the mechanism of any particular clock; it is a statement about time itself.

paras.label: B
paras.text: For most of a century the effect could only be observed where it was large. Clocks flown in aircraft, signals from satellites and light from dense stars all showed it, and all required either great speed or great distance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Satellite navigation depends on it in practice. The clocks aboard navigation satellites run measurably faster than clocks on the ground, and a system that did not correct for the difference would accumulate errors of kilometres within a day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Measuring it over a staircase is a different problem. The difference across a few metres is extraordinarily small, so detecting it requires clocks far more stable than any mechanical or quartz device can be.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Optical atomic clocks reached that stability. They count oscillations of light absorbed by trapped atoms, at frequencies far higher than earlier caesium standards, which makes them sensitive to much smaller differences.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2010 a group at NIST compared two such clocks separated vertically by about a third of a metre and detected the difference. A clock raised by roughly the height of a step was measurably ahead of one that was not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The measurement has since been pushed further, with differences detected across a vertical separation of about a millimetre within a single cloud of atoms.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What makes this remarkable is not the confirmation, which was expected. It is that a prediction formulated about stars and orbits now describes a measurable difference between the top and the bottom of an object you could hold.

articles.note: Ends the grade where it began, with a prediction made long before it could be tested. Pair it with The Case for an Asteroid and The Fossil That Was Predicted from grade 8.

articles.title: The Evidence That Birds Are Dinosaurs
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The claim that birds are dinosaurs is not a comparison or a figure of speech. It is a statement about descent: that birds sit inside the theropod group, in the way that bats sit inside the mammals, and it is now the mainstream position.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first line of evidence is skeletal and it is old. Thomas Huxley noticed in the 1860s that the hind limb of a chicken and the hind limb of certain dinosaurs share features that no other group has, and the list has since grown considerably.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Particular structures do the heaviest work. The furcula, the fused collarbone a diner calls a wishbone, is present in theropods long before any bird; so is a hollow-boned skeleton; so is a wrist bone shaped to let the hand fold sideways, which is the motion a wing makes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second line arrived in the 1990s, from a deposit in northeastern China where fine volcanic ash preserved soft tissue. The fossils there carry filaments, and in some specimens unambiguous branched feathers, on animals that could not fly and were not birds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That matters because of what it removes. Before those finds, feathers could be treated as the thing that made a bird a bird, and afterwards feathers are a theropod feature that birds inherited along with everything else.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A third line concerns behaviour, which is harder to fossilise and more persuasive when it does. Specimens of Citipati have been found sitting on nests, limbs folded over the eggs in the posture a brooding bird uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fourth is physiological, inferred from bone. Birds have an unusual breathing system with air sacs extending into hollow spaces in the skeleton, and those same spaces, in the same bones, appear in theropods that lived tens of millions of years earlier.

paras.label: H
paras.text: No one of these would carry the claim. Skeletal similarity alone could be convergence, feathers alone could be a coincidence of preservation, and a single nesting fossil could be an animal that died on a meal. Four independent lines agreeing is a different kind of argument.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The claim that birds are dinosaurs is not a comparison or a figure of speech. It is a statement about descent. Birds sit inside the theropod group, as bats sit inside the mammals. It is now the mainstream position.

paras.text: The first line of evidence is skeletal and old. In the 1860s Thomas Huxley noticed that a chicken's hind limb and certain dinosaurs' hind limbs share features no other group has. The list has grown a lot since.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second line arrived in the 1990s, from a deposit in northeastern China where fine volcanic ash preserved soft tissue. Those fossils carry filaments, and in some cases clearly branched feathers, on animals that could not fly and were not birds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That matters because of what it removes. Before those finds, feathers could be treated as what made a bird a bird. Afterwards, feathers are a theropod feature that birds inherited along with everything else.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A third line is behaviour, which is harder to fossilise and more persuasive when it does. Specimens of Citipati have been found sitting on nests, limbs folded over the eggs in the posture a brooding bird uses.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fourth is physiological, inferred from bone. Birds breathe using air sacs that extend into hollow spaces in the skeleton. Those same spaces, in the same bones, appear in theropods tens of millions of years earlier.

paras.label: H
paras.text: No single line would carry the claim. Skeletal likeness alone could be convergence. Feathers alone could be an accident of preservation. One nesting fossil could be an animal that died on a meal. Four independent lines agreeing is a different kind of argument.

questions.q: Why did the Chinese feathered fossils change the argument rather than only add to it?
questions.a: Before those finds feathers could be treated as the thing that made a bird a bird, and afterwards feathers are a theropod feature that birds inherited along with everything else.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the evidence from air sacs in bone) and paragraph H (i.e. why no single line would carry the claim).
Summarize the four lines of evidence that birds are dinosaurs.
questions.a: Skeletal features such as the furcula, hollow bones and a sideways-folding wrist appear in theropods before any bird; feathers are preserved on Chinese fossils of animals that could not fly; Citipati specimens were found brooding in a bird's posture; and the hollow spaces that carry a bird's air sacs appear in the same bones in much older theropods. Each alone has an alternative explanation and the four together do not.

questions.q:
theropod: the group of dinosaurs within which birds sit, in the way bats sit within mammals.
convergence: unrelated animals arriving at a similar feature independently, which is the alternative explanation for skeletal likeness.
Describe the connection between the wrist bone and the motion of a wing.
questions.a: The wrist bone is shaped to let the hand fold sideways, which is the motion a wing makes, and it is present in theropods before any bird.

articles.note: RI.9-10.1 at this grade means evidence from four disciplines that do not share a method. Ask which line a student would give up first and what the claim would survive on.

articles.title: Who Built Stonehenge
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Stonehenge was raised in stages over roughly fifteen hundred years, by people who left no writing. Everything claimed about them is inferred from material, and the inferences have become far stronger in the last thirty years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The stones themselves carry an origin. The smaller bluestones were matched by their chemistry to specific outcrops in the Preseli Hills in west Wales, around two hundred and forty kilometres away, and some quarry faces there show working.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The large sarsens were sourced more recently. A core removed during a repair in 1958 and returned decades later allowed a chemical comparison that placed most of them at West Woods in Wiltshire, about twenty-five kilometres from the site.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That is a claim about stone. The claim about people requires different material, and the richest source is a settlement at Durrington Walls, a short distance away, occupied while the monument was being built.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What survives there is rubbish, which for an archaeologist is better than treasure. Vast quantities of animal bone, broken pottery and hearths record what was eaten, in what season and in what quantity, by people who were not farming at the time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Isotopes in the teeth of those animals carry the decisive detail. The chemistry of an animal's teeth records the geology of the place it grew up, and the pigs and cattle eaten at Durrington came from across Britain, some from hundreds of kilometres away.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Human remains point the same way. A burial near the site, known as the Amesbury Archer, has tooth chemistry consistent with a childhood in the Alpine region, which says nothing about who built the monument and a great deal about how far people moved.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Assembled, the lines support a specific inference and refuse a looser one. They support people travelling long distances and gathering seasonally to build; they do not identify a single group, a purpose or a belief, and a confident account of why it was built is reaching past what the material holds.

questions.q: What do isotopes in animal teeth record?
questions.a: The chemistry of an animal's teeth records the geology of the place it grew up, which showed the pigs and cattle eaten at Durrington came from across Britain.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why rubbish is better than treasure) and paragraph H (i.e. what the evidence refuses to support).
Summarize what is known about the builders of Stonehenge and how.
questions.a: The bluestones were matched chemically to outcrops in west Wales and the sarsens to West Woods in Wiltshire. At Durrington Walls, animal bone and hearths record large seasonal feasting, and isotopes in the teeth show animals brought from across Britain, while a nearby burial has tooth chemistry consistent with an Alpine childhood. Together these support long-distance travel and seasonal gathering, and do not identify a purpose.

questions.q:
isotope: a form of an element whose proportions vary by region, so that teeth record where an animal grew up.
outcrop: a place where a particular rock reaches the surface, allowing stone to be matched to a source.
Describe the connection between what the evidence supports and what it refuses.
questions.a: The lines support people travelling long distances and gathering seasonally to build, and they do not identify a single group, a purpose or a belief, so a confident account of why it was built reaches past the material.

articles.note: Paragraph H is the discipline the standard is really asking for. Students will want the purpose, and the article declines to supply what the evidence cannot.

articles.title: Measuring the Distance to a Star
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Nothing about a star tells you directly how far away it is. A bright star may be luminous and distant or faint and close, and the two cases look identical from the ground.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The only direct method is geometric. As the earth moves around the sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the background of far more distant ones, and the size of that shift gives the distance by trigonometry.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shift is minute. Friedrich Bessel measured the first one in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni, and the angle involved is roughly what a coin would subtend from several kilometres away, which is why the measurement waited for the nineteenth century.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Parallax also runs out. Beyond a certain distance the shift is smaller than the instrument can resolve, so the method that is trustworthy because it rests on geometry alone covers only the nearest part of the problem.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The next rung depends on a particular kind of star. Henrietta Swan Leavitt established that certain variable stars pulse at a rate related to their true brightness, so measuring the period of one gives its luminosity, and comparing that with how bright it looks gives distance.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The relation had to be calibrated, and this is where the ladder becomes a ladder. The period and brightness relation gives relative distances on its own, and converting those into kilometres requires knowing the true distance of at least one such star, which comes from parallax.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A third rung extends further again. A particular kind of exploding star reaches a known peak brightness, and that brightness is calibrated against galaxies whose distances are already known from variable stars, which were themselves calibrated by parallax.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The structure is the point. Each rung is checked against the rung below, an error at the bottom propagates all the way up, and the figure for the most distant object depends on a trigonometric measurement of a star a few light years away.

questions.q: Why does parallax only work for nearby stars?
questions.a: Beyond a certain distance the apparent shift is smaller than the instrument can resolve, so the geometric method covers only the nearest part of the problem.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the period-brightness relation needed calibrating) and paragraph H (i.e. how an error at the bottom propagates).
Summarize how astronomical distances are established.
questions.a: Parallax measures a nearby star's apparent shift as the earth orbits and gives distance by trigonometry, but it runs out beyond a certain range. Variable stars whose pulse rate relates to true brightness extend the reach, though converting their relative distances into kilometres requires a parallax measurement, and exploding stars of known peak brightness extend it again, each rung calibrated by the one below.

questions.q:
parallax: the apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background as the observer moves.
luminosity: how much light a star actually emits, as distinct from how bright it appears from here.
Describe the connection between the lowest rung and the most distant measurement.
questions.a: Each rung is calibrated against the one below, so the figure for the most distant object depends on a trigonometric measurement of a star a few light years away.

articles.note: Thorough evidence here means a chain where every link carries the ones above it. Ask what happens to the furthest figure if the parallax of one nearby star is revised.

articles.title: The Court Records of a Village
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most people who have ever lived left no written trace of themselves. They did not write, nobody wrote about them, and the documents that survive from their societies are about taxation, landholding and the affairs of people who mattered.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There are exceptions, and they are nearly always accidental. A record created for an entirely different purpose occasionally captures ordinary lives in detail, because the purpose required asking questions nobody otherwise asked.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Court records are the richest of these. A proceeding has to establish what happened, which means recording who was where, who saw it, what time it was, what the weather was doing and who was owed money by whom.

paras.label: D
paras.text: An inquisition register from a village in the Pyrenees in the 1320s is the best-known example. It was made to identify heresy, which required interrogating almost everyone about their households, their movements, their neighbours and their beliefs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result is a document of extraordinary depth and obvious distortion. Hundreds of people describe their own lives in their own words, and every word was spoken under compulsion to an official who could imprison them.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Using it well means separating what the register was trying to establish from what it incidentally recorded. A statement about belief was the point of the question and is the least reliable part; a statement about who was in the house that evening was incidental and is far more trustworthy.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That distinction generalises to almost every official source. The thing a document was built to capture has been shaped by whoever built it, and the details it captured by accident were not worth distorting to anybody.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the strongest evidence a record contains is frequently not its subject. A tax roll is weak evidence about wealth and strong evidence about who lived next to whom, and a historian reading for the second is using the document against its own grain deliberately.

questions.q: Why do court records capture ordinary lives?
questions.a: A proceeding has to establish what happened, which means recording who was where, who saw it, what time it was and who was owed money by whom.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. separating the point of a question from what it incidentally recorded) and paragraph H (i.e. reading a document against its grain).
Summarize why records made for other purposes are valuable evidence.
questions.a: Most people left no written trace, and the records that capture them were made for other reasons, such as an inquisition register that interrogated a village about households and movements in order to identify heresy. What the document set out to establish is the least reliable part because it was shaped by its makers, while the incidental detail was not worth distorting to anyone.

questions.q:
incidental: recorded in passing rather than as the purpose of a document, which is what makes it trustworthy.
against the grain: reading a source for something other than what it was made to record.
Describe the connection between a detail being incidental and its being reliable.
questions.a: The thing a document was built to capture has been shaped by whoever built it, and the details it captured by accident were not worth distorting to anybody.

articles.note: The generalisation in paragraph G is the transferable part. Apply it to a school's own records and ask what they are accidentally strong evidence about.

articles.title: How a Drug Is Shown to Work
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Showing that a treatment works is harder than it sounds, and the difficulty is not technical. Most people given most treatments improve, improvement is the thing everybody involved was hoping for, and the question is therefore never whether patients got better but whether the treatment is why.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Conditions fluctuate, people seek help when they feel worst, and expecting to improve produces measurable change. A study that compares patients before and after cannot distinguish a drug from any of those.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So the first requirement is a comparison group receiving something else, and the second is that the two groups be alike at the start. Allocating by chance achieves that, because randomness distributes both known and unknown differences evenly.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third requirement is less obvious and is where many studies fail. The person enrolling patients must not know which group the next patient will go to, because a clinician who can predict the allocation can steer sicker patients toward the comparison.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is blinding. If patients know what they received, their reports of how they feel are affected, and if assessors know, their judgements of ambiguous findings shift in a direction nobody intends and nobody notices.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A fifth concerns what is counted. Patients who stop taking a drug are often those it suited least, so analysing only those who completed the course compares the people who tolerated the treatment with everybody in the other group.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The sixth is registration. A trial that states its main outcome in advance cannot later report whichever of twelve measures came out best, and comparing a published paper with its registration is a check anybody can run.

paras.label: H
paras.text: None of these is about the drug. They are about the ways a comparison can be spoiled, and a trial is really a set of defences against the specific errors that produce a positive result when there is nothing there.

questions.q: Why must the person enrolling patients not know the next allocation?
questions.a: A clinician who can predict the allocation can steer sicker patients toward the comparison group, which destroys the similarity randomisation created.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why analysing only completers misleads) and paragraph H (i.e. what a trial actually is).
Summarize the defences a trial is built from.
questions.a: Because most patients improve anyway, a trial needs a comparison group, allocation by chance so the groups start alike, concealment so nobody can steer who goes where, blinding so reports and judgements are unaffected, analysis including those who stopped, and registration of the main outcome in advance. Each defends against a particular way a comparison can be spoiled.

questions.q:
allocation concealment: keeping the next patient's group assignment unknown to whoever is enrolling them.
blinding: keeping patients or assessors unaware of which treatment was given.
Describe the connection between patients stopping a drug and what an analysis must include.
questions.a: Patients who stop are often those the drug suited least, so analysing only those who completed compares the people who tolerated the treatment with everybody in the other group.

articles.note: Each requirement answers a named failure. Have students match the six defences to the six ways a result could be wrong without anyone lying.

articles.title: The Discovery That Ulcers Are Infectious
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: For most of the twentieth century stomach ulcers were understood as a disease of stress and acid, and the understanding was not idle speculation but a framework with a treatment attached. The treatment was to reduce acid, it relieved symptoms reliably, and the ulcers very often came back.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as evidence against the explanation. A patient whose ulcer returned had a chronic disease, and nothing in the framework suggested that the return was telling anyone something.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In 1979 a pathologist in Perth, Robin Warren, noticed curved bacteria in biopsies from inflamed stomachs. The observation was unremarkable except that the stomach was believed too acidic for bacteria to survive in.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Barry Marshall, then a trainee, began collecting cases with him. The bacteria appeared consistently in patients with inflammation and ulcers, and the association held across a series large enough that coincidence became an uncomfortable explanation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: An association was not going to be enough, and they knew precisely why. Bacteria might colonise damaged tissue rather than cause the damage, so finding them in an ulcer is consistent with their being a consequence of it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Attempts to produce the disease in animals failed. In 1984 Marshall drank a culture of the organism himself, developed gastritis within days, had it confirmed by biopsy, and then treated it with antibiotics.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A self-experiment with one subject, unblinded and unrandomised, is weak evidence by every standard that normally applies to anything. Its force came from what it predicted rather than from what it showed: if the bacterium causes the disease, then antibiotics should cure ulcers, and controlled trials showed that they did.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea therefore shifts twice. It begins as a story about a surprising observation, becomes a story about why an observation is not enough, and ends as a story about a prediction that could have failed and did not.

questions.a: Bacteria might colonise damaged tissue rather than cause the damage, so finding them in an ulcer is consistent with their being a consequence of it.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. how recurrence was explained away) and paragraph G (i.e. where the self-experiment's force actually came from).
Summarize how the cause of stomach ulcers was established.
questions.a: Ulcers were explained by stress and acid, and recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as counter-evidence. Warren observed bacteria in inflamed stomachs believed too acidic for them, and the association held across many cases, but bacteria could have been a consequence. Marshall's self-experiment mattered because of what it predicted, and antibiotics curing ulcers in trials confirmed it.

questions.q:
biopsy: a sample of tissue taken for examination, which is where the bacteria were seen.
colonise: to settle in a place, which bacteria might do in tissue already damaged by something else.
Describe the connection between the recurrence of ulcers and the old explanation.
questions.a: The recurrence was treated as part of the condition rather than as evidence against the acid explanation, so nothing in the framework suggested the return was telling anyone something.

articles.note: Paragraph B is the quiet one and the important one. An explanation that absorbs its own failures is the thing students should learn to notice.

articles.title: The Enclosure of the Commons
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: For centuries much of England was farmed in open fields, under an arrangement that looks chaotic on a map and was not. A household held scattered strips across several large fields, and alongside them held rights over common land: to graze animals, gather fuel, cut turf or glean the grain left after a harvest.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Those rights were not ownership and they were not charity. They were customary entitlements attached to a holding, recognised in manorial courts, and for a household at the margin they were frequently the difference between sufficiency and destitution.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Enclosure replaced that arrangement with consolidated private holdings. It happened gradually by agreement over several centuries and then rapidly by statute, with several thousand individual Acts of Parliament passed between the mid-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agricultural case for it was real. Consolidated fields permit drainage, selective breeding and crop rotation that scattered strips cannot, and output per acre on enclosed land rose measurably.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distributional consequence was also real and fell on different people. A household whose entitlement was customary rather than documented had difficulty establishing it before commissioners, and compensation when granted was often a plot too small to be viable.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The central idea is therefore not that enclosure was efficient or that it was unjust. It is that the same change was both, and that the gains and the losses were not experienced by the same households.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A further detail refines it again. Many smallholders who received an allotment sold it within a generation, because an enclosed holding carried costs that a commons right did not, principally the obligation to fence it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why the episode is argued about still. It is a case where a measurable improvement in output and a measurable loss of security are both documented, and any summary that reports one of them has summarised half the evidence.

paras.label: A
paras.text: For centuries much of England was farmed in open fields. A household held scattered strips across several large fields. Alongside them it held rights over common land: to graze animals, gather fuel, cut turf or glean after a harvest.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Those rights were not ownership and not charity. They were customary entitlements attached to a holding, recognised in manorial courts. For a household at the margin they were often the difference between sufficiency and destitution.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Enclosure replaced that with consolidated private holdings. It happened gradually by agreement over centuries, then rapidly by statute, with several thousand individual Acts of Parliament between the mid-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agricultural case was real. Consolidated fields allow drainage, selective breeding and crop rotation that scattered strips cannot. Output per acre on enclosed land rose measurably.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distributional consequence was real too, and fell on different people. A household whose entitlement was customary rather than documented struggled to establish it before commissioners. Compensation, when granted, was often a plot too small to be viable.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the central idea is not that enclosure was efficient, or that it was unjust. It is that the same change was both, and that the gains and the losses were not felt by the same households.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A further detail refines it again. Many smallholders who received an allotment sold it within a generation. An enclosed holding carried costs a commons right did not, principally the obligation to fence it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why the episode is still argued about. A measurable rise in output and a measurable loss of security are both documented. Any summary reporting one of them has summarised half the evidence.

questions.q: What were common rights, and what made them precarious?
questions.a: They were customary entitlements attached to a holding, recognised in manorial courts, and a household whose entitlement was customary rather than documented had difficulty establishing it before commissioners.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. that the same change was both efficient and unjust) and paragraph G (i.e. why allotments were sold within a generation).
Summarize what enclosure did.
questions.a: Open-field farming combined scattered strips with customary common rights that mattered most to households at the margin. Enclosure consolidated holdings, which raised output per acre by allowing drainage and rotation, while households whose rights were undocumented struggled to establish them and often received plots too small to be viable, many of which were sold within a generation because fencing was required.

questions.q:
customary: held by long practice rather than by document, which made such rights hard to prove.
consolidated: brought together into a single block, as scattered strips were by enclosure.
Describe the connection between the obligation to fence and smallholders selling their land.
questions.a: An enclosed holding carried costs that a commons right did not, principally the obligation to fence it, which is why many who received an allotment sold it within a generation.

articles.note: RI.9-10.2 wants a central idea refined by detail. Paragraph G is the refinement, and without it the article's position in paragraph F looks like fence-sitting.

articles.title: The Ozone Hole
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Ozone high in the atmosphere absorbs a band of ultraviolet light that damages living tissue, and it is the only thing that does. The layer is thin, it is distributed unevenly across latitudes and seasons, and until the 1970s nobody had a reason to think anything human was affecting it at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In 1974 Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland published a chemical argument rather than an observation. Chlorofluorocarbons are so stable that nothing destroys them in the lower atmosphere, so they drift upward, and ultraviolet light eventually breaks them apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The products are destructive out of proportion to their quantity. A released chlorine atom can catalyse the destruction of ozone repeatedly without being consumed, so a small amount of gas removes a large amount of ozone over time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The prediction was for gradual thinning spread across the globe. That is what the chemistry implied, and it is what the argument was debated as, and the chemical industry's response addressed that version of the claim.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What was found in 1985 was something else. A British team working at Halley Bay in Antarctica reported a severe seasonal loss over the pole, far larger and far more localised than the theory had predicted.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The observation nearly did not surface. Satellite instruments had been recording the same low values and the processing software was discarding them as errors, on the reasonable ground that readings that extreme usually indicate a malfunction.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The explanation required a mechanism nobody had included. Ice clouds that form only in the extreme cold of the polar winter provide surfaces on which chlorine compounds convert into forms that destroy ozone rapidly when the sun returns.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The central idea develops through three stages and is different at each. A prediction from pure chemistry, an observation that did not match it, and a mechanism that explained why the observation was worse than the prediction and confined to one place.

questions.q: Why does a small quantity of chlorofluorocarbon matter so much?
questions.a: A released chlorine atom can catalyse the destruction of ozone repeatedly without being consumed, so a small amount of gas removes a large amount of ozone over time.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the satellite data being discarded) and paragraph G (i.e. the missing mechanism).
Summarize how the ozone hole was predicted, found and explained.
questions.a: Molina and Rowland argued from chemistry that stable chlorofluorocarbons would drift upward and release chlorine that destroys ozone catalytically, predicting gradual global thinning. In 1985 a British team found a severe seasonal loss over Antarctica instead, which satellite software had been discarding as error, and the explanation required polar ice clouds that convert chlorine into rapidly destructive forms.

questions.q:
catalyse: to cause a reaction repeatedly without being used up in it.
localised: confined to one area, which the observed loss was and the prediction was not.
Describe the connection between polar ice clouds and the severity of the loss.
questions.a: Ice clouds that form only in the extreme cold of the polar winter provide surfaces on which chlorine compounds convert into forms that destroy ozone rapidly when the sun returns.

articles.note: Paragraph F is worth dwelling on. Software discarding extreme readings is a defensible rule that nearly suppressed the finding, and the rule was not wrong in general.

articles.title: The Standard Gauge
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The distance between the rails on most of the world's railways is an awkward figure: four feet eight and a half inches. It is not a round number in any system, and nothing about it was calculated.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It descends from the wagonways that served collieries in the north of England, where horse-drawn wagons ran on rails to the river. George Stephenson built his early locomotives for lines of roughly that width, and his engines were the ones other companies bought.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Competitors chose differently and had reasons. Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western at just over seven feet, arguing correctly that a wider gauge permits greater stability, higher speed and a larger loading area.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The technical argument was not the one that settled it. Where two gauges met, every passenger had to change trains and every item of freight had to be unloaded and reloaded, and that cost fell on anyone shipping anything across the join.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is a different kind of problem from an engineering problem. The value of a gauge depends on how many other lines use it, so the better system loses to the more common one once the network is large enough.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Britain legislated in 1846, specifying the narrower gauge for new passenger lines, and the Great Western converted the last of its broad gauge in 1892. In the United States the conversion was largely completed over two days in 1886, with crews moving one rail inward along thousands of kilometres of track.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The central idea refines as it goes. It begins as a story about an arbitrary measurement, becomes a story about why the better design lost, and ends as a story about a property that belongs to networks rather than to things.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That property has not gone anywhere. Keyboards, electrical plugs, file formats and shipping containers are all cases where the arrangement in use is the one that was adopted early, and the question of whether it is the best arrangement is close to irrelevant.

questions.q: What was Brunel's argument for a wider gauge?
questions.a: That a wider gauge permits greater stability, higher speed and a larger loading area, which the article says was correct.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why a gauge's value depends on other lines) and paragraph H (i.e. where the same property appears today).
Summarize why the standard gauge is the standard.
questions.a: The figure descends from colliery wagonways and Stephenson's locomotives rather than from calculation. Brunel's wider gauge was technically better, but where two gauges met everything had to be unloaded, so a gauge's value depends on how many lines share it and the more common system won, which Britain legislated in 1846 and the United States largely converted in 1886.

questions.q:
gauge: the distance between the rails of a railway track.
network effect: the property by which something becomes more valuable the more others use it.
Describe the connection between the cost of a break of gauge and the outcome.
questions.a: Where two gauges met every passenger changed trains and every item of freight was unloaded and reloaded, so the value of a gauge depends on how many other lines use it and the more common one wins.

articles.note: Paragraph H generalises without overreaching. Ask students for a current case where an early choice is now effectively permanent.

articles.title: The Green Revolution
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the middle of the twentieth century a number of countries were expected to be unable to feed themselves within a generation. Population was rising faster than yields, the arithmetic was straightforward, and the projections were widely published, widely believed and taken seriously by the governments they concerned.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What changed the projection was plant breeding. Norman Borlaug and others developed wheat and then rice varieties that were short-stemmed, which sounds like a small detail and is the centre of the whole thing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A tall cereal given plenty of fertiliser grows a heavy head and falls over, which ruins the crop. A short-stemmed plant can carry a much heavier head without lodging, so it can convert fertiliser into grain rather than into stem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The yields that followed were not incremental. Wheat output in India and Pakistan roughly doubled within a decade, and the famines that had been forecast for the 1970s did not occur on anything like the predicted scale.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The central idea at that point is a technical success, and the article could stop there. The detail that complicates it is that the new varieties only outperform the old ones under particular conditions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: They require fertiliser, reliable water and often pesticide. A farmer with irrigation and access to credit gains enormously; a farmer on rain-fed land without credit gains little and may be worse off as prices fall with the larger harvest.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the same innovation widened a gap while closing another. Aggregate production rose decisively and the distribution of who benefited followed the distribution of irrigation and lending, which was not even.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The environmental account arrived later again, and it is still being written. Decades of intensive irrigation have drawn down groundwater in several of the regions where the gains were largest, which means that part of the increase was not produced at all but borrowed, from a stock that is not being replaced at anything like the rate it is used.

questions.q: Why does a short stem matter so much?
questions.a: A tall cereal given plenty of fertiliser grows a heavy head and falls over, while a short-stemmed plant can carry a heavier head without lodging and so converts fertiliser into grain rather than stem.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. which farmers gained) and paragraph H (i.e. the groundwater account).
Summarize the Green Revolution and what complicates it.
questions.a: Short-stemmed wheat and rice could carry heavy heads without lodging, so they converted fertiliser into grain and yields roughly doubled in India and Pakistan within a decade. The varieties require fertiliser, water and credit, so gains followed the distribution of irrigation and lending, and decades of intensive irrigation have drawn down groundwater in several of the regions that gained most.

questions.q:
lodging: a crop falling over under the weight of its own head, which ruins the harvest.
aggregate: the total across a whole population, which can rise while many individuals do not gain.
Describe the connection between a larger harvest and a farmer being worse off.
questions.a: A farmer on rain-fed land without credit gains little from the new varieties and may be worse off as prices fall with the larger harvest.

articles.note: The central idea is overturned twice by its own details, at paragraph F and again at H. Ask where a student would have stopped reading if the article had ended early.

articles.title: How an Outbreak Is Investigated
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An outbreak investigation has a prescribed sequence, set out in training materials and followed by public health agencies everywhere, and the sequence is not a formality. Each step produces the material the next one needs, and performing them in a different order produces answers that cannot be relied on afterwards.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first step is to establish that there is an outbreak at all. More cases than usual is a comparison, which requires knowing what usual was, and a rise can be produced by a new test, a new doctor or a new reason to look.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is to write a case definition, in advance and in writing. It states the symptoms, the place and the period that qualify someone as a case, and it is fixed before anyone starts counting.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That order matters more than it appears. A definition written after cases are known can be shaped, deliberately or not, around the people already suspected, and every count made with it will then confirm what produced it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third step is descriptive: count the cases by time, by place and by person. The resulting curve of cases against date distinguishes a single common source, which produces one sharp peak, from person-to-person spread, which produces successive waves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Only now is a hypothesis formed, and the order is the whole discipline. The description constrains what can be proposed, so a hypothesis arrived at this way has already survived a test it did not choose.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The fourth step tests it comparatively. Cases are compared with non-cases from the same population, asking what each was exposed to, and an exposure common to cases and rare among the others becomes the candidate.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The fifth is confirmation by a different method entirely, such as finding the organism in the suspected food or water. An epidemiological association and a laboratory finding are independent, and the investigation is considered closed when they agree.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what the curve of cases distinguishes) and paragraph H (i.e. confirmation by an independent method).
Summarize the order an outbreak investigation follows.
questions.a: First establish that cases exceed the usual rate, since a rise can be produced by new testing; then fix a case definition in writing before counting; then describe cases by time, place and person, which distinguishes a common source from person-to-person spread; only then form a hypothesis, test it by comparing cases with non-cases, and confirm it by an independent laboratory method.

questions.q:
case definition: the written statement of symptoms, place and period that qualifies someone as a case.
epidemiological: concerning patterns of disease across a population rather than in one patient.
Describe the connection between the descriptive step and the hypothesis that follows it.
questions.a: The description constrains what can be proposed, so a hypothesis arrived at this way has already survived a test it did not choose.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 9's accident investigation. Both encode a theory of error in a sequence, and both separate description from explanation for the same reason.

articles.title: How a Budget Is Assembled
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A public budget arrives as a single document and is produced by a process that runs for most of a year. The order of that process determines what is possible to change and when, which is rarely obvious from the document.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins with a forecast rather than a plan. Officials estimate what revenue will be available under existing arrangements, and that figure constrains everything afterwards without having been chosen by anybody.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Next comes the baseline, which is the cost of continuing to do exactly what is already being done. It is not a neutral quantity: it embeds every past decision, and it typically rises on its own through pay, prices and the number of people entitled to a service.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The gap between the forecast and the baseline is the real subject of the exercise. Departments are asked to bid against a total that is already allocated to continuing commitments, and the sum available for anything new is what remains.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Bids are then prepared, and the sequence rewards particular behaviour. A department asked to propose reductions will propose ones that are visible and unpopular, because a reduction that nobody notices invites the question of why it was not made earlier.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Decisions are taken late and quickly. The final allocations are frequently settled in a short period near the end, which means that the options considered are the ones that survived the earlier stages rather than the best ones available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Publication comes last and is the first thing the public sees. A reader meeting the document at that point is looking at the output of six months of narrowing, with no record of what was excluded at each stage.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why a budget debate rarely changes a budget. By the time the figures are public the process that produced them has finished, and an argument about a line item is an argument about the last stage of a sequence that was mostly decided earlier.

questions.a: It embeds every past decision and typically rises on its own through pay, prices and the number of people entitled to a service.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why departments propose visible reductions) and paragraph H (i.e. why a budget debate rarely changes a budget).
Summarize the order in which a budget is assembled.
questions.a: A revenue forecast made under existing arrangements constrains everything, then a baseline costing current commitments is set, and the gap between them is what departments bid against. The sequence rewards proposing visible reductions, final allocations are settled quickly near the end from options that survived earlier stages, and publication comes last, so public debate addresses a process already finished.

questions.q:
baseline: the cost of continuing existing commitments unchanged, against which new bids are measured.
allocation: the portion of a total assigned to a particular department or purpose.
Describe the connection between when a document is published and what a debate can achieve.
questions.a: By the time the figures are public the process that produced them has finished, so an argument about a line item addresses the last stage of a sequence that was mostly decided earlier.

articles.note: The order is the argument here, as in the outbreak article. Ask at which stage a student would have to intervene to change an outcome.

articles.title: How a Theorem Is Proved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mathematical paper is organised in a way that looks backwards to anyone expecting an account of how the work was actually done. It begins with definitions, proceeds through a series of small results that nobody outside the paper cares about, and reaches the theorem it is named for somewhere near the end.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That order is not chronological. Mathematicians typically start from the result they want and work toward what would establish it, and the paper presents the reverse of the route actually taken.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is that a proof is a check rather than a narrative. A reader has to be able to verify each step using only what precedes it, and an account in discovery order would require accepting things before they had been established.

paras.label: D
paras.text: So the definitions come first because nothing can be said without them. A definition in mathematics is not an explanation of a familiar word; it is a stipulation that creates the object, and everything later depends on its exact form.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then come lemmas: small results established on the way, each proved from the definitions and from earlier lemmas. Individually they are usually uninteresting, and collectively they are the structure the theorem stands on.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The main theorem is then often short. Having built the lemmas, the proof of the central claim can be a few lines, because the work was done in the pieces that came before it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The order also determines what a counterexample does. A proof is a chain, so an error anywhere breaks everything after it, and the standard question a reader asks is not whether the conclusion is plausible but which line first fails to follow.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Reading one therefore means reading for dependency rather than for narrative. The useful question at every line is what earlier statement makes this permissible, and a line that depends on nothing stated above it is where the paper is wrong.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A mathematical paper is organised in a way that looks backwards to anyone expecting an account of how the work was done. It opens with definitions, moves through small results nobody cares about, and reaches the theorem near the end.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That order is not chronological. Mathematicians usually start from the result they want and work toward what would establish it. The paper presents the reverse of the route actually taken.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is that a proof is a check rather than a narrative. A reader must verify each step using only what precedes it. An account in discovery order would require accepting things before they were established.

paras.label: D
