paras.text: Then come lemmas: small results established along the way, each proved from the definitions and from earlier lemmas. Individually they are usually uninteresting. Collectively they are the structure the theorem stands on.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The main theorem is then often short. With the lemmas built, the proof of the central claim can be a few lines, because the work was done in the pieces before it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The order also decides what a counterexample does. A proof is a chain, so an error anywhere breaks everything after it. The standard question is not whether the conclusion is plausible but which line first fails to follow.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So reading one means reading for dependency, not narrative. At every line, ask what earlier statement makes this permissible. A line depending on nothing stated above it is where the paper is wrong.

questions.q: Why is a mathematical paper not written in the order the work was done?
questions.a: A proof is a check rather than a narrative, and a reader must verify each step using only what precedes it, so an account in discovery order would require accepting things before they had been established.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what a definition does in mathematics) and paragraph G (i.e. what question a reader asks of a proof).
Summarize how a proof is ordered and why.
questions.a: Definitions come first because they stipulate the objects everything else depends on, then lemmas are proved from the definitions and from each other, and the main theorem is often short because the work was done beforehand. The order exists so each step can be verified using only what precedes it, and a reader asks which line first fails to follow rather than whether the conclusion is plausible.

questions.q:
lemma: a small result proved on the way to a larger one, usually uninteresting in itself.
stipulation: a definition that creates an object by decree rather than describing an existing one.
Describe the connection between a proof being a chain and the effect of one error.
questions.a: A proof is a chain, so an error anywhere breaks everything after it, which is why the reader's question is which line first fails to follow.

articles.note: The contrast with the outbreak and budget articles is useful. All three are about order, and only this one's order is a logical requirement rather than a defence against bias.

articles.title: How a Law Is Drafted
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A government decides to do something, and some months or years later a statute appears. Between those two events is a drafting process, largely invisible from outside, whose order shapes the law that results more than most of the public debate about it does.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It begins with instructions rather than text. A department sets out what it wants to achieve, in ordinary language, and sends that to specialist drafters, and the quality of the instructions determines most of what follows.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The drafter's first question is usually one nobody in the department asked. What exactly counts as the thing being regulated, who precisely does the obligation fall on, and what happens in the case the policy did not consider.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those questions produce the definitions section, and the definitions are written before the operative provisions because the provisions cannot be written without them. A rule about vehicles requires a boundary around the word.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then come the duties, in a deliberate order: who must do what, by when, subject to which exceptions, enforced by whom, with what consequence for failure. Each of those is a separate decision and each is capable of hollowing out the one before it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An exception drafted broadly can undo the duty it attaches to without appearing to. A provision requiring something except where it is not reasonably practicable may be a sensible limit or a complete escape, and which it is depends on words settled at this stage.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Consequential amendments come near the end. A new statute usually interacts with existing ones, and the schedule listing changes to other legislation is often longer than the Act itself and is read by almost nobody.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Debate arrives after all of it. Legislators argue about the policy, in language from the instructions, while the provisions that will decide cases were settled earlier by people whose names do not appear on anything.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how an exception can undo a duty) and paragraph H (i.e. when debate arrives).
Summarize the order in which a statute is drafted.
questions.a: A department sends instructions in ordinary language to specialist drafters, whose first questions produce a definitions section written before the operative provisions. Duties follow in order of who, by when, subject to what exceptions, enforced how, each capable of hollowing out the last, then consequential amendments to other legislation, and debate arrives after the decisive wording is settled.

questions.q:
operative provision: the part of a statute that actually imposes a duty or confers a power.
consequential amendment: a change to existing legislation made necessary by a new Act.
Describe the connection between the breadth of an exception and the duty it attaches to.
questions.a: An exception drafted broadly can undo the duty it attaches to without appearing to, so a provision requiring something except where it is not reasonably practicable may be a limit or a complete escape.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's The Definitions Section of a Law. That article read the finished document and this one shows the order in which it was built.

articles.title: How a Species Is Named
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Naming a newly recognised organism is governed by rules that are closer to law than to biology. They determine which of several proposed names is correct, and correctness here has almost nothing to do with whether a name is apt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first requirement is a type specimen. One particular individual, physically preserved and deposited in a collection anyone can consult, becomes the permanent anchor of the name, and the name refers to whatever group that specimen belongs to.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That order is the opposite of what people expect. A name is not attached to a description that organisms may or may not fit; it is attached to an object, and the description is a claim about what else resembles it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The consequence appears when a species is later split. If the group turns out to be two, the original name stays with whichever one contains the type specimen, and the other requires a new name regardless of which is more numerous or better known.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second requirement is publication in a form the rules recognise, with a date. Priority then governs: where two names have been published for the same organism, the earlier one is correct, and the later becomes a synonym.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Priority produces outcomes that nobody likes and the system accepts anyway. A familiar name can be displaced by an obscure earlier description found in a nineteenth-century journal, and the rules provide limited routes to prevent it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The point of all this is stability rather than accuracy. A name that means whatever its describer intended would change with every revision of opinion, and a name anchored to an object in a drawer does not.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the sequence encodes a decision about what names are for. Specimen, then publication, then priority, and the name is a label with a physical referent rather than a summary of what anybody currently believes.

questions.q: What happens to a name when a species is split in two?
questions.a: The original name stays with whichever group contains the type specimen, and the other requires a new name regardless of which is more numerous or better known.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. outcomes priority produces) and paragraph G (i.e. why stability is the aim).
Summarize the rules for naming a species.
questions.a: A type specimen is preserved in a consultable collection and permanently anchors the name, so the name refers to an object rather than to a description. Publication with a date follows, and priority makes the earlier of two names correct, which can displace a familiar name. The aim is stability, since a name tied to an object does not change as opinion does.

questions.q:
type specimen: the preserved individual that permanently anchors a species name.
priority: the rule that where two names exist for one organism, the earlier published name is correct.
Describe the connection between anchoring a name to an object and the stability of names.
questions.a: A name that meant whatever its describer intended would change with every revision of opinion, and a name anchored to an object in a drawer does not.

articles.note: Four articles on order and four different reasons for it: bias, politics, logic and stability. Ask students to match each article to its reason.

articles.title: The Language of a Safety Data Sheet
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Every hazardous chemical in a workplace arrives with a document in a fixed sixteen-section format. It is written to be found in an emergency, in a hurry, by somebody who has never read that particular sheet before and may never read another, and almost every feature of it follows from that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The order is prescribed and never varies. Identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, and so on down to regulatory information, so a reader looking for first aid knows it is section four before opening anything.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The vocabulary is more constrained than ordinary technical writing. Hazard statements are drawn from a fixed catalogue, each with a code, so causes severe skin burns and eye damage is one specific statement rather than a description somebody composed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That standardisation has a purpose beyond tidiness. Identical wording across manufacturers and languages means a translation is a lookup rather than an interpretation, and a worker who has learned what a statement means has learned it for every product.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Signal words are reduced to two. Danger marks the more severe category and Warning the less severe, and no third option exists, which prevents a manufacturer from softening a classification through phrasing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The sheet also distinguishes hazard from risk, and the distinction is frequently misread. A hazard is a property of the substance and does not depend on circumstances; the risk depends on how much, how often and under what controls.

paras.label: G
paras.text: This is why a sheet can look alarming for something handled routinely. Vinegar has hazard statements, and the statements describe what concentrated acetic acid can do, not what is likely while dressing a salad.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a document that reads as flat and uninflected. That is deliberate: emphasis would be a judgement by the writer, and a format that allows emphasis allows a manufacturer to decide what a reader notices first.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the distinction between hazard and risk) and paragraph H (i.e. why the document is deliberately flat).
Summarize why a safety data sheet is written as it is.
questions.a: It is built to be found in an emergency by a first-time reader, so its sixteen sections never change order, its hazard statements come from a fixed catalogue so translation is a lookup, and only two signal words exist so classifications cannot be softened by phrasing. It states hazards, which are properties of a substance, rather than risk, and avoids emphasis so no manufacturer decides what a reader notices first.

questions.q:
hazard: a property of a substance, independent of how it is used.
signal word: one of exactly two terms, Danger or Warning, marking the severity category.
Describe the connection between allowing emphasis and who controls a reader's attention.
questions.a: Emphasis would be a judgement by the writer, and a format that allows emphasis allows a manufacturer to decide what a reader notices first.

articles.note: A document whose cumulative effect is produced by removing choices rather than making them. Compare it with the patent article in grade 9 for the opposite strategy.

articles.title: The Language of a Peace Agreement
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A negotiated settlement has to be signed by parties who disagree about what happened and about what should happen next. The text has to be acceptable to all of them, and most of its characteristic features follow from that requirement.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The most important is constructive ambiguity, and it is deliberate rather than careless. A phrase that each side can read as supporting its own position allows an agreement to be signed where a precise phrase would prevent one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: This is a genuine technique with a genuine cost. The dispute has not been resolved, it has been postponed and relocated into the interpretation of a clause, and it will reappear when the clause has to be applied.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Verbs are chosen for how much they bind. Shall creates an obligation, will is weaker and often read as an expectation, and should is close to advisory, and the difference between them is frequently the subject of the longest arguments in a negotiation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Sequence words carry as much weight as verbs. Whether a clause reads after elections or following the establishment of conditions determines whether anything is actually required to happen by a particular time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The naming of parties is itself contested. A document that names an entity may be read as recognising it, so agreements are often drafted to describe parties by role, or by the places they control, rather than by the names they call themselves.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Even the title does work. Agreement, accord, framework, declaration and memorandum carry different implications about whether a binding instrument has been created, and the choice is usually made late and argued about hard.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a text that reads as evasive to an outsider and is precise about a different thing than the reader expects. It is not vague about the dispute; it is exact about what each party has agreed to be bound by, which is less.

questions.q: What is constructive ambiguity and what does it cost?
questions.a: A phrase each side can read as supporting its own position, which allows an agreement to be signed, at the cost of relocating the dispute into the interpretation of a clause where it will reappear.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why parties are described by role) and paragraph H (i.e. what the text is actually precise about).
Summarize the language of a peace agreement.
questions.a: Because all parties must sign, the text uses constructive ambiguity to allow phrases each side can read its own way, which postpones rather than resolves a dispute. Verbs are graded by how much they bind, sequence words determine whether anything must happen by a date, parties are described by role to avoid implying recognition, and the title itself signals whether a binding instrument exists.

questions.q:
constructive ambiguity: wording each party can read in its own favour, used deliberately to permit agreement.
instrument: a formal document creating legal obligations, which a title may or may not imply.
Describe the connection between the requirement that all parties sign and the vagueness of the text.
questions.a: A phrase that each side can read as supporting its own position allows an agreement to be signed where a precise phrase would prevent one.

articles.note: Compare with grade 9's diplomatic register. That article was about a scale everyone reads the same way, and this is about wording nobody reads the same way, on purpose.

articles.title: What Engineers Mean by Failure
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary use, failure means something broke and somebody is at fault. In engineering it means a component stopped performing its intended function, and the two meanings pull hard against each other whenever an engineer speaks in public.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A designed structure has a failure mode, which is not a fault but a plan. The engineer decides in advance which part will give way first and how, because a structure that fails in an unpredicted manner fails in the most dangerous one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A related term is factor of safety. It is the ratio between the load a thing can take and the load it is expected to take, and a value of three does not mean two thirds of the structure is wasted.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It means the design absorbs variation nobody can measure in advance: the material that came in slightly below specification, the load nobody anticipated, the corrosion that accumulated, the installation done imperfectly on a wet afternoon.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Ductile and brittle are the next pair, and the distinction matters more than almost any other. A ductile failure deforms visibly before it gives way, and a brittle one separates without warning, and a design is frequently chosen to make failure ductile rather than to make it less likely.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Redundancy is similarly misread. In ordinary language it means something surplus to requirements; in engineering it means a second path for a load if the first one goes, and calling it surplus is exactly the reasoning that removes it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fail-safe is not a thing that cannot fail. It is a thing whose failure leaves the system in a safe state, such as a brake held off by pressure, which engages when the pressure is lost rather than releasing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is that an engineer discussing failure in public is routinely misheard. Saying a structure is designed to fail in a particular way sounds like an admission and is a description of the safest available arrangement.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. ductile and brittle failure) and paragraph G (i.e. what a fail-safe actually is).
Summarize the technical meanings of failure and the terms around it.
questions.a: In engineering a failure is a component ceasing to perform its function, and a failure mode is a plan for which part gives way first, because unpredicted failure is the most dangerous kind. A factor of safety absorbs unmeasurable variation, a ductile failure deforms visibly while a brittle one gives no warning, redundancy is a second load path, and a fail-safe fails into a safe state.

ductile: deforming visibly before giving way, which gives warning that a brittle failure does not.
redundancy: a second path for a load, which ordinary language mistakes for something surplus.
Describe the connection between calling redundancy surplus and removing it.
questions.a: In ordinary language redundancy means something surplus to requirements, and calling it surplus is exactly the reasoning that removes a second load path.

articles.note: Every term here has an everyday meaning that is close enough to be dangerous. Ask which misunderstanding would do the most damage in a public inquiry.

articles.title: The Language of a Reference
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A written reference for a former employee is constrained in ways that make it almost unreadable by ordinary standards, and the constraints are not the writer's choice. They come from law, from institutional policy, and from the fact that the subject of the reference may eventually be entitled to see it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In many jurisdictions a reference must be fair and accurate, and a statement that damages someone can be actionable if it cannot be supported. That produces a strong incentive to say only what can be documented.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The result is a register built from verifiable facts. Dates of employment, job title, duties as recorded, and attendance figures, each of which can be defended from a file and none of which answers the question the reader is asking.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Many large organisations have reduced the problem by removing the judgement entirely. They provide only confirmation of the facts, as policy, which protects the organisation and transfers the difficulty onto whoever must now decide without information.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Where evaluation survives, it is read as a code. Experienced readers treat the absence of a positive statement as the message, so a reference describing someone as punctual and nothing else is understood to be saying something it has not said.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That reading is unreliable in both directions. A writer who is simply terse, or following a template, produces a document indistinguishable from a deliberate signal, and the reader has no way to tell which they are holding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further asymmetry worth noticing. The subject of the reference usually cannot see it at the time it matters, so a misreading that harms them is a misreading they are not able to correct.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a genre that satisfies nobody. The writer cannot say what they think, the reader cannot learn what they need, and both continue to participate because the alternative is a document with no standing at all.

questions.q: Why do references consist mainly of verifiable facts?
questions.a: A statement that damages someone can be actionable if it cannot be supported, which produces a strong incentive to say only what can be documented.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why reading the silence is unreliable) and paragraph G (i.e. the asymmetry affecting the subject).
Summarize why references are written as they are.
questions.a: Legal exposure and policy restrict a reference to facts that can be defended from a file, and many organisations supply only confirmation of employment. Where evaluation remains, readers treat the absence of praise as the message, but terseness and a deliberate signal are indistinguishable, and the subject usually cannot see the document in time to correct a misreading.

questions.q:
actionable: capable of being the subject of a legal claim.
register: the restricted kind of language a document is written in, here one built from verifiable facts.
Describe the connection between removing judgement and who bears the difficulty.
questions.a: Providing only confirmation of the facts protects the organisation and transfers the difficulty onto whoever must now decide without information.

articles.note: The code-reading in paragraph E is a real practice and an unreliable one. Ask what evidence a reader would need to distinguish a signal from a template.

articles.title: What a Statistician Means by Random
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary speech random means arbitrary, unexpected or without pattern. In statistics it means produced by a process whose outcomes have known probabilities, which is nearly the opposite of without pattern.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A random sample is not a haphazard one. It is a sample drawn by a procedure in which every member of a population had a specified chance of being selected, and that specification is what makes the sample useful.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Stopping people in a shopping street is haphazard and is not random in this sense. Nobody can say what chance a given person had of being approached, so nothing can be calculated about how the sample relates to the population.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This is why a very large haphazard sample is worth less than a small properly drawn one. Size reduces one kind of error and does nothing to the other, and a biased sample of a million is confidently wrong.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Randomness is also a property of a process rather than of a result. A sequence of ten heads can be produced by a fair coin, and judging a process by whether its output looks patternless is a reliable way to be mistaken in both directions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: People are poor at producing it and poor at recognising it. Asked to write a random sequence, most produce one with too few repetitions, because a run of four looks wrong, and genuine randomness produces runs more often than intuition allows.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is a further technical use of the word in experiments. Random assignment means allocation by a chance process, and its purpose is specifically to distribute unknown differences evenly, which no deliberate procedure can do.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The cumulative effect is a word that means almost the reverse of its everyday sense. Ordinary random means nobody chose; statistical random means the choosing was done by a specified process whose properties are known, which is a strong condition rather than an absence of one.

questions.a: Nobody can say what chance a given person had of being approached, so nothing can be calculated about how the sample relates to the population.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. randomness as a property of a process) and paragraph G (i.e. the purpose of random assignment).
Summarize the technical meaning of random.
questions.a: It means produced by a process whose outcomes have known probabilities, so a random sample is one where every member had a specified chance of selection, which a haphazard street survey does not provide. Size does not repair bias, randomness is a property of the process rather than the output, and random assignment distributes unknown differences evenly as no deliberate method can.

questions.q:
haphazard: chosen without a system, which is not the same as chosen by a specified chance process.
random assignment: allocating participants to groups by a chance process so unknown differences spread evenly.
Describe the connection between the size of a sample and the kind of error it fixes.
questions.a: Size reduces one kind of error and does nothing to the other, so a biased sample of a million is confidently wrong.

articles.note: Pairs with How a Drug Is Shown to Work in this grade. That article uses randomisation and this one says what the word is doing there.

articles.title: The Introduction of a Paper
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The introduction to a research paper is three or four paragraphs long and has a shape so consistent that a reader can predict where each sentence is going before reading it. The shape is sometimes called a funnel, and the name is accurate.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens wide. The first sentences establish that an area of work exists and matters, in terms a reader from a neighbouring field could follow, and they are frequently the only sentences in the paper written for a general audience.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then narrows to what is known. A paragraph summarises the established findings, with citations, and the summary is selective, because the author is assembling the particular background against which their own claim will look necessary.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The narrowing continues to what is not known. A sentence appears beginning however, or despite this, or it remains unclear whether, and that sentence is the hinge on which the entire paper turns.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That gap is constructed rather than discovered. There are always many things not known about any subject, and the author has selected the one their study happens to address, which is legitimate and is worth seeing clearly.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The final sentences state what the paper does. Here we show, or this study examines, and in most journals the last sentence of the introduction is the paper's claim in its most compressed form.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The structure therefore does a particular job. By the time a reader reaches the methods they have accepted that a question matters, that it is open, and that the approach taken is the reasonable one, and none of those was argued for.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A useful exercise is to read the introduction backwards, one paragraph at a time. Start at the claim, then move up to the gap, and ask whether the gap identified is the one that actually blocks the field or simply the one this study was already in a position to fill.

questions.a: In the final sentences, since in most journals the last sentence of the introduction is the paper's claim in its most compressed form.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the gap being constructed) and paragraph H (i.e. reading the introduction backwards).
Summarize the structure of a paper's introduction and what it achieves.
questions.a: It opens wide enough for a neighbouring field, narrows through a selective summary of what is known to a sentence stating what is not, and closes with what the paper does. The gap is selected rather than discovered, and by the methods section a reader has accepted that the question matters, that it is open and that the approach is reasonable, none of which was argued for.

questions.q:
funnel: the narrowing structure of an introduction, from a wide opening to a single specific claim.
hinge: the sentence on which a text turns, here the statement of what is not known.
Describe the connection between the selected gap and the study that follows it.
questions.a: There are always many things not known about any subject, and the author has selected the one their study happens to address, so the gap is constructed rather than discovered.

articles.note: RI.9-10.5 asks how a larger portion develops a claim. Here four paragraphs produce assent to three propositions before the evidence section begins.

articles.title: The First Chapter of a History
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first chapter of a serious history book is rarely the start of the story. It is usually an argument about what the story is, and a reader who treats it as throat-clearing has skipped the part that determines everything after.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It generally does four things. It states the question, defines the period, explains why the existing accounts are inadequate, and announces what this book will do differently, in that order and with varying degrees of politeness.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The definition of the period is the least obvious and most consequential. A history of a revolution that begins ten years earlier than the usual date has made a claim about causes before describing a single event.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The engagement with existing work is where the argument becomes explicit. A historian names the accounts they are writing against, summarises them fairly enough to be credible, and identifies what each one could not explain.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That summary deserves checking. A book's account of its rivals is written by someone with a reason to find them insufficient, and a reader who learns a field from one book's first chapter has learned one historian's map of it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The announcement of method matters as much. A historian saying they will use estate records rather than parliamentary debates has told a reader which people will appear in the book and which will not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Everything after is then shaped by those commitments. The chapters follow the period as defined, the evidence is of the kind announced, and the conclusion answers the question stated on page four rather than any other question.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the first chapter is the place to argue with a book, and almost nobody does. By chapter six the framework is doing its work invisibly, and a reader who accepted the period, the sources and the question has already conceded most of what was ever in dispute.

questions.q: Why is the definition of a period consequential?
questions.a: A history of a revolution that begins ten years earlier than the usual date has made a claim about causes before describing a single event.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why a book's account of its rivals needs checking) and paragraph H (i.e. where to argue with a book).
Summarize what a first chapter does.
questions.a: It states a question, defines a period, explains why existing accounts are inadequate and announces a method, each of which is a claim. The definition of the period asserts causes in advance, the summary of rivals is written by someone with a reason to find them wanting, and the choice of sources decides who appears, so by chapter six the framework is operating invisibly.

questions.q:
framework: the set of commitments a book makes early, which shapes everything that follows.
period: the span a history covers, whose boundaries are themselves an argument about causes.
Describe the connection between the sources announced and who appears in a book.
questions.a: A historian saying they will use estate records rather than parliamentary debates has told a reader which people will appear in the book and which will not.

articles.note: Pairs with the paper introduction article. Both show a text securing agreement to several propositions before any evidence is offered.

articles.title: The Discussion Section
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The discussion is the last substantial section of a research paper and the one where its claim can grow. The results section states what was measured; the discussion says what it means, and the distance between those is where the paper is most vulnerable.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens by restating the finding, usually in a single sentence and usually with the hedges intact. That sentence is worth comparing with the one in the abstract, because the two are often not the same claim.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then places the finding among existing work. Studies that agree are cited, studies that disagree are explained, and the explanation for disagreement is frequently a methodological difference the author is in no position to verify.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Next comes the mechanism, and this is where a correlational study often acquires a cause. A paragraph proposing how the effect might work is legitimate, and a reader who carries that proposal back to the result has upgraded an association without noticing.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The limitations paragraph follows, and its placement does something. Coming after the mechanism, it is read against a claim the paragraph before has already strengthened, rather than against the narrower thing actually measured.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then come implications, which is where the widening is most visible. A finding in one population at one time becomes a statement about practice, and the verbs change from past to present as it happens.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The closing sentences usually call for further research. That is uninformative on its own, and it is worth asking what specific study the authors are describing, because a precise call and a vague one say different things about how firm the finding is.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The useful comparison is therefore between two sentences a few pages apart. Take the result as stated in the results section, take the claim in the final paragraph, and the gap between them is what the discussion added rather than found.

questions.a: A paragraph proposing how the effect might work is legitimate, and a reader who carries that proposal back to the result has upgraded an association without noticing.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what the placement of the limitations does) and paragraph H (i.e. the comparison between two sentences).
Summarize what a discussion section does to a paper's claim.
questions.a: It restates the finding, places it among existing work, proposes a mechanism that can turn an association into a cause, then gives limitations read against the strengthened claim, then implications where a finding in one population becomes a statement about practice. Comparing the result as stated with the claim in the final paragraph shows what the discussion added.

questions.q:
correlational: showing that two things occur together, without establishing that one causes the other.
implication: what a finding is said to mean for practice, which is where a claim widens most.
Describe the connection between where limitations appear and how they are read.
questions.a: Coming after the mechanism, they are read against a claim the previous paragraph has already strengthened, rather than against the narrower thing actually measured.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 7's limitations article and grade 9's hedging article. Three grades, one document, and each time a different part of it.

articles.title: The Executive Summary
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A long report opens with a summary of two or three pages. It is written last, it is read first, and for most of its audience it is the only part that is read at all, which gives it a peculiar status within the document.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It is not an abstract in the scientific sense. An abstract describes a paper; an executive summary is meant to be usable on its own, so it must restate the findings rather than refer to them and must stand without the body behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That independence creates the characteristic problem. A summary that works alone cannot carry the qualifications that make the findings defensible, and a summary that carries them is too long to be read by the people it was written for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What gets dropped is predictable. Sample sizes, the basis of estimates, the range around a central figure and the conditions a recommendation depends on are the first to go, because each costs a clause and none changes the headline.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The recommendations are the part most likely to travel further. They are extracted, pasted into other documents and acted on, and they arrive in those documents without the finding they rest on, let alone its conditions.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A well-made summary resists this in a specific way. It attaches the condition to the recommendation in the same sentence, so that the two cannot be separated by a careless copy, which is the only form of protection available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: There is also a structural tell worth knowing. A summary whose recommendations are not traceable to specific findings in the body is a summary where someone has added a conclusion the evidence section does not contain.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the summary is where the report is most used and least examined. Comparing each of its claims against the section it came from takes an afternoon and is the most reliable way to find out whether a report says what it is being quoted as saying.

questions.q: Why can an executive summary not carry its own qualifications?
questions.a: A summary that works alone cannot carry the qualifications that make the findings defensible, and one that carries them is too long to be read by the people it was written for.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. attaching conditions to recommendations) and paragraph G (i.e. the structural tell).
Summarize the problem with an executive summary.
questions.a: It is written last, read first, and often alone, so it must restate findings without the body, which means sample sizes, estimate bases, ranges and conditions are dropped. Recommendations are extracted and acted on without the findings beneath them, so a good summary ties a condition to a recommendation in one sentence, and recommendations not traceable to findings signal an added conclusion.

questions.q:
qualification: a condition limiting a finding, which a short summary tends to drop.
traceable: able to be followed back to a specific finding in the body of a report.
Describe the connection between a recommendation travelling and the condition it depends on.
questions.a: Recommendations are extracted, pasted into other documents and acted on, arriving without the finding they rest on, let alone its conditions.

articles.note: The check in paragraph H is the practical one. Take a real report, trace five summary claims to their sections, and count how many narrow on the way.

articles.title: The Caveats at the End of a Model
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.3 order of ideas · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A model of a climate, an epidemic or an economy produces numbers, and the numbers are what gets reported. At the end of the document that produced them there is a section nobody quotes, and it is where the numbers are explained.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first thing it usually says is that these are projections and not predictions. A projection states what follows if stated assumptions hold, and a prediction states what will happen, and a model produces only the first.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The assumptions are then listed, and the list is the model. A climate model runs several scenarios of future emissions, and the difference between its outputs is mostly the difference between those scenarios rather than anything about the physics.

paras.label: D
paras.text: This means a single reported figure has usually had a scenario chosen for it. Which one was selected is a decision by whoever wrote the summary, and the highest and lowest are frequently both defensible and far apart.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The caveats also describe what the model does not contain. A model of an epidemic may not represent behaviour change, so its figures describe what happens if nobody responds, which is a condition that has never once held.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That omission is not a flaw and is frequently the point. A projection assuming no response is built to show why a response is needed, and quoting it as a forecast of deaths misrepresents it precisely by taking it seriously.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Uncertainty is given in the same section and in a particular form. A range is not a confidence that the truth lies inside it; it is the spread produced by the runs that were performed, and a factor nobody modelled lies outside the range entirely.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the claim a model supports is refined almost entirely at the end. The figure in the headline is the output, the conditions attached to it are the claim, and the two are published in the same document and almost never in the same place.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A model of a climate, an epidemic or an economy produces numbers, and the numbers get reported. At the end of the document that produced them is a section nobody quotes. It is where the numbers are explained.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It usually says first that these are projections and not predictions. A projection states what follows if stated assumptions hold. A prediction states what will happen. A model produces only the first.

paras.label: C

paras.label: F

paras.label: G
paras.text: Uncertainty appears in the same section, in a particular form. A range is not a confidence that the truth lies inside it. It is the spread of the runs performed. A factor nobody modelled lies outside the range entirely.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the claim a model supports is refined almost entirely at the end. The headline figure is the output. The conditions attached are the claim. Both are published in one document and almost never in one place.

questions.q: What is the difference between a projection and a prediction?
questions.a: A projection states what follows if stated assumptions hold, while a prediction states what will happen, and a model produces only the first.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why assuming no response is the point) and paragraph G (i.e. what a range actually represents).
Summarize what the caveats section does for a model's figures.
questions.a: It states that outputs are projections conditional on assumptions, lists those assumptions, and notes that differences between outputs mostly reflect chosen scenarios. It describes what the model omits, such as behaviour change, so a no-response projection shows why a response is needed, and it gives a range that reflects the runs performed rather than confidence that the truth lies inside it.

questions.q:
projection: a conditional statement of what follows if assumptions hold.
scenario: one set of assumed future conditions a model is run under, chosen rather than predicted.
Describe the connection between quoting a no-response projection as a forecast and misrepresenting it.
questions.a: A projection assuming no response is built to show why a response is needed, so quoting it as a forecast of deaths misrepresents it precisely by taking it seriously.

articles.note: The sentence about taking a projection too seriously is the hardest idea in this grade. Students assume the error is scepticism and it is the opposite.

articles.title: The Expert Witness
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An expert witness occupies a position that is structurally strange. They are paid by one side in a dispute, they are called because their opinion assists that side, and their formal duty is owed to the court rather than to whoever is paying.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That duty is not decorative. In many jurisdictions it is stated in rules and in a declaration the expert signs, requiring them to give an independent opinion and to say plainly where a question falls outside their expertise.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The rhetoric of a good expert report follows from that duty. It states the material it was given, the material it was not given, the assumptions it proceeds on and the points on which a reasonable expert could take a different view.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Those concessions are not weakness. An expert who concedes nothing is easier to attack, because an opponent need only find one overstatement to put the whole opinion in question, and a report that marks its own edges has removed that opportunity.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structural problem lies before any of this. Each side selects its expert, and a party that consults three and instructs the one most favourable has produced a sympathetic witness without anyone saying anything untrue.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The effect at trial is predictable. Two qualified experts testify to incompatible conclusions, and a jury with no means of evaluating the field is left deciding between them on manner, confidence and clarity.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some courts have changed the procedure in response. Experts may be required to meet before trial and produce a joint statement of what they agree on and precisely where they differ, which moves the disagreement into a narrower space.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What that reveals is how much of the dispute was real. Two experts who agree on nine points and differ on the tenth have given a court something usable, and the adversarial version of the same evidence would have presented it as total disagreement.

questions.q: Why is conceding points a strength in an expert report?
questions.a: An expert who concedes nothing is easier to attack, because an opponent need only find one overstatement to put the whole opinion in question.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the selection problem) and paragraph H (i.e. what a joint statement reveals).
Summarize the position of an expert witness.
questions.a: An expert is paid by one side while owing a duty to the court, stated in rules and a signed declaration, so a good report marks its assumptions and the points where others could differ. Because each side selects its own expert, sympathetic witnesses are produced without anyone lying, and joint statements before trial show how much of the apparent disagreement was real.

questions.q:
adversarial: a system in which each side presents its own case and evidence, including its own experts.
joint statement: a document produced by opposing experts setting out what they agree on and where they differ.
Describe the connection between each side choosing its expert and the appearance of total disagreement.
questions.a: A party that consults several experts and instructs the most favourable produces a sympathetic witness, so two qualified experts testify to incompatible conclusions even where they agree on most points.

articles.note: RI.9-10.6 asks how rhetoric serves a purpose. Here the persuasive move is conceding, and the reason is structural rather than moral.

articles.title: The Budget Speech
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A finance minister presenting a budget is performing a document that already exists. The figures were settled weeks earlier, the speech cannot change them, and everything in the delivery is about how they will be understood.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The order is the first instrument. Announcements that cost nothing and sound generous come early, and measures that take money arrive later, when a listener has already formed an impression of what kind of budget this is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Numbers are selected for their frame. A figure can be given as a total, as an annual amount, as a share of spending or as an increase over a previous year, and the same policy will sound large or modest depending on which is chosen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Multi-year totals do particular work. A commitment presented as a sum over five years is a larger number than the same commitment stated per year, and it is also harder to compare with anything, which is part of its appeal.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The baseline is chosen as well. An increase measured against a planned reduction is an increase; the same figure measured against last year's actual spending may be a cut, and both descriptions can be defended.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The speech also uses a particular tense. We are investing, we are backing, we are delivering, all present continuous, which describes a decision that has been taken as an action that is under way.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Independent analysis appears within hours, and the speech is written knowing that. The most contestable claims are often placed in the published documents rather than said aloud, because a sentence in an annex attracts less scrutiny than one in a broadcast.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric is about sequence and framing rather than about assertion, which is what makes it hard to rebut. Almost nothing in a budget speech is false, and the question worth asking of each sentence is what alternative description of the same figure was available and was not used.

questions.q: Why are multi-year totals used?
questions.a: A commitment presented as a sum over five years is a larger number than the same commitment stated per year, and it is also harder to compare with anything.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the use of the present continuous) and paragraph G (i.e. placing contestable claims in documents rather than the speech).
Summarize the rhetorical instruments of a budget speech.
questions.a: The figures are already settled, so the speech works by order, putting generous announcements first, and by framing, choosing whether a figure appears as a total, an annual amount or an increase, and against which baseline. The present continuous presents decisions as actions under way, and the most contestable material is placed in documents rather than spoken.

questions.q:
baseline: the figure a change is measured against, whose choice can turn the same number into a rise or a cut.
frame: the form a figure is presented in, which changes how large it sounds without changing the amount.
Describe the connection between where a claim is placed and how much scrutiny it gets.
questions.a: A sentence in an annex attracts less scrutiny than one in a broadcast, so the most contestable claims are often placed in the published documents rather than said aloud.

articles.note: Pairs with How a Budget Is Assembled in this grade. One shows the process and the other the performance, and the performance is the only part most people see.

articles.title: How a Risk Is Communicated
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A public health body has to tell people about a risk. The underlying number is the same whatever is said, and the way it is expressed changes what people decide to do, which makes the choice of expression a decision rather than a presentation.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Percentages are poorly understood by many readers and frequencies are understood better. Ten in a thousand and one per cent describe the same quantity, and the first is consistently easier for people to reason with.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Keeping the denominator constant matters as much as the format. Comparing one in a hundred with one in a thousand requires an extra step that many readers do not take, while ten in a thousand against one in a thousand does not.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Framing changes the decision even when the numbers are identical. A treatment described as having a ninety per cent survival rate is chosen more often than one described as having a ten per cent mortality rate, and this has been demonstrated repeatedly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That finding puts a communicator in an awkward position. There is no neutral framing available: survival and mortality are both accurate, one of them has to be chosen, and the choice will affect what people do.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The usual response is to give both, which helps and does not solve it. Order still matters, the first framing anchors the reader, and a document that presents both has made a smaller version of the same decision.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Visual formats carry their own effects. An array of a hundred figures with ten shaded conveys a proportion more reliably than a percentage, and a graph with a cut axis can make the same difference look like anything at all.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric here is unavoidable rather than optional. A communicator cannot decline to frame, and the honest position is to state which framing was chosen and why, rather than to present a choice as a fact.

questions.a: Comparing one in a hundred with one in a thousand requires an extra step that many readers do not take, while ten in a thousand against one in a thousand does not.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why no neutral framing exists) and paragraph H (i.e. the honest position for a communicator).
Summarize the problem of communicating a risk.
questions.a: Frequencies are understood better than percentages and a constant denominator aids comparison, but framing changes decisions even when the numbers are identical, as survival and mortality rates demonstrate. No neutral framing exists, giving both still leaves order mattering, and visual formats carry their own effects, so the honest position is to state which framing was chosen and why.

questions.q:
denominator: the base a frequency is expressed against, such as the thousand in ten in a thousand.
framing: presenting the same quantity in a way that emphasises one aspect, such as survival rather than mortality.
Describe the connection between there being no neutral framing and the communicator's duty.
questions.a: Survival and mortality are both accurate and one has to be chosen, so the honest position is to state which framing was chosen and why rather than present a choice as a fact.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 9's vocabulary of risk. That article was about which quantity is reported and this is about how the same quantity is phrased.

articles.title: The Recruitment Campaign
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Organisations that need people to join them, and that cannot compete on pay with the employers those people could otherwise choose, have to advertise something else. Armed forces, police services, teaching and nursing all run campaigns built on the same small number of appeals, in roughly the same order.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is belonging. The imagery is almost always of groups rather than individuals, and the implied offer is membership of something with a boundary around it, which is an offer competing employers find difficult to match.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is significance. The work is presented as mattering to other people in a way most work does not, and this appeal is powerful precisely because it is frequently true.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is transformation. A campaign shows a person at the end of training who is visibly not the person who began it, which is an offer about identity rather than about employment.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What is systematically absent is the ordinary content of the job. Very few campaigns show the paperwork, the shift patterns, the waiting, or the proportion of the work that is administrative, because those do not recruit anybody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That omission has a measurable consequence organisations track closely. Recruits who joined expecting the advertised version leave at higher rates when they meet the actual one, and the cost of early attrition is borne by the same organisation that ran the campaign.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some campaigns have responded by showing the difficulty deliberately. A campaign that emphasises how hard the work is can recruit fewer people and retain more of them, which is a better outcome and a harder one to defend to whoever counts applications.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric contains a tension the organisation cannot resolve by choosing better words. One metric rewards the appealing version and another punishes it, and the campaign is written for whichever metric the people commissioning it are judged on.

questions.q: What three appeals do these campaigns rest on?
questions.a: Belonging, shown through group imagery; significance, presenting the work as mattering to others; and transformation, showing a person changed by training.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the consequence of the omission) and paragraph H (i.e. the tension between two metrics).
Summarize the rhetoric of a recruitment campaign and its cost.
questions.a: Organisations that cannot offer high pay advertise belonging, significance and transformation, while systematically omitting paperwork, shifts and administration because those recruit nobody. Recruits who expected the advertised version leave at higher rates, so campaigns that show the difficulty retain more people while attracting fewer, which is hard to defend to whoever counts applications.

questions.q:
attrition: the rate at which people leave an organisation, which early departures increase.
metric: a measure an organisation is judged by, here either applications received or recruits retained.
Describe the connection between what a campaign omits and why recruits leave.
questions.a: Recruits who joined expecting the advertised version leave at higher rates when they meet the actual one, which is the consequence of omitting the ordinary content of the job.

articles.note: The tension in paragraph H is not a rhetorical failure but an incentive problem. Ask which metric a student would choose and what it would cost.

articles.title: The Science Museum Label
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A label beside an object in a museum is usually under seventy-five words. It has to work for a reader who is standing, tired, possibly with a child, and who will give it about ten seconds before moving on.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Every constraint pushes in the same direction. There is no room for qualification, no room for competing accounts, and no room to explain why the object is in a museum rather than somewhere else.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What the label chooses to say the object is for is the heart of it. The same instrument can be introduced as a tool for measuring something, as evidence in a historical dispute, or as an example of a technique, and each produces a different visit.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A label also decides which person appears. Scientific instruments were generally built by named makers, used by named researchers and operated by assistants whose names are frequently recorded somewhere and almost never on the label.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The verbs carry a position. Was discovered, was developed and was first measured each distribute credit differently, and a label using the passive throughout has made a choice about agency that a visitor will not notice.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a genuine argument for the restraint. A museum that explains every dispute produces a wall of text nobody reads, and a visitor who leaves having understood one thing clearly has had a better visit than one who skimmed four arguments.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The cost falls on what cannot be shown. An object is a thing that survived, and a gallery of surviving objects is a gallery of what was built well, kept carefully and considered worth retaining, which is not the same as what was typical.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the rhetoric of a label is mostly in its silences. The sentences present are generally accurate, and the argument is carried by what has been left out in order to fit seventy-five words.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the argument for restraint) and paragraph G (i.e. what a gallery of surviving objects represents).
Summarize how a museum label argues.
questions.a: Under seventy-five words and ten seconds of attention, a label has no room for qualification or competing accounts, so its choice of what the object is for shapes the visit, as do the people it names and the verbs that distribute credit. Restraint is defensible because a wall of text goes unread, and the cost is that surviving objects represent what was kept rather than what was typical.

questions.q:
agency: who is represented as having acted, which the choice of verb distributes.
restraint: deliberately saying less, defended here as producing a better visit than exhaustive explanation.
Describe the connection between an object surviving and what a gallery shows.
questions.a: A gallery of surviving objects is a gallery of what was built well, kept carefully and considered worth retaining, which is not the same as what was typical.

articles.note: Rhetoric carried by omission under a hard constraint. Have students rewrite one real label to include a dispute and then count the words they are over.

articles.title: A Building in Three Representations
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A building that does not yet exist is described by a drawing, by a physical model and by a rendered walkthrough. All three are produced from the same design and they are used to decide different things by different people.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The drawing is the legal and constructive document. It is dimensioned, it is to scale, and a contractor builds from it, which means that anything not drawn is not going to be built and any error in it becomes a wall in the wrong place.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its weakness is that almost nobody can read it. A plan and a section require training to convert into an experience of space, and a client looking at one is frequently agreeing to something they have not understood.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A physical model answers a different question. It shows mass, the relationship to neighbouring buildings and the shadow the new thing will cast, and those are the questions a planning committee and a neighbour actually have.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its scale is also its limit. At a model's scale a person is a few millimetres, so nothing about the experience of being inside is represented, and a model that looks elegant on a table says nothing about a corridor.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A rendered walkthrough reverses that completely. It puts a viewer at eye level inside spaces that do not exist, and it is the only one of the three that answers what it will be like to walk in.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It is also the one most able to mislead, and not by faking anything. A render is made with chosen weather, chosen time of day, chosen furniture and chosen people, and the building in it is always new, clean and lightly occupied.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the three are used in a sequence that matches their strengths. The render sells the idea, the model gets the permission, and the drawing builds the thing, and a disappointed occupant is usually someone who was shown only the first.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A building that does not yet exist is described by a drawing, a physical model and a rendered walkthrough. All three come from the same design. Different people use them to decide different things.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The drawing is the legal and constructive document. It is dimensioned and to scale. A contractor builds from it. Anything not drawn will not be built, and any error in it becomes a wall in the wrong place.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its weakness is that almost nobody can read it. A plan and a section need training to convert into an experience of space. A client looking at one is often agreeing to something they have not understood.

paras.label: D

paras.label: F
paras.text: A rendered walkthrough reverses that. It puts a viewer at eye level inside spaces that do not exist. It is the only one of the three that answers what it will be like to walk in.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It is also the most able to mislead, and not by faking anything. A render has chosen weather, time of day, furniture and people. The building in it is always new, clean and lightly occupied.

paras.label: H

questions.q: Why does a model say nothing about a corridor?
questions.a: At a model's scale a person is a few millimetres, so nothing about the experience of being inside is represented.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. how a render misleads without faking anything) and paragraph H (i.e. the sequence in which the three are used).
Summarize what each representation of a building is for.
questions.a: A dimensioned drawing is what a contractor builds from, but almost nobody can read it. A physical model shows mass, neighbours and shadow, which is what a planning committee asks, while representing nothing of the interior. A render puts a viewer inside at eye level and misleads through chosen weather, furniture and occupancy rather than through falsehood.

questions.q:
render: a computer-generated image showing a building as it would appear, with conditions chosen by its maker.
section: a drawing showing a building cut through, which requires training to read.
Describe the connection between the sequence of use and a disappointed occupant.
questions.a: The render sells the idea, the model gets the permission and the drawing builds the thing, so a disappointed occupant is usually someone who was shown only the first.

articles.note: RI.9-10.7 asks which details each medium emphasises. Here the three are used in order, and the order maps onto whose decision each one is for.

articles.title: A War in Photographs and Statistics
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A conflict is described by photographs and by numbers, and the two accounts are so different in what they can carry that they are frequently read as contradicting each other when they do not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A photograph is a record of one place at one moment, and its strength is that it cannot be argued with about what was in front of the lens. It establishes that this happened, to this person, here.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It cannot establish how often. A single image of a destroyed street is compatible with one destroyed street or ten thousand, and a viewer has no way to tell which from the photograph itself.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Statistics answer exactly that question and lose everything else. A figure for displaced people describes a scale no photograph can convey, and it describes nobody in particular, which is a loss as well as a gain.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both are produced under conditions worth knowing. Photographs come from where photographers could reach, which is where access was granted or where danger was survivable, and the places nobody could reach are not photographed at all. An absence of images from a region is evidence about access rather than about what happened there.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Casualty figures come from whoever was counting, and counting during a conflict is done by parties with positions. Different methods produce different totals, and the difference between an estimate from records and an estimate from a survey is frequently large.

paras.label: G
paras.text: They also fail in opposite directions. A photograph can be unrepresentative while being entirely genuine, and a statistic can be accurate while describing a category that nobody would recognise as the thing they were asking about.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the honest reading uses each for what it establishes. The photograph is evidence that something occurred and poor evidence of how common it was, and the number is the reverse, and a reader with only one of them has half the account.

questions.q: What can a photograph not establish?
questions.a: How often something happened, since a single image of a destroyed street is compatible with one destroyed street or ten thousand.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. where photographs come from) and paragraph G (i.e. how the two fail in opposite directions).
Summarize what photographs and statistics each establish about a conflict.
questions.a: A photograph proves that something happened in one place at one moment and cannot show how common it was, while a statistic describes scale and nobody in particular. Photographs come from where access was granted or danger survivable, casualty figures come from parties with positions and vary by method, and a photograph can be genuine but unrepresentative while a statistic can be accurate about an unrecognisable category.

questions.q:
unrepresentative: true of the case shown and not typical of the whole, which a genuine photograph can be.
displaced: forced to leave home, a category whose definition affects the figure reported.
Describe the connection between where photographers could go and what is photographed.
questions.a: Photographs come from where access was granted or where danger was survivable, so the places nobody could reach are not photographed.

articles.note: The two failure modes in paragraph G are the heart of it. Ask which failure would be harder to detect from inside the medium that produced it.

articles.title: A Protein in Three Forms
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A protein can be presented as a sequence of letters, as a three-dimensional structure and as an animation of it working. The three are derived from each other and they support completely different kinds of reasoning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sequence is the most compact and the most certain. It is a string of letters representing amino acids in order, it can be stored and searched, and comparing two sequences reveals relationships between organisms that nothing else shows as cheaply.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is also nearly uninformative about function. The sequence determines the structure in principle, and reading function from it directly is close to impossible, which is why structure had to be determined experimentally for decades.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A structure answers what the sequence cannot. It shows the folded shape, the pocket where another molecule binds, and the surfaces that face outward, and almost everything a drug designer needs is a property of the shape.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A structure is also a model rather than a photograph. It is fitted to experimental data, parts of it are less certain than others, and a published structure carries measures of that uncertainty which the picture of it does not. A loop region drawn as confidently as the rest may be the part nobody could resolve.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An animation adds the dimension both of the others lack. A protein is not rigid; it moves, and the motion is frequently the mechanism, so a static structure can be a correct picture of a thing whose behaviour it cannot show.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The animation is also the furthest from the evidence. Most such films are built from a small number of structures plus simulation plus choices about pacing and colour, and a viewer cannot tell which parts were measured and which were plausible.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So confidence runs opposite to vividness. The sequence is most certain and least illuminating, the animation is most illuminating and least constrained, and the structure sits between them, which is why all three are published together.

Summarize the three representations of a protein.
