A structure shows the folded shape and binding pockets that drug design depends on, while being a model fitted to data with uneven certainty. An animation shows motion, which is often the mechanism, but is built from few structures plus simulation, so confidence runs opposite to vividness.

questions.q:
amino acid: one of the units a protein sequence is built from, represented by a letter.
binding pocket: the shaped cavity where another molecule attaches, which only a structure can show.
Describe the connection between how vivid a representation is and how constrained it is.
questions.a: The sequence is most certain and least illuminating while the animation is most illuminating and least constrained, so confidence runs opposite to vividness.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's false-colour astronomy article. Both are about a vivid representation that is derived from measurement and is not itself a measurement.

articles.title: An Economy in Three Accounts
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An economy is described by aggregate figures, by charts and by individual accounts of how people are living. The three are usually presented as competing, and they are answering questions that do not overlap.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An aggregate figure such as total output is the only thing that permits comparison. It allows one year to be set against another and one country against another, and nothing else available does that at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It conceals distribution completely, and this is not a subtle defect. A total that rises while most people's incomes fall is arithmetically ordinary, and the figure reports the rise accurately and says nothing about the fall.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A chart adds the shape of a change over time, which a single number cannot carry. It shows whether something is accelerating, whether it has recovered and whether a recent movement is unusual against its own history.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A chart's design decisions are substantial. The period chosen determines what counts as normal, the axis determines how large a change looks, and whether a figure is shown per person or in total can reverse the direction of the line.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An individual account carries what neither can. It describes what a change consists of for a household, in terms of what is bought, what is postponed and what is given up, and that is the only form in which a number becomes legible.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It establishes nothing about how common it is. A single household's experience is compatible with it being universal or rare, which is the limitation a reporter addresses by choosing a household described as typical, on a judgement the reader cannot check.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the useful arrangement is all three in a known order. The aggregate says how much, the chart says in what pattern, the account says what it consists of, and each of them is misleading in a predictable way when it appears alone.

questions.q: How can a total rise while most people are worse off?
questions.a: A total that rises while most people's incomes fall is arithmetically ordinary, because the figure conceals distribution and reports only the rise.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the design decisions in a chart) and paragraph G (i.e. the limitation of an individual account).
Summarize what each account of an economy provides.
questions.a: An aggregate figure is the only thing permitting comparison across years and countries, and it conceals distribution entirely. A chart shows the shape of a change while its period, axis and per-person choice shape what is seen. An individual account makes a number legible and establishes nothing about how common it is.

questions.q:
aggregate: a total across a whole population, which permits comparison and hides distribution.
distribution: how something is spread across people, which a total cannot show.
Describe the connection between choosing a typical household and what a reader can verify.
questions.a: A reporter addresses the limitation of a single account by choosing a household described as typical, on a judgement the reader cannot check.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 9's index article. One is about compressing many measures into a number and this is about the number needing two other mediums to be read.

articles.title: A Species as Specimen, Photograph and Recording
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each account.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.9 seminal documents · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A newly described animal is documented in three ways at once, and each of the three answers a question the others cannot answer at all, which is why a modern description includes all of them wherever the describing team is able to.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The specimen is the anchor. It is a physical individual, preserved and deposited, and it remains available for measurement by people who were not born when it was collected and who have instruments nobody then imagined.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That permanence is what distinguishes it absolutely. A specimen collected in 1890 can now be sampled for genetic material and examined by scanning, so a decision made then is still producing evidence that nobody could have intended.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its limitation is equally absolute. A specimen is dead, it has usually been altered by preservation, and the colours of many organisms begin changing within hours of death, so a drawer records shape far better than appearance.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A photograph answers appearance and behaviour. It shows posture, living colour, what the animal was doing and the habitat around it, and all of that is lost from a specimen before the specimen reaches a collection.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It records only what was pointed at. A photograph is taken by someone who decided what mattered, from where they could stand, and the feature a later researcher wants is frequently just outside the frame. Nothing in the image indicates that it was ever there.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A recording answers what neither can, and for many groups it is decisive. Species of bird, frog and insect that are visually almost identical are separated reliably by sound, and the sound is a behaviour rather than a structure.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the three divide along a clear line. The specimen holds structure permanently, the photograph holds appearance at a moment, the recording holds behaviour, and a description with only the first is unable to distinguish species that a listener can tell apart in a field.

questions.q: Why can a specimen collected in 1890 still produce new evidence?
questions.a: It remains available for measurement by people who were not born when it was collected, so it can now be sampled for genetic material and examined by scanning.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what a photograph records) and paragraph G (i.e. why a recording is decisive for some groups).
Summarize what each record of a species holds.
questions.a: A preserved specimen anchors the name permanently and still yields evidence with instruments invented since, but it is dead and altered so it records shape better than appearance. A photograph shows posture, living colour and habitat but only what the photographer pointed at, and a recording captures behaviour, which separates species that look almost identical.

questions.q:
specimen: a preserved individual deposited in a collection as a permanent physical record.
habitat: the surroundings an organism lives in, which a photograph captures and a drawer does not.
Describe the connection between sound being a behaviour and its value for identification.
questions.a: Species that are visually almost identical are separated reliably by sound, and the sound is a behaviour rather than a structure, which a specimen cannot hold.

articles.note: Pairs with How a Species Is Named earlier in this grade. That article explains why the specimen anchors the name, and this explains what the anchor cannot hold.

articles.title: Survivorship Bias
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study of successful companies identifies the habits they share and recommends those habits to everybody else. The reasoning seems unimpeachable at first reading: the data are real, the habits were measured carefully, and the companies in question did in fact succeed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The error is in which companies were available to measure. The study examined the ones that still existed, and a company that adopted the same habits and failed was not in the sample because it was not there to be studied.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That omission can produce any conclusion at all. If a habit is common among both survivors and failures, examining only survivors makes it look like a cause of success, when it may be a cause of nothing or a cause of failure.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The classic case concerns aircraft returning from missions in the Second World War, inspected to decide where to add armour. The returning planes showed damage concentrated in certain areas, and the obvious response was to armour those areas.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Abraham Wald's observation was that the sample consisted of aircraft that came back. Damage in those areas was survivable by definition, and the places with no damage on returning aircraft were the places where a hit meant the plane did not return.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The correction is counterintuitive in a specific way. The right response was to armour exactly where the data showed no damage, which inverts the apparent reading of a perfectly accurate dataset.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Identifying it in a new case requires asking a particular question before looking at any figures: what would have had to happen for a case to be absent from this data, and is that thing related to what is being measured?

paras.label: H
paras.text: Where the answer is yes, the dataset cannot support the conclusion however large it is. Adding more survivors adds more of the same selection, and a confident finding from a complete census of survivors is still a finding about survival.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study of successful companies finds the habits they share and recommends those habits. The reasoning looks unimpeachable. The data are real, the habits were measured, and the companies did succeed.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Abraham Wald observed that the sample was aircraft that came back. Damage in those areas was survivable by definition. The places with no damage on returning aircraft were where a hit meant the plane did not return.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Spotting it in a new case means asking one question before looking at figures. What would have had to happen for a case to be absent from this data? Is that thing related to what is being measured?

paras.label: H

questions.q: What was wrong with armouring the areas where returning planes were damaged?
questions.a: Damage in those areas was survivable by definition, so the places with no damage on returning aircraft were where a hit meant the plane did not return.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why the omission can produce any conclusion) and paragraph G (i.e. the question to ask before looking at figures).
Summarize survivorship bias and how to detect it.
questions.a: A conclusion drawn only from cases that survived can be wrong because the failures are absent, so a habit shared by survivors and failures alike looks like a cause of success. Wald showed that armour belonged where returning aircraft showed no damage, and detection requires asking what would make a case absent and whether that is related to what is being measured.

questions.q:
sample: the cases actually examined, which may have been selected by the very thing being studied.
selection: the process determining which cases are available, which can produce a bias no amount of data removes.
Describe the connection between adding more data and the strength of the conclusion.
questions.a: Adding more survivors adds more of the same selection, so a confident finding from a complete census of survivors is still a finding about survival.

articles.note: RI.9-10.8 at this grade means a fallacy where the arithmetic is correct. Nothing in the aircraft data was wrong and the conclusion was backwards.

articles.title: The Appeal to Consequences
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A claim is put forward and someone objects that if it were true, something bad would follow from it. The objection is often entirely sincere, it is frequently persuasive to an audience, and it is not an argument about whether the claim is true.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The structure is easy to state and harder to notice in use. We cannot accept this, because accepting it would mean accepting that, and the second clause describes a consequence rather than offering evidence.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It appears in both directions. If this result holds, decades of work were wasted, and if this result holds, our approach is vindicated, are the same move, and the second is less often challenged because the people making it are pleased.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is a legitimate neighbour that must not be confused with it. If a claim implies something already known to be false, that is a genuine argument against the claim, because a true statement cannot entail a false one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distinction is between implying something false and implying something unwelcome. The first is a logical relation and the second is an assessment of consequences, and an argument slides between them easily because both begin the same way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a legitimate use in deciding what to do. If a claim might be true and acting on it would be catastrophic, the consequence is a sound reason to act cautiously, and it remains no reason at all to believe the claim is false.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That separation is the whole of it. What is true and what it would be convenient to be true are different questions, and the appeal collapses them so smoothly that a listener can agree without noticing a question has been swapped.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The test is therefore mechanical. Remove the clause describing what would follow, and ask whether anything remains that bears on whether the claim is correct, and frequently nothing does.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A claim is put forward and someone objects that if it were true, something bad would follow. The objection is often sincere and frequently persuasive. It is not an argument about whether the claim is true.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The structure is easy to state and harder to notice in use. We cannot accept this, because accepting it would mean accepting that. The second clause describes a consequence rather than offering evidence.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It appears in both directions. If this result holds, decades of work were wasted. If this result holds, our approach is vindicated. Same move. The second is challenged less, because the people making it are pleased.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is a legitimate neighbour that must not be confused with it. If a claim implies something already known to be false, that is a genuine argument against it. A true statement cannot entail a false one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The distinction is between implying something false and implying something unwelcome. The first is a logical relation. The second is an assessment of consequences. An argument slides between them because both begin the same way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is also a legitimate use in deciding what to do. If a claim might be true and acting on it would be catastrophic, the consequence is a sound reason to act cautiously. It is no reason to believe the claim is false.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That separation is the whole of it. What is true and what it would be convenient to be true are different questions. The appeal collapses them so smoothly a listener can agree without noticing a swap.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the test is mechanical. Remove the clause describing what would follow. Ask whether anything remains that bears on whether the claim is correct. Frequently nothing does.

questions.q: What is the legitimate neighbour of this fallacy?
questions.a: If a claim implies something already known to be false, that is a genuine argument against the claim, because a true statement cannot entail a false one.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the legitimate use in deciding what to do) and paragraph H (i.e. the mechanical test).
Summarize the appeal to consequences.
questions.a: It objects that a claim cannot be accepted because accepting it would mean something unwelcome, which describes a consequence rather than offering evidence, and it appears both when the consequence is feared and when it is hoped for. It must be distinguished from a claim implying something known to be false, and a consequence can justify acting cautiously without being a reason to think the claim false.

questions.q:
entail: to imply as a logical consequence, so that if the first is true the second must be.
unwelcome: unpleasant to accept, which is different from false.
Describe the connection between acting cautiously and believing a claim.
questions.a: If a claim might be true and acting on it would be catastrophic, the consequence is a sound reason to act cautiously and remains no reason at all to believe the claim is false.

articles.note: Paragraph C is the half students miss. The version that flatters is the same fallacy and is almost never objected to.

articles.title: The Pattern Drawn Afterwards
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study measures many things at once and reports the one that came out striking. Nothing has been fabricated, every measurement was really taken, and the conclusion is still unreliable in a way that cannot be detected by reading the paper alone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The arithmetic is the reason. If twenty independent comparisons are made and the usual threshold is applied, roughly one is expected to pass it by chance even where nothing whatever is going on.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A paper reporting that one comparison has reported a true measurement. What it has not reported is how many others were made, and without that number a reader cannot tell a finding from a lottery result.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The name usually given to this comes from a story about a marksman who fires at a barn and then paints a target around the tightest cluster of holes. The shooting is genuine and the accuracy is created afterwards.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It arises most naturally in subgroup analysis. A treatment showing no overall effect may show one in men over sixty, and if twelve subgroups were examined the appearance of one such result is what chance alone predicts. The published paper frequently names only that subgroup.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The correction is not to forbid such analysis, which would discard real discoveries. It is to state in advance which comparison is the main one, and to treat everything else as a question for a later study rather than as a finding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is what registration provides, and it is why the gap between a registered protocol and a published paper is so informative. A main outcome that changed between the two is a specific and checkable event.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The underlying lesson is uncomfortable. A striking result from a study that looked at many things is weaker evidence than an unremarkable result from a study that looked at one, and nothing visible in the two papers shows that.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study measures many things and reports the one that came out striking. Nothing was fabricated. The measurement was real. The conclusion is still unreliable in a way the paper alone cannot show.

paras.label: C

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is what registration provides, and it is why the gap between a registered protocol and a published paper is so informative. A main outcome that changed between the two is a specific, checkable event.

questions.q: Why does making twenty comparisons matter?
questions.a: If twenty independent comparisons are made and the usual threshold is applied, roughly one is expected to pass it by chance even where nothing whatever is going on.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the correction is not to forbid the analysis) and paragraph H (i.e. the uncomfortable lesson).
Summarize the fallacy and its remedy.
questions.a: Reporting the one striking result from many comparisons is unreliable because chance alone produces about one pass in twenty, and a reader cannot tell a finding from a lottery result without knowing how many were made. The remedy is not to forbid subgroup analysis but to state the main comparison in advance, which registration records and which makes a changed outcome checkable.

questions.q:
subgroup: a smaller set within a study's participants, whose separate analysis multiplies the comparisons made.
registration: recording a study's plan and main outcome in advance so later changes are visible.
Describe the connection between how many things a study measured and how strong its result is.
questions.a: A striking result from a study that looked at many things is weaker evidence than an unremarkable result from a study that looked at one, and nothing visible in the two papers shows that.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's significance article. That one explained the threshold and this one explains what happens when it is applied twenty times.

articles.title: The Slippery Slope
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: An argument against a proposal says that allowing it will lead to something nobody wants. The chain may be three steps or ten, and the form is the same: not this is bad, but this leads to that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The form is not automatically fallacious, which is why it is difficult. Some chains are real, institutions do set precedents, and an argument that a measure will be extended is sometimes a correct prediction with evidence behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What distinguishes a sound version is that each step is defended. A claim that A leads to B requires a reason why, and a claim that B leads to C requires another, and an argument that asserts the chain without supporting the links has asserted a story.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Probability compounds in a way intuition handles badly. If each of five steps is eighty per cent likely, the whole chain is about a third likely, and an argument that feels overwhelming step by step may be unlikely taken whole.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fallacious version also tends to describe the final step vividly and the intermediate ones briefly. Attention is drawn to the destination, which is doing emotional work, and away from the links, which is where the argument would have to be checked.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A useful counter-question is whether the intermediate steps have independent defences. If step three would be opposed on its own terms by the same people and institutions, then arriving at it is not automatic and the chain has a stopping point.

paras.label: G
paras.text: History supplies cases in both directions, which is why neither side can settle this generally. Some measures were extended exactly as predicted, and others were adopted and not extended for decades, and pointing at either set proves nothing about a new case.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the assessment has to be specific. Name the steps, ask what evidence supports each transition, and ask what would prevent it, and an argument that cannot answer those about step two has not earned step seven.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. how probability compounds) and paragraph F (i.e. the counter-question about intermediate steps).
Summarize how to assess a slippery slope argument.
questions.a: The form asserts that one step leads to another, which is sometimes a sound prediction, so each link must be defended separately. Probabilities compound, making a chain of likely steps unlikely as a whole, the fallacious version describes the destination vividly and the links briefly, and the test is whether the intermediate steps would be opposed on their own terms.

questions.q:
precedent: an earlier decision treated as a reason for a later one, which is what makes some chains real.
compound: to multiply together, so that several likely steps produce an unlikely chain.
Describe the connection between the vividness of the final step and where attention goes.
questions.a: Attention is drawn to the destination, which is doing emotional work, and away from the links, which is where the argument would have to be checked.

articles.note: The compounding arithmetic in paragraph D is the part that settles most real cases. Work one example through with five plausible steps.

articles.title: Absence of Evidence
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.5 development · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: A search finds nothing, and two opposite conclusions are drawn from the same result. One side says this shows the thing does not exist, the other says this shows nothing at all, and both are sometimes right.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The phrase absence of evidence is not evidence of absence is widely quoted and is only half true. Whether an absence is informative depends entirely on how hard anyone looked and on what they would have found.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A search that would certainly have detected the thing, and did not, is strong evidence that the thing is not there. That is an ordinary and sound inference, and it is what a negative medical test is for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A search that might have missed it says far less, and how much less is calculable rather than a matter of opinion. The quantity is the probability of finding the thing if it were present, which is what a study's power measures.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the question to ask of any negative result is never whether something was found. It is what the search would have detected, and a report that does not state that has not reported enough to be interpreted either way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The error runs in both directions and the second is less often noticed. Treating a weak search as decisive overstates it; treating a powerful search as uninformative because absence is not evidence is a misuse of a slogan to dismiss a real finding.

paras.label: G
paras.text: An example makes the asymmetry concrete. If a careful survey of a small island reports no large mammals, that is strong evidence, and if the same method is applied once to a continent it establishes very little.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The slogan survives because it is a useful correction to one specific error. Used as a general principle it licenses ignoring any negative result at all, which is the opposite of what the people who coined it were arguing for.

questions.q: When is finding nothing strong evidence?
questions.a: When the search would certainly have detected the thing and did not, which is an ordinary and sound inference and is what a negative medical test is for.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the error in the other direction) and paragraph G (i.e. the island and the continent).
Summarize how to interpret a negative result.
questions.a: Whether an absence is informative depends on how hard anyone looked and what they would have found, which is measured by a study's power. A search certain to detect something is strong evidence it is not there, a weak search says little, and using the slogan that absence is not evidence as a general principle licenses dismissing real findings.

questions.q:
power: the probability a search or study would detect the thing if it were present.
inference: a conclusion drawn from evidence, here from the failure to find something.
Describe the connection between the size of an area searched and the strength of a negative result.
questions.a: A careful survey of a small island reporting no large mammals is strong evidence, and the same method applied once to a continent establishes very little.

articles.note: A slogan that is correct in one direction and is used in both. Ask students where they have heard it used to dismiss something rather than to qualify it.

articles.title: The Preamble to the Constitution
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Constitution of the United States opens with a single sentence of fifty-two words, and nearly every phrase in it was contested by the people who agreed to it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first three words are the most argued over. We the People locates the authority of the document in a population rather than in the states that sent delegates, and an earlier draft had begun by naming the states individually.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That change was partly practical. The document would take effect when nine states ratified, so naming thirteen would have been inaccurate the moment it was signed, and the general formulation avoided the problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It was not only practical, and both sides understood that. If the authority comes from a people, then the union is not an agreement among states that states might revisit, and the question of who the parties were is not settled by the text.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The purposes that follow are a list of six, and they are not in a random order. A more perfect union comes first, justice and domestic tranquillity next, the common defence after that, and the general welfare and liberty last.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The phrase to form a more perfect union is doing quiet work. It concedes that a union already existed under the Articles of Confederation and claims that this document improves rather than replaces it, which was the politically necessary claim.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The preamble creates no powers and grants no rights, and courts have long held that nothing can be founded on it alone. It is a statement of purpose, and its legal function is to inform the reading of the clauses that follow.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Declaration, the difference in task is visible immediately. The Declaration argues that a government may be dissolved, and the Preamble states what a government is being constituted to do, and the same people wrote both within eleven years.

questions.a: The document would take effect when nine states ratified, so naming thirteen would have been inaccurate the moment it was signed.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the work done by a more perfect union) and paragraph G (i.e. the preamble's legal function).
Summarize what the Preamble does.
questions.a: Its fifty-two words locate authority in a people rather than in states, which was partly practical given ratification by nine and partly a claim about what the union is. It lists six purposes in a deliberate order, concedes a union already existed while claiming to improve it, and creates no powers, functioning instead to inform how later clauses are read.

questions.q:
ratify: to approve formally, which nine states had to do for the document to take effect.
preamble: an opening statement of purpose that creates no powers and guides the reading of what follows.
Describe the connection between locating authority in a people and the status of the union.
questions.a: If the authority comes from a people, then the union is not an agreement among states that states might revisit.

articles.note: RI.9-10.9 wants documents read against each other. This grade's five all argue about what a union is for, and this is where the question is first posed.

articles.title: Federalist Number Ten
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Federalist papers were written to persuade New York to ratify the Constitution. They are advocacy, published under a pseudonym, and the tenth of them is the most studied because it answers the strongest objection the other side had.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That objection came from accepted theory. Republics were understood to work only in small territories, because a large and diverse population would contain too many competing interests for any common good to emerge.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Madison accepts the premise about interests and reverses the conclusion. He argues that faction is not a defect to be eliminated but a permanent consequence of liberty, since people free to think differently will form groups around different interests.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument that follows turns on what can be done about it. Removing the causes of faction would require destroying liberty or making everyone think alike, and both remedies are described as worse than the disease.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So the question becomes how to control the effects. A minority faction can be outvoted, which leaves the hard case: a faction that constitutes a majority, which cannot be outvoted and which ordinary republican machinery does not restrain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The solution is where the essay inverts the received view entirely. In a large republic there are more interests, so a majority is harder to assemble, and any majority that forms must be built from groups that agree about less.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The size that was supposed to be fatal therefore becomes the protection. The essay is not arguing that a large republic is tolerable despite being large; it is arguing that it is safer than a small one, for the reason small ones were praised.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Preamble, the two do different halves of one job. The Preamble states what the union is for, and this essay argues why an institution of that size could achieve it, which is the claim the Preamble assumes and does not defend.

questions.a: Removing them would require destroying liberty or making everyone think alike, and both remedies are described as worse than the disease.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the hard case of a majority faction) and paragraph F (i.e. why a large republic is safer).
Summarize the argument of Federalist Ten.
questions.a: Accepted theory held that republics work only in small territories because diversity prevents a common good. Madison accepts that faction follows from liberty and cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so the effects must be controlled, and since a minority can be outvoted the problem is a majority faction. In a large republic more interests make a majority harder to assemble, so size becomes the protection.

questions.q:
faction: a group united by an interest adverse to the rights of others or to the general good.
republic: a government by elected representatives, which theory held could only work in a small territory.
Describe the connection between the number of interests and the difficulty of a majority faction.
questions.a: In a large republic there are more interests, so a majority is harder to assemble and any majority that forms must be built from groups that agree about less.

articles.note: The reversal in paragraph G is the move worth isolating. The same fact that was the objection becomes the answer, and nothing about the fact changed.

articles.title: The Bill of Rights
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution were ratified in 1791, four years after the document they amend was signed. Their existence is the result of an argument that the original text had lost, and the terms of that argument are still visible in how they are written.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Several states had ratified the Constitution only on the understanding that amendments protecting individual rights would follow. Without that understanding the document would probably not have been adopted, and the amendments are therefore part of the price of ratification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument against them was not that rights do not matter. Hamilton argued in Federalist 84 that a list would be dangerous, because enumerating some rights implies that the ones not listed were not protected.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That objection was taken seriously enough to be answered inside the text. The Ninth Amendment states that listing certain rights shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people, which is a clause written to answer an argument.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The drafting is also notable for what it restrains. Most of the amendments limit what government may do rather than describing what a person may do, so the First begins with a prohibition on Congress rather than a grant to a speaker.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That form matters for how they were originally understood. A restriction on Congress is a restriction on the federal government, and applying these limits to states happened much later, through a long sequence of decisions under the Fourteenth Amendment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The Tenth closes the set by stating a principle about everything unstated. Powers not delegated to the federal government, and not prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states or to the people.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside Federalist Ten, the two sit uneasily together, which is the interesting part. One argues that structure and scale are what protect liberty, and the other was demanded by people who did not find that argument sufficient.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution were ratified in 1791, four years after the document they amend. They exist because of an argument the original text had lost.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Several states ratified the Constitution only on the understanding that amendments protecting individual rights would follow. Without that understanding the document would probably not have been adopted. The amendments are part of the price of ratification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument against them was not that rights do not matter. Hamilton argued in Federalist 84 that a list would be dangerous. Naming some rights implies the ones not named were not protected.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That objection was taken seriously enough to be answered inside the text. The Ninth Amendment says that listing certain rights shall not be construed to deny or disparage others retained by the people. It was written to answer an argument.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The drafting is notable for what it restrains. Most amendments limit what government may do rather than describing what a person may do. The First begins with a prohibition on Congress, not a grant to a speaker.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That form matters for how they were first understood. A restriction on Congress restricts the federal government. Applying these limits to states came much later, through a long sequence of decisions under the Fourteenth Amendment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The Tenth closes the set with a principle about everything unstated. Powers not delegated to the federal government, and not prohibited to the states, are reserved to the states or to the people.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Beside Federalist Ten the two sit uneasily, which is the interesting part. One argues that structure and scale protect liberty. The other was demanded by people who did not find that argument sufficient.

questions.q: What was Hamilton's objection to a bill of rights?
questions.a: That enumerating some rights implies the ones not listed were not protected, which he argued in Federalist 84 made a list dangerous.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the amendments restraining government rather than granting to persons) and paragraph H (i.e. the tension with Federalist Ten).
Summarize why the Bill of Rights exists and how it is drafted.
questions.a: States ratified on the understanding that amendments protecting rights would follow, so the ten are part of the price of ratification. Hamilton's objection that a list implies unlisted rights are unprotected is answered by the Ninth Amendment, most of the amendments restrain government rather than grant to persons, and they applied only to the federal government until much later decisions.

questions.q:
enumerate: to list individually, which Hamilton argued would endanger rights left off the list.
reserved: kept by someone else, as the Tenth Amendment keeps unlisted powers with the states or the people.
Describe the connection between the Bill of Rights and the argument of Federalist Ten.
questions.a: Federalist Ten argues that structure and scale protect liberty, and the Bill of Rights was demanded by people who did not find that argument sufficient.

articles.note: Paragraph H is the comparison the standard asks for. These documents do not simply complement each other, and students should be able to say where they disagree.

articles.title: Lincoln's Second Inaugural
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Lincoln's second inaugural address, delivered in March 1865, is about seven hundred words long. The war was nearly over, his side was going to win, and the speech does almost nothing that the occasion would predict.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It does not claim victory, name a general or describe a battle. It spends its first third on the situation four years earlier, in the measured tone of a man recounting something both audiences already knew.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then names the cause of the war directly, which the first inaugural had not. Slavery is identified as the interest over which the parties divided, and the sentence is constructed so that no reader can take it as referring to anything else.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The section that follows is the strangest and the most carefully built. It observes that both sides read the same Bible, pray to the same God, and each invokes that God's aid against the other.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The symmetry is doing deliberate work. By placing the two sides in the same sentence, with the same practices, the speech removes the usual structure of a victory address, in which one side is the subject and the other is the problem.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The passage then declines to resolve the symmetry in his own favour. Lincoln says that the prayers of neither have been answered fully, and that the Almighty has his own purposes, which is a refusal to claim divine endorsement at a moment when it was available.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The closing is the most quoted and is frequently detached from what precedes it. With malice toward none, with charity for all follows an argument that has already refused to describe the enemy as different in kind.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Gettysburg Address, the pair shows the same method at two scales. One dates a nation to make a claim about its principle, and the other describes a war without an enemy to make a claim about what follows it.

questions.q: What does the speech do instead of claiming victory?
questions.a: It spends its first third on the situation four years earlier, names slavery as the cause of the war, and places both sides in the same sentence as people who read the same Bible and pray to the same God.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the refusal of divine endorsement) and paragraph G (i.e. what the closing follows from).
Summarize what Lincoln's second inaugural does.
questions.a: Delivered as the war was ending, it claims no victory and names no general, spending its first third on the situation four years earlier and then identifying slavery as the cause. It places both sides in one sentence as people with the same practices, declines to claim that either side's prayers were answered, and closes with charity for all after refusing to describe the enemy as different in kind.

questions.q:
inaugural: the address given on taking office, usually an occasion for programme and celebration.
symmetry: the deliberate placing of two sides in the same terms, which removes the structure of a victory speech.
Describe the connection between the symmetry passage and the closing line.
questions.a: With malice toward none, with charity for all follows an argument that has already refused to describe the enemy as different in kind.

articles.note: The closing line is quoted constantly on its own. Give students the last sentence first, then the speech, and ask what changed.

articles.title: What the Emancipation Proclamation Did
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.6 rhetoric · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on the first of January, 1863, in the middle of a war whose outcome was not yet decided. It is among the most famous documents in American history and among the most frequently misdescribed, because what it actually did and what it is remembered for are not the same thing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It did not abolish slavery. It declared enslaved people free in the areas then in rebellion, and it explicitly exempted the border states that had remained in the Union and the parts of the Confederacy already under federal control.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That exemption produced the obvious objection at the time and since. The proclamation freed people in the places where the federal government had no power to free anyone and left slavery untouched where it did.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The legal reasoning behind the exemption is the explanation. The document was issued as a war measure under the president's authority as commander in chief, which could reach enemy property in a rebellion and could not reach a loyal state.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So its immediate effect was conditional on military advance. As federal armies took territory, the proclamation applied there, which made every advance an act of emancipation and gave the army a function it had not previously had.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It also changed who could fight. The proclamation authorised the enlistment of Black soldiers in the United States forces, and roughly two hundred thousand served, which altered the manpower position and the meaning of the war simultaneously.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The international effect is frequently overlooked and was substantial. After January 1863 the war was explicitly about slavery, which made recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible for European governments whose populations opposed it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, which is the document that did the thing the proclamation is remembered for. Read together they show a familiar pattern: the famous text changed the terms, and a less famous one changed the law.

questions.q: Why did the proclamation exempt the border states?
questions.a: It was issued as a war measure under the president's authority as commander in chief, which could reach enemy property in a rebellion and could not reach a loyal state.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the enlistment of Black soldiers) and paragraph G (i.e. the effect on European recognition).
Summarize what the Emancipation Proclamation did.
questions.a: It declared enslaved people free in areas in rebellion while exempting loyal border states, because it was a war measure reaching only enemy property, so its effect followed military advance. It authorised the enlistment of Black soldiers, about two hundred thousand of whom served, and made European recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible, while abolition came with the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865.

questions.q:
war measure: an action taken under wartime authority, whose reach is limited to the enemy.
recognition: formal acknowledgement of a government by another state, which the proclamation made politically difficult.
Describe the connection between the proclamation and the Thirteenth Amendment.
questions.a: The proclamation changed the terms of the war while the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865 is the document that abolished slavery, which is what the proclamation is remembered for.

articles.note: Five documents that argue about what a union is for and what it owes people inside it. Ask students to place each of the five on that question.

articles.title: The Eclipse That Tested a Theory
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: General relativity predicted in 1915 that gravity bends light, and predicted a specific amount: twice the deflection that Newtonian reasoning gives for a star's light passing the edge of the sun.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The prediction was testable only under one circumstance. The sun's own light drowns the stars beside it, so the only way to photograph them is during a total eclipse, and the only way to measure a shift is to compare that photograph with one of the same stars months later.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Two expeditions went out in May 1919, one to Príncipe off West Africa and one to Sobral in Brazil, organised in Britain by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson. The war had ended six months earlier.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The measurement is extremely difficult and the numbers involved are tiny. The expected shift is a fraction of a second of arc, which required photographic plates compared with instruments operating close to their limits.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The conditions were poor. Príncipe was clouded for most of totality, and of the plates taken there only two were usable; Sobral had better weather and one of its two instruments produced images affected by heating of the mirror.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The results were announced in November 1919 and reported worldwide as a confirmation. The Príncipe plates and the better Sobral instrument agreed with Einstein's figure, and the problematic Sobral instrument gave a value closer to the Newtonian one.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The handling of that third dataset has been argued about ever since. It was given less weight on the stated ground that the instrument was known to have a defect, which is a legitimate reason and is also what one would say if one wanted a particular answer.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Later measurements settled the question independently and repeatedly, which is why the episode is now interesting for a different reason. It is a case where the conclusion was right, the data were marginal, and a judgement was made that only subsequent work could justify.

questions.a: The sun's own light drowns the stars beside it, so they can only be photographed when the sun is covered, and a shift is measured by comparing with an image taken months later.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the handling of the third dataset) and paragraph H (i.e. why the episode is interesting now).
Summarize the 1919 eclipse expeditions.
questions.a: Relativity predicted twice the Newtonian deflection of starlight, testable only during a total eclipse, so expeditions went to Príncipe and Sobral in May 1919. Cloud left only two usable plates at Príncipe and one Sobral instrument suffered from mirror heating, and that instrument's Newtonian-leaning result was downweighted for a stated defect, a judgement only later measurements could justify.

questions.q:
deflection: the amount light is bent from a straight path, which the two theories predicted differently.
totality: the period when the sun is completely covered, the only time the nearby stars can be photographed.
Describe the connection between the defect in one instrument and the dispute since.
questions.a: Downweighting that dataset on the ground of a known defect is a legitimate reason and is also what one would say if one wanted a particular answer, which is why it has been argued about ever since.

articles.note: A famous confirmation with marginal data and a defensible judgement. Ask what would have had to be true for the downweighting to be wrong.

articles.title: The Manuscripts of Timbuktu
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, was a centre of scholarship for several centuries, with universities and a trade in books. It held libraries of manuscripts written in Arabic and in African languages using Arabic script, covering astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law, poetry and the practical business of commerce.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The existence of those manuscripts contradicts a claim that was once widely made. Written scholarship in West Africa before European contact was frequently denied, and the denial survived partly because the evidence was held in private family collections rather than in public institutions.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That privacy was a preservation strategy rather than secrecy for its own sake. Collections passed down within families were kept out of sight during periods when they might have been seized or destroyed, and the same practice preserved them and kept them unavailable to anyone attempting to catalogue what existed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Estimates of the number run to hundreds of thousands across the region, and the range is wide because many have never been seen by anyone outside the family holding them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Their physical condition is the permanent problem. The climate is hostile to paper, insects are a continuous threat, and a manuscript that has survived four hundred years in a chest may not survive being moved, opened or photographed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2012, when armed groups took control of the city, a large-scale evacuation was organised. Manuscripts were packed into footlockers and moved out by road and by river over several months, in an operation that depended on secrecy.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The evacuation saved an enormous number and created a second problem immediately. Material that had been stable in a dry northern climate was moved to a humid southern one, where the threat is mould rather than seizure.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode shows a tension that applies to any endangered archive. Material survives by being left alone and becomes useful by being catalogued and read, and every act that makes a collection accessible also makes it more vulnerable.

questions.a: Collections kept within families were out of sight during periods when they might have been seized, which preserved them and kept them unavailable to anyone cataloguing.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the problem the evacuation created) and paragraph H (i.e. the general tension for an archive).
Summarize the manuscripts of Timbuktu and what has happened to them.
questions.a: Libraries of manuscripts on astronomy, law, medicine and poetry contradict the claim that West Africa had no written scholarship, and they survived in private family collections that kept them safe and uncatalogued. The climate and insects threaten them, and a 2012 evacuation moved great numbers south by road and river, exchanging the risk of seizure for the risk of mould.

questions.q:
archive: a collection of documents preserved for their long-term value.
catalogue: to record what a collection contains, which makes it usable and also makes it known.
Describe the connection between making a collection accessible and making it vulnerable.
questions.a: Material survives by being left alone and becomes useful by being catalogued and read, so every act that makes a collection accessible also makes it more vulnerable.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 8's paper-and-server article. Both are about preservation as an active practice with costs, in very different circumstances.

articles.title: The Island That Rose From the Sea
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In November 1963 a volcanic eruption began on the sea floor south of Iceland, was first noticed by the crew of a fishing boat, and continued for more than three years. What emerged from it was an entirely new island, named Surtsey, covering about two and a half square kilometres at its largest.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A new island is an unusual scientific opportunity because it supplies something that is otherwise impossible to obtain: a surface of known age with nothing living on it, in a region where the surrounding biology is thoroughly documented.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Iceland protected it almost immediately. Landing is restricted to a small number of researchers, nothing may be brought ashore that could introduce an organism, and the island has been surveyed on a schedule ever since.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The arrivals were recorded in order, which is the entire value of the exercise. Bacteria and fungi were present early, the first vascular plant was found in 1965, mosses followed, and lichens appeared several years after that.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Birds changed the rate decisively. Gulls began nesting in 1986, and the area around their colony developed vegetation far faster than the rest of the island, because the birds brought both seeds and the nutrients plants needed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a result nobody could have obtained from a mature ecosystem. The causal relationship between seabird colonies and plant establishment is visible at Surtsey because the before state was observed rather than inferred.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The island is also eroding, and faster than it formed. Much of the original area has been lost to the sea, and the long-term projection is that what remains will be a small core of harder material.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The protection is therefore the experiment. A single unauthorised landing with a seed on a boot would not destroy the island and would destroy the record, which is why the restriction is absolute and why it has held for sixty years.

questions.q: What makes a new island scientifically valuable?
questions.a: It supplies a surface of known age with nothing living on it, in a region where the surrounding biology is thoroughly documented.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the effect of the gull colony) and paragraph H (i.e. why the protection is the experiment).
Summarize what Surtsey has provided.

Arrivals were recorded in order, from bacteria and the first vascular plant in 1965 to mosses and lichens, and gulls nesting from 1986 accelerated vegetation around their colony, a causal relationship visible because the earlier state was observed rather than inferred.

questions.q:
vascular plant: a plant with tissue for conducting water, distinguishing it from mosses and lichens.
colonisation: the arrival and establishment of organisms on ground that held none.
Describe the connection between the landing restriction and the value of the data.
questions.a: A single unauthorised landing with a seed on a boot would not destroy the island and would destroy the record, which is why the restriction is absolute.

articles.note: An experiment whose method is a prohibition. Ask what the island would be worth scientifically if visitors had been allowed in 1964.

articles.title: The Village That Shut Its Gates
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1665 plague reached the village of Eyam in Derbyshire, probably carried in a consignment of cloth sent from London. Over the following fourteen months a substantial proportion of the inhabitants died, in a community small enough that the dead were known individually to everyone left.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What is remembered about Eyam is the decision that followed. The villagers agreed to isolate themselves, not to leave, and to accept supplies left at boundary stones, in order to prevent the disease spreading to surrounding settlements.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The account rests on a mixture of sources of very different quality. Parish burial registers are contemporary and reliable; the narrative of a collective decision rests substantially on accounts written considerably later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That distinction matters because the two support different claims. The registers establish who died and when, with dates, and the later accounts establish what people in the following century believed about why.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Historians have used the registers for something the villagers could not have intended and would not have recognised as a use. The burial dates, combined with surviving records of which households stood where and who lived in them, allow transmission within the village to be reconstructed with unusual precision.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The results have revised the traditional picture in a specific way. Mortality varied enormously between households, and the pattern is more consistent with transmission within families and dwellings than with a single uniform exposure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The quarantine's effectiveness is harder to assess and is genuinely disputed among historians. Surrounding villages were not devastated, which is consistent with the isolation having worked and equally consistent with several other explanations that nobody is now in a position to exclude.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So Eyam supports two claims of different strength, and conflating them is the usual error. That a community isolated itself and that many died is well evidenced; that the isolation saved the surrounding region is a reasonable inference and not a demonstrated fact.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1665 plague reached the village of Eyam in Derbyshire, probably in a consignment of cloth from London. Over the following fourteen months a substantial proportion of the inhabitants died.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What is remembered is the decision that followed. The villagers agreed to isolate themselves, not to leave, and to take supplies left at boundary stones, to stop the disease reaching surrounding settlements.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The account rests on sources of very different quality. Parish burial registers are contemporary and reliable. The narrative of a collective decision rests substantially on accounts written considerably later.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That distinction matters because the two support different claims. The registers establish who died and when, with dates. The later accounts establish what people in the next century believed about why.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Historians have used the registers for something the villagers cannot have intended. Burial dates, combined with surviving household records, allow transmission within the village to be studied with unusual precision.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The results revise the traditional picture in a specific way. Mortality varied enormously between households. The pattern fits transmission within families and dwellings better than a single uniform exposure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The quarantine's effectiveness is harder to assess and genuinely disputed. Surrounding villages were not devastated. That is consistent with the isolation having worked, and with several other explanations nobody can exclude.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So Eyam supports two claims of different strength, and conflating them is the usual error. That a community isolated itself and many died is well evidenced. That the isolation saved the region is a reasonable inference, not a demonstrated fact.

questions.q: What do the parish registers establish that later accounts do not?
questions.a: Who died and when, with dates, while the later accounts establish what people in the following century believed about why.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what the household pattern shows) and paragraph H (i.e. the two claims of different strength).
Summarize what is known about Eyam and how firmly.
questions.a: Plague reached the village in 1665 and the inhabitants are said to have isolated themselves, taking supplies at boundary stones. Contemporary burial registers reliably record who died and when, allowing household transmission to be studied, while the narrative of a collective decision rests on later accounts, and the claim that the isolation saved surrounding villages is an inference rather than a demonstrated fact.

questions.q:
parish register: a contemporary record of burials, baptisms and marriages kept by a church.
transmission: the passing of a disease from one person to another, which household records allow to be traced.
Describe the connection between the burial registers and a use nobody intended.
questions.a: The burial dates, combined with surviving records of households, allow transmission within the village to be studied with unusual precision, which the villagers could not have intended.

articles.note: Pairs with The Court Records of a Village earlier in this grade. Both show a record answering a question it was not made for.

articles.title: The Signal That Came From a Microwave
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.9-10.1 citing evidence · RI.9-10.2 central idea · RI.9-10.4 word meaning · RI.9-10.8 claims and evidence
 Lower range: LL 970 – 1070

paras.label: A
paras.text: Radio telescopes at Parkes in Australia had for some years been recording occasional bursts of radio energy lasting only milliseconds. Some of them were genuinely astronomical and are now an established field of study, and some belonged to a second category that behaved strangely from the beginning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The strange ones were given their own name, perytons. They appeared at roughly the right frequencies, they were short, and they looked enough like the real signals that distinguishing them was not immediately possible.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Several features did not fit. Perytons were detected across the whole sky rather than from a direction, which is not how an astronomical source behaves, and they clustered around the middle of the day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: They also came in groups. A single astronomical event does not repeat on a schedule, and perytons tended to arrive in clusters separated by minutes, which pointed clearly at a terrestrial source without doing anything at all to identify which one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The investigation took years and was not glamorous at any point. A radio-frequency interference monitor was installed at the site, and the team then waited for a peryton to occur while that second instrument was running and recording everything else happening nearby.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In 2015 they found it. The signals were produced by the kitchen microwave ovens in the observatory building, and specifically by a door being opened before the timer finished, which stops the magnetron mid-cycle and releases a brief burst.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The clustering around midday was lunch. The whole-sky detection was because the source was inside the building rather than in a direction, and the resemblance to real bursts was a coincidence of frequency and duration.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is not a failure, and it is told as one too often. The team suspected a local source for years, investigated systematically and eventually identified it, which is what an instrument's noise characterisation is supposed to do.

questions.a: The kitchen microwave ovens in the observatory building, specifically a door opened before the timer finished, which stops the magnetron mid-cycle and releases a brief burst.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the features that did not fit) and paragraph H (i.e. why the episode is not a failure).
Summarize the peryton investigation.
questions.a: Short radio bursts at Parkes resembled real astronomical signals but were detected across the whole sky, clustered around midday and arrived in groups, which pointed to a terrestrial source. An interference monitor was installed and in 2015 the source was identified as microwave oven doors opened before the timer finished, and the clustering was lunch.

questions.q:
terrestrial: originating on earth rather than in space, which the whole-sky detection suggested.
interference: unwanted signal from a local source, which a monitor is installed to identify.
Describe the connection between whole-sky detection and the location of the source.
questions.a: The signals were detected across the whole sky rather than from a direction because the source was inside the building rather than at a point in space.

articles.note: Closes the grade on the same discipline it opened with at Penzias and Wilson in grade 9: eliminating what the instrument itself is doing before claiming anything about the sky.

articles.title: What the Fossil Record Cannot Say
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fossil record is the primary evidence for the history of life, and it is a sample rather than a census. Understanding what it can establish requires understanding, first, what had to happen for anything to be in it at all.

paras.label: B
paras.text: An organism becomes a fossil only under a narrow set of conditions. It has to be buried quickly, in sediment, in a place where the sediment will survive, and it has to have parts durable enough to persist while the surrounding material turns to rock.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each of those conditions filters. Hard parts survive and soft ones rarely do, so a world of worms and jellyfish leaves almost nothing, and the apparent abundance of shelled animals in the record is partly a fact about shells.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Environment filters as well. Sediment accumulates in river deltas, lake beds and shallow seas, and an animal that lived on a mountainside is in a place that erodes rather than accumulates, so entire habitats are nearly absent.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This produces a specific and well-known trap. The last fossil of a species is almost never the last individual, because rarity precedes extinction and a rare animal is unlikely to be preserved, so the record consistently makes extinctions look earlier and more abrupt than they were.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What palaeontologists do about this is instructive. A date for an extinction is published with a range rather than a point, and that range is calculated from how often the species appears in the layers below, which converts an unknown into a stated uncertainty.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some questions remain genuinely open and are marked as such in the literature. Whether a particular lineage declined over a million years or vanished in a decade is frequently not resolvable with the material available, and the honest papers say which of those they cannot distinguish.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the record supports two kinds of statement with very different strength. That an organism existed at a time and place is as firm as evidence gets, because the specimen is physical. That something did not exist is an inference from absence, and its strength depends entirely on how thoroughly the relevant rocks have been searched.

questions.a: A date published with a range calculated from how often a species appears in the layers below states the uncertainty rather than hiding it, and papers also say which possibilities they cannot distinguish.

articles.note: RI.11-12.1 adds determining where a text leaves matters uncertain. Paragraph G is that clause in one sentence, and students should be able to point at it.

articles.title: How Confident Is a Climate Projection
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An assessment report on climate runs to thousands of pages and is summarised in a few. The summaries are what circulate, and the thing most frequently lost in the compression is the vocabulary the report uses to say how sure it is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That vocabulary is defined rather than conversational. Terms such as virtually certain, very likely, likely and about as likely as not each correspond to a stated probability range, and the definitions are printed in the report so that a reader can convert a word into a number.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Likely, for instance, means at least a two in three chance. A reader who takes it in its ordinary sense, as meaning probably or expected, has read a hedge as a prediction, and the report has done what it could to prevent that.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second scale operates alongside the first and is often confused with it. Confidence describes how good the underlying evidence is, and a finding can be assigned high confidence and a wide probability range at the same time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those two are genuinely independent. High confidence that a quantity lies somewhere in a broad range is a coherent position, and so is low confidence about a narrow one, and a summary that reports only the number has dropped the half that says how much to trust it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reports also distinguish between what is being projected. Physical quantities such as warming under a stated emissions scenario are treated differently from consequences that depend on how societies respond, and the second carry wider ranges for reasons that are not about physics.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Where the science does not support a statement, the reports say so in the same formal register. Phrases marking limited evidence or low agreement appear throughout, and they are statements about the literature rather than about the world.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the uncertainty is not a weakness the documents are admitting. It is the most carefully constructed part of them, built to let a reader distinguish a well-constrained finding from a poorly constrained one, and it is the first thing a short summary removes.

questions.a: At least a two in three chance, which is a defined probability range rather than the ordinary sense of probably or expected.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the two scales are independent) and paragraph G (i.e. phrases marking limited evidence).
Summarize how these reports express uncertainty.
