questions.q: Why does a continuous cause disappear in a chronological report?
questions.a: It appears nowhere in particular because it was everywhere, so a reader following the timeline meets it as a series of unconnected moments.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what a thematic report costs) and paragraph G (i.e. how the terms of reference decide).
Summarize the choice between chronological and thematic structure.
questions.a: A chronological report establishes what was known to whom and when, but a cause operating throughout appears as unconnected moments. A thematic report states a persistent failure once with instances from the whole period and loses the sequence needed to judge individual conduct, so the right choice depends on whether the inquiry was asked about a system or a person.

questions.q:
terms of reference: the question an inquiry was formally set, against which its structure can be assessed.
thematic: organised by topic rather than by time.
Describe the connection between the question asked and the structure chosen.
questions.a: An inquiry asked whether a system failed is well served by themes, and one asked whether a person should have acted differently is not, so the terms of reference make the choice evaluable.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's accident investigation article, which showed why the factual phase comes first. This asks how the findings should then be arranged.

articles.title: The Textbook That Starts With the Answer
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Textbook chapters are written in two opposite shapes, and the difference is not stylistic. One begins with the conclusion and explains it; the other reconstructs the problem and arrives at the conclusion at the end.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the standard modern form, and its advantages are real rather than merely conventional. A chapter that states the principle in its opening paragraph gives a reader a framework to hang everything else on, and all the subsequent material is easier to follow because its destination is already known.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also reflects how the field itself now thinks, which is not a trivial consideration. Presenting a settled result first is honest about the present state of knowledge, and a student is not asked to spend a week inside a confusion that the discipline resolved two centuries ago and has not revisited.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What it removes is the reason the result is believed. A principle stated first arrives with the authority of the textbook, and the evidence that follows reads as illustration of something already accepted rather than as the argument that established it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The reconstructive shape makes the opposite trade. A chapter that begins with the observations that puzzled people, and lets the reader feel the difficulty, produces understanding of why the answer is the answer, and does so slowly and at the cost of frustration.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is evidence that the slower form produces better retention and transfer, and evidence that it produces worse examination performance in the short term, and both findings can be true because they measure different things.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decisive consideration is usually what comes next. A chapter that is a prerequisite for ten more is better written in the efficient form, and a chapter intended to show what the subject is actually like has a different job.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So a structure can be evaluated against a stated purpose rather than in the abstract. The question is not which shape is better but what the chapter is for, and a textbook that uses the same shape for everything has not asked.

questions.q: What does stating the principle first remove?
questions.a: The reason the result is believed, because the evidence that follows reads as illustration of something already accepted rather than as the argument that established it.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the two kinds of evidence about the slower form) and paragraph H (i.e. evaluating against a purpose).
Summarize the two textbook structures and how to choose.
questions.a: Stating the conclusion first gives a framework and reflects settled knowledge, while removing the reason the result is believed. Reconstructing the problem produces understanding of why the answer is the answer, slowly and frustratingly, and evidence suggests better retention but worse short-term examination performance, so the choice depends on what the chapter is for.

questions.q:
transfer: the ability to apply something learned to a new situation, which the two forms affect differently.
reconstructive: rebuilding the problem that produced a result, rather than stating the result first.
Describe the connection between two conflicting findings both being true.
questions.a: Evidence of better retention and transfer and evidence of worse short-term examination performance can both hold because they measure different things.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's paper introduction. One text secures agreement before the evidence, and this asks whether that is the right thing for a textbook to do.

articles.title: Chronological or Thematic in a History
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A history of a long period has to be arranged, and the two available arrangements are incompatible in a way that cannot be resolved by careful writing. A book proceeds by time or by subject, and whichever it chooses, it loses what the other would have shown.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A chronological history preserves contingency, which is its great strength. A reader moving forward in time meets events in the order the participants did, without knowing what will happen, and the sense that things could have gone otherwise survives.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What it cannot show is a slow change. A shift in landholding or in family size happens across a century and appears in a chronological account as a series of small mentions, none of which conveys the magnitude of the whole.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A thematic history can state that change directly and support it properly. A chapter on landholding can compare the beginning and the end of the period, present the evidence together, and give the reader a quantity rather than an impression.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its cost is that everything happens at once. A reader finishing a thematic chapter on agriculture and beginning one on religion returns to the start of the period, and the connections between the two domains, which operated in time, are hard to see.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those connections are frequently the point of the book. A change in landholding that caused a change in religious practice is a claim about sequence, and a structure that separates the two domains into different chapters makes that claim harder to state than to assert.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Some historians solve this by nesting. Large chronological sections contain thematic chapters, so the sequence is preserved at one scale and the themes are developed at another, which works where the period divides naturally and not otherwise.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Evaluating the structure therefore means asking what the book claims. A book arguing that one development caused another needs the sequence visible, and a book arguing that a society had a particular character does not, and a structure that fights the argument is a real defect rather than a preference.

questions.a: Contingency, because a reader meets events in the order participants did without knowing what will happen, so the sense that things could have gone otherwise survives.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why connections are often the point) and paragraph G (i.e. the nesting solution).
Summarize the trade between the two arrangements.
questions.a: A chronological history preserves contingency and cannot show a slow change, which appears only as scattered mentions. A thematic history states such changes with the evidence gathered, while returning the reader to the start each chapter and obscuring connections that operated in time, so nesting is sometimes used and the right choice depends on what the book argues.

questions.q:
contingency: the quality of events that could have turned out otherwise, which a timeline preserves.
nesting: placing one organising structure inside another, such as thematic chapters within chronological sections.
Describe the connection between a book's claim and the structure it needs.
questions.a: A book arguing that one development caused another needs the sequence visible, and a structure that separates the domains makes that claim harder to state than to assert.

articles.note: The companion to the inquiry article earlier in this standard. The same choice, the same trade, and a different reason for making it.

articles.title: The Argument Built on a Diagram
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Some expositions are built around a single diagram, and the prose exists to explain it. That is a structural choice as substantial as any ordering of paragraphs, and it has consequences the writer may not have intended.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first effect is that the argument becomes available at a glance. A reader who understands the figure has the claim, and the text that follows is confirmation rather than construction, which is why such pieces are easy to remember.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its second effect is that the diagram's limitations become the argument's limitations. A figure showing two axes can represent two variables, so a third one has to appear in the prose, and material that appears only in the prose of a diagram-led piece is routinely forgotten.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third effect concerns what a diagram asserts by its form. Boxes joined by arrows assert that the relationships are directional and discrete, and a process that is continuous or that runs in both directions has been misrepresented by the shape before any label is read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A well-made piece turns these into strengths deliberately. The figure carries the claims that are genuinely discrete and directional, the prose carries what cannot be drawn, and the text says explicitly that the diagram simplifies in a stated way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A badly made one lets the figure do work it cannot support. An arrow drawn between two boxes looks like a demonstrated relationship whether the evidence for it is strong or absent, and a reader cannot tell which arrows are which.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Evaluating such a structure means reading the figure and the text against each other. Every arrow should correspond to a claim defended somewhere in the prose, and every claim that matters should be visible in the figure or explicitly marked as not drawn.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Where that correspondence holds, the structure is extremely effective and deserves the reputation it has. Where it does not, the piece has acquired the persuasive force of a diagram without the evidence a diagram implies, and the mismatch is invisible to a reader looking only at the picture.

questions.a: That the relationships are directional and discrete, which misrepresents a process that is continuous or runs in both directions before any label is read.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. arrows that look alike regardless of evidence) and paragraph G (i.e. reading figure and text against each other).
Summarize the effects of building an argument on a diagram.
questions.a: The claim becomes available at a glance so the prose reads as confirmation, the diagram's limits become the argument's limits so a third variable in the text is forgotten, and the form asserts that relationships are discrete and directional. A good piece puts drawable claims in the figure and marks what simplifies, and the test is whether every arrow corresponds to a defended claim.

questions.q:
discrete: separate and distinct, which a box-and-arrow form asserts whether or not the process is.
correspondence: a match between what a figure shows and what the prose defends.
Describe the connection between an arrow's appearance and the evidence behind it.
questions.a: An arrow drawn between two boxes looks like a demonstrated relationship whether the evidence for it is strong or absent, and a reader cannot tell which arrows are which.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 9's The Figure That Carries the Paper. That article read figures to find the claim, and this asks whether the figure should be carrying it.

articles.title: The Shortest Important Paper
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April 1953 Nature published a paper about the structure of DNA that runs to roughly a page. It is among the most consequential scientific papers of the century, and much of its effect comes from decisions about style that could have been made differently.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The opening sentence does something unusual for a technical paper. It announces a structure and calls it of considerable biological interest, which is a claim about significance offered before any evidence and in a register closer to understatement than to announcement.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second paragraph disposes of a rival. It describes an earlier proposed structure, states precisely why it cannot be right, and moves on, which takes four sentences and removes the main competing account from the reader's mind before the new one is presented.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The description itself is almost entirely geometric. Two chains, coiled around a common axis, running in opposite directions, with the bases on the inside and the backbones outside, and the whole arrangement is conveyed without a single equation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The pairing rule arrives as a constraint rather than a discovery. The text observes that only specific pairs of bases can fit the available space, which presents a chemical fact as a consequence of the geometry rather than as an additional assumption.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Then comes the sentence the paper is remembered for. It observes that the specific pairing immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material, and declines to say more, and the restraint is the effect.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The restraint was also strategic, which the authors did not conceal in later accounts. Stating the implication fully would have required evidence they did not have, and stating it this way claimed the territory without making a claim that could be refuted.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the power of the piece comes from compression and from what it refuses to do. It has no speculation, no survey of the field and no discussion section, and a reader finishes it in three minutes having been shown a structure and handed its most important consequence in one clause.

questions.a: As a constraint rather than a discovery, by observing that only specific pairs of bases can fit the available space, which makes a chemical fact a consequence of the geometry.

articles.note: RI.11-12.6 names power and beauty as well as persuasiveness. This is a case where the three are produced by removal rather than addition.

articles.title: The Last Sentence of a Book
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The closing sentence of On the Origin of Species is one of the most quoted in English scientific writing, and its effect is produced by techniques that can be described precisely, which is what makes it worth studying rather than merely admiring.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The passage begins by asking the reader to look at a tangled bank, with plants, birds, insects and worms, and the choice of scene is doing work. It is ordinary, it is local, and it is the kind of place a reader has stood in without thinking about it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sentence then lists the laws that produced everything on the bank, and the list is long. Growth, reproduction, inheritance, variability, a struggle for life, and the consequences that follow from them, delivered in a sequence that accumulates rather than resolves.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The accumulation is the technique. Each clause adds a law, the sentence refuses to end, and the reader's sense of how much is being accounted for grows with the syntax rather than being stated by it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The final movement reverses the scale without changing the subject. From a bank in a field, the sentence moves to the planet cycling according to a fixed law, and places the whole of the preceding list inside that motion.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The last clause has been the subject of attention for a century and a half. Endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved: three adjectives, a tense that includes the present, and a passive construction that names no agent.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That absence of an agent is the argument of the book compressed into a grammatical choice. A sentence written actively would require a subject doing the evolving, and the passive leaves the forms arriving from the laws listed earlier and from nothing else.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the beauty and the content are not separable here, which is the strongest version of what this standard asks. The passage is moving because of its structure, and its structure is a statement of the theory, and a paraphrase loses the argument along with the cadence.

Summarize how the passage achieves its effect.
questions.a: It begins at an ordinary local scene, lists the laws producing everything there in a sequence that accumulates rather than resolves, then reverses scale to the planet cycling under a fixed law. The final clause uses three adjectives, a tense including the present, and a passive construction naming no agent, which states the theory grammatically.

questions.q:
cadence: the rhythm of a sentence, which here cannot be separated from what it asserts.
passive construction: a sentence form in which no agent is named, used here to leave the forms arriving from laws alone.
Describe the connection between the grammar and the argument.
questions.a: An active sentence would require a subject doing the evolving, and the passive leaves the forms arriving from the laws listed earlier and from nothing else.

articles.note: The claim is that style carries content, and the article demonstrates it rather than asserting it. Ask students to rewrite the clause actively and say what changed.

articles.title: The Letter That Is Not Angry
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter written in reply to a public and unjust accusation has two available registers, and the choice between them is made in the first sentence. It determines almost everything about what the letter can subsequently accomplish, and it cannot be revised halfway through without the revision itself becoming the subject.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is anger, and it has real advantages. It conveys the scale of the wrong, it is honest about what the writer feels, and it will satisfy readers who already agree, which is a larger group than writers usually estimate.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its disadvantage is specific rather than moral. An angry letter allows a reader who wishes to avoid the substance to discuss the tone instead, and the discussion of tone can proceed indefinitely without anyone addressing the accusation.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second register is controlled, and its power depends entirely on the reader understanding that it is controlled rather than merely mild. A letter that is measured about something outrageous produces a gap between the matter and the manner, and the reader fills that gap themselves, which is the whole of the effect.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The technique that makes this work is usually understatement. A writer who describes a serious wrong in plain and unemphatic language invites the reader to supply the emphasis, and an emphasis a reader supplies is held more firmly than one they were given.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A second technique is the conceded point. Granting something to the accuser, early and without qualification, establishes that the writer is capable of concession, which makes every subsequent refusal to concede weigh more than it otherwise would.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The third is the question that cannot be answered comfortably. A direct question, asked politely, leaves a reader composing an answer in their own head, and a reader who cannot produce one has been persuaded by their own silence.

paras.label: H
paras.text: None of this is a recommendation of calm over anger as a general matter. It is an observation about what each register makes possible, and the controlled letter is harder to write, harder to sustain and considerably harder to dismiss.

Summarize the two registers and their techniques.

A controlled letter creates a gap between matter and manner that the reader fills, using understatement so the reader supplies the emphasis, early concession so later refusals weigh more, and direct questions a reader cannot answer comfortably.

understatement: describing something in plainer terms than it warrants, so a reader supplies the force.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 9's Letter from Birmingham Jail. Read that letter after this article and have students identify each of the three techniques in it.

articles.title: The Understatement in a Report
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Official reports into serious failures are written in a register that strikes many first-time readers as inadequate to the subject. The language is flat, the verbs are weak, and the findings arrive in sentences that seem to be working hard not to be interesting.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of that flatness is defensive, and the legal pressures producing it have been discussed elsewhere. What is less often noticed is that the restraint, in a well-written report, is also a deliberate rhetorical instrument, and that it is frequently the most effective one available to the people writing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The mechanism is contrast. A sentence recording that a request for additional staffing was submitted on four occasions and not acknowledged is doing nothing dramatic, and the drama is supplied entirely by the reader placing it beside the outcome.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Juxtaposition without comment does similar work. A paragraph that gives the date of a warning and then, in the next sentence, the date of the failure has made an argument without a single evaluative word appearing anywhere in it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The technique depends absolutely on the surrounding register being consistent. A report that is flat throughout makes each factual sentence land, and a report that permits itself one indignant paragraph has taught the reader that the flatness was a choice and can be departed from.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There is a further effect that is specific to this genre. A reader who has supplied the outrage themselves will defend the conclusion more firmly than one who was handed it, because they have done the work and will not lightly treat it as having been done for them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The register also has a cost, and the better reports know it. Families and those directly affected frequently find the flatness unbearable, and a document that is maximally persuasive to a minister can be experienced as an institution refusing to say plainly what happened.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Some reports address this directly by changing register once, in a preface, where a chairman writes in the first person. That single departure works precisely because the rest does not, which is the whole technique stated in a paragraph.

Summarize how restraint works in an official report.

The effect requires the register to be consistent, a reader who supplies the outrage defends the conclusion more firmly, and the cost is that those directly affected may experience the flatness as a refusal to say what happened.

juxtaposition: placing two facts beside each other so that the relation is implied rather than stated.
evaluative: expressing a judgement, which the register deliberately avoids.
Describe the connection between a single indignant paragraph and the rest of a report.
questions.a: A report that permits itself one indignant paragraph has taught the reader that the flatness was a choice and can be departed from, which weakens the effect elsewhere.

articles.note: Paragraph G is the one that keeps this honest. The most persuasive document and the most humane one are not always the same document.

articles.title: The Speech Built on One Repetition
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Anaphora is the repetition of the same words at the beginning of successive clauses, and it is the oldest device in persuasive speech. It survives because it does several things at once that are difficult to achieve separately.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first function is structural, and it is felt by an audience rather than consciously noticed by them. A repeated opening tells a listener where each new unit begins, which matters enormously in speech, where a listener cannot see a paragraph break, cannot go back, and has only the sound to navigate by.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second function is accumulation. Each repetition adds an instance to a set the listener is assembling, and the force comes from the number rather than from any individual item, which is why removing three examples from such a passage weakens it more than removing three ordinary sentences.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is anticipation. After the third repetition a listener knows the form of the fourth, and the brief moment of knowing what is coming produces a kind of participation that passive listening does not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That anticipation is also what makes the ending dangerous and powerful. A speaker who breaks the pattern deliberately at the last item produces a sharp effect, and one who breaks it accidentally produces an anticlimax the audience will feel without being able to name.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The device is not neutral between arguments, which is worth stating plainly. It works best for claims that are genuinely multiple, where many instances exist, and it can create an impression of multiplicity where a speaker has two real examples and three weak ones.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A listener can test this directly and in real time. Take the repeated passage, remove the repetition, and read the items as a plain list, and a set of strong instances survives that treatment while a padded one visibly collapses.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the device is powerful because it is doing legitimate work and is available for illegitimate work with the same syntax. The form tells a listener that there are many reasons, and whether there are is a separate question the form does not address.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the device is not neutral) and paragraph G (i.e. the test a listener can run).
Summarize what anaphora does and how to test it.

Describe the connection between the form of the device and the strength of an argument.
questions.a: The form tells a listener that there are many reasons, and whether there are is a separate question the form does not address.

articles.note: The test in paragraph G is runnable on any speech in two minutes. Try it on a famous passage and on a mediocre one and compare what survives.

articles.title: Deciding Whether a Bridge Is Safe
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A local authority has to decide whether a bridge can remain open. The question is concrete, the answer has to be given by a date, and the information available to answer it arrives in four forms that do not resemble each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the original design. Drawings and calculations from the period of construction state what the structure was built to carry, and they are the only document that says what the designer intended, which is not the same as what was built.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the inspection record, which is not a measurement at all but a sequence of judgements made by people. Inspectors record visible condition against defined categories, and a series of such records shows a trajectory over time, which is frequently far more informative than any single assessment taken on its own.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is instrumental. Strain gauges, crack monitors and displacement sensors produce continuous numerical data, and they measure precisely what they are placed to measure and nothing at all about anywhere they are not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is a model. A structural analysis predicts how loads distribute through the bridge, and its output is as good as its assumptions about material condition, which are supplied by the inspections and the measurements rather than by the model.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Integrating these is not a matter of averaging. They disagree in a structured way: the design says what should be there, the inspection says what can be seen, the instruments say what one point is doing, and the model says what follows if the first three are right.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The decisive questions are usually about the gaps between them. A model predicting stress at a location nobody can inspect, and nobody has instrumented, is producing a number with nothing behind it, and knowing that is worth more than the number.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the engineer's judgement is about which source governs where. Visible deterioration overrides a model, an instrument reading that contradicts an inspection prompts a second inspection rather than a conclusion, and the design drawing is evidence about intention and never about present condition.

articles.note: RI.11-12.7 is about solving a problem with sources in different formats. The useful move is paragraph H, which ranks them by situation rather than in general.

articles.title: Deciding Where to Put a School
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A district has to site a new school, and the decision is irreversible for sixty years. The inputs arrive from different places, in different formats, with different reliabilities, and none of them answers the question on its own.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Demographic projections come first and are the least certain thing in the process. A forecast of how many five-year-olds will live in an area in eight years depends on birth rates, on migration and on housing that has not been built.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Housing plans are a separate source and they interact with the first. Approved developments supply a number of dwellings with a timescale, and converting dwellings into children requires an assumption about household composition that varies with the kind of housing built.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Travel data answers a different question again. Catchment modelling shows how far children would travel to each candidate site and by what mode, and a site that is central on a map can be badly placed once a river, a main road or a railway is taken into account.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Cost information constrains everything and is the most precise and least flexible input. Land acquisition, ground conditions and construction costs are quantified to a degree the other sources cannot match, which gives them an influence their importance may not justify.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Consultation supplies something none of the others can. Residents know which crossings are dangerous, which routes are walked and which are not, and a site that models well can be opposed for reasons the models had no way to contain.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Integrating these means noticing that they have different time horizons. Cost is a figure for next year, travel patterns change over a decade, and demography is a projection about a generation, and a decision that optimises the precise short-term input will be judged against the uncertain long-term one.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The usual failure is therefore predictable rather than exotic. The most quantified source dominates because it is the easiest to defend in a document, and the least quantified one turns out to have been describing the thing that mattered.

articles.note: Pairs with the bridge article. One problem is physical and one is social, and both fail in the same way when precision substitutes for relevance.

articles.title: Deciding Whether to Evacuate
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: An official has to decide whether to order an evacuation ahead of a storm, and the decision has to be made before the information that would settle it exists. Everything available at the moment of decision is a projection, and the costs of being wrong are asymmetric and both large.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The forecast is the first input and it is a distribution rather than a path. Models produce a range of possible tracks, the commonly published cone represents where the centre is likely to go, and a reader who treats the cone's edge as the edge of the danger has misread it entirely.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Physical exposure data is a separate layer. Elevation models, flood mapping and storm surge projections state which areas go under at which water heights, and these are static, well-understood and among the most reliable things in the whole picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Population data answers who is there, and it is reliable in a way that is also misleading. A census records residence, and the number of people in a coastal area on a given weekend can differ from the resident population by a very large factor.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Transport capacity determines whether the decision is executable at all. Road capacity, fuel availability and the time required to move a given population out are calculable, and they set a deadline that is independent of the storm and earlier than the storm.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Vulnerability information is the least quantified and the most consequential. Which residents cannot drive, which require medical equipment and which will not leave are questions that determine whether an order produces an evacuation or produces a traffic jam containing the people most at risk.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that these have incompatible update rates. The forecast changes every six hours, the transport deadline is fixed, and the vulnerability information is months old, so the decision has to be made on the schedule set by the slowest component.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why an evacuation decision is made earlier than the evidence justifies, and why that is correct rather than cautious. Waiting for a better forecast means passing the point at which the roads can still clear, and the choice is between acting on a distribution and losing the ability to act.

paras.text: Transport capacity decides whether the decision is executable at all. Road capacity, fuel availability and the time needed to move a population are calculable. They set a deadline independent of the storm and earlier than it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Vulnerability information is the least quantified and the most consequential. Which residents cannot drive, which need medical equipment, which will not leave. Those decide whether an order produces an evacuation or a traffic jam containing the people most at risk.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that these update at incompatible rates. The forecast changes every six hours. The transport deadline is fixed. The vulnerability information is months old. The decision must be made on the schedule set by the slowest component.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is why an evacuation decision is made earlier than the evidence justifies, and why that is correct rather than cautious. Waiting for a better forecast means passing the point at which the roads can still clear. The choice is between acting on a distribution and losing the ability to act.

questions.q: What does the published cone represent?
questions.a: Where the centre of the storm is likely to go, so a reader who treats its edge as the edge of the danger has misread it entirely.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. vulnerability information) and paragraph H (i.e. why the decision is made early).
Summarize the sources and why the decision must be early.
questions.a: A forecast gives a distribution of tracks, exposure mapping reliably states what floods at what height, census population may differ greatly from who is present, transport capacity sets a fixed deadline, and vulnerability data determines whether an order works. These update at incompatible rates, so waiting for a better forecast means passing the point at which roads can still clear.

questions.q:
asymmetric: unequal in kind or size, as the costs of evacuating unnecessarily and of not evacuating are.
exposure: which areas are physically affected at a given water height, as distinct from who is in them.
Describe the connection between update rates and the timing of a decision.
questions.a: The forecast changes every six hours while the transport deadline is fixed and vulnerability data is months old, so the decision has to be made on the schedule set by the slowest component.

articles.note: The closing paragraph reframes an apparent failure as a requirement. Ask what information would have to exist for a later decision to be better.

articles.title: Deciding What a Painting Is
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A painting is offered for sale as the work of a particular artist, and the question of whether it is cannot be answered by looking, although looking is where it starts and sometimes where it ends.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Connoisseurship is the oldest source and much the hardest to evaluate from outside the discipline. A specialist who has examined hundreds of works by an artist recognises handling in a way they frequently cannot articulate, and such judgements have been right often enough to matter and wrong often enough that they cannot be allowed to stand alone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Provenance is documentary rather than physical. An unbroken chain of ownership running back to the artist's own studio is the strongest single piece of evidence available, and its weakness is that documents can be fabricated and that gaps in a chain are extremely common for entirely innocent reasons.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Technical analysis supplies constraints rather than attributions. X-ray and infrared imaging reveal underdrawing and changes beneath the surface, and those reveal how a picture was built, which is a different question from who built it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Material analysis answers questions with dates attached. A pigment that was not manufactured until 1830 cannot be in a painting from 1780, and that is a decisive negative result which no amount of connoisseurship can overturn.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The asymmetry there is the key to the whole exercise. Material evidence can refute an attribution absolutely and can never confirm one, because a skilled forger using period materials leaves nothing for the analysis to find.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the sources are not of equal kind and cannot be weighed on one scale. One can disprove, one can establish a chain, one describes method, and one is expert judgement, and a case is built by seeing whether any of them produces a refutation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What follows is a specific and unsatisfying conclusion that the field accepts. An attribution is a best current judgement rather than a determination, and a painting can move between categories as evidence accumulates, which is why catalogues record the reasoning as well as the conclusion.

questions.a: A pigment manufactured after the claimed date is decisive against an attribution, while a skilled forger using period materials leaves nothing for the analysis to find.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what technical imaging reveals) and paragraph H (i.e. what an attribution actually is).
Summarize the sources used to attribute a painting.
questions.a: Connoisseurship recognises handling and cannot stand alone, provenance traces ownership and can be fabricated or broken innocently, technical imaging shows how a picture was built rather than by whom, and material analysis can date pigments. Material evidence refutes absolutely and never confirms, so an attribution is a best current judgement that catalogues record with its reasoning.

questions.q:
provenance: the documented chain of ownership of a work back toward its origin.
attribution: the assignment of a work to a particular artist, which remains a judgement rather than a determination.
Describe the connection between the asymmetry of evidence and how a case is built.
questions.a: Because one source can disprove and none can confirm, a case is built by seeing whether any of the sources produces a refutation.

articles.note: An integration problem where the sources are not commensurable at all. Ask which single source a student would want if they could have only one.

articles.title: Deciding Whether to Approve a Drug
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: A regulator has to decide whether a medicine may be sold. The decision is binary, the evidence is not, and the material presented arrives in formats that have to be assessed against each other rather than added together.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Trial results are the centre of the submission and are by a long way the most structured input the regulator receives. They state effects in defined populations with stated statistical properties, and their principal limitation lies in who was studied rather than in how carefully the study was conducted.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Trial populations are routinely narrower than the population that will receive the drug. Participants are often younger, with fewer other conditions and fewer other medications, so the evidence is strongest about people least like the average eventual patient.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Safety data arrives from a different direction and in a quite different shape from efficacy data. Adverse events are counted as rates across the whole programme, and a serious effect occurring in one patient in five thousand will frequently not appear even once in a trial programme that enrolled three thousand people.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Manufacturing information is assessed separately and is not about the molecule. It establishes that what was tested can be produced consistently, and a product that cannot be made to specification reliably is not approvable however well it performed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Patient testimony enters through formal channels and supplies something the trials do not measure. It describes what a condition is like and which outcomes matter to people living with it, which is frequently not what the trial chose as its endpoint.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that these answer different questions and none is decisive. Efficacy, safety, manufacturability and relevance are separate assessments, and a submission can be strong in three and fail on the fourth.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What the decision ultimately rests on is a comparison against the alternative rather than against perfection. A drug for a condition with no existing treatment is assessed on terms that a fourth drug for a well-treated condition is not, and the same evidence can support approval in one case and refusal in the other.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what patient testimony supplies) and paragraph H (i.e. the comparison against the alternative).
Summarize what a regulator must integrate.
questions.a: Trials give structured effects in populations narrower than those who will receive the drug, safety data cannot detect rare events at trial sizes, manufacturing evidence shows the product can be made consistently, and patient testimony identifies outcomes that matter and may not be the endpoint. These answer different questions, and the decision compares the drug against the existing alternative rather than against perfection.

questions.q:
endpoint: the outcome a trial was designed to measure, which may not be what patients most care about.
adverse event: a harmful occurrence recorded during a trial, counted as a rate.
Describe the connection between the existing alternative and the evidence required.
questions.a: A drug for a condition with no existing treatment is assessed on terms a fourth drug for a well-treated condition is not, so the same evidence can support approval in one case and refusal in the other.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's How a Drug Is Shown to Work. That article was about producing the evidence and this is about deciding on it.

articles.title: Marbury and the Power to Decide
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1803 the Supreme Court of the United States decided a case about a commission that had not been delivered, and the decision established that the Court may declare an act of Congress unconstitutional. The reasoning by which it got there is more interesting than the holding.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The facts of the case were small and the politics surrounding it were not. A departing administration had made a series of appointments at the last possible moment, the incoming Secretary of State declined to deliver some of the resulting commissions, and William Marbury went to the Court and asked it to order delivery.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Court faced a trap with no comfortable exit. Ordering delivery would produce an order the administration could simply ignore, demonstrating that the Court could be defied, and refusing would concede that the executive could withhold what the law required.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The opinion takes the questions in a deliberate order, and the order is the whole manoeuvre. It asks first whether Marbury has a right to the commission, and answers yes; second whether the law affords a remedy, and answers yes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those two answers are a rebuke to the administration delivered before anything else happens, and they cost the Court nothing, because no order has yet been issued that anybody could refuse to obey.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third question is whether this Court can supply that remedy, and here the opinion turns. The statute under which Marbury applied gave the Court power the Constitution had not given it, so the statute conflicted with the Constitution.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conclusion follows from a premise stated as though it were obvious. A written constitution is superior law, a court deciding a case must apply the law, and where two laws conflict a court must say which governs, which is a chain any reader can follow and which nothing in the text explicitly authorises.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the Court declined jurisdiction and acquired a power. It gave the administration the outcome it wanted, refused Marbury his commission, and established in the course of doing so a principle that has been the foundation of its authority ever since.

questions.a: Ordering delivery would produce an order the administration could ignore, showing the Court could be defied, and refusing would concede that the executive could withhold what the law required.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the first two answers cost nothing) and paragraph G (i.e. the premise stated as obvious).
Summarize the reasoning of the decision.
questions.a: The Court answered first that Marbury had a right and second that the law afforded a remedy, rebuking the administration without issuing any order that could be defied. It then held that the statute granting it jurisdiction exceeded what the Constitution gave, reasoning that a constitution is superior law and a court must say which law governs, so it declined jurisdiction and established judicial review.

questions.q:
jurisdiction: the authority of a court to decide a particular kind of case.
judicial review: the power of a court to declare a law unconstitutional, established by this decision.
Describe the connection between the order of the questions and the Court's position.
questions.a: Answering the first two questions rebuked the administration while costing nothing, because no order had yet been issued that anybody could refuse to obey.

articles.note: RI.11-12.8 asks students to delineate and evaluate legal reasoning. Here the structure of the argument is the strategy, which is unusually visible.

articles.title: The Dissent That Became the Law
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1896 the Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railway carriages for Black and white passengers. The decision was seven to one, and the single dissent is now better known than the majority opinion it failed to prevent.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The majority's reasoning proceeded from a distinction it treated as straightforward. A law requiring separation, it held, does not of itself impose inequality, so a requirement applying to both races equally is not a discrimination that the Fourteenth Amendment reaches.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then addressed the obvious objection with an argument about perception. If separation is felt as a badge of inferiority, the opinion stated, that is because the group affected chooses to construe it so, which locates the harm in the reaction rather than in the law.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Justice John Marshall Harlan's dissent attacks both steps and attacks the second first. He states that everyone knows what the statute is for, that nobody is deceived about which carriage is which, and that the Court's reasoning depends on a pretence it does not believe.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The dissent's central passage is a claim about what a constitution does rather than about railways. It argues that the document neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens, and that this is the principle the majority has set aside while claiming to apply it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: He then makes a prediction, which is the most quoted element and the part a reader should examine most carefully. He writes that the judgement will in time prove as pernicious as an earlier decision the Court had by then repudiated entirely.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The dissent is not an unqualified document and is weaker in places that are usually omitted. The same opinion contains a passage asserting the enduring dominance of one race, which sits uneasily beside the sentence it is best known for.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Nearly sixty years later a unanimous Court reached the conclusion the dissent had argued for, which is why this is the standard case for the proposition that a losing argument can be the correct one and can be preserved by being written down.

questions.a: It argued that if separation is felt as a badge of inferiority, that is because the group affected chooses to construe it so, locating the harm in the reaction rather than in the law.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the prediction) and paragraph G (i.e. the passage usually omitted).
Summarize the reasoning of the majority and the dissent.

Harlan's dissent answered that nobody is deceived about the statute's purpose, argued that a constitution tolerates no classes among citizens, and predicted the decision would prove pernicious, though the same opinion contains a passage usually omitted.

dissent: an opinion by a judge disagreeing with the decision, which binds nobody at the time.
pernicious: causing serious harm gradually, the word used in the dissent's prediction.
Describe the connection between writing a dissent down and its later effect.
questions.a: A losing argument can be the correct one and can be preserved by being written down, which is why a unanimous Court could reach its conclusion nearly sixty years later.

articles.note: Paragraph G is included deliberately. Students should be able to admire an argument and also read the document it is actually in.

articles.title: The Concurrence That Became the Framework
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1952, during a labour dispute that threatened steel production in wartime, the President ordered the seizure of the steel mills. The Supreme Court held the seizure unlawful, and the opinion that has governed the question since was not the opinion of the Court.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The majority opinion reasoned from the absence of authorisation. No statute permitted the seizure, Congress had considered and rejected such a power, and the Constitution does not grant the executive a general power to take property, so the action had no legal basis.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Justice Robert Jackson agreed with the outcome and wrote separately, beginning with an observation about the method rather than the case. He noted that arguments about executive power are usually conducted by quoting isolated clauses and historical materials selectively, and that this produces confident conclusions in both directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: His alternative was to sort the question into three categories according to what Congress had done. That move is the entire contribution, and it converted a question about the extent of a power into a question about a relationship between two branches.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In the first category the President acts with express or implied authorisation from Congress, and the authority is at its maximum, because it combines what the office holds with what the legislature has granted.

paras.label: F
paras.text: In the second the President acts where Congress has neither granted nor denied, a zone Jackson called twilight, in which the outcome is likely to depend on practice and circumstance rather than on an abstract allocation.

paras.label: G
paras.text: In the third the President acts against the expressed or implied will of Congress, and the authority is at its lowest, because it rests on the office's own powers minus whatever the legislature may constitutionally exercise over the matter.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The seizure fell into the third category, which decided the case, and the framework has been applied far beyond it since. A concurrence joined by no other justice became the operative law because it supplied a structure rather than an answer, which is a specific and unusual kind of persuasive achievement.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what the three categories converted the question into) and paragraph H (i.e. why a concurrence became the law).

questions.a: A concurrence joined by no other justice became the operative law because it supplied a structure rather than an answer, which could be applied far beyond the case.

articles.note: Pairs with the Harlan dissent. Both are opinions that did not command a majority and both became the law, for entirely different reasons.

articles.title: Federalist Fifty-One
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Federalist 51 addresses a problem that the earlier papers in the series had raised repeatedly and had not solved. A government has to be strong enough to actually govern and limited enough not to become dangerous to the people it governs, and those two requirements pull directly against each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The essay rejects the obvious remedy before it proposes its own, which is why the rejection comes first. Relying on the quality of the people who hold office is dismissed, not from cynicism about any particular individual, but because an arrangement that works only when the officials are good is not really an arrangement at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The famous formulation states the problem with unusual symmetry. If men were angels no government would be necessary, and if angels governed men no controls on government would be necessary, which locates the whole difficulty in the fact that neither condition holds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The proposed mechanism is structural and is stated plainly as a design principle. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition, so the interest of the person must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That sentence does something specific that is easy to pass over. It does not ask officials to restrain themselves; it arranges for each branch to defend its own position out of self-interest, which converts a moral requirement into an institutional one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The essay then extends the argument to society rather than only to government. A multiplicity of interests makes oppressive combinations harder to assemble, which is the argument of Federalist 10 reappearing in a different application.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The reasoning is open to a direct objection that the essay does not fully answer. The design assumes that officeholders identify with their branch rather than with a party spanning several branches, and party loyalty can align the interests the structure assumed would conflict.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That objection is worth holding because it is testable against two centuries of practice. The question is whether a structure designed to set institutions against each other works when the people in them are organised into groups the design did not anticipate.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Federalist 51 addresses a problem the earlier papers raised and did not solve. A government must be strong enough to govern and limited enough not to become dangerous, and those requirements pull against each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The essay rejects the obvious remedy before proposing its own. Relying on the quality of the people in office is dismissed, not from cynicism about any individual, but because an arrangement that works only with good officials is not an arrangement at all.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The famous formulation states the problem with unusual symmetry. If men were angels no government would be necessary. If angels governed men no controls on government would be necessary. The whole difficulty is that neither condition holds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The proposed mechanism is structural and is stated plainly as a design principle. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the person must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place.

paras.label: H

questions.q: Why does the essay reject relying on the quality of officials?
questions.a: Not from cynicism about any particular individual, but because an arrangement that works only with good officials is not an arrangement at all.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. converting a moral requirement into an institutional one) and paragraph G (i.e. the objection about party).
Summarize the argument of Federalist 51 and its weakness.
questions.a: A government must be strong and limited at once, and relying on good officials is not a design, so the essay proposes that ambition counteract ambition by connecting a person's interest to the rights of their office. It extends this to a multiplicity of social interests, and the objection it does not answer is that party loyalty can align interests the structure assumed would conflict.

questions.q:
multiplicity: a large number of distinct interests, which makes oppressive combinations harder to assemble.
counteract: to work against, which the design arranges for one ambition to do to another.
Describe the connection between self-interest and the design's mechanism.
questions.a: The design connects the interest of the person with the constitutional rights of the place, so each branch defends its own position out of self-interest rather than from restraint.

articles.note: Pairs with Federalist 10 in grade 10. One argues that scale protects liberty and this argues that structure does, and the objection in paragraph G applies to both.

articles.title: The Reasoning of Brown
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1954 the Supreme Court held unanimously that segregated public schools violate the Fourteenth Amendment. The opinion is short, it is deliberately plain, and the reasoning by which it reaches its conclusion is not the reasoning most people assume.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The Court begins by examining the history of the Amendment and declines to rest on it. The evidence about what its framers intended for public education is described as inconclusive, partly because public education in 1868 was so limited that the question had barely arisen.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That move is significant and is a choice rather than a necessity. Having found the historical argument indeterminate, the Court states that it cannot turn the clock back and must consider public education as it exists now, which is a decision about how a constitution should be read.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The opinion then establishes the importance of education in contemporary terms. It describes schooling as the foundation of citizenship and the principal instrument by which a child is prepared for life, and this paragraph is doing work that the historical section could not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The central question is then narrowed with precision. The issue is not whether facilities are equal in buildings and salaries, because the Court assumes they are; the issue is whether separation itself deprives children of equal educational opportunity.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The answer rests on a claim about effect, and the opinion supports it with a citation that has been argued about ever since. A footnote lists psychological and social scientific studies, which is unusual in constitutional reasoning and was understood as unusual at the time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Critics have objected that resting a constitutional holding on social science makes it vulnerable to the next study, and defenders reply that the studies were corroboration rather than foundation, and that the sentence they support states something the law already implied.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The opinion then does something procedurally distinctive. It declines to order a remedy, setting that question for later argument, which produced a second decision and a much slower implementation than the clarity of the first opinion suggested.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the footnote citing social science) and paragraph H (i.e. declining to order a remedy).
Summarize the reasoning of the decision.

Its answer rested on effect, supported by a footnote citing social science that has been argued about since, and it deferred the question of remedy.

indeterminate: not settling the question either way, which the Court found the historical evidence to be.
corroboration: supporting evidence for a conclusion reached on other grounds, as defenders describe the footnote.
Describe the connection between narrowing the question and the answer given.
questions.a: By assuming facilities equal, the Court made the issue whether separation itself deprives children of equal educational opportunity, which is a claim about effect rather than about resources.

articles.note: Five texts across RI.11-12.8, three of them opinions and two advocacy. Ask which of the five would be weakest if its structure were rearranged.

articles.title: The Mayflower Compact
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In November 1620 a group aboard a ship off the coast of what is now Massachusetts signed a document of about two hundred words. It is among the earliest surviving instruments of self-government written by Europeans in North America, and its brevity is part of what makes it readable as an argument.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The circumstances explain the document better than any description of its contents. The ship had been authorised to settle considerably further south, had arrived outside the territory of its patent, and some aboard had said that no authority over them would exist once they landed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The compact is a response to that specific claim. It is not a constitution, it establishes no offices and describes no procedure, and what it does is create an obligation by agreement where the signatories had concluded no obligation otherwise existed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its opening is conventional and is doing necessary work. The signatories identify themselves as loyal subjects of the king, which locates the document inside existing authority rather than against it, and that framing was essential to anyone who might later be asked about it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The operative sentence is the one that matters. The signatories covenant and combine themselves into a civil body politic, for better ordering and preservation, and agree to enact such laws as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Two features of that sentence are worth isolating. The authority is created by the act of agreeing rather than conferred from outside, and the standard for future laws is the general good, which is a criterion the signatories set for themselves.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The document's limitations should be stated as plainly as its significance. It was signed by forty-one men, it did not extend to the women aboard or to servants, and it says nothing about the people already living where the ship had arrived.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Read beside the Declaration of Independence, written a hundred and fifty-six years later, the resemblance is structural rather than textual. Both documents respond to a claim that authority is absent or illegitimate, and both answer by asserting that a body of people may constitute a government by agreeing to.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the two features of the operative sentence) and paragraph G (i.e. the limitations).
Summarize what the Mayflower Compact does.

covenant: to bind oneself by solemn agreement, which is the act the document performs.
body politic: a group of people constituted as a political unit capable of making law.
Describe the connection between the compact and the Declaration of Independence.

articles.note: RI.11-12.9 names the seventeenth century, and this is the document that makes that range meaningful. Two hundred words, read in full in one lesson.

articles.title: Common Sense
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Thomas Paine's pamphlet appeared in January 1776 and sold in numbers that remain extraordinary relative to the population. Its argument had been made before in various forms, and the reason this version mattered is almost entirely a matter of how it was written.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The prose is the first thing to notice because it was the first thing contemporaries noticed. Paine writes in short declarative sentences, uses almost no Latin, cites scripture rather than classical authority, and addresses a reader who is assumed to be intelligent and not educated.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That choice had a political consequence beyond its literary one. A pamphlet written in this register could be read aloud in a tavern to people who could not read it themselves, which made the argument available to an audience that previous political writing had not addressed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The structure attacks monarchy in general before reaching Britain in particular, and the order matters. By the time the pamphlet discusses the current king, it has already argued that hereditary succession is absurd in principle, so the specific grievances arrive as instances rather than as the case.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The argument against hereditary rule is made by reduction rather than by assertion. Paine observes that it requires believing that the merit of an original ruler, itself usually obtained by force, transmits through a bloodline indefinitely, and that nothing in observation supports this.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The economic argument is made in the same plain terms and is frequently underestimated. The pamphlet asserts that the connection to Britain damages American trade by involving the colonies in European wars they have no interest in, which is an argument addressed to merchants.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Paine then refuses the available compromise explicitly. Reconciliation, he argues, would leave the same arrangement in place and would simply postpone the question, which closes off the position most of his readers currently held.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The rhetorical achievement is therefore the removal of a middle. Before the pamphlet, a reader could want redress without wanting independence; after it, the pamphlet has argued that those are the same question, and that is the shift its enormous circulation carried.

Summarize the argument and method of Common Sense.

reconciliation: a settlement short of independence, which Paine argues would merely postpone the question.
Describe the connection between the order of the argument and how grievances are read.
questions.a: By arguing that hereditary succession is absurd in principle first, the pamphlet makes the specific grievances arrive as instances rather than as the case itself.

articles.note: A document whose rhetorical features are the historical cause. Ask what the same argument in the register of a legal brief would have achieved.

articles.title: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom was drafted by Thomas Jefferson in 1777 and was not enacted until 1786, after a legislative fight that ran for most of a decade. Jefferson asked that it be named on his gravestone, alongside the Declaration and the founding of a university, and that his presidency should not be.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its structure is unusual for a statute and is the reason it reads as an argument. The operative provision is brief, and it is preceded by a long preamble that sets out the reasoning at a length no modern drafter would permit.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The preamble begins from a claim about the mind rather than about rights. It asserts that God created the mind free, and that attempts to influence it by punishment produce only hypocrisy, which is an argument about efficacy before it is one about justice.

paras.label: D
paras.text: It then makes a claim about what compulsion actually achieves. A person compelled to support an opinion they disbelieve is not persuaded, and the practice corrupts the religion it is meant to serve by filling it with people who do not hold it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third argument concerns the capacity of officials. The preamble observes that magistrates who judge opinions are fallible and will impose their own, and that the same power used well by one will be used badly by the next.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The operative sentence is then short and absolute. No person shall be compelled to attend or support any religious worship, nor suffer on account of religious opinion, nor shall their civil capacities be affected by it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The final paragraph does something rare in legislation and is worth reading closely. It acknowledges that a legislature cannot bind its successors, declares the rights asserted to be natural rights, and states that any future repeal would be an infringement of natural right.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That is a statement about the status of the law rather than its content. The statute cannot prevent its own repeal and says so, and then characterises repeal in advance, which is a rhetorical device operating entirely outside the law's enforceable effect.

questions.a: Only hypocrisy, since a person compelled to support an opinion they disbelieve is not persuaded, and the practice corrupts the religion it is meant to serve.
