articles.note: A statute that argues rather than only commands, which is why it belongs in this standard. Compare its preamble with the one in grade 10's Constitution article.

articles.title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Frederick Douglass delivered an address in Rochester, New York, on the fifth of July, 1852, having been invited by a local society to speak on the occasion of Independence Day. The date on which he chose to deliver it is the first element of the argument, and it was understood as such by everybody present.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The opening third of the speech praises the founders without qualification. It describes them as great men, calls their act brave, and affirms the principles of the Declaration in terms that any audience at such an event would expect and approve.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That section is not preliminary and it is not insincere. It establishes that the speaker accepts the standard the occasion invokes, which is the only position from which the rest of the speech can be delivered at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The turn is marked by a single pronoun and is among the most studied transitions in American oratory. Douglass moves from the achievements of your fathers to the question of what those achievements mean to him and to those he speaks for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The question that follows is the title and it is constructed to be unanswerable in the terms of the occasion. He asks what the Fourth of July is to the American slave, and answers that it reveals to him the injustice and cruelty of which he is the constant victim.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What follows is not an accusation of falsehood but of inconsistency, and the distinction is the engine of the entire speech. The principles are not disputed; they are accepted, and the argument is that the nation does not apply them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The method is therefore to use the audience's own document against their practice. A listener who had agreed with the opening third has already granted the premise from which the indictment follows, and cannot withdraw it without abandoning the occasion.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That makes this the clearest case in nineteenth-century American oratory of a foundational text being turned on the people who honour it. The speech does not ask for new principles, which is what makes it difficult to answer.

oratory: the art of formal public speaking, of which this transition is a studied example.
Describe the connection between accepting the principles and the strength of the argument.
questions.a: The principles are not disputed but accepted, so the argument is that the nation does not apply them, and the speech does not ask for new principles, which is what makes it difficult to answer.

articles.note: Pairs with the Declaration of Sentiments in grade 9. Both take a founding document at its word, four years apart, and ask who it covers.

articles.title: Civil Disobedience
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: Henry David Thoreau's essay was published in 1849, following a night he spent in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax. The refusal was a protest against a war he opposed and against slavery, and the essay reasons outward from an act that was, in itself, extremely small.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its starting claim is about the relationship between a citizen and a law. Thoreau argues that a person's first obligation is to do what they believe right, and that obedience to law is owed only where law and right coincide.

paras.label: C
paras.text: He is explicit about the consequence for majority rule. A majority decides questions not because it is more likely to be right but because it is stronger, which he states plainly, and that observation is the premise from which the rest proceeds.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The essay then distinguishes between kinds of complicity, which is where its argument becomes specific. A person who disapproves of an injustice while paying for it is participating in it, and the payment is the point at which an opinion becomes an action.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The remedy proposed is withdrawal rather than resistance. He does not advocate the overthrow of a government or violence against it; he argues for refusing to lend it practical support, which is a narrower position than the essay is often remembered as holding.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The willingness to accept punishment is essential and is frequently omitted from summaries. Thoreau's argument requires that the person refusing accept the legal consequence, because accepting it is what distinguishes the position from simple evasion.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The essay has a weakness its admirers acknowledge. It addresses a person who can afford to withdraw, and a man who can spend a night in jail and return to his life is differently placed from somebody whose dependents rely on their continued liberty.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Its later influence is nevertheless documented rather than asserted. Figures including Gandhi and King described reading it and taking from it the argument that an unjust law may be disobeyed openly by a person willing to accept the penalty, which is precisely the structure the essay set out.

questions.a: Not because it is more likely to be right but because it is stronger, which he states plainly as the premise for the rest.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. accepting the punishment) and paragraph G (i.e. the weakness admirers acknowledge).
Summarize the argument of the essay.
questions.a: Obedience is owed only where law and right coincide, and a majority decides because it is stronger rather than likelier to be right. Paying for an injustice is participating in it, so the remedy is withdrawal of practical support rather than resistance, and the person refusing must accept the legal penalty, which distinguishes the position from evasion.

questions.q:
complicity: participation in a wrong through support rather than direct action.
evasion: avoiding a legal obligation without accepting a penalty, which the essay's position is defined against.
Describe the connection between accepting punishment and the nature of the act.
questions.a: Accepting the legal consequence is what distinguishes the position from simple evasion, which is why the willingness is essential to the argument.

articles.note: Five documents across three centuries, each creating or refusing an obligation. Ask students to order them by how much authority each claims for an individual.

articles.title: The Man Who Lived Without a Clock
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1962 a French geologist named Michel Siffre spent two months in a cave beneath a glacier, deliberately and entirely without any means of telling the time. He had gone there to study the ice underground and ended up conducting, more or less by accident, a long experiment on himself.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The arrangement was deliberate and the conditions underground were severe. He had no watch, no daylight and no indication of the hour at any point, and a surface team logged the times at which he telephoned them while telling him nothing whatever about when those calls had occurred.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What he reported afterwards was a discrepancy. He believed he had been underground considerably less time than he had, and his own count of days had fallen behind the calendar by a substantial margin.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The explanation offered then was that an internal clock continues running without external cues and runs slightly slow. In the absence of light to reset it, a person's day drifts longer than twenty-four hours, and the accumulated difference is what Siffre had experienced.

paras.label: E
paras.text: He conducted considerably longer isolations afterwards, including six months in a Texas cave in 1972, and the later work recorded sleep and waking in far more detail, with better instrumentation, continuous monitoring and medical oversight throughout.

paras.label: F
paras.text: What those records showed was less tidy than the first account. Cycles were not uniformly long; some stretched to forty-eight hours, a few participants in related studies settled near twenty-five, and the pattern varied between individuals and over time.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Later research has substantially revised the interpretation while confirming the phenomenon. The free-running period is now understood to be close to twenty-four hours in most people, and several early estimates were affected by the lighting the participants themselves controlled.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is therefore a useful case of how a finding matures. A striking first result turned out to be real in its central claim and wrong in its numbers, corrected by work that was possible only because the first result made the question seem worth asking.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what the later records showed) and paragraph G (i.e. how the interpretation was revised).
Summarize the isolation experiments and what they established.

free-running: operating without external cues to reset it, which is the condition the experiments created.

Describe the connection between the first result and the later corrections.
questions.a: The first result was real in its central claim and wrong in its numbers, and the corrections came from work that was possible only because the first result made the question seem worth asking.

articles.note: A finding that is famous in its original form and has since been revised. Ask what the popular version still asserts and what the literature now says.

articles.title: The Census That Burned
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The United States census of 1890 was taken, tabulated and published, and almost all of the original returns no longer exist. A fire in 1921 damaged the records, and what the fire did not destroy was largely disposed of some years later.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The loss is unusual among archival disasters because the scale is so complete. For most censuses a researcher can consult the original schedules and see individual households, and for 1890 that is impossible for all but a tiny fraction of the population.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What survives is the published statistical summary, which answers different questions entirely. A researcher can learn how many people lived in a county and how they were distributed by broad categories, and cannot learn who any of them were.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The gap falls in a place that makes it worse than its size suggests. The decades on either side were a period of very large migration into and within the country, and 1890 sits between two surveys that would otherwise allow households to be followed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Genealogical research is the most visible casualty and is not the most significant one. A family traceable through 1880 and 1900 can usually be bridged, and the missing decade is more damaging for people who moved, changed name or arrived during it, which is a particular population rather than a random sample.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The 1890 census is also the one that produced a famous administrative claim, which is now read differently because of the loss. Its superintendent observed that a frontier line could no longer be identified, and that observation became the basis of an influential thesis about American development.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Historians who later questioned that thesis wanted to re-examine the underlying returns, which is precisely what cannot be done. An argument built on a census is unusually difficult to evaluate when the census itself is gone.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The episode is why archival practice changed afterwards. Duplicate storage, dispersal of copies and formal retention schedules exist substantially because of losses like this one, and the 1890 census is the example invoked when the cost of not doing so has to be explained.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. who the gap damages most) and paragraph G (i.e. the thesis that cannot be re-examined).
Summarize what was lost with the 1890 census.
questions.a: Fire and subsequent disposal destroyed almost all the original returns, leaving only published summaries that give counts without households. schedule: the original form on which individual household details were recorded.
retention schedule: a formal policy stating how long records are kept and in how many copies.
Describe the connection between the loss and later archival practice.
questions.a: Duplicate storage, dispersal of copies and formal retention schedules exist substantially because of losses like this one, which is the example invoked when the cost is explained.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's article on historical population figures. One is about estimates built from thin evidence, and this is about evidence that existed and was lost.

articles.title: The Archive of Ordinary Days
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1937 a group in Britain began a project with an unusual premise. They proposed to record what ordinary people did and thought, on the grounds that nobody was recording it and that the newspapers purporting to represent public opinion were not evidence of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The methods were deliberately plural and the plurality was the point. Volunteers kept diaries, observers recorded conversations in public places, and panels of correspondents answered open questions sent to them each month.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The directives are the richest of the three and the most unusual as evidence. A question such as what did you do yesterday evening, or what do you think about the news, produced hundreds of long answers from people with no reason to perform for anybody.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The material has obvious limitations that its own founders described. The volunteers were self-selected, they were disproportionately literate and left-leaning, and a person who agrees to write a monthly essay about their life is not typical of people in general.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What it captures that other sources do not is nevertheless substantial. Official records say what was decided, newspapers say what was said publicly, and these diaries say what somebody thought was worth mentioning about a Tuesday, which no other source preserves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The project also captured changes of mind, which almost no historical source does. A diarist who held one view in 1938 and a different one in 1940 recorded both without knowing which would look better later, because the later view had not yet arrived.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It lapsed in the 1950s and was revived in 1981, and the revival produced a second difficulty of a different kind. Later volunteers knew the archive existed and knew they were writing for it, which changes what a diary is in a way that cannot be subtracted afterwards.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the collection supports a specific range of claims and not others. It is weak evidence about what people in general believed, strong evidence about how particular people reasoned, and unique evidence about what the texture of an ordinary day was understood to consist of.

Summarize what the archive contains and what it supports.

Describe the connection between the revival and what a diary is.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's village court records. Both are sources that capture ordinary life, one by accident and one on purpose, with opposite kinds of bias.

articles.title: The Experiment That Outlived Its Experimenters
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1927 a professor of physics at an Australian university heated a quantity of pitch, poured it into a sealed glass funnel, and allowed it to settle for three years before cutting the stem. The apparatus has been running ever since.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The purpose was demonstrative rather than investigative. Pitch at room temperature shatters when struck with a hammer, which is the behaviour of a solid, and the experiment was set up to show students that it is in fact an extremely viscous liquid.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The rate at which it behaves as one is the striking part. A drop forms over a period of years and detaches roughly once a decade, which means the entire visible result of a year's running is a very small change in the shape of a hanging blob of tar.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Fewer than ten drops have fallen in the whole period. The experiment has outlasted its originator, several custodians and the building it started in, and the intervals between drops have varied with temperature, particularly after air conditioning was installed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: For most of its existence nobody actually saw a drop fall. Drops were found to have fallen, which is a different thing, and the detachment itself went unobserved for more than eighty years through a sequence of near-misses that reads as comic.

paras.label: F
paras.text: One custodian stepped out for a cup of tea and missed one. A camera installed for the purpose malfunctioned at the critical moment on another occasion, and a drop fell during a period when the apparatus was unattended.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fall was finally recorded on camera in 2013, not in Australia but at a similar experiment in Dublin that had been set up decades later and had attracted far less attention.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The experiment is often told as a joke and is a serious demonstration of something that is otherwise hard to convey. The distinction between a solid and a liquid is a matter of timescale, and the only way to show that is to pick a timescale longer than the patience of everyone involved.

articles.note: The lightest article in the grade and the one that states a real conceptual point most plainly. Worth reading last.

articles.title: The Animal Nobody Had Filmed
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1020 – 1120

paras.label: A
paras.text: The giant squid was known to science from carcasses for well over a century before anybody obtained an image of a living one. Specimens washed ashore on beaches, were taken up in fishing nets and were recovered from the stomachs of whales, and every single one of them was dead when it was examined.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That situation produced a strange kind of knowledge. The animal's anatomy was well described, its maximum size was argued about from measured specimens, and nothing whatever was known about how it moved, hunted or behaved.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The difficulty was a combination of depth and behaviour. The animal lives deep, the volume of ocean at those depths is enormous, and the methods available for exploring it were loud, bright and slow, which is a description of exactly what a deep-sea predator avoids.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first photographs of a live animal were obtained in 2004 by a Japanese team using a baited line with a camera, which caught an individual attacking the bait at depth and recorded the sequence over several hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first video of one in its own environment followed in 2012, and the method that produced it is the interesting part. Rather than illuminating the animal, the team used a lure that imitated the bioluminescent display of a jellyfish under attack.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reasoning behind that lure is worth stating because it is a piece of inference rather than engineering. A jellyfish displaying in that way is signalling to attract something large enough to attack whatever is attacking it, which makes the display an advertisement a predator has reason to investigate.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The camera system was also designed around the assumption that light drives the animal away. It used far red illumination, which the squid is believed not to see, so the recording is made in a wavelength outside the animal's own experience.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the result came from treating the failure as information. Decades of expeditions had established what does not work, and the successful method was built by assuming that every element of the standard approach was the reason for the standard outcome.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reasoning behind that lure is worth stating, because it is inference rather than engineering. A jellyfish displaying that way is signalling to attract something large enough to attack whatever is attacking it. The display is an advertisement a predator has reason to investigate.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The camera system was also built around the assumption that light drives the animal away. It used far red illumination, which the squid is believed not to see, so the recording is made in a wavelength outside the animal's own experience.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the result came from treating the failure as information. Decades of expeditions had established what does not work, and the successful method was built by assuming that every element of the standard approach was the reason for the standard outcome.

questions.q: Why did the standard methods fail?
questions.a: They were loud, bright and slow, which is a description of exactly what a deep-sea predator avoids.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the reasoning behind the lure) and paragraph H (i.e. treating the failure as information).
Summarize how a giant squid was finally filmed.
questions.a: Known only from dead specimens, the animal's anatomy was described while its behaviour was unknown, because exploration methods were loud, bright and slow. Photographs came in 2004 from a baited camera line, and video in 2012 from a lure imitating a jellyfish's distress display, filmed in far red light the squid is believed not to see.

questions.q:
bioluminescent: producing light biologically, which the lure imitated.
far red: a wavelength at the edge of visible light, used because the animal is believed not to detect it.
Describe the connection between decades of failure and the successful method.
questions.a: The successful method was built by assuming that every element of the standard approach was the reason for the standard outcome, so the failures established what does not work.

articles.note: Closes the grade on inference rather than equipment. Ask what the team would have concluded if the lure had not worked.

articles.title: What a Brain Scan Shows
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Functional magnetic resonance imaging produces pictures of a brain with regions highlighted, and those pictures appear in news coverage with captions describing what a person was thinking. Almost every step between the instrument and the caption involves an inference that the picture does not display.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The instrument does not measure thought and does not measure neural activity. It measures a magnetic property that depends on how much oxygen is carried by blood in a small volume of tissue, and that signal changes when a region becomes more active and demands more supply.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The relationship between activity and blood flow is real, well established and indirect. The blood response follows the neural event by a matter of seconds, which is enormously slower than the processes being studied, so the measurement smears in time what the brain did sharply.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The spatial unit is also larger than the thing of interest. A single volume element in a typical scan contains on the order of a million neurons, so a region described as active contains cells doing different things, some increasing their firing and some suppressing it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The statistics introduce a separate difficulty that was widely underestimated for years. A whole-brain analysis performs a test at every one of many thousands of locations, and at conventional thresholds a number of those will pass by chance alone even when nothing is there.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That point was demonstrated in a way that made it memorable. A team scanned a dead salmon, ran a standard analysis without correcting for the number of comparisons, and found a region of apparent activity, which is exactly what the arithmetic predicts.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The inference from a region to a mental state is a further step and is the one most often made invisibly. Knowing that a task activates a region is not the same as knowing that the region's activity indicates the task, because most regions participate in many different tasks.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Researchers call that reverse inference and are careful about it in papers. The care frequently does not survive the press release, where a region associated with reward lighting up becomes evidence that a person found something rewarding, which the data cannot establish.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What the method does establish is genuine and considerable. It shows where blood flow changes under a condition, it has produced reliable maps of sensory and motor organisation, and it supports claims about location far better than claims about what a located activity means.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the dead salmon demonstration) and paragraph H (i.e. reverse inference in a press release).

questions.a: A whole-brain analysis performs a test at every one of many thousands of locations, so at conventional thresholds a number of them will pass by chance alone even when nothing is there.

articles.note: RI.11-12.1 at this grade means separating four different uncertainties in one method. Ask which of the four a better scanner would remove and which it would not.

articles.title: The Evidence for a Lost Language
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two scripts were found on Crete and the Greek mainland at the beginning of the twentieth century, written on clay tablets that had been baked by the fires that destroyed the buildings holding them. One of them has been read since 1952 and the other has not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The one that was read is called Linear B, and the decipherment is worth describing because it shows what the word decipherment actually requires. Michael Ventris established that the language written in the script was an early form of Greek, which nobody had expected.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The method proceeded without any bilingual text, which is what makes it unusual. Ventris built grids relating signs by their likely vowel and consonant patterns, worked from the structure of word endings, and used place names from the tablets' own find spots as probable anchors.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The claim was then tested in the way that matters. A tablet found after the proposal was published, and not available when it was made, turned out to contain words for tripods and vessels beside pictures of tripods and vessels, in the forms the decipherment predicted.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is the criterion a decipherment has to meet, and it is a high one. A proposal must produce sense in material it was not built from, and a system flexible enough to produce plausible readings for anything produces evidence for nothing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Linear A has resisted every attempt, and the reasons are specific rather than mysterious. The corpus is small, most of it is administrative lists rather than connected prose, and crucially the underlying language is not known to be one that anybody speaks or has recorded elsewhere.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The signs themselves are partly readable, which makes the situation stranger. Many Linear A signs resemble Linear B signs closely enough that their probable sound values can be assigned, so scholars can pronounce the words and cannot say what any of them mean.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Proposed decipherments appear regularly and the field's response to them is instructive. Each is assessed against the same test: whether it produces coherent readings in tablets the proposer did not use, and so far each has failed that test rather than been rejected on authority.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What the evidence supports is therefore narrow and firm. The script records a language, that language is probably not Greek, the administrative content can be partly understood from context and numerals, and the identity of the language is open in a way no amount of further analysis of the existing tablets is likely to close.

questions.a: It must produce sense in material it was not built from, since a system flexible enough to produce plausible readings for anything produces evidence for nothing.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. signs that can be pronounced without being understood) and paragraph I (i.e. what remains open).
Summarize why one script was deciphered and the other was not.
questions.a: Ventris read Linear B without a bilingual text by building sign grids, using word endings and place names, and the proposal was confirmed when a later tablet matched its predictions. Linear A has a small corpus of administrative lists in an unknown language, its signs can be given probable sound values without meaning, and proposals fail the same predictive test.

questions.q:
corpus: the complete body of surviving text in a script, whose size limits what can be established.
bilingual: a text in two languages, normally essential to decipherment and absent in this case.
Describe the connection between a flexible system and weak evidence.
questions.a: A system flexible enough to produce plausible readings for anything produces evidence for nothing, which is why a decipherment must produce sense in material it was not built from.

articles.note: The uncertainty here is marked by the field itself rather than by the article. Ask what evidence would settle Linear A and whether it is likely to exist.

articles.title: How Many Species Are There
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Roughly two million species have been formally described, each with a published name attached to a type specimen. The number that exist is unknown, and the published estimates differ from one another by an order of magnitude.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The difficulty is not laziness and is not solvable by more collecting alone. Describing a species requires specialist expertise in a particular group, the number of people with that expertise is small and falling in several fields, and the rate of description has not changed much in decades.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The groups that are well known are well known for reasons that bias the whole picture. Birds and mammals are large, visible, studied for centuries and probably described nearly completely, and they are an extremely small fraction of the animals that exist.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The groups that dominate the real total are the ones hardest to survey. Insects, nematodes, fungi and bacteria contain most of the diversity, live in places that are difficult to sample, and in several cases cannot be distinguished without genetic work.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Estimates are therefore produced by extrapolation rather than by counting, and the method chosen drives the answer. One approach samples a small area exhaustively and scales up; another uses the relationship between how many groups exist at each taxonomic level; another counts how often new specimens turn out to be new species.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A widely cited study published in 2011 used the taxonomic ratio method and produced a figure near nine million eukaryote species. The same paper reported a substantial range around that figure, and other methods applied to the same question have produced numbers several times higher.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The disagreement concentrates in particular groups rather than being spread evenly. Estimates for beetles and for fungi vary enormously between methods, and because those groups are a large share of any total, the overall figure inherits their uncertainty directly.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Microbial diversity is a separate problem that may not have a stable answer. Where organisms exchange genes readily and reproduce without mating, the species concept that the counting depends on becomes difficult to apply, so part of the uncertainty is about definition rather than about data.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What the evidence supports is therefore a shape rather than a number. Most species are undescribed, the undescribed ones are concentrated in a few groups and a few habitats, and anyone citing a single figure for global diversity is citing one method's output rather than a measurement.

questions.q: Why are birds and mammals a misleading guide to the whole?
questions.a: They are large, visible, studied for centuries and probably described nearly completely, and they are an extremely small fraction of the animals that exist.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. where the disagreement concentrates) and paragraph H (i.e. uncertainty about definition rather than data).
Summarize what is known about how many species exist.
questions.a: About two million are described and the total is unknown, since estimates come from extrapolation and the method drives the result. A 2011 study using taxonomic ratios gave about nine million eukaryotes with a wide range, disagreement concentrates in beetles and fungi which dominate any total, and microbial diversity raises a definitional problem rather than a data one.

questions.q:
extrapolation: estimating beyond what has been observed by projecting an observed pattern.
taxonomic ratio: the relationship between numbers of groups at successive levels of classification, used as an estimating method.
Describe the connection between the method chosen and the figure produced.
questions.a: Estimates are produced by extrapolation rather than counting, and different approaches applied to the same question have produced numbers several times apart.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's historical population article. Both are cases where a precise-looking figure is one method's output and the range is the finding.

articles.title: Counting the Dead After a Disaster
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: After a hurricane, an earthquake or an epidemic, a death toll is published and is then revised, sometimes by a factor of many. The revisions are frequently reported as corrections of error, and most of them are not: they are the results of a different method answering a different question.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A direct count is the first figure available and the narrowest. It records deaths attributed to the event on a certificate, usually by physical cause, and it can be produced quickly because it comes from documents that already exist.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its limitations follow from how certification works. A death is attributed to the event if somebody wrote that down, so a person who died because a hospital had no power, or because a road was impassable, will often be certified with the condition that killed them and not the cause of that condition.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Excess mortality answers the other question. It compares the number of deaths in a period against the number that would have been expected without the event, and the difference, whatever its individual causes, is attributed to the event as a whole.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That method captures everything the direct count misses and introduces a dependence of its own. The expected figure is a model built from previous years, so the estimate is only as good as the baseline, and a place with poor or incomplete vital registration has a poor baseline.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two methods also diverge in time. Direct counts peak during the event and stop; excess mortality can continue accumulating for months as interrupted treatment, displacement and damaged infrastructure take their toll, which is why a toll revised upward a year later is often not a correction at all.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Both can be affected by factors that are not statistical. Governments have reasons to prefer a lower figure, certification practices vary, and in several documented cases the official count was maintained long after independent studies using excess mortality had produced much larger estimates.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The difference between them is also the policy question rather than a technicality. A direct count measures what the event did physically, and excess mortality measures what the event and the response to it did together, which is the number relevant to judging preparation.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So a published toll cannot be read without knowing which it is. Two figures differing by a factor of ten can both be correct, and the gap between them is itself a measurement of how much of the harm came from the failure of systems rather than from wind or water.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's unemployment article. Both show two defensible definitions producing very different numbers, and both say which question each answers.

articles.title: The Disagreement About the Age of the Universe
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: The rate at which the universe is expanding can be measured in two independent ways, and for most of the past decade the two have not agreed. The disagreement has narrowed in neither direction, the measurements have both improved, and the gap has become more significant rather than less.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first method works outward from nearby objects and is the descendant of the distance ladder. Variable stars calibrated by parallax establish distances to nearby galaxies, exploding stars of known brightness extend that reach, and the recession speeds of those galaxies give an expansion rate directly.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second works from the earliest light in the universe. The pattern of fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background encodes the composition and geometry of the early universe, and running a well-tested model forward from that pattern predicts what the present expansion rate should be.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Both are mature, both have been refined by many groups, and both now quote uncertainties small enough that the difference between them cannot be explained as noise. The late-universe measurement sits near seventy-three kilometres per second per megaparsec and the early-universe prediction near sixty-seven.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The first response of any field to a disagreement like this is to suspect the measurements. Enormous effort has gone into finding an error in the distance ladder's calibration, and into checking the microwave background analysis, and neither search has produced a resolution.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A second route is to use a method that depends on neither. Gravitational wave events provide distances without reference to the ladder, lensed quasars provide another independent route, and these have so far produced figures with uncertainties too large to settle the question.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The third possibility is the interesting one and is why the disagreement matters. The early-universe figure is not a measurement of the expansion rate but a prediction from a model, so if the measurements are both right, something in the model between then and now is wrong.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Proposals of that kind exist and none has been accepted. Additional forms of radiation in the early universe, changes in the behaviour of dark energy and modifications to gravity have all been suggested, and each tends to improve agreement on this question while worsening it on another.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What the situation supports is a statement that is uncomfortable and precise. Two well-understood methods disagree, the disagreement is probably not an error, and the resolution is more likely to require a change to the standard model of cosmology than a correction to either measurement.

paras.text: Proposals of that kind exist and none has been accepted. Additional radiation in the early universe, changes in dark energy and modifications to gravity have all been suggested. Each tends to improve agreement here while worsening it elsewhere.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the situation supports a statement that is uncomfortable and precise. Two well-understood methods disagree, the disagreement is probably not an error, and the resolution is more likely to require a change to the standard model of cosmology than a correction to either measurement.

questions.q: Why is the early-universe figure not strictly a measurement?
questions.a: It is a prediction from running a well-tested model forward from the pattern of fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. what follows if both measurements are right) and paragraph H (i.e. why proposals have not been accepted).
Summarize the disagreement and what it may mean.
questions.a: A distance-ladder measurement of the expansion rate gives about seventy-three while a prediction from the cosmic microwave background gives about sixty-seven, with uncertainties too small for the gap to be noise. Searches for errors have not resolved it, independent methods are not yet precise enough, and since the second figure is a model prediction, the resolution may require changing the model.

questions.q:
cosmic microwave background: the earliest light in the universe, whose fluctuations encode early conditions.
recession speed: how fast a galaxy is moving away, which combined with distance gives an expansion rate.
Describe the connection between proposals improving one agreement and worsening another.
questions.a: Additional radiation, changes in dark energy and modifications to gravity each tend to improve agreement on this question while worsening it on another, which is why none has been accepted.

articles.note: The clearest available case of an open question that is not an absence of evidence. Ask what observation would make a model change unavoidable.

articles.title: The Problem With Measuring Pain
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost everything a clinician measures has an instrument behind it. Temperature, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and blood chemistry are all read from a device, and the reading does not depend on what the patient says about themselves.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Pain has no such instrument. The standard measure is a person's own report, usually on a scale from zero to ten, and the definition used in practice treats pain as whatever the person experiencing it says it is.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That definition is deliberate and is a considered position rather than a default. The alternative is for a clinician to judge how much pain a patient is in, and the evidence on how accurately clinicians do that is not encouraging.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Self-report nevertheless has a property that makes it awkward as a measurement. The scale has no shared anchor, so one person's seven and another's seven are not demonstrably the same quantity, and comparison between patients rests on an assumption nobody can test.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Within a single patient the scale works much better, which is how it is mostly used. A person's seven yesterday and five today is a meaningful change, because the two readings come from the same instrument, and tracking change is the clinical question most of the time.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The second idea begins where the measurement problem ends. Because the figure is a report rather than a reading, how it is received depends on whether the person receiving it believes the person giving it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Studies across several health systems have found that reported pain is treated differently depending on the patient. Differences in analgesic prescribing by race, by sex and by whether a patient has a history of substance use have been documented repeatedly and are not explained by clinical factors.

paras.label: H
paras.text: So the two ideas meet in a specific place. A measurement that can only be obtained by asking is a measurement that can be discounted by not believing, and that is a route to unequal treatment which no amount of improving the scale would close.

paras.label: I
paras.text: Efforts to build an objective measure continue and would change the problem rather than solve it. Even a physiological correlate of pain would then require a decision about what to do when the instrument and the patient disagree, and the history above suggests which would be trusted.

questions.a: Both readings come from the same instrument, so a change from seven to five is meaningful, while one person's seven and another's are not demonstrably the same quantity.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. differences in prescribing) and paragraph I (i.e. what an objective measure would not solve).
Summarize the two ideas about measuring pain.
questions.a: Pain has no instrument, so the standard measure is self-report, which lacks a shared anchor between patients while tracking change within one patient well. Because the figure is a report, it can be discounted by not believing the patient, and differences in prescribing by race, sex and substance-use history are documented, so an objective measure would relocate rather than remove the problem.

questions.q:
anchor: a shared reference point that would let two people's ratings be compared.
correlate: a physiological signal that accompanies pain, which would not settle what to do when it disagrees with the patient.
Describe the connection between obtaining a measurement by asking and unequal treatment.
questions.a: A measurement that can only be obtained by asking is a measurement that can be discounted by not believing, which is a route to unequal treatment that improving the scale would not close.

articles.note: RI.11-12.2 wants ideas that build into a complex analysis. The second idea here is only possible because of the first, and paragraph I refuses the technological escape.

articles.title: Who Owns a Shipwreck
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A wreck is found on the seabed with cargo aboard, and the question of who may take it has at least four possible answers depending on which body of law applies and where the wreck is lying.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The oldest framework is salvage, which rewards rescue. A salvor who recovers property at risk is entitled to a payment from the owner, the entitlement arises from the service rather than from possession, and the ownership of the goods does not change.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A second framework treats a long-abandoned wreck as a find. Where an owner cannot be identified and the property is treated as abandoned, the person who recovers it may acquire title, which is the rule that makes commercial recovery financially attractive.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A third applies to government vessels and operates differently again. A sunken warship generally remains the property of its flag state indefinitely, regardless of how long ago it sank or in whose waters it lies, and many such wrecks are also war graves.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The fourth is heritage law, and it reverses the assumptions of the first two. A wreck may be protected as an archaeological site, in which case the question is not who may recover the cargo but whether anybody may disturb the site at all.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That difference is not a technicality and is where the second idea begins. Salvage law values recovery and measures success by what is brought up; archaeology values context and measures loss by what is removed from its position before being recorded.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The conflict is therefore about what a wreck is. The same object is an asset whose value is realised by lifting it and a document whose information is destroyed by lifting it, and those two descriptions cannot both govern a single operation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: International instruments have attempted to settle this. A convention adopted in 2001 favours preservation in place and discourages commercial exploitation, and it has been ratified by a substantial number of states and not by several of the largest maritime powers.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The two ideas together explain why these disputes recur rather than resolving. Ownership can be determined by a court, and what a wreck is for cannot, so a case that settles the first question leaves the second exactly where it was.

questions.q: How does salvage differ from treating a wreck as a find?
questions.a: Salvage entitles a recoverer to payment from the owner without ownership changing, while treating a wreck as abandoned allows the recoverer to acquire title.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how the two fields measure success) and paragraph I (i.e. why disputes recur).
Summarize the two ideas about shipwrecks.
questions.a: Four legal frameworks may apply: salvage pays for rescue, the law of finds allows title in abandoned property, warships remain their flag state's indefinitely, and heritage law may forbid disturbance. Salvage measures success by what is lifted and archaeology measures loss by what is lifted, so the dispute is about what a wreck is, which a court cannot settle.

questions.q:
salvor: a person who recovers property at risk and is entitled to payment for the service.
context: the position and surroundings of an object, which carry information destroyed when it is moved.
Describe the connection between the two descriptions of a wreck.
questions.a: The same object is an asset whose value is realised by lifting it and a document whose information is destroyed by lifting it, and those cannot both govern a single operation.

articles.note: The second idea reframes the first from a legal question into a definitional one. Ask which of the four frameworks a student would apply to a wreck found tomorrow.

articles.title: Why Reinforced Concrete Fails
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, which is why almost all structural concrete contains steel. The combination works because the two materials expand at nearly the same rate with temperature, so they do not tear each other apart through the seasons.

paras.label: B
paras.text: There is a second and less obvious reason the pairing works. Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, and in that chemical environment steel forms a thin passive oxide layer on its surface which prevents it from rusting even though it is surrounded by moisture.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The structure's working life therefore depends on a chemical condition rather than a mechanical one. As long as the concrete around the steel stays alkaline and intact, the steel is protected, and the assembly can last a very long time.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two processes attack that condition from outside. Carbon dioxide from the air reacts with the concrete and gradually lowers its alkalinity from the surface inward, and chloride ions from sea spray or de-icing salt penetrate the pore structure and break down the passive layer directly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What follows once the steel begins to corrode is the part that makes the failure structural. Rust occupies substantially more volume than the steel it replaces, so corrosion generates pressure from inside the concrete, which cracks, which admits more water and more chloride.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is a self-accelerating loop and it is the characteristic failure mode of twentieth-century construction. A structure can appear sound for decades while the cover over its reinforcement is thinning chemically, and then deteriorate visibly over a few years.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The second idea concerns what is being optimised when such a structure is designed. Concrete is specified by its strength at twenty-eight days, which is a number available quickly and which says very little about whether the cover will resist chloride for sixty years.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Durability design addresses this directly and is newer than the material. Specifying cover depth, limiting permeability and choosing cement types for the environment are decisions about service life rather than about strength, and they cost money at a stage where nothing is yet visible.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The two ideas meet in an uncomfortable conclusion. A structure that is strong enough and will not last is indistinguishable at handover from one that will, and the difference becomes visible only after everyone who made the decision has left the project.

questions.a: Fresh concrete is strongly alkaline, and in that environment steel forms a thin passive oxide layer that prevents rusting even in the presence of moisture.

Summarize the two ideas about reinforced concrete.

cover: the depth of concrete between the surface and the reinforcement, which determines how long protection lasts.
Describe the connection between what is specified and what fails.
questions.a: Concrete is specified by its strength at twenty-eight days, which says very little about whether the cover will resist chloride for sixty years, so durability is not what the specification optimises.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's What Engineers Mean by Failure. That article defined the terms and this shows a failure mode they were built to describe.

articles.title: What a Passport Became
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Documents permitting safe passage are very old, and the system in which almost every person belongs to a state that issues them, and in which crossing a border without one is generally impossible, is about a century old.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Before the First World War the position was closer to the opposite in much of the world. Passports existed and were frequently not required, several European states had abolished systematic checks, and large movements of people took place with no document of the modern kind.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The war ended that arrangement and the arrangement did not return afterwards. Controls introduced for security were retained, an international conference in the early 1920s standardised the booklet's format, and the document became a requirement rather than a convenience.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first idea the history develops is that a passport identifies a person to a state. It carries a name, a photograph, a number and increasingly biometric data, and the identification is what the document is usually understood to be for.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second idea is that a passport allocates mobility, and this is where the system becomes unequal in a way the first idea does not predict. What a passport permits depends almost entirely on which state issued it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The difference is large and measurable. Holders of some passports can enter well over a hundred and fifty countries without applying in advance, and holders of others can enter fewer than forty, for reasons that have nothing to do with the individual.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Those two functions sit in the same object and pull apart under pressure. Identification is about a person, and permission is about a nationality, so a document that performs both means that a question about who somebody is answers a question about where they may go.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The case of people without a state makes the interaction visible. A stateless person can be identifiable beyond doubt and still unable to travel, which is why a special document was created in the 1920s for refugees who had no government willing to issue them one.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the modern passport is an identity document that became an allocation of rights. The two ideas are now inseparable in practice, and almost every argument about borders is an argument about which of the two the document should primarily be.

Summarize the two functions of a passport.

It identifies a person to a state, and it also allocates mobility according to which state issued it, so holders of some can enter over a hundred and fifty countries and others fewer than forty, and a stateless person can be fully identifiable and unable to travel.

stateless: having no nationality that any state recognises, and therefore no government to issue a document.
biometric: based on measurable physical characteristics, increasingly carried in the document.
Describe the connection between the two functions and arguments about borders.
questions.a: Identification is about a person and permission is about a nationality, so almost every argument about borders is an argument about which of the two the document should primarily be.

articles.note: Paragraph H is the test case that makes the two ideas separable. Ask what a document that did only the first job would look like.

articles.title: The Fish That Are Not Counted
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis; provide an objective summary of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Managing a fishery requires knowing how many fish there are, and nobody can count them. The population is mobile, invisible from the surface and distributed through a volume, so every figure used in management is an estimate built from indirect evidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The traditional source of that evidence is the catch itself. Records of how much was landed, by how many boats, over how much time, produce a measure of catch per unit of effort, which is treated as a proxy for abundance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That proxy has a failure mode that took decades to be taken seriously. As fish become scarcer, boats fish harder, navigate better and target the remaining concentrations more precisely, so catch per unit of effort can hold steady while the population beneath it falls.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Scientific surveys avoid that problem by sampling independently. A research vessel tows a standard net along a standard route at a standard time, so the result does not depend on what a fleet chose to do, and a series of such surveys measures change directly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Those surveys are expensive, and the second idea begins there. The quality of a stock assessment depends almost entirely on how much money has been spent observing a species, and money follows commercial value rather than ecological importance.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The result is a sharp division in what is known. A handful of high-value stocks are assessed annually with age-structured models and independent surveys, and the great majority of exploited species are classified as data-poor, meaning the catch is recorded and almost nothing else is.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Discards make the record worse in a way that is systematic rather than random. Fish caught and returned dead do not appear in landings data, and the quantity discarded depends on quotas and prices, so the gap between what is caught and what is recorded moves with regulation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two ideas interact to produce the characteristic pattern of fishery collapse. A species is managed on a proxy that holds steady as the stock declines, in a system where the money to detect that is spent elsewhere, and the failure becomes visible when the catch itself falls.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What follows for management is a shift in what counts as evidence. Several systems now set catch limits more conservatively where the data are poor, which treats the absence of information as a reason for caution rather than as an absence of a problem.

questions.q: Why can catch per unit of effort mislead?
questions.a: As fish become scarcer, boats fish harder, navigate better and target remaining concentrations more precisely, so the measure can hold steady while the population falls.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. how discards distort the record) and paragraph I (i.e. treating absence of data as a reason for caution).
Summarize the two ideas about fishery data.
questions.a: Abundance is estimated from catch per unit of effort, which can hold steady as a stock declines because fleets improve, while independent surveys measure change directly and are expensive. Survey money follows commercial value, so most exploited species are data-poor, discards distort landings in step with regulation, and several systems now set limits conservatively where data are weak.

questions.q:
catch per unit of effort: landings divided by fishing effort, used as a proxy for how many fish remain.
data-poor: a stock for which catch is recorded and little else, which is most exploited species.
Describe the connection between where money is spent and where collapse is detected.
questions.a: Survey money follows commercial value rather than ecological importance, so a species can be managed on a misleading proxy in a system where the money to detect the decline is spent elsewhere.

articles.note: Paragraph I is the policy move the two ideas produce. Ask what a management system would do differently if it treated no data as no information rather than as no problem.

articles.title: How Radiocarbon Dating Was Corrected
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Willard Libby's method, published in the late 1940s, dates organic material by measuring how much of a radioactive form of carbon remains in it. The principle is simple, it won a Nobel Prize, and the first decade of results were systematically wrong in a way nobody could detect from inside the method.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The method rests on a chain of assumptions, each reasonable. Carbon-14 is produced in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays, it mixes through the atmosphere and the oceans, living things take it up, and when they die the intake stops and the clock begins.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The assumption that failed is the one about production. Libby's calculation required that the atmospheric concentration of carbon-14 had been constant through the period being dated, and he was explicit that this was an assumption rather than a finding.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first evidence against it came from the method's own results. Dates for Egyptian material of known historical age came out consistently too young, by amounts that grew with age, which is the signature of a systematic error rather than of scattered inaccuracy.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The correction required a source of material whose age was known independently and exactly. Tree rings supply that: a ring is one year, rings can be counted, and overlapping sequences from living and dead trees extend a continuous record thousands of years back.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Hans Suess and others then measured carbon-14 in rings of known age, which converts the problem into a measurement. The resulting curve shows what the atmospheric concentration actually was in each year, and it is not flat.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The reasons for the variation turned out to be several and physical. Changes in solar activity alter the cosmic ray flux, the earth's magnetic field modulates it over longer periods, and ocean circulation changes how much old carbon is exchanged with the atmosphere.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Human activity then added two large disturbances in opposite directions. Burning fossil fuels released carbon containing no carbon-14 and diluted the atmosphere, and atmospheric nuclear testing in the 1950s and 1960s roughly doubled the concentration within a few years.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The method today is therefore a measurement plus a calibration curve, and the curve is the accumulated work of many laboratories over decades. A radiocarbon date reported without calibration is not a date, which is why published results carry a notation stating which curve was used.

Describe the connection between tree rings and the correction.
questions.a: A ring is one year and overlapping sequences extend a continuous record thousands of years back, which supplies material of exactly known age in which carbon-14 can be measured directly.

articles.note: RI.11-12.3 wants a sequence of interacting ideas. Here the method's own results exposed its assumption, and a different discipline supplied the fix.

articles.title: How the Penny Post Was Argued For
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1840 sending a letter in Britain was expensive and the charge depended on distance and on the number of sheets. Postage was normally paid by the recipient, who could refuse to accept a letter, and many people routinely did.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rowland Hill's pamphlet of 1837 made an argument that was counterintuitive and turned out to be arithmetically correct. He proposed a single low rate for any letter to anywhere in the country, prepaid by the sender, and predicted that revenue would not fall.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument rested on an analysis of where the cost actually lay. Hill examined the operation and concluded that the expensive part was handling: receiving, sorting, accounting for and collecting on each item, and that the distance a letter travelled added almost nothing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That finding reframed the whole question. If distance is not the cost, charging by distance is not a recovery of expense but an administrative apparatus that is itself expensive, and the accounting required to charge differently for every route was a substantial part of the operation.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Collection on delivery was the second expense he identified and the one most visible to the public. A postman waiting at a door for payment, and frequently not receiving it, represented wasted time on every undelivered item.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The proposal for prepayment required a mechanism that did not exist, and the mechanism is what the reform is remembered for. An adhesive label sold in advance proved that postage had been paid, which removed the transaction from the doorstep entirely.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The institutional response was hostile and the reasons were not foolish. The Post Office objected that revenue would collapse, that the volume increase Hill predicted was speculative, and that a service designed around a small number of valuable letters could not absorb a flood of cheap ones.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What happened was partly what each side predicted. Volume rose immediately and very substantially, revenue fell at first and took years to recover to its previous level, and the service was transformed in a way that made the earlier arrangement politically impossible to restore.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The episode therefore shows an argument winning on one ground and being vindicated on another. Hill's cost analysis was correct and his revenue forecast was optimistic, and the reform survived because the thing it produced, a country in which ordinary people wrote to each other, was not a thing anybody proposed to undo.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's standard gauge article. Both are cases where an argument about cost produced an institution nobody could later unmake.

articles.title: How Anaesthesia Was Established
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Surgery before the 1840s was conducted on conscious patients, and the surgical virtue most prized was speed. Operations were limited to what could be done in minutes, and the interior of the body was effectively unreachable.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The substances that would change this were already known and were not being used medically. Nitrous oxide and ether had been investigated decades earlier, their effects were understood well enough to be a form of entertainment, and nobody had connected them to the problem of surgical pain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first person to use ether for surgery appears to have been Crawford Long, in Georgia, in 1842. He operated on a patient under ether, repeated it, and did not publish for several years, which removed him from the history that was about to be made without him.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Horace Wells, a dentist, attempted a public demonstration with nitrous oxide in 1845 and it failed. The patient cried out, the audience concluded the method did not work, and Wells's reputation did not recover from a demonstration in which the gas had probably been withdrawn too early.

paras.label: E
paras.text: William Morton's demonstration at the Massachusetts General Hospital in October 1846 succeeded, and the differences from Wells's attempt are instructive. He used ether rather than nitrous oxide, he controlled the delivery with an apparatus he had designed, and he had practised on his own patients first.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The news moved faster than any medical development had moved before. Reports crossed the Atlantic within weeks, operations under ether were performed in London and Paris within months, and the adoption was essentially complete in a few years.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The priority dispute that followed consumed the lives of several of the people involved. Morton attempted to patent the agent under a disguised name, Charles Jackson claimed to have supplied the essential idea, Wells pressed his own claim, and Long's earlier work surfaced late and was never decisive.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The patent attempt is the element that matters most for how the episode is read. Concealing the identity of a substance that was already widely known could not hold, the profession objected on ethical grounds, and the attempt made Morton's claim harder to accept rather than easier.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the sequence is one in which an available idea waited for a combination of circumstances. The substance, a reliable method of delivery, a public institution willing to host a demonstration and a result that could not be argued with, and the dispute about who deserved credit turned on everything except whether it worked.
