articles.title: How the Suffrage Campaign Divided
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Campaigns for women's suffrage in Britain and in the United States both split, at roughly the same period, over the same question. The question was not whether women should vote but what should be done to achieve it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The older organisations had worked by the methods available to people without the vote. Petitions, meetings, pamphlets, lobbying of sympathetic legislators and the patient accumulation of parliamentary support had been pursued for decades and had produced very little.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That record is the premise of the argument that followed. A newer organisation concluded that the constitutional route had been tried thoroughly enough to be judged, and that its failure was evidence about the method rather than about the amount of effort applied.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The alternative proposed was disruption, and the reasoning behind it was specific rather than merely angry. An issue that can be ignored will be ignored, so the campaign's task was to make ignoring it more expensive than conceding, which required action that could not be filed away.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The older organisations objected on grounds that were also strategic. They argued that disruption alienated the legislators whose votes would eventually be needed, that it supplied opponents with evidence of unfitness, and that it set back support that had taken decades to build.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both predictions were partly borne out, which is why the question is still argued. Militant action produced enormous publicity and genuine political pressure, and it also produced a hardening among some legislators and a withdrawal of some support.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The relationship between the two wings was more complicated than a simple opposition. Each could use the other: the constitutional organisations gained from being the reasonable alternative, and the militants gained from an established movement that kept the question respectable.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The war interrupted both and changed the terms entirely. Campaigning was suspended, women entered occupations that had excluded them, and the legislation that followed is frequently attributed to that experience rather than to either campaign.

paras.label: I
paras.text: That attribution is itself contested and the dispute is unresolvable in principle. There is no way to run the period again without the campaigns, so the question of what the militancy achieved is a counterfactual, and historians who disagree about it are not disagreeing about any fact that can be checked.

articles.title: How Forecasting Became Possible
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Weather prediction older than the nineteenth century consisted of local signs and accumulated experience. Nothing about it was contemptible, it produced useful rules of thumb, and it could not predict a storm that had not yet arrived in the observer's sky.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The telegraph changed the situation by changing what could be known. For the first time, conditions at distant places could be learned faster than the weather itself travelled, which made it possible to draw a picture of a whole region simultaneously.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Robert FitzRoy built a system on that possibility in the 1860s, collecting telegraphed observations, plotting them, and issuing storm warnings to ports. He also coined the word forecast, choosing it deliberately to signal that the output was a reasoned estimate rather than a prophecy.

paras.label: D
paras.text: His warnings were criticised when they were wrong and the criticism was public and sustained. The method was defensible and the product was not reliable enough to satisfy its critics, and the service was discontinued after his death before being restored under pressure from the ports.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Vilhelm Bjerknes reframed the problem in 1904 in a way that made it a different subject. He argued that the atmosphere obeys known physical laws, so prediction is in principle an initial-value problem: given the present state with sufficient accuracy, the future state follows by calculation.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That formulation is correct and it was, at the time, useless. Lewis Fry Richardson attempted the calculation by hand during the First World War, spending months to produce a six-hour forecast that was badly wrong, partly through an error in handling the initial data.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Richardson understood exactly why it had failed and what would be needed. He estimated that keeping pace with the weather would require tens of thousands of human computers working simultaneously in a coordinated hall, which he described in detail and which was not a practical proposal.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The machine that made it practical arrived in 1950, when a team produced the first numerical forecast on an electronic computer. The calculation took about as long as the period it predicted, which was useless operationally and demonstrated that Richardson's approach was correct.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the sequence required four separate things that arrived over a century: a way to gather simultaneous observations, a theoretical reformulation, a demonstration of the method's failure that diagnosed itself, and a machine fast enough to make the arithmetic worth doing.

questions.a: To signal deliberately that the output was a reasoned estimate rather than a prophecy.

Summarize how numerical forecasting became possible.

articles.note: Four requirements across a century, none sufficient alone. Ask which of the four would have been hardest to predict in 1860.

articles.title: What a Calorie Measures
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A figure on a food package states an energy content in calories, and the figure is produced by a chain of conventions that have been refined repeatedly over a century. The word does not mean one thing, and the differences between its meanings are large enough to matter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The original definition is purely physical and belongs to chemistry. A calorie is the energy required to raise the temperature of a gram of water by one degree, and that quantity can be measured directly by burning a substance and recording the heat released.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A device for doing exactly that exists and is where food energy figures began. A bomb calorimeter burns a sample completely in oxygen and measures the temperature rise, which gives the total chemical energy the substance contains.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That number is not the number a person obtains from eating the food, and the gap is the first refinement. A human digestive system does not burn food completely; some of it passes through, and the fraction that does varies with what the food is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The figures in use therefore come from a second definition. Metabolisable energy is what the body actually extracts, and it is calculated by applying fixed factors to the protein, fat and carbohydrate a food contains rather than by measuring anything about that particular food.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those factors are averages established in the early twentieth century and are known to be approximations. They were derived from a limited set of foods, they assume a typical digestive efficiency, and they are applied to foods that differ considerably from the ones that produced them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A third refinement concerns the cost of digestion. Extracting energy requires energy, and the amount varies by nutrient, so protein delivers less usable energy than its figure implies because more of it is consumed in the processing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A fourth concerns the food's physical state, which the figures do not represent at all. The same nuts whole and ground yield different amounts to a person, and cooking changes availability substantially, so the number on a package describes a food's composition rather than a specific meal.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the term has narrowed and been qualified four times while keeping one name. A calorie on a label is a convention built from averages for ingredients, and reading it as a measurement of what a particular body will obtain from a particular plate is reading it as the first definition when it is the second.

bomb calorimeter: a device that burns a sample completely and measures the heat released.
metabolisable energy: the portion of a food's energy a body actually extracts, estimated from average factors.
Describe the connection between the factors being averages and what a label can claim.
questions.a: The factors were derived from a limited set of foods and assume a typical digestive efficiency, so a label describes a food's composition rather than what a particular body will obtain.

articles.note: RI.11-12.4 asks how a term is refined over a text. Four refinements, one word, and the article is careful that none of them makes the label useless.

articles.title: The Word Refugee in Law
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Refugee in ordinary use describes anybody who has fled something. In law it describes a person satisfying a definition written in 1951, and the distance between the two meanings determines what happens to people at a border.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The legal definition has several elements that must all be present. A refugee is a person who is outside their country of nationality, who has a well-founded fear of persecution, and whose fear arises for one of five stated reasons.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each element excludes a group that ordinary usage includes. A person who has fled and remains inside their own country is not a refugee under this definition, however severe their situation, and such people are described by a separate term with weaker protections.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The requirement that fear be well-founded does two things at once. It excludes fear that is not objectively supportable, and it also means that a person need not have been persecuted already, which is a significant inclusion that is frequently misunderstood.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The five reasons are the element doing the most work and the most argued over. Persecution must be on grounds of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group, and a person persecuted for a reason outside that list is not covered.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The fifth category has absorbed most of the development since. Membership of a particular social group was not defined in the convention, and decades of decisions have shaped what it covers, which is how the definition has expanded without the text changing.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A person fleeing a general situation rather than targeted persecution presents the hardest case. Somebody escaping a war that endangers everybody, or a country that has become uninhabitable, may satisfy nobody's definition of safe and may not satisfy this definition of a refugee.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Regional instruments have widened the term where the original was found insufficient. Several agreements extend protection to people fleeing generalised violence or events seriously disturbing public order, which is an admission that the 1951 definition did not cover everyone it should.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the word in law is narrower than the word in use and is being widened case by case rather than by amendment. A person described accurately as a refugee in a newspaper may be refused that status in a hearing, and both uses can be correct in their own register.

questions.a: A refugee in law is outside their country of nationality with a well-founded fear of persecution on one of five stated grounds, so people displaced internally or fleeing general danger may be excluded. The undefined fifth category has absorbed most development through decisions, and regional instruments have extended protection to people fleeing generalised violence.

instrument: a formal international agreement, several of which have widened the term regionally.
Describe the connection between an undefined category and a changing definition.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's article on terrorism in three statutes. Both are terms whose legal meaning decides outcomes and whose ordinary meaning is wider.

articles.title: What Intelligence Means on a Test
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Intelligence testing began with a practical question and a narrow one. Alfred Binet was asked in 1904 to identify children who would need additional help in French schools, and he built a scale for that purpose and said what it was for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: His own statements about the instrument are unusually clear and are frequently quoted against later use of it. He wrote that the scale did not measure a fixed quantity, that intelligence was not a single thing that could be given a number, and that the results should not be treated as a permanent classification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The term changed meaning as the instrument travelled. Translated and revised in the United States, the scale acquired a quotient, that quotient acquired a reputation for stability, and the number came to be treated as a property of a person rather than a position on a scale built for a purpose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A second refinement arrived from the statistics rather than from the theory. Scores on different mental tasks correlate with one another, and a factor extracted from those correlations is commonly labelled general intelligence, which gives the word a technical meaning derived from the structure of the data.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That derivation is real and is also circular in a way worth stating. The factor summarises correlations among whichever tasks were included, so what it describes depends on what was tested, and naming it intelligence imports a meaning the statistics did not supply.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A third refinement came from asking what the tests predict. Scores do predict educational and occupational outcomes to a measurable degree, which is the strongest argument for their usefulness, and prediction is a different claim from measurement of a capacity.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A fourth came from populations rather than individuals. Average scores rose substantially across many countries through the twentieth century, by amounts too large to be genetic change, which tells against any reading of the number as a fixed natural quantity.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What the term now carries in careful use is therefore heavily qualified. It names performance on a defined set of tasks, under defined conditions, relative to a norm group, at a particular time, and each of those qualifications was added because a reading without it went wrong.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The ordinary meaning has absorbed none of this, which is the practical problem. A number produced by an instrument whose author denied it measured a fixed quantity is still reported as though it describes something a person simply has.

Summarize how the term has been refined.

norm group: the population a score is expressed relative to, which a careful use of the term must specify.
factor: a statistical summary of correlations among tasks, which carries no meaning beyond what was tested.
Describe the connection between rising averages and reading the number as fixed.
questions.a: Average scores rose substantially across many countries by amounts too large to be genetic change, which tells against reading the number as a fixed natural quantity.

articles.note: A term whose author's own qualifications were discarded as it spread. Ask which of the four refinements a newspaper report would have to include to be accurate.

articles.title: The Word Genocide
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: The word genocide did not exist before 1944. Raphael Lemkin constructed it from a Greek root and a Latin one in order to name something he argued had no name, and his account of why a new word was necessary is part of the term's meaning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: His argument was that existing vocabulary described the wrong unit. Murder and massacre describe what is done to individuals, and Lemkin held that there was a distinct crime whose object is the destruction of a group as such, which is not the sum of the individual crimes committed in it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: He also used the word more broadly than the later legal definition does. His writing includes the destruction of a group's institutions, language, culture and social structure, on the view that a group can be destroyed without every member being killed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The definition adopted in the 1948 convention narrowed it substantially, and the narrowing was a negotiation rather than a clarification. Proposals to include political groups and to cover cultural destruction were made and were not adopted, for reasons that were political at the time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What survived is a list of acts and a requirement about intent. The acts include killing, causing serious harm, imposing conditions calculated to bring about destruction, preventing births and transferring children, and all of them must be committed with intent to destroy a group in whole or in part.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The intent requirement is where almost all the legal difficulty concentrates. Proving that acts occurred is frequently straightforward, and proving that they were committed with the specific purpose of destroying a group as such is a much higher threshold than proving that a group was in fact destroyed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: In whole or in part has generated its own body of interpretation. Tribunals have held that the part must be substantial, and have considered whether a geographically limited portion of a group can count, which produces outcomes that turn on definitions rather than on facts about what happened.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The gap between the scholarly and the legal term has therefore widened rather than closed. Scholars use a wider definition closer to Lemkin's, courts apply the convention, and a situation can be genocide in a journal and not in a judgment without either being careless.

paras.label: I
paras.text: That gap is itself the thing to understand about the word. It was invented to make a crime nameable, narrowed so that states would sign, and has since been argued over continuously, so every use of it carries a position on which definition is operating.

questions.a: Because murder and massacre describe what is done to individuals, while he held there was a distinct crime whose object is the destruction of a group as such.

Summarize how the meaning of the term has developed.
questions.a: Lemkin coined it in 1944 to name the destruction of a group as such, including cultural and institutional destruction. The 1948 convention narrowed it by negotiation, excluding political groups and cultural destruction, and required specific intent, which is the hardest element to prove, so scholarly and legal usage have diverged rather than converged.

questions.q:
specific intent: the requirement that acts be committed with the purpose of destroying a group, not merely that destruction occurred.
tribunal: a court established to try such cases, whose interpretations have shaped the phrase in whole or in part.
Describe the connection between the negotiation of 1948 and the term's present use.
questions.a: Proposals to include political groups and cultural destruction were not adopted for political reasons, so the legal term is narrower than Lemkin's and scholars continue to use the wider one.

articles.note: A term invented by one person, narrowed by a treaty and contested ever since. Ask what the convention would look like if the 1948 proposals had been adopted.

articles.title: What Sustainable Came to Mean
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Sustainable originated as a technical term in forestry and fisheries and meant something narrow and checkable. A harvest is sustainable if it does not exceed the rate at which the stock replaces itself, which is a quantity that can in principle be measured.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That meaning has a property worth noting before any of the later ones. It is falsifiable: a claim that a given harvest is sustainable can be shown to be wrong by the stock declining, and the term is doing work that a vaguer word could not do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The word entered general use through a definition published in 1987, in a report prepared for the United Nations. Sustainable development was defined as development meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That formulation did something the forestry definition had not. It extended the term from a physical stock to an open-ended set of human needs, and it introduced an obligation to people who do not yet exist and cannot state what they will need.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The extension was deliberate and the report said why. Confining the idea to resource yields would exclude the questions the report existed to address, which concerned poverty and development as much as forests, so the widening was a choice with a reason behind it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The cost of the widening is that the term stopped being checkable. A claim that an activity is sustainable in the original sense can be tested against a stock, and a claim that it meets present needs without compromising future ones cannot be tested against anything available now.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Subsequent use has widened it further still, to the point where a reader cannot assume any content at all. Products, buildings, business strategies and investment funds are described as sustainable, and in most of those uses the word is a commendation rather than a claim.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Attempts to restore checkability have taken the form of standards rather than definitions. Certification schemes specify what an activity must do to use the word, which replaces an untestable claim with a testable one about compliance, and moves the question to whether the standard is any good.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the word has travelled from a measurable rate to an ethical obligation to a marketing term, and all three meanings are in use simultaneously. A reader meeting it has to decide which is operating, and the most common answer is the third.

questions.a: It is falsifiable, since a claim that a given harvest is sustainable can be shown wrong by the stock declining.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. why the report widened the term) and paragraph H (i.e. how standards restore checkability).
Summarize how the meaning of sustainable has changed.
questions.a: It began as a measurable claim that a harvest does not exceed a stock's replacement rate, was extended in 1987 to development meeting present needs without compromising future ones, which introduced an untestable obligation to people who do not yet exist, and has since become a commendation, with certification schemes replacing the claim with compliance against a standard.

questions.q:
falsifiable: capable of being shown wrong by evidence, which the original meaning was and the later ones are not.
certification: a scheme specifying what must be done to use a term, replacing a claim with a testable compliance.
Describe the connection between widening the term and losing the ability to check it.
questions.a: The original claim can be tested against a stock, and a claim about meeting present needs without compromising future ones cannot be tested against anything available now.

articles.note: Three meanings in simultaneous use, one of them checkable. Ask students to find the word on five real products and say which meaning each is using.

articles.title: The Abstract That Must Stand Alone
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Journals in several fields now require a structured abstract: a short summary divided under fixed headings such as background, methods, results and conclusions, in that order and with a word limit for each.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The alternative is an unstructured paragraph, which is older and is still standard in some disciplines. It permits a writer to shape the summary to the paper, emphasising what that particular study did that was unusual, which a fixed template cannot do.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The argument for structure rests on what abstracts are used for. A reader scanning search results is comparing many studies rather than reading one, and comparison requires that the same information appear in the same place in each.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There is evidence behind that argument rather than only a rationale. Studies comparing the two forms have found that structured abstracts contain more of the information a reader needs, including sample sizes and effect measures that unstructured versions frequently omit.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The structure also constrains a specific failure. A results heading that must be filled makes it awkward to summarise a study without stating what it found, and an abstract reporting only that something was investigated is harder to write when a heading demands the outcome.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The costs are real and are mostly about proportion. A fixed allocation gives the same space to methods in a study whose method is routine and in one whose method is the entire contribution, and the second is badly served by the format.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A second cost is that headings can be satisfied without being answered. A conclusions field can be filled with a sentence calling for further research, which occupies the slot, meets the requirement and tells a reader nothing.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Evaluating the structure therefore depends on which failure is more common, and that is an empirical question rather than a matter of taste. If omission is the usual problem, a template fixes more than it costs; if distortion by proportion is, it does not.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The evidence as it stands favours structure for the fields that adopted it, which are those where studies are numerous and comparable. The fields that have not adopted it are generally those where each paper's contribution is of a different kind, and that pattern is itself the argument.

questions.q: What is the argument for a structured abstract?
questions.a: A reader scanning search results compares many studies rather than reading one, and comparison requires the same information to appear in the same place in each.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. headings satisfied without being answered) and paragraph I (i.e. which fields adopted the form).
Summarize the case for and against structured abstracts.
questions.a: Fixed headings make comparison across studies possible and demonstrably increase the information present, including sample sizes, and a results heading makes it awkward to omit an outcome. The costs are a fixed proportion that serves an unusual method badly and headings that can be filled without being answered, so the right choice depends on which failure is more common in a field.

questions.q:
structured abstract: a summary divided under fixed headings with allocated space for each.
empirical: settled by evidence rather than by argument from principle.
Describe the connection between a field's papers and the form it adopted.
questions.a: Fields where studies are numerous and comparable adopted structure, while fields where each paper's contribution is of a different kind did not, and that pattern is itself the argument.

articles.note: RI.11-12.5 asks for evaluation rather than description. This article reaches a verdict and states the condition under which it would reverse.

articles.title: The Shape of an Obituary
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: An obituary in a serious newspaper has a form that is almost invariant, and the form was arrived at rather than designed. Reading several in sequence makes the pattern obvious and raises the question of whether it is a good one.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence states who died, what they were known for and when, in one clause each. It is written to be complete on its own, because a substantial number of readers will read nothing else, and the entire judgement of a life is compressed into its middle clause.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second paragraph usually gives the single achievement the piece will organise around. That choice is the most consequential decision in the whole document, and it is made by a writer who may be working from a file prepared years earlier.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The body then runs chronologically, from origins through the achievement to the later life, which is where the form shows its main weakness. A person whose significant work came early is followed through decades of less interesting material because the structure requires it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The convention of candour about the subject's faults is handled by placement rather than by omission. Difficulties are generally stated plainly and placed in the second half, after a reader has absorbed the achievement, so the ordering does evaluative work that no sentence states.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The closing is formulaic and the formula is load-bearing. A list of survivors returns the subject from a public figure to a person with a family, and its position at the end means a reader leaves with that rather than with the assessment.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The strongest argument for the form is that it is reliable under pressure. Obituaries are frequently written quickly, by people who did not know the subject, and a template that produces a competent piece under those conditions is worth a great deal.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The strongest argument against is that it imposes a narrative shape on lives that did not have one. A chronological structure implies development toward the achievement, and a life in which the significant thing was accidental or early is distorted by being told that way.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the form is well suited to its production conditions and badly suited to a particular kind of subject, which is a specific and defensible verdict rather than a complaint. The papers that depart from it do so for exactly those subjects, which suggests the editors know.

questions.q: How are a subject's faults usually handled?
questions.a: By placement rather than omission: stated plainly but placed in the second half, after a reader has absorbed the achievement.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. reliability under pressure) and paragraph H (i.e. the narrative shape imposed).
Summarize the form of an obituary and how it should be judged.
questions.a: A first sentence complete on its own carries the judgement of a life, a second paragraph names the organising achievement, and the body runs chronologically with faults placed in the second half and survivors at the end. The form is reliable when written quickly by people who did not know the subject, and it distorts lives whose significant work was early or accidental.

questions.q:
invariant: unchanging across instances, which this form very nearly is.
load-bearing: doing structural work rather than being decorative, as the closing list is.
Describe the connection between where faults are placed and the reader's judgement.
questions.a: Difficulties are placed in the second half after a reader has absorbed the achievement, so the ordering does evaluative work that no sentence states.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's A Life in Three Tellings. That article compared forms and this evaluates one of them against its own conditions.

articles.title: The Protocol a Technician Follows
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A laboratory protocol is a document written to be executed rather than read, and its structure follows from that almost completely. It is numbered, imperative, and arranged so that a person can find their place again after being interrupted.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The numbering does more than order the steps. It creates a reference that two people can use in conversation, so a technician can be asked what happened at step seven, and an error can be localised in a way a prose description would not allow.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The imperative mood removes an ambiguity that ordinary prose carries. Add five millilitres is an instruction, and the sample is treated with five millilitres describes what usually happens, which leaves open whether the reader is being told to do it now.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Quantities and conditions are placed in a fixed position within each step, and the consistency matters more than the position chosen. A technician scanning for a volume knows where in the sentence to look, which is a property that only holds if every step is written the same way.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Checkpoints are the structural feature that distinguishes a good protocol from a complete one. A step reading confirm the solution is clear before proceeding stops the sequence at a point where an error is still correctable, and placing those well is most of the skill.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Timing constraints are the hardest thing for the form to carry. A step that must begin within two minutes of the previous one is a relationship between steps rather than a property of either, and a numbered list represents sequence naturally and simultaneity badly.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Protocols address that with devices that are visibly awkward. A note in bold before a step, a timing column alongside the list, or an instruction to read the next three steps before starting any of them, and the awkwardness is evidence that the structure is being used past its limit.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The deeper evaluation is about what the form assumes. A numbered list assumes a single linear path, so a procedure with branches must either flatten them into conditions inside steps or split into separate protocols, and both solutions lose something.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the structure is close to optimal for a linear sequence executed under interruption and is a poor fit for anything else. A protocol that has grown branches and timing dependencies is usually a sign that the work has outgrown the document, rather than that the document was written badly.

questions.a: A reference two people can use in conversation, so an error can be localised by asking what happened at a particular step.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what checkpoints do) and paragraph H (i.e. what a numbered list assumes).
Summarize the structure of a protocol and its limits.

The form represents sequence well and timing relationships and branches badly, so awkward devices in a protocol usually indicate work that has outgrown the document.

questions.q:
imperative: the grammatical form that instructs, distinguishing a step from a description.
checkpoint: a step requiring confirmation before proceeding, placed where an error can still be corrected.
Describe the connection between awkward devices and the structure's limits.
questions.a: Bold notes, timing columns and instructions to read ahead are awkward, and the awkwardness is evidence that the structure is being used past its limit.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 7's checklist article. A checklist catches an expert who will miss something, and a protocol directs someone following it exactly.

articles.title: How a Dictionary Entry Is Built
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dictionary entry has a structure that encodes a theory of what a word is, and two dictionaries can present the same word differently because they hold different theories rather than because one is more careful.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The headword and pronunciation are uncontroversial and the first real decision follows them. The senses of a word have to be put in an order, and there are two defensible orders which produce substantially different entries.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Historical order places the oldest attested sense first and the newest last. An entry built this way is a record of how a word moved, and a reader can see that a present meaning developed from an earlier one that may now be obsolete.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Frequency order places the most common current sense first. An entry built this way serves a reader who has encountered a word and wants to know what it probably means, which is the overwhelmingly common reason for opening a dictionary.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The two orders can put the same sense in first position and last, and the choice signals what the dictionary is for. A historical dictionary is a work of record, a learner's dictionary is a tool, and the ordering is the clearest statement of which a given book is.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Citations do similar work and are similarly revealing. A dictionary that supports each sense with dated quotations is making an evidential claim about when the sense existed, and one that supplies invented examples is helping a reader use the word rather than documenting it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Etymology is placed differently in different traditions, and the placement is an argument. At the head of an entry it implies that origin explains meaning, and at the foot it implies the opposite, which is a position on a question linguists do not agree about.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Labels are the most contested element and the hardest to execute. Marking a sense as informal, offensive or dated is a judgement about usage that changes faster than editions, and a label that is accurate when printed can be wrong within a decade.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the structure is an argument about what a word is, and evaluating it means asking what the book is for. A historical arrangement serves a scholar badly served by frequency, a frequency arrangement serves a learner badly served by history, and no single order serves both.

questions.q: What do the two possible orders of senses signal?
questions.a: What the dictionary is for, since a historical dictionary is a work of record and a learner's dictionary is a tool, and the ordering is the clearest statement of which a book is.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the placement of etymology) and paragraph H (i.e. why labels are hardest).
Summarize what a dictionary entry's structure encodes.
questions.a: Senses can be ordered historically, recording how a word moved, or by frequency, serving a reader who wants a probable meaning, and the choice states what the book is for. Dated citations make evidential claims while invented examples teach use, etymology's placement implies whether origin explains meaning, and usage labels date faster than editions.

attested: evidenced in recorded use, which determines where a sense falls in a historical ordering.
etymology: the account of a word's origin, whose placement in an entry implies how much it explains.
Describe the connection between the order chosen and who is served.
questions.a: A historical arrangement serves a scholar badly served by frequency, a frequency arrangement serves a learner badly served by history, and no single order serves both.

articles.note: Bring two dictionaries and look up one polysemous word in both. The difference in sense order is usually visible immediately and is the whole lesson.

articles.title: The Structure of an Error Message
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.3 complex ideas · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: An error message is a piece of writing produced under the worst possible conditions for communication. The reader is frustrated, is not looking for information, wants to resume what they were doing, and will give the text approximately one second.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The structure that has emerged from that constraint has three parts and a conventional order. What went wrong, why it went wrong where that is knowable, and what the reader can do about it, with the third part being the one most often missing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The order is not arbitrary and is defended by evidence about how people read under stress. A reader who learns the action first may act without understanding the problem, and a reader who is given the cause first will frequently stop reading before reaching the action.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The hardest structural decision is where to put technical detail. A reference code is useless to most readers and essential to anybody helping them, so it has to be present and must not occupy the position the action needs.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The usual solution is a hierarchy rather than a sequence. A short message with the action, and a disclosure control revealing the detail, which serves both readers without making either read the other's material.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The characteristic failure of the form is a message that describes an internal state. A message reporting that a null reference was encountered in a module is accurate, is addressed to somebody who is not reading it, and leaves the actual reader with nothing to do.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A second failure is the message that assigns blame to the reader. Phrasing an error as something the user did wrong is frequently inaccurate, since most such errors are a system failing to accommodate ordinary input, and it makes the reader less likely to attempt the action again.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The third is the message that is reassuring and empty. Something went wrong, please try again contains no information, occupies the structural position where information belongs, and trains readers to dismiss messages without reading them.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the structure is evaluable against a stated purpose, which is rare for such a short text. The purpose is to get a reader to a successful action, and a message can be measured against whether readers who see it complete the task, which makes this one of the few kinds of writing with a usable outcome measure.

questions.a: What went wrong, why it went wrong where that is knowable, and what the reader can do about it, with the third most often missing.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the hierarchy solution) and paragraph I (i.e. the outcome measure).
Summarize the structure of an error message and how it fails.
questions.a: Written for a frustrated reader giving it a second, the form states what went wrong, why, and what to do, with the action last so readers understand before acting. Technical detail is placed behind a disclosure control, and the characteristic failures are describing an internal state, blaming the reader, and filling the information position with reassurance.

questions.q:
disclosure control: an element that reveals additional detail on request, keeping it out of the main message.
internal state: a description of what the system encountered, addressed to someone who is not the reader.
Describe the connection between an empty message and future reading.
questions.a: A reassuring message carries no information, occupies the position where information belongs, and trains readers to dismiss messages without reading them.

articles.note: The only text in this grade with a measurable outcome. Ask what a controlled comparison between two messages would look like.

articles.title: The Eulogy That Is About Something Else
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A eulogy is understood to be about the person who has died, and the most effective examples are frequently about something else as well, delivered to an audience that has gathered for a reason nobody has to explain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That audience is unusual in a way that shapes everything. It is unified by an occasion rather than by agreement, it is in a state in which ordinary resistance to persuasion is lowered, and it will not interrupt or heckle whatever is said.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A speaker aware of that has a responsibility and an opportunity in the same moment. The responsibility is that the occasion belongs to the dead person and to the people who knew them, and the opportunity is that a claim made here will be heard without the defences a political meeting would raise.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The technique that resolves the tension is to let the subject's life carry the argument. A speaker who describes what somebody worked for, in particular rather than abstract terms, has made a case for that work without appearing to argue for anything.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Specificity is what makes that work and generality is what destroys it. A sentence describing a person as devoted to justice is an abstraction that could apply to anyone, and a sentence describing what they did on a particular Tuesday in 1971 is evidence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The best examples also give the audience something to do. A eulogy that ends by naming what remains unfinished converts grief into a task, which is a rhetorical move of considerable power and is also the point at which it can be misused.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That misuse is the risk the form carries and it is worth stating directly. A speaker can enlist the dead for a position they did not hold, the audience is in no condition to object, and nobody present can be contradicted by the person being described.

paras.text: The constraint that keeps the form honest is specificity again, acting in the other direction. A claim about what somebody believed can be tested against what they did, so a eulogy made of particulars is harder to turn than one made of qualities.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the power and the danger have the same source. An occasion that suspends disagreement makes a speaker unusually persuasive, and the only thing distinguishing an honest use from a dishonest one is whether the argument would survive being made somewhere else.

paras.text: A eulogy is understood to be about the person who has died, and the most effective examples are frequently about something else as well, delivered to an audience gathered for a reason nobody has to explain.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That audience is unusual in a way that shapes everything. It is unified by an occasion rather than by agreement, it is in a state in which ordinary resistance to persuasion is lowered, and it will not interrupt whatever is said.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A speaker aware of that has a responsibility and an opportunity in one moment. The responsibility is that the occasion belongs to the dead person and the people who knew them. The opportunity is that a claim made here is heard without the defences a political meeting would raise.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The technique that resolves the tension is to let the subject's life carry the argument. A speaker who describes what somebody worked for, in particular rather than abstract terms, has made a case for that work without appearing to argue for anything.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Specificity makes that work and generality destroys it. A sentence describing a person as devoted to justice is an abstraction that could apply to anyone. A sentence describing what they did on a particular Tuesday in 1971 is evidence.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The best examples also give the audience something to do. A eulogy ending by naming what remains unfinished converts grief into a task. That is a rhetorical move of considerable power, and it is also where it can be misused.

paras.label: G

paras.label: H

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the power and the danger share a source. An occasion that suspends disagreement makes a speaker unusually persuasive, and the only thing separating an honest use from a dishonest one is whether the argument would survive being made somewhere else.

questions.q: What makes the audience at a eulogy unusual?
questions.a: It is unified by an occasion rather than by agreement, its ordinary resistance to persuasion is lowered, and it will not interrupt whatever is said.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the risk the form carries) and paragraph H (i.e. how specificity constrains it).
Summarize how a eulogy persuades and what keeps it honest.
questions.a: An audience unified by occasion rather than agreement has lowered resistance, so describing what a person worked for in particular terms makes a case without appearing to argue. Ending by naming unfinished work converts grief into a task, which can be misused since the subject cannot object, and specificity constrains it because claims about belief can be tested against actions.

questions.q:
eulogy: a speech in praise of someone who has died, delivered to an audience gathered by occasion.
enlist: to claim someone's support for a position, which the dead cannot refuse.
Describe the connection between the source of the power and the source of the danger.
questions.a: An occasion that suspends disagreement makes a speaker unusually persuasive, and the test of an honest use is whether the argument would survive being made somewhere else.

articles.note: RI.11-12.6 asks how style and content produce power. Here the article names the misuse the same technique enables, which is the harder half.

articles.title: The Lecture Given on Receiving a Prize
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A scientist receiving a major prize gives a lecture, and the genre has a problem built into it. The work being honoured is usually decades old, the audience is mixed, and the occasion rewards a kind of speech that the discipline's ordinary writing forbids.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The ordinary writing forbids it for good reasons. A paper removes the person, states what was done in the passive, excludes the false starts, and presents a result in an order that bears no relation to how it was found.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A lecture on such an occasion is the one place where the removed material is expected. The audience wants to know how the question arose, what the speaker believed that turned out to be wrong, and which of the steps now described as inevitable was a guess.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The strongest examples use that permission to do something specific. They describe the state of ignorance before the work, in enough detail that the audience can feel why the question was hard, which no paper can do because a paper is written for people who already know.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Credit is the second element the form handles differently. A lecture can name the graduate student who did the experiment, the technician who built the apparatus and the rival whose objection forced a change, and the convention is that it should.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The rhetorical effect of that naming is larger than its fairness. A speaker who distributes credit precisely is describing how the work actually happened, and the resulting account is more convincing than one in which a single person reasoned their way to a result.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The most quoted passages are usually at the end and are usually not about the work. A lecture that closes by describing what remains unknown, or what the speaker would do with another lifetime, is using the authority of the prize for something other than the prize.

paras.label: H
paras.text: That move is available because of the occasion rather than the argument. Nobody would attend a lecture by the same person on the same subject the previous year, and the prize supplies an audience to whom a claim about the future of a field can be made.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the form converts recognition into a platform, and the best examples are honest about doing it. A lecture that spends its first half on the work and its second on an argument the speaker has wanted to make for twenty years is using the genre exactly as the genre permits.

questions.q: What does ordinary scientific writing remove?
questions.a: The person, the false starts, and the order in which the work was actually done, presenting the result in an order unrelated to how it was found.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the effect of distributing credit) and paragraph H (i.e. why the move is available).
Summarize what this kind of lecture does.
questions.a: It is the one occasion where the material papers remove is expected, so the strongest examples describe the state of ignorance before the work and name the people who contributed, which is both fairer and more convincing. The closing passages typically use the prize's authority for a claim about the field's future that no ordinary occasion would supply an audience for.

questions.q:
platform: an occasion supplying an audience for a claim, which the prize converts recognition into.
convention: an expected practice, here that credit should be distributed by name.
Describe the connection between naming contributors and persuasiveness.
questions.a: A speaker who distributes credit precisely is describing how the work actually happened, and that account is more convincing than one in which a single person reasoned their way to a result.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 10's grant application article. Both are genres where the rhetoric is shaped by what the discipline's ordinary writing is not allowed to say.

articles.title: The Resignation Letter
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A resignation letter written over a disagreement is an unusual document because its author has already lost. The decision has been taken, the letter will not reverse it, and everything in it is written in the knowledge that the writer's leverage is gone.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That fact determines what the form can achieve. A letter cannot change the decision and can change what the decision is understood to have been, which is a smaller objective and is sometimes the only one available.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The rhetoric that follows is almost entirely about restraint. A letter that catalogues grievances reads as the complaint of a person who has been overruled, and a letter that states one disagreement and resigns over it reads as a judgement.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The choice of a single ground is therefore the central decision. A writer who objects to six things and names one has made the one unavoidable, and a writer who names six has allowed a reader to select whichever is easiest to dismiss.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Timing is the second instrument and is frequently more powerful than the text. A resignation on the day a decision is announced attaches itself to that decision permanently, and the same letter sent a month later is a personnel matter.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The convention of courtesy is doing work that is easy to misread as weakness. A letter that thanks colleagues and praises the institution removes every available response except engaging with the disagreement, which is exactly what an angry letter does not do.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The most effective examples state the principle rather than the incident. An objection framed as a disagreement about what the organisation is for outlasts the particular decision, and one framed around a specific episode expires when the episode is settled.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The form has an obvious limit that honest examples acknowledge. A resignation is available only to people who can afford to make one, and a letter of this kind is written from a position that most people objecting to most decisions do not occupy.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the genre is powerful in proportion to how rarely it is used. A person who resigns over a disagreement spends something that cannot be recovered, and the rhetorical force of the letter comes from the cost rather than from any sentence in it.

questions.q: What can a resignation letter achieve and not achieve?
questions.a: It cannot change the decision, and it can change what the decision is understood to have been.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the effect of timing) and paragraph H (i.e. who can use the form).
Summarize the rhetoric of a resignation letter.
questions.a: Written after the decision is lost, it aims to change how the decision is understood, which requires restraint: naming one ground rather than six, resigning on the day the decision is announced, and courtesy that leaves no response except engaging with the disagreement. Framing the objection as a principle outlasts the episode, and the form is available only to those who can afford it.

questions.q:
leverage: the ability to affect an outcome, which the writer no longer has.
ground: the single stated reason for resigning, whose selection is the central decision.
Describe the connection between the cost of resigning and the letter's force.
questions.a: A person who resigns over a disagreement spends something that cannot be recovered, and the rhetorical force comes from that cost rather than from any sentence in the letter.

articles.note: Paragraph H keeps the article honest about who the genre is available to. Ask what the equivalent move is for somebody who cannot afford to leave.

articles.title: The Warning That Works
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A warning is a piece of writing with a measurable purpose, which is unusual, and the research on what makes one effective contradicts several things that intuition suggests.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first finding is that more warnings produce less warning. A product covered in cautions trains a reader that the labels are boilerplate, and the specific caution that matters is read with the same attention as the one about not using a toaster in a bath.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second concerns where a warning sits. A caution in a manual is almost never read, a caution on packaging is read once, and a caution on the thing itself at the moment of use is the only placement with a reliable effect.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third concerns what a warning must contain to change behaviour. Naming the hazard is insufficient on its own; research consistently finds that effectiveness depends on stating the consequence and the specific action that avoids it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That is why the strongest warnings are grammatically peculiar. They are short, imperative and concrete, and a sentence reading do not open until the pressure gauge reads zero does three jobs in nine words that a paragraph of explanation does worse.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The fourth finding is the least intuitive and the most important. A warning competes with the reader's own model of the situation, and a person who believes they understand a machine will not read a label that contradicts them.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That is why the most effective interventions are frequently not writing at all. A connector that cannot be inserted the wrong way round solves the problem that a warning about orientation only describes, and the design literature treats a required warning as evidence of a design that failed.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Legal considerations push against all of this and are the reason labels proliferate. A warning that was present is a defence, so the incentive is to warn about everything, which is precisely the condition the first finding identifies as destroying effectiveness.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So this is a genre where the rhetorical goal and the institutional goal diverge sharply. Writing to be read means saying one thing clearly at the moment of use, and writing to be defensible means saying everything, and the labels most people encounter are the output of the second.

questions.a: A product covered in cautions trains a reader that the labels are boilerplate, so the caution that matters is read with the same attention as a trivial one.

Summarize what makes a warning effective.
questions.a: Effectiveness falls as warnings multiply, placement on the object at the moment of use is the only reliable position, and a warning must state the consequence and the specific avoiding action rather than only naming a hazard. Warnings compete with a reader's own model, design that prevents the error is better, and legal incentives to warn about everything undermine all of it.

questions.q:
boilerplate: standard text included as a matter of routine, which readers learn to skip.
imperative: the instructing grammatical form, which the strongest warnings use.
Describe the connection between the legal incentive and ineffective labels.
questions.a: A warning that was present is a defence, so the incentive is to warn about everything, which is the condition that destroys effectiveness.

articles.note: Pairs with the error message article under RI.11-12.5. Both are short texts with measurable purposes and institutional pressures against achieving them.

articles.title: The Oath
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: An oath is a short text that does something rather than describing something. Saying the words is the act, in the way that saying I do at a wedding is not a report of a decision but the making of one.

paras.label: B
paras.text: That property is what makes the form worth studying rhetorically. An oath does not need to persuade anybody, it does not argue, and it contains no evidence, and yet the wording of oaths is argued over with great intensity whenever one is revised.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reason is that the words determine what has been undertaken. An oath to uphold an institution and an oath to obey a person commit the speaker to different things in a conflict, and the difference is invisible until the conflict arrives.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first-person singular is the near-universal feature and it is load-bearing. A collective undertaking distributes responsibility and an individual one does not, so an oath spoken by each person separately binds in a way a group statement would not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Public performance does similar work and is almost always required. A commitment made before witnesses is one the speaker cannot later claim to have made with reservations, and the witnesses are part of the instrument rather than an audience for it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The archaism of the language, which is often criticised, has a defensible function. Words that are not used elsewhere mark the utterance as separate from ordinary speech, which is how a reader knows that something is being done rather than said.

paras.label: G
paras.text: What an oath cannot do is the thing it is frequently assumed to do. It does not make a person trustworthy, it creates no mechanism for enforcement by itself, and a person willing to break the undertaking is not prevented by having stated it.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Its actual function is to fix a standard in advance. Once spoken, the oath exists as a public statement of what the speaker accepted, and a later departure can be measured against their own words rather than against somebody else's expectation.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the rhetoric of an oath is about a future argument rather than a present one. The text is written to be quoted back, which is why the drafting matters so much and why disputes about a single word in an oath are not pedantry.

questions.a: A collective undertaking distributes responsibility and an individual one does not, so an oath spoken by each person separately binds differently.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. what an oath cannot do) and paragraph H (i.e. what it actually does).
Summarize what an oath is and what it achieves.
questions.a: An oath performs an act rather than describing one, so its wording determines what has been undertaken, and uphold an institution commits differently from obey a person. The singular binds individually, witnesses are part of the instrument, archaic language marks the utterance as separate, and the oath fixes a standard that a later departure can be measured against.

performative: an utterance that performs an act rather than reporting one, which an oath is.
archaism: language no longer used in ordinary speech, which marks the utterance as a different kind of act.
Describe the connection between the wording and a future conflict.
questions.a: An oath to uphold an institution and one to obey a person commit the speaker differently in a conflict, and the difference is invisible until the conflict arrives.

articles.note: The only text in this grade whose rhetoric is aimed at a reader who does not yet exist. Ask what wording a drafter should choose for a conflict nobody has foreseen.

articles.title: Deciding Whether a Glacier Is Retreating
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier appears in a photograph taken in 1890 and in one taken last year, and the difference between them is dramatic. That comparison is the image used to communicate the change and is the weakest source available for establishing it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The weakness is not that the photographs are false. It is that a glacier's terminus advances and retreats on timescales of years for reasons including snowfall, and two images a century apart cannot distinguish a trend from two points on a fluctuating line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Length records are the next source and are the longest series available. Some European glaciers have had their terminus position measured annually since the nineteenth century, which converts the photographic impression into a curve with a direction.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Length is nevertheless an indirect measure of what matters. A glacier's terminus responds to changes in mass with a delay of years to decades depending on its size, so a retreating front may be responding to conditions from a generation earlier.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Mass balance measures the quantity directly and is far more expensive to obtain. Stakes drilled into the ice record accumulation and melting at points across the surface, and the sum across a year says whether the glacier gained or lost, with no lag.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those measurements exist for a small number of glaciers and cannot be extended backwards. A reference glacier with sixty years of mass balance data is an exceptional case, and most glaciers have none, which is where the next source becomes necessary.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Satellite measurement resolves the coverage problem and introduces a different limit. Gravitational and altimetric data give mass change for whole regions, consistently and everywhere, and the record begins only when the satellites were launched.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Integrating these means using each over the interval where it is strongest. Satellites give the recent period comprehensively, mass balance gives direct measurement where it exists, length records give the long trend indirectly, and photographs establish nothing that the other three do not establish better.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The photograph retains a function the others lack entirely, and it is not evidential. It makes a quantity visible to people who will never read a mass balance series, which is a communication problem rather than a measurement one, and confusing the two is how the comparison gets attacked.

paras.text: A glacier appears in a photograph taken in 1890 and in one taken last year, and the difference is dramatic. That comparison is the image used to communicate the change and is the weakest source available for establishing it.

paras.text: The weakness is not that the photographs are false. A glacier's terminus advances and retreats over years for reasons including snowfall, and two images a century apart cannot distinguish a trend from two points on a fluctuating line.
