paras.text: Length records are the next source and the longest series available. Some European glaciers have had their terminus position measured annually since the nineteenth century, which turns the photographic impression into a curve with a direction.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Length is still an indirect measure of what matters. A terminus responds to changes in mass with a delay of years to decades depending on size, so a retreating front may be responding to conditions from a generation earlier.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Mass balance measures the quantity directly and is far more expensive to obtain. Stakes drilled into the ice record accumulation and melting at points across the surface, and the sum across a year says whether the glacier gained or lost, with no lag.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those measurements exist for a small number of glaciers and cannot be extended backwards. A reference glacier with sixty years of mass balance data is exceptional, and most glaciers have none. That is where the next source becomes necessary.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Satellite measurement solves the coverage problem and brings a different limit. Gravitational and altimetric data give mass change for whole regions, consistently and everywhere, and the record begins only when the satellites were launched.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Integrating these means using each over the interval where it is strongest. Satellites cover the recent period comprehensively. Mass balance gives direct measurement where it exists. Length records give the long trend indirectly. Photographs establish nothing the other three do not establish better.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The photograph keeps a function the others lack entirely, and it is not evidential. It makes a quantity visible to people who will never read a mass balance series, which is a communication problem rather than a measurement one, and confusing the two is how the comparison gets attacked.

questions.q: Why is a terminus position an indirect measure?
questions.a: A terminus responds to changes in mass with a delay of years to decades, so a retreating front may be responding to conditions from a generation earlier.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. what satellites add and cannot reach) and paragraph I (i.e. the photograph's actual function).
Summarize the sources and how they are combined.
questions.a: Paired photographs are dramatic and cannot distinguish a trend from fluctuation, length records give a long indirect series lagged by years to decades, mass balance measures directly but exists for few glaciers, and satellites cover everywhere only since launch. Each is used where it is strongest, and the photograph's role is communication rather than evidence.

questions.q:
mass balance: the net gain or loss of ice over a year, measured directly at points on the surface.
terminus: the lower end of a glacier, whose position responds to mass changes with a delay.
Describe the connection between the photograph's function and the attacks on it.
questions.a: It makes a quantity visible to people who will never read a mass balance series, which is a communication problem rather than a measurement one, and confusing the two is how the comparison gets attacked.

articles.note: RI.11-12.7 asks students to integrate and evaluate. Paragraph I separates a source's evidential value from its communicative value without dismissing either.

articles.title: Deciding Whether a Document Is Authentic
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A manuscript appears and is offered as the work of a known hand, or as a record of a known event. Establishing whether it is genuine requires sources from several disciplines that do not share a vocabulary.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Physical analysis of the materials can refute and cannot confirm, which is the same asymmetry that governs painting. Paper manufactured after the claimed date settles the question absolutely, and paper of the right date tells you only that a forger had access to old paper.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Ink chemistry works the same way with an additional complication. Modern components are decisive against authenticity, and period-appropriate ink can be made deliberately, so the test eliminates careless forgeries and not careful ones.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Handwriting comparison is the source that is expected to be decisive and is the weakest of the technical ones. Hands vary with age, health, speed and writing surface, and the discipline's own literature is candid about the limits of comparison from small samples.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Internal evidence frequently settles what the physical evidence cannot. A document referring to an event that had not happened, using a word not yet in use, or describing an institution by a name it acquired later, has dated itself independently of its materials.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That kind of evidence requires knowing the period well enough to notice an absence as well as a presence. The strongest internal arguments are often about what a genuine document would have mentioned and this one does not.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Provenance is a documentary source and is the one most often fabricated. A convincing chain of custody is easier to construct than a convincing manuscript, and investigators have learned to treat an unusually complete provenance as a reason for suspicion rather than comfort.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The strongest integrated cases combine a refutation with a motive. Showing that a document cannot be genuine is a conclusion, and showing who produced it, when and why explains the evidence rather than only rejecting it.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The honest position when those do not converge is that the matter is unresolved, and it is a position institutions find difficult to hold. A document that cannot be authenticated and cannot be refuted remains in that state indefinitely, and the pressure to classify it is institutional rather than evidential.

internal evidence: what a document's own content reveals about when it could have been written.
chain of custody: the documented record of who has held an object, which can be constructed falsely.
Describe the connection between refutation and explanation.
questions.a: Showing that a document cannot be genuine is a conclusion, and showing who produced it, when and why explains the evidence rather than only rejecting it.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's painting attribution article. Same asymmetry, different materials, and this one adds internal evidence which has no equivalent for a painting.

articles.title: Deciding What Killed a Patient
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Establishing a cause of death is frequently presented as a technical determination and is in practice an integration of sources that disagree, assessed against a question that must be answered in a form the law specifies.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The clinical record is the first source and is both detailed and partial. It records what was observed, measured and done, and it records it through the lens of the working diagnosis at the time, so a condition nobody suspected may leave no trace in the notes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The autopsy supplies physical findings the record cannot. It establishes what was structurally present in the body, which frequently differs from what was being treated, and studies comparing autopsy findings with clinical diagnoses have consistently found significant discrepancy rates.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its limitation is that structure is not always function. A heart can show disease sufficient to kill and not be what killed on that occasion, and an autopsy can establish that a condition existed without establishing that it was the mechanism.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Toxicology answers a narrow question precisely and is easy to over-read. It establishes what substances were present and at what concentrations, and the interpretation of a concentration depends on tolerance, timing and post-mortem changes that can alter a reading substantially.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Witness accounts supply the sequence, which none of the physical sources carry. When symptoms began, what was taken and when, and how quickly a change occurred are often decisive, and they come from people who were distressed and are recalling under pressure.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The integration problem is that the question asked is not the question the sources answer. The sources establish what was present, and the determination required is what caused death, which is a judgement about mechanism that frequently cannot be read off any finding.

paras.label: H
paras.text: This is why the formal output distinguishes levels. A certificate separates the immediate cause from the conditions leading to it and from other significant conditions, which converts a single judgement into a chain whose links can be assessed separately.

paras.label: I
paras.text: Where the sources cannot support that chain, the honest answer is recorded as such. A determination of undetermined is not a failure of the process but a statement about the evidence, and systems that discourage it produce certificates more confident than anything behind them.

questions.a: It records observations through the lens of the working diagnosis at the time, so a condition nobody suspected may leave no trace in the notes.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the mismatch between question and sources) and paragraph I (i.e. what undetermined means).
Summarize the sources and the difficulty of combining them.

The sources establish presence while the question asks mechanism, so a certificate separates immediate from underlying causes and undetermined is a statement about evidence.

questions.q:
mechanism: the physiological process that actually caused death, as distinct from a condition that was present.
discrepancy rate: how often autopsy findings differ from the clinical diagnosis.
Describe the connection between discouraging undetermined and the quality of certificates.
questions.a: Systems that discourage a determination of undetermined produce certificates more confident than anything behind them.

articles.note: The hardest integration problem in this set, because the output format is fixed by law and the sources were not collected to fill it.

articles.title: Deciding Where a Boundary Runs
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dispute arises about where a boundary lies between two properties, or two states, and the sources available to settle it were produced at different times by people answering different questions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The written description in a deed or treaty is the primary source and is frequently the least usable. It describes a line in words, referring to features that may have moved, been removed or never been precisely identified, and a river named in 1820 may not run where it ran then.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Historical maps are the second source and carry a problem that is easy to overlook. A map is a representation at a scale, and a line drawn with a pen at one inch to the mile covers a width on the ground measured in tens of metres.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That width is frequently larger than the disputed strip. A boundary shown on an old map is therefore consistent with several positions on the ground, and reading precision into a cartographic line is the commonest error in these disputes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Physical monuments are the most authoritative where they survive. A marked stone or a surveyed post was placed to record the line, and the law in many systems gives such a monument priority over a written description that contradicts it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The reason for that priority is instructive. A monument records what the parties actually agreed on the ground, and a description records what somebody wrote down afterwards, and where the two differ the written version is the more likely to contain an error.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Modern survey resolves position to within centimetres and cannot resolve the dispute by itself. It establishes exactly where a monument now stands, and whether that monument is in its original position is a separate question requiring different evidence.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Occupation supplies evidence the documents cannot. Where a fence has stood for generations, where crops have been worked and where rates have been paid are facts about what the parties treated as the boundary, and many legal systems give that long practice substantial weight.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The integration therefore runs in a defined priority in most systems: monuments first, then natural features, then courses and distances, then area. That order encodes a judgement that evidence closer to the original act of agreement is more reliable than evidence derived from it afterwards.

questions.a: A map is a representation at a scale, and a pen line at one inch to the mile covers a width on the ground measured in tens of metres, frequently larger than the disputed strip.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why monuments take priority) and paragraph I (i.e. what the priority order encodes).
Summarize the sources and the order in which they are used.
questions.a: A written description refers to features that may have moved, a map line covers tens of metres on the ground, and a surviving monument records what the parties agreed on the spot. Modern survey fixes where a monument now stands without showing whether it moved, occupation shows what was treated as the boundary, and most systems rank monuments, natural features, courses and distances, then area.

questions.q:
monument: a physical marker placed to record a boundary, given priority over a conflicting description.
occupation: the long-standing practical use of land, which evidences what parties treated as the boundary.
Describe the connection between proximity to the original agreement and reliability.
questions.a: The priority order encodes a judgement that evidence closer to the original act of agreement is more reliable than evidence derived from it afterwards.

articles.note: The only article in this set where the integration order is formally specified by law. Ask why area comes last and what that implies about what people get wrong.

articles.title: Deciding Whether a Building Can Be Saved
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats, as well as in words, in order to address a question or solve a problem.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.9 foundational documents · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A historic building is damaged, by fire, by subsidence or by long neglect, and a decision has to be made about whether it is repaired, partially rebuilt or demolished. The sources that bear on that decision answer different questions and are owned by different people.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The structural assessment comes first and sets the outer boundary. An engineer establishes what is carrying load, what has lost capacity and what can be stabilised, and nothing that follows can propose a building that will not stand up.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its limitation is that it describes a present condition rather than a possible one. An element that is failing can frequently be repaired, so a report stating that a wall is unsafe is not a conclusion about demolition until it is read alongside what repair would require.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Cost estimates supply that and are the source most likely to be decisive. They are also the least stable, because the cost of repairing a damaged historic structure cannot be known until it is opened up, and estimates before that routinely move by large margins.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The historical assessment answers a question the other two do not address. It establishes what about the building matters: whether the significance lies in the fabric itself, in the design, in the use, or in the way it sits among its neighbours.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That distinction determines what a defensible repair looks like. Where significance lies in the original fabric, replacing material destroys the thing being saved, and where it lies in the form, a faithful rebuilding preserves it, and the two cases support opposite decisions from the same damage.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Community evidence introduces a kind of value the technical sources cannot measure. A building can matter because of what happened in it, which is not visible in its structure and is not recorded in a listing, and consultation is the only route by which that evidence enters at all.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The decision also has an asymmetry that the sources do not state and that should be stated. Demolition is irreversible and repair is not, so an uncertain assessment argues for delay rather than for either option, and the cost of delay is the thing usually weighed against that.

paras.label: I
paras.text: So the integration is a sequence of constraints rather than a weighing of equals. Structure sets what is possible, significance sets what is worth doing, cost sets what is affordable, and the irreversibility of one option means that the burden falls on the case for demolition rather than on the case for keeping.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. how significance changes what repair means) and paragraph I (i.e. where the burden falls).
Summarize how such a decision is made.
questions.a: A structural assessment sets what is possible, cost estimates are decisive and unstable until the building is opened, and a historical assessment establishes whether significance lies in fabric, form or setting, which makes the same damage support opposite decisions. Community evidence enters only through consultation, and because demolition is irreversible the burden falls on the case for it.

questions.q:
fabric: the original physical material of a building, which replacing destroys where significance lies in it.
irreversible: incapable of being undone, which demolition is and repair is not.
Describe the connection between where significance lies and what counts as saving a building.
questions.a: Where significance lies in the original fabric, replacing material destroys the thing being saved, and where it lies in the form a faithful rebuilding preserves it.

articles.note: The asymmetry in paragraph H is the move worth carrying elsewhere. Ask which other decisions in this grade have an irreversible option on one side.

articles.title: The Bank a State Tried to Tax
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: Maryland taxed the branch of a national bank operating inside it, the branch's cashier refused to pay, and the case that followed required the Supreme Court to answer two questions the Constitution's text does not answer directly.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first was whether Congress could create a bank at all, since no clause grants that power. The Court's answer did not claim to find the power in the text, and argued instead that a government given great ends must be understood to possess ordinary means.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The reasoning turned on the word necessary, in the clause permitting laws necessary and proper. Maryland read it to mean indispensable, the Court read it to mean convenient or useful, and the opinion supported that reading from the word's ordinary use elsewhere in the document.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The argument's foundation was placed deeper than the clause. The Court held that the Constitution derives its authority from the people rather than from the states, which meant a state's objection to a federal instrument could not rest on the state's own sovereignty.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second question was whether Maryland could tax the bank once it existed. The opinion's answer rests on a consequence: a power to tax an instrument of the federal government is a power to destroy it, and the two cannot coexist.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That step is where the reasoning is most often examined, because a consequence is not by itself a legal rule. The opinion strengthens it with an argument from representation, noting that a state legislature taxing a federal body acts on people who had no voice in electing it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The famous sentence about it being a constitution that is being expounded states the interpretive principle the whole opinion depends on. A document meant to last through unforeseen circumstances cannot be read in the way a statute drafted for a known situation is read.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The weakness critics have pressed on since is that the principle has no stated limit. If the means need only be appropriate to a legitimate end, then the question of what counts as appropriate is largely left to the body exercising the power.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The opinion anticipates that objection and answers it briefly, which is the part most worth reading closely. It says that a pretextual use of means to reach an end not entrusted to the government would be the Court's duty to strike down, and says nothing about how a pretext would be identified.

It says a pretextual use of means to reach an end not entrusted to the government would be the Court's duty to strike down. It says nothing about how a pretext would be identified.

questions.q: How did the Court read the word necessary?
questions.a: Not as indispensable but as convenient or useful, supported by the word's ordinary use elsewhere in the document.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the argument from representation) and paragraph I (i.e. what the opinion says about pretext).
Summarize the reasoning in the opinion.
questions.a: A government given great ends must possess ordinary means, so necessary means convenient rather than indispensable, and the Constitution's authority comes from the people rather than the states. A power to tax a federal instrument is a power to destroy it, strengthened by the fact that a state taxes people who did not elect it, and the limiting principle against pretext is stated without any test for identifying one.

questions.q:
implied powers: powers not listed in the text but treated as means to listed ends.
pretext: a stated purpose that is not the real one, which the opinion says the Court would strike down.
Describe the connection between the taxing consequence and the representation argument.
questions.a: A consequence is not by itself a legal rule, so the opinion strengthens it by noting that a state legislature taxing a federal body acts on people who had no voice in electing it.

articles.note: RI.11-12.8 asks students to delineate and evaluate reasoning. Paragraph I is the evaluation: the opinion names the limit and supplies no way to apply it.

articles.title: Two Dissents That Do Not Agree
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A wartime order excluded a group of citizens from a region on the basis of ancestry, a conviction for remaining followed, and the Supreme Court upheld it. The reasoning in the two principal dissents is now studied more closely than the majority opinion, and the two run in different directions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The majority's structure was narrow by design. It held that the order was a military measure taken in wartime, that courts owed deference to the judgement of those charged with defence, and that the exclusion was therefore a response to danger rather than a racial classification.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first dissent attacked the factual premise directly. It examined the military's own report, found the assertions about disloyalty unsupported by evidence, and concluded that the order rested on assumptions about a group rather than on findings about persons.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its conclusion was correspondingly direct. The exclusion fell, in its phrase, into the ugly abyss of racism, and deference to military judgement does not extend to accepting claims for which no evidence has been offered.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second dissent accepted something the first did not. It granted that a court is not equipped to assess whether a military measure was necessary, having neither access to the information nor the competence to weigh it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: From that concession it built a different objection. If a court cannot evaluate the order, it should not validate it, because an order that expires with the emergency does less lasting harm than a judicial opinion holding such an order constitutional.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The image it used has outlasted the case. A judicial validation lies about like a loaded weapon, available to any authority that can plead an urgent need, long after the circumstances that produced it have gone.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The two dissents cannot both be fully accepted, which is what makes them worth studying together. One says the Court should have examined the facts and found them wanting, and the other says the Court was never in a position to examine them at all.

paras.label: I
paras.text: History has endorsed the conclusion without settling which route was right. The conviction was vacated decades later, after evidence emerged that the government had withheld its own contradictory intelligence reports, and the Court has since said the decision was wrong on the day it was decided.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the objection built from the concession) and paragraph H (i.e. why the two cannot both be accepted).

Describe the connection between the concession and the loaded weapon image.
questions.a: If a court cannot evaluate the order it should not validate it, because the validation remains available to any authority that can plead an urgent need long after the circumstances have gone.

articles.note: Two dissents reaching the same verdict by incompatible routes. Ask which one a student would have signed, and what each commits a court to in the next emergency.

articles.title: The Letter Written in Pencil
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A man convicted in a Florida court of breaking into a poolroom had asked for a lawyer and been told the state supplied one only in capital cases. He conducted his own defence, lost, and wrote to the Supreme Court in pencil from prison.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The petition raised a question the Court had already answered. Twenty years earlier it had held that the right to appointed counsel bound state courts only where special circumstances made a fair trial impossible without one.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That rule had produced two decades of case-by-case litigation. Each defendant had to show that his own circumstances were special enough, which meant the question of whether counsel was required could only be answered after the trial counsel would have altered.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The opinion that overruled it is unusually short, and its central argument is unusually concrete. It does not reason from the nature of rights or from the text alone, and points instead at what governments and defendants can be observed to do.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Governments hire lawyers to prosecute, and defendants who can afford lawyers hire them to defend. The opinion treats those two facts as the strongest available evidence that lawyers in criminal courts are necessities rather than luxuries.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The move is worth noticing for what it avoids. An argument from practice does not require the Court to define a fair trial in the abstract, and it is hard to answer without claiming that the settled practice of every prosecutor's office is mistaken.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The opinion also had to explain why the earlier decision should be abandoned rather than distinguished. Its answer was that the earlier case had itself departed from older precedent, so overruling it was a return rather than an innovation.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What the reasoning establishes is narrower than the principle usually attributed to it. It holds that a lawyer must be provided, and says nothing about what that lawyer must have time to do, how many other clients they may carry, or what resources they are owed.

paras.label: I
paras.text: Those questions were left to later litigation and have not been settled since. A right established by an argument from practice can be satisfied in practice by a system that appoints counsel and funds the appointment at a level the argument never addressed.

Summarize the argument and its limit.

questions.a: A right established by an argument from practice can be satisfied in practice by a system that appoints counsel and funds the appointment at a level the argument never addressed.

articles.title: The Speech Built in a Library
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A politician preparing an address for a city where he was not well known chose to build the whole speech around a single sentence spoken by his opponent, which is an unusual decision and turned out to be the source of its force.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The sentence asserted that the men who framed the Constitution had understood the question of federal authority over slavery in the territories better than the present generation did. It was offered as a flourish, and it was a claim about identifiable people who had left records.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The speaker accepted the premise completely rather than disputing it. If the framers' understanding settles the question, the task is to establish what that understanding was, which converts a political dispute into a research problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: He defined the group precisely, taking the thirty-nine signers of the Constitution, and then worked through the recorded congressional votes bearing on federal control of slavery in the territories to establish how each of them had acted.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The result was a count. A clear majority of those who had voted on the question had voted consistently with federal authority to restrict slavery in the territories, and the speech names the men and the occasions rather than summarising them.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The rhetorical effect of a count differs from that of an argument. An audience can disagree with reasoning and cannot easily disagree with a list of names and votes, and an opponent is left either to produce a different count or to abandon the premise.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Having established that, the speech turns and addresses the opposing section directly, in a passage that concedes a great deal. It accepts that the complaints being made are sincerely held and answers them on their own terms rather than dismissing them.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The final section addresses the speaker's own side and is the most demanding part of the text. It warns against positions that would be satisfying to hold and would not survive the premise the speech has just spent its length establishing.

paras.label: I
paras.text: What makes the structure hard to imitate is the labour behind it. The argument depends entirely on research done over weeks in a library, and the strategy of granting an opponent's premise is available only to a speaker who has already checked where that premise leads.

questions.q: What did the speaker do with his opponent's premise?
questions.a: He accepted it completely rather than disputing it, which turned a political dispute into a research problem about what the framers' understanding had been.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why a count persuades differently) and paragraph I (i.e. the labour the structure requires).

It then concedes a great deal to the opposing section and closes by warning its own side against positions the premise will not support.

premise: a claim an argument starts from, which this speech adopts rather than attacks.
concede: to grant a point to an opponent, which the speech does at length before answering.
Describe the connection between the research and the rhetorical strategy.
questions.a: Granting an opponent's premise is available only to a speaker who has already checked where that premise leads, and here that meant weeks of work in a library.

articles.note: Pairs with grade 11's advocacy articles. The move students can carry is adopting an opponent's premise, which is only safe after the checking.

articles.title: The Power Argued For Before It Existed
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.5 structure · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: An essay published in a newspaper during a ratification debate made the case for an independent judiciary and, in the course of making it, set out an argument for a power that no American court had yet claimed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens by minimising the institution it is defending. The judiciary, it says, has no influence over the sword or the purse, commands neither force nor will but merely judgment, and must depend on another branch even for the execution of its decisions.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That characterisation does real work in the argument. A branch described as the least dangerous is easier to grant independence to, and the independence being argued for is the one the essay wants: tenure during good behaviour rather than at another body's pleasure.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The case for judicial review then follows as a deduction. A constitution is fundamental law, a legislative act contrary to it cannot be valid, and some body must decide when the two conflict, since an unresolved conflict would leave the fundamental law meaningless.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The obvious objection is anticipated and answered in the sentence that carries the most weight in the essay. Preferring the constitution to the statute does not make the judiciary superior to the legislature, but makes the people superior to both.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The force of that answer depends on an assumption the essay does not examine. It assumes that a court reading the constitution is reporting what the people enacted rather than supplying a meaning of its own, which is the point every later critic has pressed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The essay then argues that permanent tenure follows from the same reasoning. A judge who can be removed over a decision is not in a position to prefer the constitution to a statute, so independence is a condition of the function rather than a privilege attached to the office.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The whole argument was made without institutional experience to draw on. No American court had set aside a federal statute, the practice the essay describes did not yet exist, and it would be some fifteen years before a court claimed the power in those terms.

paras.label: I
paras.text: That is the feature worth examining. An argument deduced from the nature of a written constitution rather than from how courts behave is strong exactly where the deduction holds, and silent about everything the deduction does not reach, which is most of what the power has since been used for.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. the unexamined assumption) and paragraph I (i.e. what a deduction cannot reach).
Summarize the essay's argument and what it leaves open.

questions.q:
judicial review: a court's power to hold a statute invalid as contrary to the constitution.
deduction: an argument from stated premises rather than from observed practice.
Describe the connection between the absence of experience and the essay's limits.
questions.a: An argument deduced from the nature of a written constitution rather than from how courts behave is strong where the deduction holds and silent about everything it does not reach.

articles.note: The only text in this set arguing for a practice that did not exist. Ask what evidence could have refuted it at the time.

articles.title: The Ordinance That Promised Equal States
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A congress sitting in New York passed an ordinance for governing the territory west of the mountains in the same summer that a convention in Philadelphia was writing the Constitution. The two documents came from different bodies, and the ordinance did something the Constitution did not attempt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its central provision concerned what the territory would become. States formed there were to be admitted on an equal footing with the original states in all respects, which converted a system of colonies into a procedure for manufacturing equals.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That is the clause worth dwelling on, because nearly every empire before it had done the opposite. A territory acquired by a European power remained a possession, and this ordinance committed in advance to giving away the authority it had just asserted.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The articles of compact that follow were declared unalterable except by common consent, which gave a statute something of the character of a constitution. A later congress could repeal an ordinary law, and these provisions were written to resist that.

paras.label: E
paras.text: One of them prohibited slavery in the territory in a single sentence, with a proviso returning people who escaped into it. The prohibition drew a line that shaped the following seventy years, and the proviso undercut it for anyone who crossed.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Another declared that religion, morality and knowledge being necessary to good government, schools and the means of education should forever be encouraged. It is the sentence most often quoted in the states formed from that territory, and it imposed no obligation on anybody.

paras.label: G
paras.text: A third promised that the utmost good faith would be observed towards the Indians, that their lands and property would never be taken from them without their consent, and that laws founded in justice would be made to prevent wrongs being done to them.

paras.label: H
paras.text: What followed is the hardest thing in the document to teach. The same ordinance that made that promise established the machinery by which the land was surveyed, sold and settled, and the promise was broken continuously by the government that had given it.

paras.label: I
paras.text: Reading the document honestly means holding both at once. It contains an innovation that changed how states are made and a commitment that was never kept, and treating either as the whole of it produces a version of the past that will not survive the archive.

questions.a: It turned a system of colonies into a procedure for manufacturing equals, committing in advance to giving away the authority the ordinance had just asserted.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. the slavery clause and its proviso) and paragraph H (i.e. the promise and the machinery).
Summarize what the ordinance contains.
questions.a: It provided that new states would be admitted on an equal footing with the original states, made its articles unalterable except by common consent, prohibited slavery with a proviso for people who escaped into the territory, encouraged schools without obliging anyone, and promised utmost good faith to the Indians. The same document established the machinery by which that land was surveyed, sold and settled.

questions.q:
equal footing: admission to the union on the same terms as the original states, rather than as a possession.
proviso: a clause qualifying what precedes it, here undercutting the prohibition for anyone who escaped into the territory.
Describe the connection between the good faith promise and what the ordinance set up.
questions.a: The same ordinance established the machinery by which the land was surveyed, sold and settled, and the promise was broken continuously by the government that had given it.

articles.note: RI.11-12.9 asks for themes, purposes and rhetorical features. Paragraph I is the instruction: hold the innovation and the broken promise together rather than choosing one.

articles.title: The Letter That Refused the Word Toleration

Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the summer of 1790 a congregation in Rhode Island addressed the president during a visit, and he replied in a letter of a few hundred words that is now read as one of the country's foundational statements about religious liberty.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its form matters to how it works. The letter is a reply, written to people who had addressed him first, and it takes up their register and their biblical imagery rather than announcing a principle from above to people who had not asked.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The sentence at its centre refuses a word. It says that toleration is no longer to be spoken of, as though it were by the indulgence of one class of people that another enjoyed the exercise of their inherent natural rights.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That refusal is the whole argument compressed into a distinction. Toleration describes a permission a majority grants and could therefore withdraw, and the letter replaces it with a claim that the rights were already held and are not anybody's to extend.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The best-known phrase follows from it, describing a government that gives to bigotry no sanction and to persecution no assistance. Both halves of the construction are negative, which is a precise description of what a government is actually in a position to promise.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It is worth noticing what the letter does not say. It does not promise that the congregation will be welcomed, liked, or shielded from their neighbours' opinions, and a government that assists no persecution has not undertaken to make anybody agreeable.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The closing image comes from scripture and is addressed to the recipients in terms they would recognise. Everyone is to sit in safety under his own vine and fig tree with none to make him afraid, which describes ordinary life rather than rights.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The letter had no legal force of any kind and was the expression of one man's view while holding office. Its authority is entirely rhetorical, which is why it has been quoted continuously in arguments it was never written to settle.

paras.label: I
paras.text: That is also its limitation and should be stated plainly. A principle stated in a letter binds nobody, and the practice the letter describes was contradicted at the time by states that still maintained establishments and religious tests.

questions.a: Toleration describes a permission a majority grants and could withdraw, and the letter claims instead that the rights were already held and are not anybody's to extend.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. what the letter does not promise) and paragraph I (i.e. its limitation at the time).
Summarize the letter's argument and its standing.
questions.a: Written as a reply in the recipients' own register, it refuses the word toleration because toleration is a permission that could be withdrawn, and describes a government giving bigotry no sanction and persecution no assistance, both negative promises. It does not promise welcome, it had no legal force, and states with establishments and religious tests contradicted it at the time.

questions.q:
toleration: permission to practise granted by a majority, which the letter rejects as the wrong word.
establishment: an officially supported church, which several states still maintained when the letter was written.
Describe the connection between the negative construction and what a government can promise.
questions.a: Both halves of the phrase are negative, which is a precise description of what a government is actually in a position to promise, since it has not undertaken to make anybody agreeable.

articles.note: A foundational statement with no legal force, written only because somebody wrote first. Ask what that says about how such documents acquire authority.

articles.title: The Address Given After a Disputed Election
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: The election had been bitter and was decided only after thirty-six ballots in the House, and the man taking office led the party that had spent four years attacking the one leaving it. His address was the first American speech whose job was to make a transfer of power look unremarkable.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The circumstances made that difficult. No government under this constitution had yet handed authority to its opponents, and nobody present knew whether the arrangement would hold once it was tested by a side that had genuinely lost.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The speech's famous sentence is usually quoted as a gesture of goodwill and is doing something more specific. In saying that we are all republicans and all federalists, the words name principles rather than parties, and the claim is that the disagreement was never about the form of the government.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Whether that claim was true is a separate question from what it accomplished. A speech describing a division as shallower than it is can help make it shallower, and an incoming administration asserting that its opponents accept the constitution makes the opposite assertion harder to make.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The passage on dissent goes considerably further than goodwill. It says that those who would dissolve the union or change its form should be left undisturbed, as monuments to the safety with which an error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The structure of that sentence carries the argument. It does not claim the opinions are harmless, it claims that leaving them alone demonstrates something about the government, which converts tolerance from an apparent weakness into evidence of confidence.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The address also states a limit on majorities that is easy to read past. The will of the majority must prevail and must be reasonable in order to be rightful, and the minority possess equal rights which equal laws must protect.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Delivery worked against every part of it. The speaker read quietly in a crowded chamber, much of the audience could not hear him, and the text reached the country as print, which is how most people met it then and how it has been read since.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The gap between the speech and the administration that followed is evidence rather than a reason to dismiss it. A government that had been attacked in the press pursued some of its critics afterwards, and a standard a speaker fails to meet is still a standard that speaker put on record.

Summarize the speech's purpose and its argument about dissent.
questions.a: Delivered after a bitter election decided in the House, its job was to make the first transfer of power to opponents look unremarkable, which it did by naming principles rather than parties. It argues that leaving dangerous opinions undisturbed demonstrates the government's confidence, states that a majority's will must be reasonable to be rightful, and was inaudible to much of the audience.

questions.q:
transfer of power: the handing of authority from one administration to its opponents.
rightful: justified rather than merely victorious, which the speech says a majority's will must be.
Describe the connection between the speech's claim and what it accomplished.
questions.a: A speech describing a division as shallower than it is can help make it shallower, and an incoming administration asserting that its opponents accept the constitution makes the opposite assertion harder to make.

articles.note: Pairs with the resignation letter under RI.11-12.6. Both are texts written at a moment of transfer, by someone whose leverage has just changed.

articles.title: Four Sentences and the Noun That Changes
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: One section of one amendment, four sentences long, has produced more litigation than any other passage in the Constitution. Its drafting choices repay close reading because very nearly every one of them was contested when it was written.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first sentence settles citizenship by definition rather than by argument. Everyone born or naturalised in the country and subject to its jurisdiction is a citizen, which reversed a decision of the Supreme Court without naming it or explaining why it had been wrong.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Defining rather than arguing was a deliberate choice with a predictable effect. A reasoned repudiation invites a counter-argument, and a definition inserted into the constitutional text leaves nothing available to dispute except what the words themselves mean.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The remaining sentences change who is being addressed. They do not grant rights to anybody, and are written as prohibitions on the states, which makes the section a limit on governments rather than a list of entitlements held by persons.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The most consequential drafting decision is a change of noun partway through. Privileges and immunities belong to citizens, and due process and equal protection are owed to any person within a state's jurisdiction, which extends them to people who are not citizens at all.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The generality of the language was chosen as well. Due process of law and equal protection of the laws are phrases with no specified content, and the drafters declined to enumerate what they would cover, leaving that to be settled case by case.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That generality is why the section is quoted so often and is also the standing objection to it. A clause whose content is supplied by later interpretation transfers a decision from the body that ratified the words to the courts that afterwards read them.

paras.label: H
paras.text: One clause was effectively removed within five years. A decision in the 1870s read the privileges and immunities of national citizenship so narrowly that the clause did almost no work thereafter, and the arguments it was drafted to carry moved to the other two.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The section as it now operates is therefore not the section as drafted. Two clauses are doing the work of three, by a route nobody voting on the text anticipated, which is a fact about constitutional language generally rather than about this amendment alone.

questions.q: What changes partway through the section?
questions.a: The noun: privileges and immunities belong to citizens, while due process and equal protection are owed to any person within a state's jurisdiction.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why a definition beats an argument) and paragraph H (i.e. the clause read almost out of the text).
Summarize the section's drafting choices and what became of them.
questions.a: It settles citizenship by definition rather than argument, writes the rest as prohibitions on states rather than grants of rights, and shifts from citizens to persons so due process and equal protection reach non-citizens. Its language was left general on purpose, which moved content to the courts, and one clause was read so narrowly in the 1870s that two now do the work of three.

questions.q:
enumerate: to list specifically, which the drafters declined to do for these phrases.
ratify: to approve a text formally, done here by bodies that could not know how the words would be read.
Describe the connection between the general language and the standing objection.
questions.a: A clause whose content is supplied by later interpretation transfers a decision from the body that ratified the words to the courts that afterwards read them.

articles.note: The closest reading in the grade. Four sentences, and the whole article turns on a single change of noun.

articles.title: The Speech That Survives in Two Versions
articles.standard_text:
Standard: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.6 rhetoric · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A speech given at a women's rights convention in Ohio in 1851 is among the most quoted in American history, and the version everybody quotes was written down by somebody else twelve years after it was delivered.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The speaker could not read or write. Everything that survives of her words reaches us through other people's hands, including the account of her life, which she dictated to a writer who shaped it for publication.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A report of the speech appeared within weeks, written by a man who was present at the convention and knew the speaker. It is plain, it is in standard English, and it contains no refrain and no famous question.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The version that became famous was published in 1863 by a woman who had chaired the convention. It adds a repeated question, a southern dialect and a dramatic scene in the hall, and it is the version that reaches most students.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Several of its details can be checked and do not hold. The speaker had been enslaved in New York and spoke Dutch as a child, so a southern dialect belongs to the writer rather than to her, and the number of children the famous version gives is too high.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The purpose of the later version explains a good deal about it. It was published during the war, when the speaker was nationally known, by a writer with an argument of her own to make, for an audience the 1851 report was never written for.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Discarding it is less straightforward than it first sounds. The famous version is the one that moved people for a century, and the question it repeats has done work in the world that the accurate report has not, which is a fact about the text's history.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The defensible position is to teach both and to say which is which. The earlier report is the better evidence of what was said, the later version is the better evidence of what the speech became, and the two answer different questions.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The case is useful because it makes a general problem visible. Every speech delivered before recording reaches us through a transcriber, and the features we remember best are the ones most likely to have been supplied or sharpened by the person writing them down.

questions.q: Why does a southern dialect belong to the writer rather than the speaker?
questions.a: The speaker had been enslaved in New York and spoke Dutch as a child, so the dialect was supplied by the person writing the later version.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. why discarding the famous version is not simple) and paragraph I (i.e. the general problem it makes visible).
Summarize the problem with this speech.
questions.a: A report written within weeks by someone present is plain and has no refrain, while the famous version published twelve years later adds a repeated question, a dialect the speaker did not use and a child count that is too high. The later version was shaped for a wartime audience, and the honest approach teaches both, since one evidences what was said and the other what the speech became.

questions.q:
transcriber: the person who writes down what a speaker said, and whose choices reach us as the speaker's.
refrain: a repeated line, here supplied by the later writer rather than recorded at the convention.
Describe the connection between how a speech reaches us and which features we remember.
questions.a: Every speech delivered before recording reaches us through a transcriber, and the features remembered best are the ones most likely to have been supplied or sharpened by the person writing them down.

articles.note: The hardest case for the standard's phrase about rhetorical features, since the most famous feature of this text was not the speaker's. Ask which version belongs on a wall and which in a footnote.

articles.title: The Ship That Was Frozen In on Purpose
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1880s wreckage from a ship crushed by ice north of Siberia was found on the coast of Greenland, having crossed the top of the world in about three years. A Norwegian scientist read the report and drew a conclusion nobody else was willing to act on.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The conclusion was that a current carries ice across the polar basin, and the test he proposed was to put a ship into that ice deliberately and let it be carried. Senior figures in the field described the plan as suicide and said so in public.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Their objection was sound as far as it went. Ice had destroyed every vessel caught in it, and a plan that depends on surviving the thing that had killed everybody else requires something more than confidence to recommend it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What made the plan serious was that it answered the objection with a hull. The ship was built short, broad and rounded below the waterline, so that pressure from converging ice would push it upward rather than inward and squeeze it out onto the surface.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It was frozen in near the New Siberian Islands in the autumn of 1893 and began to drift. The ice lifted it as designed, the drift ran in the predicted direction, and the central claim was effectively settled within the first year.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The drift was also slower and further south than hoped, and by early 1895 it was clear the ship would not pass near the pole. At that point the expedition's leader left the vessel with one companion, dogs and two kayaks, and went north on foot.

paras.label: G
paras.text: They reached a higher latitude than anyone had and turned back short of the pole, which was the correct decision and left them a year away from anywhere. They wintered in a hut of stone and walrus hide and were found by another expedition the following summer.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The ship came out of the ice north of Spitsbergen that August with every member of its crew alive, which was the unprecedented part. Polar expeditions of the period routinely lost men, and this one lost nobody in three years.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The episode is usually told as an adventure and is better understood as an experiment. A hypothesis about a current was tested by a design that made the test survivable, and the part everybody remembers is the dash for the pole, which proved nothing at all.

questions.q: How did the hull answer the objection to the plan?
questions.a: It was built short, broad and rounded below the waterline, so pressure from converging ice would push it upward rather than inward and squeeze it onto the surface.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. what the first year established) and paragraph I (i.e. how the episode should be understood).
Summarize what happened and what it proved.
questions.a: Wreckage carried from Siberia to Greenland suggested a current across the polar basin, so a ship was built with a rounded hull and frozen into the ice deliberately. The drift ran as predicted within the first year, the leader left on foot when it became clear the pole would be missed, and the ship emerged after three years with every man alive.

questions.q:
drift: the movement of ice carrying whatever is frozen into it, which the voyage was designed to test.
hypothesis: a proposed explanation put to a test, here a claim about a current.
Describe the connection between the design and the test being possible at all.
questions.a: A hypothesis about a current was tested by a design that made the test survivable, since ice had destroyed every vessel caught in it before.

articles.note: RI.11-12.10 is range and independence. The last paragraph separates the famous part of the story from the part that carried the evidence.

articles.title: The Letters That Were Read Without Opening Them
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A trunk in a Dutch museum holds about two thousand six hundred letters that were never delivered. Six hundred of them have never been opened, and until recently the only way to learn what they said was to break the seals and destroy the thing being studied.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The letters survived because of the way postage worked. The recipient paid on delivery, so a letter that could not be delivered could not be paid for, and a postmaster kept undeliverable letters in the hope that somebody would eventually claim one and settle the charge.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The couple who kept this trunk were postmasters in The Hague in the seventeenth century. The hope was never realised, the trunk passed into a collection, and what had been preserved by an accounting problem became a sample of ordinary correspondence that historians almost never have.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Most surviving letters from the period are the ones somebody chose to keep, which means they are the letters of people whose papers were thought worth preserving. These are the letters of anybody who happened to write, including people who left no other trace at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The sealed ones posed the problem. A letter of the period was its own envelope, folded, slit, tucked and sealed in patterns that secured it, so opening one destroys the evidence of how it was closed as well as any chance of studying it intact.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The solution came from an imaging technique developed for something else. A scanner of the kind used on teeth records the internal structure of a folded packet in enough detail to distinguish the ink lying on a surface from the paper around it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The scan is only half the work. What it produces is a solid block of data in which the writing lies on folded surfaces, and an algorithm has to work out the geometry of the folds and flatten them computationally into a page somebody can read.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The first letter read this way was unremarkable in content, which is part of the point. A man wrote to a relative asking for a certified copy of a death notice, and that ordinariness is exactly what the collection preserves and what an archive of eminent men does not.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The technique also changed what counts as evidence in the collection. How a letter was folded and secured turns out to carry information about trust, distance and urgency, and that information had been destroyed every previous time a scholar opened one in order to read it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A trunk in a Dutch museum holds about two thousand six hundred letters that were never delivered. Six hundred have never been opened, and until recently the only way to learn what they said was to break the seals and destroy the thing being studied.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The letters survived because of the way postage worked. The recipient paid on delivery, so a letter that could not be delivered could not be paid for. A postmaster kept undeliverable letters in the hope that somebody would claim one and settle the charge.

questions.q: Why were these letters kept rather than discarded?
questions.a: The recipient paid on delivery, so an undeliverable letter could not be paid for, and the postmaster kept it in the hope somebody would claim it and settle the charge.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why this collection differs from most) and paragraph I (i.e. what opening a letter destroyed).
Summarize how the letters survived and how they are now read.
questions.a: Undelivered letters could not be paid for, so a postmaster kept them, preserving ordinary correspondence rather than the papers of people thought worth preserving. The sealed ones were folded to be their own envelopes, so a dental-type scanner records the packet's internal structure and an algorithm flattens the folds computationally, which also preserves the folding itself as evidence.

questions.q:
algorithm: a defined procedure, here one that works out fold geometry and flattens a scan into a readable page.
undeliverable: incapable of being handed over, which under paid-on-delivery postage also meant unpaid.
Describe the connection between the technique and what now counts as evidence.
questions.a: How a letter was folded and secured carries information about trust, distance and urgency, and that information had been destroyed every previous time a scholar opened one to read it.

articles.title: The Seed Bank Held Through a Siege
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research institute in a besieged city held the largest collection of seeds in the world, several hundred thousand samples gathered from six continents. The staff who stayed with it through the winter of 1941 had food in the building and did not eat it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The collection existed because of a programme to find the origins of cultivated plants. Expeditions had been sent to the regions where crops were first domesticated, on the theory that the greatest variety of a plant survives where it has been grown longest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That theory is why the collection mattered. A variety from a centre of origin may carry resistance to a disease that has not appeared yet, and a seed bank is an argument that the useful traits of the future already exist somewhere and have to be kept.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The city was surrounded in September 1941 and the siege ran for nearly nine hundred days. Supplies failed, the ration fell below what sustains life, and people in the city ate whatever could be eaten and a good deal that could not.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The building held tonnes of edible material. Rice, wheat, maize, potatoes and groundnuts, catalogued and boxed, in a city where people were dying of hunger in the street outside, in rooms occupied by the people guarding them.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Several of the staff died of starvation that winter without touching the collection. Accounts differ on how many and agree on the fact, and one of them is recorded as having been found dead in a room of the rice he had been responsible for.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The reasoning they left is not sentimental and is worth reading as an argument. The collection could feed the institute briefly and could not feed the city, so eating it would have converted something irreplaceable into a delay measured in days.

paras.label: H
paras.text: The potatoes posed a harder problem than the seeds. Tubers cannot be stored indefinitely and have to be replanted, so staff grew them in ground outside the city, under shelling, in order to keep the varieties alive at all.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The man who assembled the collection was not there. He had been arrested before the war over a dispute about genetics and died of starvation in a prison some distance away, while the people he had trained were starving in order to protect what he had gathered.

questions.q: Why were the regions where crops were first domesticated chosen for collecting?
questions.a: Because the greatest variety of a plant survives where it has been grown longest, and a variety from such a region may carry resistance to a disease that has not appeared yet.

questions.q: Paragraph G (i.e. the argument for not eating the collection) and paragraph H (i.e. the problem the potatoes posed).
Summarize what the staff protected and why.
questions.a: The institute held several hundred thousand seed samples collected from the regions where crops were first domesticated, because the variety that survives there may carry traits not yet needed. During a siege of nearly nine hundred days, staff starved rather than eat tonnes of edible material, reasoning that it could not feed the city, and grew the potatoes outside under shelling.

questions.q:
centre of origin: a region where a crop was first domesticated and where its greatest variety survives.
tuber: a storage organ such as a potato, which cannot be kept indefinitely and must be replanted.
Describe the connection between the argument they left and the decision they made.
questions.a: The collection could feed the institute briefly and could not feed the city, so eating it would have converted something irreplaceable into a delay measured in days.

articles.note: The hardest article in the grade to discuss well. The argument in paragraph G is the thing to examine, not the sacrifice.

articles.title: The Tunnel That Copied a Worm
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: In the 1820s a tunnel was begun beneath a tidal river in a city, which had not been done under a navigable waterway anywhere. The ground was soft, waterlogged and in places barely coherent, and the mining methods of the day were useless in it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The method that made it possible was taken from an animal. A shipworm bores through submerged timber by advancing behind a hard shell that protects the part doing the cutting, and an engineer who had examined one patented a frame working on the same principle.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The frame was a grid of cells, each holding one man facing the clay. A worker took out a board, cut back a few inches, replaced the board, and when every cell had advanced the whole frame was screwed forward while bricklayers lined the space behind it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The principle is that the ground is never left unsupported. Every part of the face is either being worked at that moment or is held by a board, which is what allows a tunnel to be driven through material that would otherwise flow into it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It worked, and it did not work reliably. The river broke in repeatedly, the worst inundation killing six men and nearly drowning the engineer's son, who was in the workings when the water came through and was carried out on the flood.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The project then stopped for seven years for want of money, with the workings sealed and the shaft standing open in the middle of a city. The halt was financial rather than technical, which is the usual reason large works stop and is rarely the reason they are remembered.

paras.label: G
paras.text: It opened in 1843 as a foot tunnel and became an attraction rather than a thoroughfare. Crowds came to walk under the river, stalls were set up in the arches, and the commercial purpose for which it had been dug was never achieved.

paras.label: H
paras.text: Its value turned out to lie in the method rather than in the tunnel. Every soft-ground tunnel driven since has used a descendant of that frame, and the underground railways of a dozen cities exist because the problem of holding a working face had been solved.

paras.label: I
paras.text: The tunnel itself still carries trains, which is an unusual afterlife for a failed investment. A work can be a commercial disaster and a technical foundation at the same time, and the accounts that judged it in the 1840s were measuring the wrong thing.
