questions.a: That the ground is never left unsupported, since every part of the face is either being worked at that moment or held by a board.

questions.q: Paragraph F (i.e. why the work stopped) and paragraph I (i.e. what the accounts of the 1840s measured).
Summarize the method and what came of the project.
questions.a: A frame modelled on a shipworm's shell let men cut a few inches at a time behind boards, so the face was never unsupported, which made tunnelling through soft waterlogged ground possible. The river broke in repeatedly, the work stopped seven years for money, it opened as an attraction rather than a thoroughfare, and every soft-ground tunnel since has used a descendant of the frame.

questions.q:
face: the exposed ground at the front of a tunnel, which the frame holds while it is cut.
inundation: a flooding, which happened repeatedly and killed six men on the worst occasion.
Describe the connection between the commercial result and the technical result.
questions.a: A work can be a commercial disaster and a technical foundation at the same time, since the value lay in the method rather than in the tunnel.

articles.note: Pairs with the reinforced concrete article under RI.11-12.2. Both are about a technique outliving the structure that introduced it.

articles.title: What Happens When a Whale Dies
articles.standard_text:
Standard: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.11-12.1 citing evidence · RI.11-12.2 central ideas · RI.11-12.4 key terms · RI.11-12.8 reasoning
 Lower range: LL 1050 – 1160

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1987 a submersible working on the floor of a basin off the California coast came upon the skeleton of a whale. The scientists aboard had not been looking for one, and what was living on it did not belong at that depth by anything then understood.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The deep sea floor is a place of scarcity. Almost nothing grows there, and the animals living on it depend on what sinks from the lit water far above, which arrives as a thin and more or less continuous rain of particles.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A dead whale is therefore an event out of all proportion. Thirty or forty tonnes of flesh and bone arrive at once in a place that receives a few grams per square metre in a year, and the arrival supports a sequence of communities rather than one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first stage is scavenging and is comparatively quick. Sleeper sharks, hagfish and amphipods strip the soft tissue over months to a couple of years, in numbers that can run to thousands of animals around a single carcass.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The second stage belongs to animals living in the enriched sediment. Worms and molluscs colonise the material that has fallen around the skeleton, at densities far above anything the surrounding seabed supports, and that phase can continue for years.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The third stage is the one that surprised everybody. Bacteria break down the fats held inside the bones and release sulphide, and a community grows that lives on chemical energy rather than on anything derived from sunlight, as the communities at hot vents do.

paras.label: G
paras.text: That resemblance raised a question which is still open. If vent communities are separated by long stretches of ordinary seabed, whale skeletons may act as stepping stones letting those animals cross, which would make their distribution depend on where whales happened to die.

paras.label: H
paras.text: A further discovery came much later. A worm described in 2004 has neither mouth nor gut, grows root structures into bone and digests it with the help of bacteria, and its males are microscopic and live by the dozen inside the female's tube.

paras.label: I
paras.text: All of it rests on a small number of observed falls, which is the honest limit on the subject. A carcass sinking in deep water is almost never witnessed, most of what is known comes from skeletons found by chance or from whales deliberately sunk by researchers, and the sample is tiny.

questions.a: Thirty or forty tonnes arrive at once in a place that receives a few grams per square metre in a year.

articles.note: Last of the six hundred and fifty. It ends on the sample size, which is the habit this whole grade has been building.
